The commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah 7, verses 4–7:

Allah's saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿How many a town have We destroyed! Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were resting at midday.﴾ ﴿Their only plea, when Our might came upon them, was to say, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers.﴾ ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were never absent.﴾

"Kam" (how many) is in the place of raising (rafʿ) as the subject (mubtadaʾ). The predicate (khabar) is "ahlaknāhā" (We destroyed it). It is also permissible that the predicate is in "fajāʾahā" (then Our punishment came upon it) and "ahlaknāhā" is a descriptive clause (ṣifa). It is also permissible that it is in the place of accusative (naṣb) by a verb supplied after it, whose estimate is: "How many a town did We destroy, We destroyed it." The verb is supplied after it, although it is a declarative (khabariyya) form, by analogy to the interrogative (istifhāmiyya), in that it always holds the front position of the sentence. Some have said that the meaning is "How many of the people of a town," where the modified noun is omitted and the modifier (muḍāf ilayhi) takes its place. Some have said that Allah only expressed it as "town" because it is more severe in punishment when He destroys humans together with their town. In the end of the verse, by His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿"or they"﴾, He has made clear that humans are included in the destruction. So the verse, according to this interpretation, includes the destruction of the town and its people together. According to the first interpretation, it includes the destruction of the people.

The purpose of the verse is to express abundance. Ibn Abī ʿAblah recited: "How many a town We destroyed them, then Our punishment came upon them." Allah's saying "fajāʾahā" (then it came upon it) apparently implies that the coming happened after the destruction, and that is impossible. So there remains only the option of departing from the apparent sense of this sequence. It was said: the particle "fāʾ" (then) may come in the sense of "wāw" (and), and does not necessarily indicate order.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak.

It was also said: He expressed the intention of destruction by the destruction itself. Makkī said in "al-Mushkil": like His saying ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge﴾ [al-Naḥl: 98].

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is what those who say that the "fāʾ" in this verse indicates sequence of speech rely upon.

It was also said: the meaning is: "We destroyed them through abandonment and lack of success, then Our punishment came upon them after that." Al-Farrāʾ, as related by al-Ṭabarī, said: the destruction is the coming of the punishment, and the coming of the punishment is the destruction; since the two are mutually entailed, it does not matter which one is placed first in order. It was also said: the "fāʾ" is only for the sequence of the account, as if He informed about many towns that He destroyed, then said: "So the matter concerning them was the coming of the punishment."

"Bayātan" (by night) is accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). "Qāʾilūn" (resting at midday) is from "al-qāʾila" (the midday rest). He specified the two times of ease and tranquility only because the arrival of punishment during them is more dreadful and more terrifying, due to the suddenness and surprise in them. The "aw" (or) in this place is like when you say: "The people concerning so-and-so are of two kinds: one who praises him or one who blames him." It is as if He said: "Our punishment came upon them in two groups, spending the night or resting at midday." This is what is called "al-laff" (the wrapping, i.e., a concise expression of alternatives, which the listener's mind separates without difficulty). "Al-baʾs" (the might) means the punishment. It was said: the intended meaning is "or they were resting at midday," and the two conjunctions were disliked together, so the "wāw" was omitted. This is a forced interpretation, because the meaning of "al-laff" remains.

Allah's saying ﴿Their only plea﴾, the verse; this verse makes clear beyond any explanation that the intended people in the verse before it are the people of the towns. "Al-daʿwā" in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings: first, supplication (duʿāʾ). Al-Khalīl said: you say, "O Allah, make us share in the good supplication (daʿwā) of the Muslims." From this is Allah's saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿That remained their cry﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 15]. And from it is the saying of the poet:

"If my foot became numb, I call you, seeking relief
through your calling me, from the numbness, so it becomes easy."

Second, claim (iddiʿāʾ). Al-Ṭabarī said: in this place it means supplication.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is also possible that it means claim (iddiʿāʾ), because whoever is struck by something disagreeable or afflicted by a calamity is inclined to supplicate, as the commentators understood about the deeds of those mentioned in this verse. It is also in their nature to claim excuses and other things that improve their state and establish their argument in their own view. So it is possible that these people were in the condition of one who claims excuses and the like. Thus Allah, Exalted is He, informed about them that they had no claim. Then He made an exception from a non-first (i.e., a different category) as if He said: "There was no supplication, or claim, except acknowledgment and confession." That is, this acknowledgment was in place of supplication or claim.

The verse may also mean: "Their claim which they had in the state of their disbelief did not lead to anything except confession." A similar verse is the saying of the poet:

"Qays witnessed, and their help was nothing
for Qutayba except biting with the thumbs."

Their confession and their saying, "Indeed we were wrongdoers," occurs in the period between the appearance of the punishment and its arrival upon them personally; and within that there is a respite, depending on the type of punishment, that accommodates this statement and others. Ibn Masʿūd related from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No people perished until they were given an excuse from themselves." ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Maysara interpreted this hadith with this verse. "Daʿwāhum" (their claim) is the predicate of "kāna" (was), and its subject is "illā an qālū" (except that they said). It was also said the reverse.

Allah's saying ﴿We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾, the verse; it is a threat from Allah, Exalted and Majestic, to all the world. He informed that He will question all nations about what was conveyed to them from Him, Exalted is He, and about all their deeds; and He will question the prophets, peace be upon them, about what they conveyed.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Questioning is negated in some verses, and that is the questioning of genuine inquiry; and it is affirmed in verses like this one, and this is questioning for the purpose of establishing (taqrīr) the matter. For Allah, Exalted is He, has encompassed all of that in knowledge before the questioning. As for the prophets, peace be upon them, and the believers, their answer will be followed by mercy and honor. As for the disbelievers, and those among the disobedient upon whom the threat is carried out, their answer will be followed by punishment and rebuke. Whoever among them denies, Allah, Exalted is He, will relate to him with knowledge. Ibn Masʿūd recited: "Then We will surely question those to whom Our messengers were sent before you, and We will surely question the messengers."

Allah's saying ﴿"Then We will surely relate"﴾, that is: "We will surely narrate to them their deeds, story by story." And "with knowledge" means with reality and certainty. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The Book will be placed on the Day of Resurrection, and it will speak about what they used to do.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It seems that the speech here is a metaphor (istiʿāra), since everything in it is recorded.

﴿"And We were never absent"﴾, that is: "We were never one who does not know all their conduct," like the absent person concerning something, who does not know its condition.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 8–9:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth. As for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls because they used to wrong Our signs.﴾

(p-515) "Al-wazn" (the weighing) is a verbal noun from "wazana, yazinu"; it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "al-haqq" (the truth) is its predicate (khabar). "Yawma'idhin" (on that Day) is an adverbial phrase in the accusative governed by "al-wazn". It is also permissible for "yawma'idhin" to be the predicate of the subject, and "al-haqq" to be an adjective (na't) of "al-wazn"; the sense would then be: "The weighing is true and established, or manifest, on that Day." "Yawma'idhin" refers to the Day of Resurrection and the Judgement between the creatures.

People have differed about the meaning of "al-wazn" and "al-mawazin" (the scales). One group said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to inform His servants that the reckoning and the assessment on the Day of Resurrection are of the utmost precision and the ultimate justice. So He gave them an image of this through weighing and the balance, since humans know nothing more precise than it. Thus the words "al-wazn" and "al-mizan" were borrowed for justice and the precise assessment, just as Abu Talib borrowed it in his saying:

"With a balance of justice that does not short a single barleycorn,
For it has a judge from its own self, not partial."

This view is reported from Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and others. Likewise, "heaviness" and "lightness" were borrowed to mean the abundance and scarcity of good deeds.

The majority of the community said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to present to His servants on the Day of Resurrection the precision of assessment and the utmost justice through a matter they have known in this world and that their understanding is accustomed to. So the scale of the Resurrection has a pillar and two pans, in the form of the scales of this world. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The one in charge of the scales on the Day of Resurrection is Jibril, peace be upon him." They said: This is what the Qur'an requires, and no reasoning has rejected it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is more correct than the first for several reasons. The first is that the apparent meanings of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, require it, and the hadith of the Messenger, peace be upon him, speaks to it. Among that is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to one of the Companions, who had said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, where shall I find you on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "Seek me at the Pool; if you do not find me, then by the scale." Had the scale not been visible and perceptible, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have referred him to seeking him there. (p-516) The second reason: the assessment by the scale, the weighing, heaviness and lightness, which are connected with the reckoning, is not corrupted in any part of it, nor is its soundness disturbed. If this is so, why should we depart from the real meaning of the word to its figurative meaning without a reason? The third reason: the discussion of the scale is one of the articles of the Shari'ah that is known only through revelation (sam'). If we open the door of metaphor concerning it, the statements of the heretics (mulhidah) and the zindiqs would overwhelm us, saying that the scale, the Sirat, Paradise, Hell, the Gathering, and similar things are merely words intended to mean other than their apparent sense.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: As for heaviness and lightness, the reports are consistent that the records of good and bad deeds are placed in the two pans of the scale, and Allah, may He be exalted, produces heaviness and lightness in whichever pan He wills, in the same way that He produced it in the body of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at the time of revelation descending upon him. In the Sahih, from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit, he said: "I was writing when there was revealed ﴿other than those with a disability﴾ [al-Nisa: 95]; and the thigh of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was upon my thigh until it nearly crushed my thigh." And in the hadith: "When revelation came to him while he was on his she-camel, she would kneel down with him," being unable to bear him because of the heaviness that occurred in him. We must know that the heaviness produced together with the good deeds is connected only with a body, since an accident does not subsist in an accident. It is therefore permissible that He produce heaviness in the records, and this is the nearest of them to what is likely; and it is also permissible that He produce it in bodies adjacent to that condition. Abu al-Ma'ali went to the view that it is produced in the records. Reports concerning the scale have come from Companions and Successors about its shape, its length, and its conditions, but they are not established by sound chains, so we see no benefit in lengthening by them. al-Hasan said, as is reported from him: "It has reached me that every person on the Day of Resurrection will have a separate scale."

(p-517) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This statement is rejected; people hold the opposite view. Rather, each person has a weighing specific to him, while the scale is one. It is reported from Mujahid, regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿whose scales are heavy﴾, that "al-mawazin" means the good deeds themselves.

"Be successful with whatever you wish, for with weakness one may reach [his goal], and the shrewd may be deceived."

As for the saying of the poet:

"................. and the evening and the morning, there is no falah with them,"

it has been said that it means "al-baqa'" (remaining). The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Remaining is the attaining of an aim, so the two meanings are close. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 8–9:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth. As for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls because they used to wrong Our signs.﴾

(p-515) "Al-wazn" (the weighing) is a verbal noun from "wazana, yazinu"; it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "al-haqq" (the truth) is its predicate (khabar). "Yawma'idhin" (on that Day) is an adverbial phrase in the accusative governed by "al-wazn". It is also permissible for "yawma'idhin" to be the predicate of the subject, and "al-haqq" to be an adjective (na't) of "al-wazn"; the sense would then be: "The weighing is true and established, or manifest, on that Day." "Yawma'idhin" refers to the Day of Resurrection and the Judgement between the creatures.

People have differed about the meaning of "al-wazn" and "al-mawazin" (the scales). One group said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to inform His servants that the reckoning and the assessment on the Day of Resurrection are of the utmost precision and the ultimate justice. So He gave them an image of this through weighing and the balance, since humans know nothing more precise than it. Thus the words "al-wazn" and "al-mizan" were borrowed for justice and the precise assessment, just as Abu Talib borrowed it in his saying:

"With a balance of justice that does not short a single barleycorn,
For it has a judge from its own self, not partial."

This view is reported from Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and others. Likewise, "heaviness" and "lightness" were borrowed to mean the abundance and scarcity of good deeds.

The majority of the community said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, intended to present to His servants on the Day of Resurrection the precision of assessment and the utmost justice through a matter they have known in this world and that their understanding is accustomed to. So the scale of the Resurrection has a pillar and two pans, in the form of the scales of this world. Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The one in charge of the scales on the Day of Resurrection is Jibril, peace be upon him." They said: This is what the Qur'an requires, and no reasoning has rejected it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is more correct than the first for several reasons. The first is that the apparent meanings of the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, require it, and the hadith of the Messenger, peace be upon him, speaks to it. Among that is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to one of the Companions, who had said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, where shall I find you on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "Seek me at the Pool; if you do not find me, then by the scale." Had the scale not been visible and perceptible, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would not have referred him to seeking him there. (p-516) The second reason: the assessment by the scale, the weighing, heaviness and lightness, which are connected with the reckoning, is not corrupted in any part of it, nor is its soundness disturbed. If this is so, why should we depart from the real meaning of the word to its figurative meaning without a reason? The third reason: the discussion of the scale is one of the articles of the Shari'ah that is known only through revelation (sam'). If we open the door of metaphor concerning it, the statements of the heretics (mulhidah) and the zindiqs would overwhelm us, saying that the scale, the Sirat, Paradise, Hell, the Gathering, and similar things are merely words intended to mean other than their apparent sense.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: As for heaviness and lightness, the reports are consistent that the records of good and bad deeds are placed in the two pans of the scale, and Allah, may He be exalted, produces heaviness and lightness in whichever pan He wills, in the same way that He produced it in the body of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at the time of revelation descending upon him. In the Sahih, from the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit, he said: "I was writing when there was revealed ﴿other than those with a disability﴾ [al-Nisa: 95]; and the thigh of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was upon my thigh until it nearly crushed my thigh." And in the hadith: "When revelation came to him while he was on his she-camel, she would kneel down with him," being unable to bear him because of the heaviness that occurred in him. We must know that the heaviness produced together with the good deeds is connected only with a body, since an accident does not subsist in an accident. It is therefore permissible that He produce heaviness in the records, and this is the nearest of them to what is likely; and it is also permissible that He produce it in bodies adjacent to that condition. Abu al-Ma'ali went to the view that it is produced in the records. Reports concerning the scale have come from Companions and Successors about its shape, its length, and its conditions, but they are not established by sound chains, so we see no benefit in lengthening by them. al-Hasan said, as is reported from him: "It has reached me that every person on the Day of Resurrection will have a separate scale."

(p-517) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This statement is rejected; people hold the opposite view. Rather, each person has a weighing specific to him, while the scale is one. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 10–11:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood. Little are you grateful.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly created you and then formed you; then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis. He was not among those who prostrate.﴾

The address is to all of mankind, and what is meant is that the species as a whole is established on the earth. "Al-ma'ayish" (livelihoods) is the plural of "ma'ishah," a word that encompasses the food by which one lives and the trade (taharruf) that leads to it. The majority of readers recited "ma'ayish" with a kasra on the ya', without hamza. Al-A'raj and others recited "ma'a'ish" with hamza, like "madaa'in" and "safa'in." This was transmitted by Kharijah from Nafi'. It is also reported from Warsh as "ma'aysh," with the ya' sukun. Whoever recites "ma'ayish" with the ya' kept sound is the most correct, because it is the plural of "ma'ishah," whose pattern is "maf'ilah." It may also be "maf'ulah" with a damma on the 'ain; this is what Sibawayh said both of them. Al-Farra' said it is "maf'alah" with a fatha on the 'ain. So the ya' in "ma'ishah" is original. "Ma'ishah" was made weak (i'lal) because it agrees with the verb "ya'ish" in the ya', that is, in the moving and the still. "Ma'ayish" was kept sound in the broken plural, because the agreement mentioned in the wording disappears, and because the broken plural, as a meaning, does not occur in the verb; it is peculiar to nouns. As for whoever recites "ma'ayish" (with the ya' sukun), it is by way of lightening from "ma'ayish." Whoever recites "ma'a'ish," having made the ya' weak, that is an error. As for its justification, it is by likening the original to the augmented letter, because "ma'ishah" resembles "sahifah" in form, so just as "sahaif" is said, "ma'a'ish" was said. The ya' of "sahaif" and its counterparts, in which the ya' is augmented, is made hamza because it has no original basis in movement; its pattern is "fa'ilah" with the ya' still. When it was compelled to move it in the plural, it was replaced by something sturdier than it.

"Qalilan" (little) is in the accusative governed by "tashkurun" (you give thanks). It may be that "ma" is superfluous, and it may be that it is with the verb by way of interpretation as a verbal noun. "Qalilan" is then an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "little is your thanks" or "thanks little do you give."

As for His exalted saying, ﴿And We have certainly created you and then formed you﴾, the verse, the meaning of this verse is to draw attention to the place of lesson and wonder, from the wondrous craftsmanship and the bestowal of blessing. He began with creation, which is bringing into existence after non-existence, then with forming in this specific structure for humans. Otherwise, a created thing was never devoid of a form.

People have differed about the order of this verse, because its apparent meaning requires that the creating and forming of the children of Adam occurred before the saying to the angels to prostrate. The Shari'ah has established that the matter was not so. One group said: what is meant by His exalted saying ﴿And We have certainly created you and then formed you﴾ is Adam himself, peace be upon him, even though the address is to his descendants. This is because he, peace be upon him, was the cause of the existence of his descendants, so what was done to him is validly said, with some figurative usage, to have been done to his descendants. Mujahid said: the meaning is, "And We have certainly created you and then formed you in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, and at the time of bringing forth the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, from his back, like specks, in the form of humans."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On these two views, "thumma" (then) follows its own sense of sequence and interval.

'Ikrimah and al-A'mash said: what is meant is, "We created you in the backs of the fathers and formed you in the wombs of the mothers." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "As for 'We created you,' it is Adam, peace be upon him; as for 'We formed you,' it is his progeny in the wombs of the mothers." Qatadah and al-Dahhak said the same. Ma'mar ibn Rashid, from some of the people of knowledge, said: rather, all of that is in the wombs of the mothers, both creation and formation.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This group said that "thumma" is for the ordering of the reports conveyed by these clauses, not for the ordering of the clauses themselves. Al-Akhfash said: "thumma" in this verse has the meaning of "wa" (and). The grammarians of Basra refuted him.

"Malaikah" (angels): its pattern is either "mafa'ilah" or "ma'afilah," according to the derivation mentioned earlier in Surat al-Baqarah. There we mentioned the manner of prostration, its intended meaning, and the meaning of "Iblis," and how he was before disobedience. As for His exalted saying in this verse, ﴿except Iblis﴾, al-Zajjaj said: it is an exception that is not from the first group. Rather, Iblis was commanded to prostrate, based on His exalted saying ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. Other than al-Zajjaj said: the exception is from the first group, because if we made it disjunctive, according to the view of one who says that Iblis was not among the angels, it would necessarily follow that Iblis was not commanded to prostrate, unless the speaker of this view says that Iblis's command was in another way, other than His exalted saying "Prostrate." That is clearly weak.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "li-l-malaikatu usjudu" with a damma on the ha', and this is a weak reading. Its justification is that he dropped the hamza of "usjudu" and placed its vowel on the ha'. That is not tenable, because it is a dropped hamza with the ha' carrying a vowel by way of genitive, that is, something to be nullified; and nullification occurs only in continuous speech (wasl).

قَوْلُهُ - عَزَّ وجَلَّ -:

﴿Allah said: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?" He said: "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ ﴿He said: "Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein, so get out. Indeed, you are of the debased."﴾ ﴿He said: "Reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, you are of those reprieved."﴾ ﴿He said: "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path."﴾

"Mā" is an interrogative, and what is intended by it is rebuke and reproach. As for the "lā" in His words, "allā" (an allā), it has been said that it is redundant (zāʾidah, extra), and the meaning is: "What prevented you from prostrating?" It is like the "lā" in the words of the poet:

*His generosity refused "no" to stinginess, so "yes" hastened toward him from a youth who does not withhold generosity from its killer.*

This is according to one of the opinions regarding this verse. It has been said that the "lā" in it is redundant. Al-Zajjāj said: it is an object (mafʿūl), and "al-bukhl" (stinginess) is a substitute (badal) for it. Al-Ṭabarī related from Yūnus, from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, that the narration in it is "lā al-bukhli" with the letter lām in the genitive case, because "lā" may contain generosity when one says it in a matter that withholds rights and withholds stinginess from obligations. Among the verses in which "lā" came redundant is the saying of the poet:

*Is it from you, no lightning, as if its flash is a thicket crowned by a pierced flame?*

It has been said regarding the verse that "lā" is not redundant; rather, the meaning is: "What prevented you, so that it made you need not to prostrate?" It has also been said: since "mā manaʿaka" carries the meaning of "Who commanded you?" and "Who said to you?", it was fitting that "allā tasjuda" should follow it.

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The summary of this is that a verb should be assumed in the speech upon which the negation can properly be placed, as if he said: "What compelled you, or carried you, or forced you?" The answer of the accursed Iblīs was not in response to what he was asked about; rather, he came with speech that contains the answer and the argument against him. It is as if he said: "My own superiority prevented me, since I am better than him, when You created me from fire and created him from clay." It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "I will not prostrate, and I am better than him, older than him, and stronger in creation." He means: fire is stronger than clay. Iblīs thought that fire is superior to clay, and this is not so; rather, they are on one level in that both are created inanimate matter. When Iblīs thought that the rising and lightness of fire necessitate a superiority over the stillness and dullness of clay, he analogized that what was created from it is superior to what was created from clay. So his analogy (qiyās, analogical reasoning) was mistaken, and he overlooked that the spirit which was breathed into Ādam is not of clay. Al-Ṭabarī said: He overlooked what is in fire of restlessness, lightness, and agitation, and what is in clay of gravity, deliberation, forbearance, and steadfastness.

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: There is scrutiny in the words of al-Ṭabarī. It is related from al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn that they both said: "The first to analogize was Iblīs, and the sun and the moon were only worshipped through analogy." 

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Al-Ṭabarī said: They mean the wrong analogy, and there is no evidence from their words for it, and their statement cannot be interpreted as denying analogy in general. Their speech came only as a prohibition against what existed in their time of the faulty analogies of the Khawārij and others, and so they wanted to bring people back to the right path.

As for His words, "Then descend from it" (fa-ihbiṭ minhā), up to the end of the verse, it is a command from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to Iblīs to descend at the time of his disobedience in prostration. From this it appears that he was first made to descend and was expelled from Paradise, and he came to be in the heavens. This is because the reports are consistent that he misled Ādam, peace be upon him, and Ḥawwāʾ from outside Paradise. Then he was commanded, at last, to descend from the heavens together with Ādam, peace be upon him, Ḥawwāʾ, and the serpent.

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: All of this is according to the wording of the story, and Allah knows best.

As for His words, "for it is not [for you]" (fa-mā yakūnu laka), its meaning is: "it is not valid for you and not complete for you." This wording does not imply that arrogance is permitted for him elsewhere, as some critics have claimed.

The verse includes that Allah, Exalted, informed Iblīs that greatness does not belong to him and is not valid for him in Paradise, along with His prohibiting him and others from arrogance in every place. But if we take "fa-mā yakūnu" to mean "it is not good and not becoming," as you say to a man, "It was not for you not to maintain your kinship ties," the sense of severity toward Iblīs would be diminished.

As for His words, "Indeed, you are of the debased" (innaka mina al-ṣāghirīn), it is a ruling against him with the opposite of the disobedience through which he disobeyed, which is arrogance. So he was punished by being driven to it, in contrast to his desire and his hope. Al-ṣaghār means humiliation; this was said by al-Suddī.

Then Iblīs asked his Lord, Exalted, to delay him until the Day of Resurrection, hoping that he would not die, since he knew that death ends after resurrection. The meaning of "anẓirnī" is: "delay me." Allah, Exalted, granted him the reprieve until the Day of the appointed time. Most people said: the appointed time is the first blast of the Trumpet, by which everyone in the heavens and everyone on earth among the creatures will be struck senseless. This is according to one of the opinions regarding this verse. It has been said that the "lā" in it is redundant. Al-Zajjāj said: it is an object (mafʿūl), and "al-bukhl" (stinginess) is a substitute (badal) for it. Al-Ṭabarī related from Yūnus, from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, that the narration in it is "lā al-bukhli" with the letter lām in the genitive case, because "lā" may contain generosity when one says it in a matter that withholds rights and withholds stinginess from obligations. Among the verses in which "lā" came redundant is the saying of the poet:

*Is it from you, no lightning, as if its flash is a thicket crowned by a pierced flame?*

It has been said regarding the verse that "lā" is not redundant; rather, the meaning is: "What prevented you, so that it made you need not to prostrate?" It has also been said: since "mā manaʿaka" carries the meaning of "Who commanded you?" and "Who said to you?", it was fitting that "allā tasjuda" should follow it.

From this it appears that he was first made to descend and was expelled from Paradise, and he came to be in the heavens. This is because the reports are consistent that he misled Ādam, peace be upon him, and Ḥawwāʾ from outside Paradise. Then he was commanded, at last, to descend from the heavens together with Ādam, peace be upon him, Ḥawwāʾ, and the serpent.

As for His words, "for it is not [for you]" (fa-mā yakūnu laka), its meaning is: "it is not valid for you and not complete for you." This wording does not imply that arrogance is permitted for him elsewhere, as some critics have claimed.

The verse includes that Allah, Exalted, informed Iblīs that greatness does not belong to him and is not valid for him in Paradise, along with His prohibiting him and others from arrogance in every place. But if we take "fa-mā yakūnu" to mean "it is not good and not becoming," as you say to a man, "It was not for you not to maintain your kinship ties," the sense of severity toward Iblīs would be diminished.

As for His words, "Indeed, you are of the debased" (innaka mina al-ṣāghirīn), it is a ruling against him with the opposite of the disobedience through which he disobeyed, which is arrogance. So he was punished by being driven to it, in contrast to his desire and his hope. Al-ṣaghār means humiliation; this was said by al-Suddī.

Then Iblīs asked his Lord, Exalted, to delay him until the Day of Resurrection, hoping that he would not die, since he knew that death ends after resurrection. The meaning of "anẓirnī" is: "delay me." Allah, Exalted, granted him the reprieve until the Day of the appointed time. Most people said: the appointed time is the first blast of the Trumpet, by which everyone in the heavens and everyone on earth among the creatures will be struck senseless. Another group said: rather, He deferred it to an appointed time known to Him, Mighty and Majestic, meaning the day of Iblīs's death and the arrival of his term, without specifying that to him. He left him in the fog of ignorance about it so that this would distress him as long as he lived.

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Some of those who held this view said that Iblīs was killed by the angels on the day of Badr, and they related a weak report (athar) regarding that.

The author, Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The first of these opinions is more sound and more widely known in the Sharīʿa.

The meaning of "among those reprieved" (min al-munẓarīn) is: among the group whose lifespans were greatly extended until their terms came, according to the differences in their times. Thus a reprieve encompassed that group, even though they were not alive for the entire span of time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 17–18:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful.﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "Get out of it, reproached and expelled. Whoever follows you among them – I will surely fill Hell with all of you."﴾

This is an assertion by Iblis (Iblis, the devil) that he will strive hard to mislead the children of Adam. This had not been the case until Iblis knew that Allah, the Exalted, was going to place a khalifa (successor, vicegerent) on the earth, and he knew that this was Adam, peace be upon him. Otherwise there is no way for him to know about the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him, from the wording of these verses.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The purpose of this verse is that Iblis informed about himself that he comes to lead the son of Adam astray from every direction and on every path. He corrupts for him whatever belief he can, makes him forget the good deeds of the Hereafter, and incites him to the ugly deeds of this world. He expressed this with words that imply encompassing them, and in the wording there is a figure of speech (tajawwuz, figurative usage). This is the view of a group of exegetes (mufassirun).

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, as it has been transmitted from him: By His saying ﴿from before them﴾ he meant the Hereafter; ﴿and from behind them﴾, this world; ﴿and from their right﴾, the truth; ﴿and from their left﴾, falsehood. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as it has been transmitted from him: ﴿from before them﴾ is this world; ﴿and from behind them﴾ is the Hereafter; ﴿and from their right﴾ is the good deeds; ﴿and from their left﴾ is the bad deeds. Mujahid said: "from before them and from their right" means: where they can see; and "from behind them and from their left" means: where they cannot see.

As for His saying ﴿and You will not find most of them grateful﴾, it informs that his scheming does this, out of his own assumption and conjecture about the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, when he saw his creation from various different things. So he knew that they would have dispositions that call for obeying him, such as rancor, envy, desires, and the like. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: However, Iblis did not say that he would come to the children of Adam from above them, and Allah, the Exalted, did not give him a way to come between them and the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, His pardon and His favor. What Iblis assumed, Allah, the Exalted, made true. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a group of the believers﴾ [Saba': 20]. Thus He made most of the world disbelievers. This is clarified by the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in the hadith: "Allah, Blessed and Exalted, will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'O Adam, bring forth the portion of the Fire.' He will say: 'O my Lord, what is the portion of the Fire?' He will say: 'Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine, and one to Paradise.'" And similar to it, what specifically concerns the community of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him: "You are among the nations only like the white hair on a black ox."

(p. 527) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, "like the hair", may possibly mean a single hair, but this is far-fetched, because the coherence of the first hadith rejects it. It may possibly mean, by the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the hair that is generic (lil-jins, a collective noun), and the intention is to liken them to a black ox in whose blackness a white hair has grown. It may also possibly mean the gleam of white hair, but this is a distant interpretation.

His saying "shakirin" (grateful) means "mu'minin" (believers), because the son of Adam does not thank the favor of Allah, the Exalted, except by believing. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿[Allah] said, "Get out of it"﴾: the pronoun in "minha" (from it) refers to Paradise. "Mazu'man" means "reproached"; it is said "dha'amahu" when he found fault with him. From this comes "al-dha'm", which is blame. In the proverb: "The beautiful woman will never be without a detractor" (lan tu'dama al-hasna'u dhamman), i.e., a fault. The hamza in it has been eased (tas-hil, softening of the glottal stop). From this is the saying of a speaker of Himyar: "You wanted to blame him, so you praised him" (aradta an tudhimahu fa-madahtahu), meaning: "fa-madahtahu" (so you praised him). Al-Tabari related that this verse is transmitted:

"I kept company with you when my eye had a film over it, / but when it cleared I cut my breath (regretting) to blame it."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The well-known transmission is "uluma-ha" (I blame it). Among the evidence for the wording is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"They are the nearest of all good, / and they are the farthest from all blame."

Among the evidence for "madhuran" (expelled/rejected): the saying of the poet:

"I drove the sons of al-Husayb back to Qudayd, / though they had been people of pride and boasting."

Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash read in this verse "madhumuman" (with easing of the hamza) and "madhuran" means: distanced and removed. A group read "li-man tabi'aka" (for whoever follows you) with a fatha on the lam; on this reading it is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam, the particle of swearing) which moves the speech from doubt to an oath. 'Asim al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read "li-man tabi'aka" with a kasra on the lam, and the meaning is: "for the sake of whoever follows you, I will surely fill Hell with all of you"; thus, by the particle of "minkum" (from you), he included him in the threat along with them.

'Asim al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read "li-man tabi'aka" with a kasra on the lam, and the meaning is: "for the sake of whoever follows you, I will surely fill Hell with all of you"; thus, by the particle of "minkum" (from you), he included him in the threat along with them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿And O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾

When a person is commanded to do something that he is already engaged in, the purpose of the command is that he continue in his state and persist in his condition. The saying of the Exalted to Adam, peace be upon him, "dwell" (uskun), belongs to this category. He emphasized the pronoun in His saying "uskun" with "anta" (you), and at that point it became permissible to coordinate (ʿataf) upon it. The pronoun here is one that may not be expressed separately and is not a standalone word, and coordinating upon a pronoun that is pronounced is not permissible except after emphasizing it, as in your saying "qumta anta wa-Zaydun" (you stood, you and Zayd), because the pronoun is like a letter of the verb. This pronoun in "uskun" is weaker than the one that is pronounced, so it is all the more fitting that coordinating upon it not be valid except after emphasis.

His saying, exalted is He, "fa-kulā" (so eat), is from "akala" (to eat). Its original form was "uʾkulā," so the first radical of the verb was deleted because two similar letters came together (ijtimaʿ al-mithlayn), and the other was dispensed with when what followed it became vowelled. Deleting the first radical of the verb was also considered good, because they found the vowel on a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah) burdensome. This is the rule for every verb whose first letter is a hamza and whose pattern is faʿala, like "akhadha" (he took) and "amara" (he commanded) and the like. Analogically, the first radical of the verb should not have been deleted, but their usage came down in this way.

It is said: "qaruba, yaqrabu" (he approached). As for "hādhihi al-shajara" (this tree), the apparent meaning is that the Exalted indicated a single individual tree of a kind and intended it. It is also possible that He indicated a specific tree while meaning the species as a whole, and He expressed it with the name of the singular, just as you say, "The people obtained the dinar and the dirham," while you mean the category.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On both possibilities, Adam, peace be upon him, intended, at the time of his disobedience, only to do what he had been forbidden. This is what the majority of the interpreters said, and with this Iblis, may Allah curse him, seduced him by his saying: "You were only forbidden lest you become immortal, or become kings." Thereby the saying of one who says that Adam, peace be upon him, erred only by interpretation, by supposing that the prohibition was attached to one specific tree, so he ate from the species, is refuted, and he is not excused for error.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That is because this speaker only supposes Adam believing that the prohibition attached only to a specific tree. How then can it be said to him, with this belief: "You were only forbidden lest you become immortal," and then he himself seeks immortality by committing what he was not forbidden? There is no difference between his eating what he believes he was not forbidden and his eating all the other permissible things for him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The final "h" in "hādhihi" is a substitute for the "y" in "hādhī"; it was substituted in pausal form, and then remained as "h" in continuous speech, by analogy with pause. There is no feminine "h" preceded by a kasra in speech other than this one. Ibn Muhaysin read "hādhī al-shajara" according to the original form. His saying, exalted is He, "fa-takūnā" (so you would be), is in the subjunctive as the answer to the prohibition.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: People have invoked this verse in the question of prohibition (ḥaẓr) and permissibility (ibāḥa). The question of prohibition and permissibility has been discussed by people in two ways. As for the jurists (fuqahāʾ), what prompted them to discuss it is that calamities (nawāzil) occur that are not found explicitly stated in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, nor in the Sunnah of His Prophet, Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor in a consensus (ijmāʿ). The way of deriving them from one of these three, and analogizing them to what is in them, is hidden; so the examiner then looks in which direction to carry it, from permission and prohibition. Some of them said: When the like of this occurs, we carry it upon prohibition, and we take in it the stricter course, and we seek to clear ourselves, since Allah, the Exalted, has explained for us in His Book all that needs explaining, and permitted what He willed to permit, and He did not leave mention of this calamity except deliberately; so our burdening ourselves with it is not required by the Law. Others said: Rather, we carry it upon permissibility, because Allah, the Exalted, has perfected our religion for us, and has prohibited for us what He willed to prohibit; and He did not neglect to state a ruling for a calamity except that He left it within the general body of the permitted; and it is far-fetched that He would intend a prohibition in something without mentioning it to us, leaving us in the blindness of ignorance of it. So we carry it upon permissibility until prohibition arises. Others said: Rather, we carry that upon suspension (waqf) forever, and we do not judge in it by prohibition or permissibility; rather we seek consideration and analogy in it forever. That is because we find Allah, the Exalted, saying in His Book, "It is forbidden to you" in many places, and saying, "It is made lawful for you" in many places. This indicates that every calamity needs a legal ruling and command, either specific to it or encompassing it and other things. Had things been upon prohibition, He would not have said of anything, "It is forbidden to you"; and had they been upon permissibility, He would not have said of anything, "It is made lawful for you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the clearest of the sayings. The jurists, in this question, did not address the examination of the intellect's making things good or bad; rather they adhered in these sayings to the causes of the Law and proceeded to extract their doctrines from them.

As for the second type of human discourse on prohibition and permissibility: the Mu'tazila, and whoever says what they say, that reason makes things good and bad, examined the question from this aspect. They said: We posit a time with no law in it, or a man who grew up in a wilderness and never perceived any law, command, or prohibition; or we suppose Adam, peace be upon him, at the time of his descent to earth, left to himself and his intellect before being commanded and forbidden; how were things for him? Or how does reason require regarding the time and the man posited? Some of them said: What is good according to reason is that everything be prohibited until permission to make use of it arrives, because making use of it is a transgression upon the property of another; and if that is ugly among created beings, then regarding the right of Allah, the Exalted, it is greater in sanctity. Some of this group went on to exempt breathing and movement from this prohibition, and they said: These cannot be otherwise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad said: It is possible to posit the necessity of them as making them permissible. Others said: Rather, it is good according to reason that they be permissible, since disposing of another's property in a way that causes him no harm is permitted, like seeking shade under walls and the like. If this is permissible among created beings, then regarding the greatness of the rank of Allah, the Exalted, and His existence, it is more permissible; since there is no harm in our disposing of His property, and nothing of that touches His right.

The people of truth and the Sunnah said, in this kind of consideration: Rather, the matter in itself is upon suspension; reason does not by itself require making good or making bad; nothing is owed by it; and the judgment of good and bad is not determined except by the Law. Others said: Reason has never been free of law; so there is no point in plunging into this question, nor in positing what does not occur. They argued that Adam, peace be upon him, was addressed by commands and prohibitions in the Garden, by the saying of the Exalted to him when the spirit entered his body and he sneezed: "Say: 'All praise is for Allah,' O Adam," and by His saying, "Dwell," "Eat," "Do not approach," and the like. Al-Qadi Ibn al-Baqillani said in "al-Taqrib wal-Irshad": The jurists who spoke of prohibition and permissibility did not intend to agree with the Mu'tazila in their error; rather they saw in their words a composite, embellished speech, and they found it attractive without realizing what corruption it leads to regarding the claim that reason makes good and bad.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this statement there is an imputation against the jurists of the Law and a belittling of them; the correct view is that this defect should not be attributed to them. Rather, they sought to attach the ruling of prohibition and permissibility to their calamities from the Law; and, moreover, it should not be imputed to them that they deny the truth that reason does not make good or bad apart from the Law.

The discussion of the difference concerning the tree and its identification has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 20–21:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Then Satan whispered to them, to reveal to them what was hidden from them of their private parts, and said, "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortal."﴾ ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisors."﴾

"Al-waswasa" (whispering): speech in concealment, in a murmur, and a faint, secret sound. "Al-waswas" is the sound of ornaments (ḥulī), and whispering was likened to it. The casting of Satan into the soul of the son of Adam was called "waswasa" because it is the most eloquent and most hidden form of secret speech. This is Satan's condition with us now. As for Adam, peace be upon him, it is possible that the whispering was by proximity, covertly, or by casting into the soul. From this is the saying of Ru'ba:

﴿Whispered, striving to call upon the Lord of the daybreak...﴾

This is an expression for hidden speech. "Satan" here is meant to be Iblis himself. Narrators of the stories differed about the form of his whispering. It is narrated that he used to enter Paradise within the mouth of the serpent, concealed—by his own claim—and thus he was able to whisper. It is also narrated that Adam, peace be upon him, and Eve used to go out beyond Paradise, and Iblis was then able to reach them. It is also narrated that God Exalted empowered him to cast into their souls, so he misled them while he was on earth.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a weak opinion, and the wording of the Qur'an refutes it.

The lam in His saying, Exalted, "li-yubdiya" (that he might reveal), is—according to the view of many scholars—the lam of becoming and outcome (lam al-sayrura wa al-'aqiba). This applies to Adam and Eve, and to Iblis, in this particular punishment, because he had no knowledge of it so as to intend it.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is possible that the lam is the lam of purpose (kay) in its proper sense, according to Iblis's intention to degrade their status and cast them into a punishment other than the particular one. "Ma wuriya" means "what was concealed," from your saying "wārā, yuwārī" when he concealed. The apparent form of this word is "mufā'ala" from one party, but it may be considered as from two, because the thing that is concealed [yuwārī] is also from one side.

Ibn Wathhab read "ma wuriya" with a single waw. Some people said that this word in this verse is derived from "warā'" (behind). 

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an opinion that morphology weakens.

"Al-sawʾa" means the private parts, both the front and the rear. It is likely that it is so named because its sight is displeasing (yasū'u). Mujahid and al-Hasan read "min sawwatihima" with a single letter, softening the hamza and doubling the waw. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shayba ibn Nassah, al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read "min sawwatihima," softening the hamza and doubling the waw; Sibawayh related it as a dialect form. Abu al-Fath said: its basis is the deletion of the hamza and placing its vowel on the waw, so they say "sawa", and some double the waw. 

A group said: this expression is intended to mean that their meanings were uncovered for them, and what would displease them, and it does not refer to nakedness.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an opinion the wording could bear; however, the mention of the sewing of leaves refutes it, unless the pronoun in "'alayhima" is taken to refer to their bodies, since the garments of Paradise were stripped from them, so that the aforementioned view would be sound.

As for His saying, Exalted, ﴿And he said, "Your Lord has not forbidden you..."﴾ etc.: this saying attributed to Iblis is subject to the same interpretation as the whispering. It is possible that he said this in direct address and dialogue, and it is possible that it was cast into the soul as inspiration.

"Illa an": according to Sibawayh and the Basrans, its estimate is "illa karahiyyata an" (except out of dislike that); according to the Kufans, its estimate is "illa alla," by the omission of "la."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The view of the Basrans is preferred, since the omission of nouns is better than the omission of particles.

The majority of people read "malakayn" with a fatha on the lam. Ibn 'Abbas, Yahya ibn Kathir and al-Dahhak read "malikayn" with a kasra on the lam. This reading is supported by His saying, Exalted, in another verse: ﴿and a kingdom that does not decay﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120].

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Some people said: it follows from these wordings that the angels are superior to humans. This is a question on which people differed, and each party clung to apparent evidences from the Sharia, and bounty is in the hand of Allah Exalted.

Ibn Furak said: there is no proof in this verse, since it is possible that it means "two angels" in that they would have no desire for food.

﴿"And he swore to them"﴾: i.e., he swore to them by Allah Exalted. It is of the form "mufā'ala," since the acceptance by the one sworn to and his turning toward the meaning of the oath, like the swearing and its confirmation, is conveyed; although at first glance it suggests it is from one party. Similar to it is the saying of al-Huzali:

﴿And he swore to them by Allah with striving, that you are sweeter than the quail when it is roasted...﴾

It is narrated in the accounts that Adam, peace be upon him, said, in the course of his excuse: "I did not think, O Lord, that anyone would swear falsely by You." Some scholars said: Satan deceived Adam, peace be upon him, by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and so he was deceived; and we, whoever deceives us by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, we are deceived by him. Something similar is narrated from Qatada.

The lam in His saying, Exalted, "lakuma" is connected to "al-nasihin" (the sincere advisors). Some people—Makki and others—said: this is on the basis that the alif and lam are for defining the genus, not in the sense of "alladhi" (who), because if they were in the sense of "alladhi," then His saying, Blessed and Exalted, "lakuma" would be within the relative clause, and it would not be permissible to front it. I think Abu 'Ali al-Farisi allowed its fronting even when the alif and lam mean "alladhi." The apparent view is that if it is taken to mean "alladhi," then the lam in "lakuma" is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: "Indeed I am a sincere advisor to you of the sincere advisors." Abu al-'Aliya, in some readings, read: "wa qasamahuma billah."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 22–23:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So he lured them with deception. And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden. And their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?" They said, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾

(p-535) ﴿So he lured them with deception﴾: he means, he deceived them with his words and beguiled them with his cunning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In my view, it resembles a metaphor drawn from "a man lowering another from a precipice by a rope that has rotted, or by a weak means in which he trusts; when he lets himself down by it and leans his weight upon it, it snaps and he perishes." Thus the one who is deceived by speech until he believes it, and so falls into calamity, is likened to one who is lowered into a pit by a weak means.

The ruling of punishment was attached to tasting, since it is the beginning of eating, and by it the prohibition is violated. In another verse: ﴿So they both ate from it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121].

As for His saying, exalted is He, "became apparent" (بَدَتْ): it was said that the garments of the Garden were torn away from them and their clothing scattered, disassociating itself from them. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: there was a light over each of them that covered the nakedness of each one, and by disobedience that light was dispersed. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: there was a covering of nails upon them, and when they disobeyed it shrank away from them, so their private parts became apparent, and a remnant of it remained on the fingers, enough for them to remember the disobedience, so that they would renew their regret.

"And they began" (وَطَفِقا): its meaning is "they took up and began to," and it is a verb not restricted to a particular time, like "bāta" and "ẓalla."

"Fasten" (يَخْصِفانِ): its meaning is that they stick them on and join some of them to others. "Al-mikhsaf" is the awl, and joining leaves one to another resembles stitching with beads more than sewing.

The majority of readers recited "yakhṣifān," from "khaṣafa." 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah recited "yakhaṣṣifān," with the ṣād doubled. Al-Zuhri recited "yukhṣifān," from "akhṣafa." Al-Hasan, as transmitted from him by Mahbub, recited "yakhaṣṣifān" with a fatḥa on the yā' and the khā', a kasra on the ṣād, and doubled. It is also reported from Ibn Buraydah and from Ya'qub. Its origin is "yakhtaṣifān," as you say "sami'tu al-ḥadīth" and "istama'tuhu." The tā' was assimilated into the ṣād and its vowel transferred to the khā'. Likewise the underlying form of the reading with a kasra on the khā' after this is the same; but when the tā' was made quiescent and assimilated into the ṣād, two quiescent letters came together, so the khā' was given a kasra according to the usage for meeting of two quiescent letters. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Mujahid recited "yakhiṣṣifān," with a fatḥa on the yā', a kasra on the khā', a kasra on the ṣād, and doubled; its explanation has already been given.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: the leaves from which they fastened were fig leaves. Ubayy reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Adam (peace be upon him) used to walk in the Garden as if he were a tall palm tree. When he committed the disobedience and his state became apparent to him, he fled headlong, and a tree caught hold of the hair of his head; it is said that it was the olive tree. He said to it, 'Release me.' It said, 'I will not release you.' His Lord called to him: (O Adam, do you flee from Me?) He said: 'No, O Lord, but I was shy before You.' He said: (Did you not have, among what I granted you of the Garden, an ample alternative to what I forbade you?) He said: 'Yes, O Lord, but by Your might, I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely.' He said: (By My might, I will surely cause you to descend to the earth; then you will not attain sustenance except with toil)."

As for His saying, "And their Lord called to them" (وَناداهُما) and the rest of the verse: the majority said this call was an inspired call, through an intermediary. This is supported by the fact that we receive from the Shari'ah that Musa (peace be upon him) is the one singled out among the worlds for speech. Also, in the hadith of intercession, "the believing children of Adam will say to Musa (peace be upon him) on the Day of Resurrection: 'You are the one whom Allah singled out with His speech and chose with His message; go and intercede for the people.'" Its apparent meaning is that he is singled out. Another group said: rather, it is a call of direct address.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The proof of this position is that it occurred in the first folio of the History of Ibn Abi Khaythamah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Adam (peace be upon him), and he said: 'a prophet who was spoken to.'" Also, Musa was singled out among the humans dwelling on the earth, whereas Adam, while in the Garden, was not in the rank of the earth's inhabitants; so there is nothing in his being addressed that negates the singling out of Musa (peace be upon him). What supports that it was an inspired call is that Hawwa' shared in it, and it was never narrated that Allah, exalted is He, spoke to Hawwa'. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "a prophet who was spoken to," is interpreted to mean that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, reached him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did I not forbid﴾: is a question of confirmation that includes rebuke. His saying, exalted is He, "that" (تِلْكُما): by the apparent wording, it indicates that He was pointing to the individual tree. ﴿And tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy﴾: is a reference to the verse in Surah Ta-Ha, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let him not expel you from the Garden, lest you be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the covenant that Adam (peace be upon him) forgot, according to the view of those who keep forgetting on its literal basis. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "Were you not forbidden from that tree, and was it not said to you..." Their saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ is an acknowledgment from Adam and Hawwa' (peace be upon them both), and a request for repentance, covering, and enveloping in mercy. Adam (peace be upon him) asked for this, while Iblis asked for respite and did not ask for repentance, so he was left to his own opinion. Al-Dahhak said: this verse is the words that Adam (peace be upon him) received from his Lord, exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 22–23:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So he lured them with deception. And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden. And their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?" They said, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾

(p-535) ﴿So he lured them with deception﴾: he means, he deceived them with his words and beguiled them with his cunning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: In my view, it resembles a metaphor drawn from "a man lowering another from a precipice by a rope that has rotted, or by a weak means in which he trusts; when he lets himself down by it and leans his weight upon it, it snaps and he perishes." Thus the one who is deceived by speech until he believes it, and so falls into calamity, is likened to one who is lowered into a pit by a weak means.

The ruling of punishment was attached to tasting, since it is the beginning of eating, and by it the prohibition is violated. In another verse: ﴿So they both ate from it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121].

As for His saying, exalted is He, "became apparent" (بَدَتْ): it was said that the garments of the Garden were torn away from them and their clothing scattered, disassociating itself from them. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: there was a light over each of them that covered the nakedness of each one, and by disobedience that light was dispersed. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: there was a covering of nails upon them, and when they disobeyed it shrank away from them, so their private parts became apparent, and a remnant of it remained on the fingers, enough for them to remember the disobedience, so that they would renew their regret.

"And they began" (وَطَفِقا): its meaning is "they took up and began to," and it is a verb not restricted to a particular time, like "bāta" and "ẓalla."

"Fasten" (يَخْصِفانِ): its meaning is that they stick them on and join some of them to others. "Al-mikhsaf" is the awl, and joining leaves one to another resembles stitching with beads more than sewing.

The majority of readers recited "yakhṣifān," from "khaṣafa." 'Abdullah ibn Buraydah recited "yakhaṣṣifān," with the ṣād doubled. Al-Zuhri recited "yukhṣifān," from "akhṣafa." Al-Hasan, as transmitted from him by Mahbub, recited "yakhaṣṣifān" with a fatḥa on the yā' and the khā', a kasra on the ṣād, and doubled. It is also reported from Ibn Buraydah and from Ya'qub. Its origin is "yakhtaṣifān," as you say "sami'tu al-ḥadīth" and "istama'tuhu." The tā' was assimilated into the ṣād and its vowel transferred to the khā'. Likewise the underlying form of the reading with a kasra on the khā' after this is the same; but when the tā' was made quiescent and assimilated into the ṣād, two quiescent letters came together, so the khā' was given a kasra according to the usage for meeting of two quiescent letters. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Mujahid recited "yakhiṣṣifān," with a fatḥa on the yā', a kasra on the khā', a kasra on the ṣād, and doubled; its explanation has already been given.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: the leaves from which they fastened were fig leaves. Ubayy reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "Adam (peace be upon him) used to walk in the Garden as if he were a tall palm tree. When he committed the disobedience and his state became apparent to him, he fled headlong, and a tree caught hold of the hair of his head; it is said that it was the olive tree. He said to it, 'Release me.' It said, 'I will not release you.' His Lord called to him: (O Adam, do you flee from Me?) He said: 'No, O Lord, but I was shy before You.' He said: (Did you not have, among what I granted you of the Garden, an ample alternative to what I forbade you?) He said: 'Yes, O Lord, but by Your might, I did not think that anyone would swear by You falsely.' He said: (By My might, I will surely cause you to descend to the earth; then you will not attain sustenance except with toil)."

As for His saying, "And their Lord called to them" (وَناداهُما) and the rest of the verse: the majority said this call was an inspired call, through an intermediary. This is supported by the fact that we receive from the Shari'ah that Musa (peace be upon him) is the one singled out among the worlds for speech. Also, in the hadith of intercession, "the believing children of Adam will say to Musa (peace be upon him) on the Day of Resurrection: 'You are the one whom Allah singled out with His speech and chose with His message; go and intercede for the people.'" Its apparent meaning is that he is singled out. Another group said: rather, it is a call of direct address.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The proof of this position is that it occurred in the first folio of the History of Ibn Abi Khaythamah that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Adam (peace be upon him), and he said: 'a prophet who was spoken to.'" Also, Musa was singled out among the humans dwelling on the earth, whereas Adam, while in the Garden, was not in the rank of the earth's inhabitants; so there is nothing in his being addressed that negates the singling out of Musa (peace be upon him). What supports that it was an inspired call is that Hawwa' shared in it, and it was never narrated that Allah, exalted is He, spoke to Hawwa'. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "a prophet who was spoken to," is interpreted to mean that the speech of Allah, exalted is He, reached him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did I not forbid﴾: is a question of confirmation that includes rebuke.
