[p. 538]

**The Exalted's saying:**

﴿He said: "Go down, some of you being enemies to others. On earth you will have a dwelling-place and provision for a time."﴾ ﴿He said: "Therein you will live, therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth."﴾ ﴿Children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts, and finery. But the clothing of God-consciousness (taqwa), that is best. That is among the signs of God, so that they may take heed.﴾

The address in His saying "Go down" (ihbitu): Abu Salih, al-Suddi, al-Tabari and others said it is addressed to Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, and to Iblis and the serpent. A group said it is addressed to Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring, and to Iblis and his offspring.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This view is weak, because they did not exist at that time. If it is said that He addressed them and commanded them on the condition of their existence, this is remote in this case, because a command conditional on existence is valid only when it applies to the one commanded after he exists, and its meaning is realised in him, as with prayer, fasting and the like. But here, the meaning of descent (hubut) cannot be conceived for the children of Adam after their existence, and no part of the command to descend applies to them. As for His saying in another verse, "Go down" (ihbita), in dual form, it is addressed to Adam, peace be upon him, and to Iblis, by the evidence of His stating the enmity between them.

"Enemy" ('aduww) is singular in form but has the meaning of plural. You say: "a people 'aduww; and a people sadiq (friend)." From this is the poet's saying:

"By my life, if you were, in distance and in wealth, to me as I am to you, you would indeed be friends."

The enmity of serpents is well known. Qatada narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have not made peace with them since we went to war against them." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Whoever abandons them is not of us." 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, said: "Whoever leaves a serpent out of fear of its vengeance, upon him is the curse of God, the angels and all people."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The matter of serpents is raised only by the story of the young man at the Battle of the Trench, and the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Jinn in Medina have embraced Islam. So whoever sees any of these serpents in his house, let him warn it three times; if he sees it after that, let him kill it, for it is then a disbeliever."

His saying "a dwelling-place" (mustaqarr) is a general term that covers the time of life and the time of residence in graves. Abu al-'Aliya explained it as the time of life, and said it is like His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqara 2:22]. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, explained it as residence in graves. The wording includes both, and it is like His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat 77:25–26]. As for "provision" (mata'), it depends on each individual during the time of life, unless one judges that dwelling in the grave is in some way a provision. Mata' is enjoyment and gaining of benefits. "For a time" (ila hin) means, in general, the establishing of the Hour, and for each individual, the reaching of the appointed term and death. "Hin" in the speech of the Arabs means an unspecified time.

It is related that Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down in India, and Eve in Jeddah. He longed for her at Mina, recognised the reality of their situation at 'Arafa, and met her at Jam'. Iblis was sent down at Maysan. It was also said at Basra, and it was said at Egypt, where he laid eggs and hatched them. Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said: Iblis spread his silk brocade there. Salih, the client of al-Tawama, mentioned that in some books it is said: When Iblis was sent down, he said: "My Lord, where is my dwelling?" He was told: "Your dwelling is the bathhouse, your seat is the markets, your amusement is the flutes, your food is what my name is not mentioned over, your drink is the intoxicant, your messengers are the desires, and your snares are women." The serpent was sent down at Isfahan. It is related that it had legs like a camel, and as punishment it was made to crawl on its belly.

It is related that when Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to the hardship of the world, he was taught the craft of iron, then he was taught tillage. He ploughed, watered, harvested, winnowed, ground, kneaded, baked, cooked and ate. He did not attain this until he reached the degree of hardship that God the Exalted willed. It is related that it was said to Eve: "O Eve, just as the tree bled, so you bleed every month, and you bear only with pain and give birth only with pain." She then wailed, and it was said to her: "Wailing be upon you and upon your offspring."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This story contains much of the reports, which I have abridged, since the wording does not require them.

His saying, "Therein you will live…" and so on, is a judgement from God the Exalted that He enforced and made binding upon the necks of the servants: they live on earth, die in it, and are raised from it alive at the gathering, as He originated the first creation and will restore it.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Abu 'Amr recited "tukhrajun" (you will be brought forth) with a dammah on the ta' and a fatha on the ra' here, and in al-Rum, and likewise wherever it recurs, except in al-Rum: ﴿when you come forth﴾ [al-Rum 30:25], and in "Sa'ala sa'il": ﴿the Day they come forth﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:43]. These two are with a fatha on the ta' and the ya', and a dammah on the ra'; people did not differ over them. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited in al-A'raf: "wa-minha takhrujun" with a fatha on the ta' and a dammah on the ra'. Ibn 'Amir put a fatha on the ta' in al-A'raf and a dammah in the rest.

His saying, "Children of Adam…" and so on, is an address to all nations at the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him. The occasion and the intended group were the Quraysh, and those among the Arabs who used to go naked while circling the House. Al-Naqqash mentioned Thaqif, Khuza'a, Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'a, Banu Mudlij, and the two sons of 'Abd Manaf, 'Amir and al-Harith, for this was their custom, men and women alike; this is the utmost of shame and disobedience. Mujahid said: "It was concerning them that these four verses were revealed."

His saying, "We have sent down" (anzalna), may mean gradual descent: that is, when We sent down the rain, from which came all that is worn, and He said of clothing "We have sent down", and this is like the saying of the poet describing rain:

"It came forward from its clouds, humps of camels in its rain."

That is, with wealth. It may also mean "We created", and the expression came with "sent down", like His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which is might﴾ [al-Hadid 57:25], and His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar 39:6]. Also, God's creation and His actions are from a high rank and station. "Libas" (clothing) is general for everything worn. "Yuwari" means covers. In the reading of Ubayy: "sau'atikum wa-zinatan wa-libsu al-taqwa." In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-libasu al-taqwa khayrun dhalikum," and it is reported from him "dhalika," and the first "dhalika" is dropped. Sakan the grammarian recited "wa-lbusu al-taqwa" with a waw, with the sin in the nominative. The majority of people recited "wa-rishan." Al-Hasan, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, 'Asim as transmitted from him by Abu 'Amr as well, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and Qatada recited "wa-riyashan." Abu al-Fath said: This is the recitation of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Abu Hatim said: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, transmitted it from him. Both words express abundance of provision, comfort of life, the availability of clothing, and enjoyment. Some explained it as furnishings. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, explained it as wealth, and al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said the same. Ibn Zayd said: "al-Rish" is beauty. It was also said that "al-riyash" is the plural of "rish", like "bir" and "biyar", "dhib" and "dhiyab", "lisb" and "lisab", "shi'b" and "shi'ab." It was also said that "al-riyash" is a verbal noun from "arashahu Allah yarishuhu," when God bestows favour upon him, and "al-rish" is also a verbal noun from that. In a hadith: "A man whom God has enriched with wealth."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It seems that all of this is from the meaning of the feathers of a bird or the feathers of an arrow, since it is its clothing, its covering, and its aid in flight. "Rasha Allah" is derived from that. Do you not see that it is paired with "bara" (to shape)? From this is the poet's saying:

"Feather me with goodness, since you have long shaped me, and the best of patrons is the one who feathers and does not shape."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i recited "wa-libasa" with a fatha, coordinated with what preceded. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamza recited "wa-libasu" with a dammah. It was said that it is the predicate of a suppressed subject, its estimate being "wa-huwa libasu" (and it is the clothing). It was also said that it is the subject, and "dhalika" is another subject, and "khayrun" is the predicate of "dhalika," and the clause is the predicate of the first. It was also said that it is the subject and "khayrun" is its predicate, and "dhalika" is an apposition, an explicative apposition, or an attribute. This is the most excellent of the opinions, mentioned by Abu 'Ali in al-Hujja.

His saying, "That is among the signs of God", refers to all that was sent down: the clothing and the feathers. al-Naqqash related that the reference is to "wa-libasu al-taqwa", that is, it is a sign in the servant, an indication and token from God that He is pleased with him and has mercy on him. "La'allahum" (so that they may) expresses hope, according to their capacity and their level of knowledge. Ibn Jurayj said: "The clothing of God-consciousness" is faith. Ma'bad al-Juhani said it is modesty. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said it is righteous deeds, and also said it is good bearing in the face. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, said this from the pulpit. 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said it is fear of God the Exalted. Ibn Zayd said it is covering the nakedness and good bearing in this world. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "The clothing of God-consciousness" is chastity. Zayd ibn 'Ali said: "The clothing of God-consciousness" is weapons and the instruments of jihad.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: All of these are examples, and they are all from the clothing of God-consciousness.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The attribute that Abu 'Ali related in his saying "dhalika" can be conceived, because demonstrative nouns are described in the sense of pointing, as you say: "Zayd came to me, this one," as if you said: "Zayd, the one pointed to, came to me." On this basis, nouns are described by demonstratives. As for his saying about it, "explicative apposition" and "substitution", these two are identical in wording; the difference between them lies only in meaning and purpose. For in substitution you intend as if you had removed the first and applied the governing word to the second, with the intention of repeating the governing word. In explicative apposition, you intend as if you had kept the first and then repeated it exactly when mentioning the second. The difference between substitution and explicative apposition becomes clear in the matter of the vocative: when you say, "O 'Abd Allah, Zayd," then the substitution in this case is on this basis, with "Zayd" in the nominative, because you suppose the removal of "'Abd Allah" and the attachment of "O" to "Zayd." If you used explicative apposition, you would say, "O 'Abd Allah, Zayda," because you intended to clarify it, and did not suppose the removal of the first. This verse is recited:

"Indeed I, and lines written in writing, are one who says: O Nasr, Nasran, Nasra."

"Nasr" the first is in explicative apposition, and the second is in substitution.

Abu al-Fath said: This is the recitation of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Abu Hatim said: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, transmitted it from him. Both words express abundance of provision, comfort of life, the availability of clothing, and enjoyment. Some explained it as furnishings. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, explained it as wealth, and al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said the same. Ibn Zayd said: "al-Rish" is beauty. It was also said that "al-riyash" is the plural of "rish", like "bir" and "biyar", "dhib" and "dhiyab", "lisb" and "lisab", "shi'b" and "shi'ab." It was also said that "al-riyash" is a verbal noun from "arashahu Allah yarishuhu," when God bestows favour upon him, and "al-rish" is also a verbal noun from that. In a hadith: "A man whom God has enriched with wealth."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It seems that all of this is from the meaning of the feathers of a bird or the feathers of an arrow, since it is its clothing, its covering, and its aid in flight. "Rasha Allah" is derived from that. Do you not see that it is paired with "bara" (to shape)? From this is the poet's saying:

"Feather me with goodness, since you have long shaped me, and the best of patrons is the one who feathers and does not shape."

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i recited "wa-libasa" with a fatha, coordinated with what preceded. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamza recited "wa-libasu" with a dammah. It was said that it is the predicate of a suppressed subject, its estimate being "wa-huwa libasu" (and it is the clothing). It was also said that it is the subject, and "dhalika" is another subject, and "khayrun" is the predicate of "dhalika," and the clause is the predicate of the first. It was also said that it is the subject and "khayrun" is its predicate, and "dhalika" is an apposition, an explicative apposition, or an attribute. This is the most excellent of the opinions, mentioned by Abu 'Ali in al-Hujja.

His saying, "That is among the signs of God", refers to all that was sent down: the clothing and the feathers. al-Naqqash related that the reference is to "wa-libasu al-taqwa", that is, it is a sign in the servant, an indication and token from God that He is pleased with him and has mercy on him. "La'allahum" (so that they may) expresses hope, according to their capacity and their level of knowledge. Ibn Jurayj said: "The clothing of God-consciousness" is faith. Ma'bad al-Juhani said it is modesty. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said it is righteous deeds, and also said it is good bearing in the face. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, said this from the pulpit. 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said it is fear of God the Exalted. Ibn Zayd said it is covering the nakedness and good bearing in this world. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "The clothing of God-consciousness" is chastity. Zayd ibn 'Ali said: "The clothing of God-consciousness" is weapons and the instruments of jihad.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: All of these are examples, and they are all from the clothing of God-consciousness.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The attribute that Abu 'Ali related in his saying "dhalika" can be conceived, because demonstrative nouns are described in the sense of pointing, as you say: "Zayd came to me, this one," as if you said: "Zayd, the one pointed to, came to me." **The Exalted's saying:**

But the clothing of God-consciousness (taqwa), that is best. That is among the signs of God, so that they may take heed.﴾

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This view is weak, because they did not exist at that time. If it is said that He addressed them and commanded them on the condition of their existence, this is remote in this case, because a command conditional on existence is valid only when it applies to the one commanded after he exists, and its meaning is realised in him, as with prayer, fasting and the like. But here, the meaning of descent (hubut) cannot be conceived for the children of Adam after their existence, and no part of the command to descend applies to them. As for His saying in another verse, "Go down" (ihbita), in dual form, it is addressed to Adam, peace be upon him, and to Iblis, by the evidence of His stating the enmity between them.

"Enemy" ('aduww) is singular in form but has the meaning of plural. You say: "a people 'aduww; and a people sadiq (friend)." From this is the poet's saying:

"By my life, if you were, in distance and in wealth, to me as I am to you, you would indeed be friends."

The enmity of serpents is well known. Qatada narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have not made peace with them since we went to war against them." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Whoever abandons them is not of us." 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, said: "Whoever leaves a serpent out of fear of its vengeance, upon him is the curse of God, the angels and all people."

"For a time" (ila hin) means, in general, the establishing of the Hour, and for each individual, the reaching of the appointed term and death. "Hin" in the speech of the Arabs means an unspecified time.

It is related that when Adam, peace be upon him, was sent down to the hardship of the world, he was taught the craft of iron, then he was taught tillage. It is related that it was said to Eve: "O Eve, just as the tree bled, so you bleed every month, and you bear only with pain and give birth only with pain." She then wailed, and it was said to her: "Wailing be upon you and upon your offspring."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This story contains much of the reports, which I have abridged, since the wording does not require them.

Mujahid said: "It was concerning them that these four verses were revealed."

His saying, "We have sent down" (anzalna), may mean gradual descent: that is, when We sent down the rain, from which came all that is worn, and He said of clothing "We have sent down", and this is like the saying of the poet describing rain:

That is, with wealth. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 27–28:

And His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿O Children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden, stripping off from them their clothing to show them their private parts. Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them. Indeed, We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe.﴾ ﴿And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers upon it, and Allah has commanded us with it." Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality. Do you say about Allah that which you do not know?"﴾

This address is to the whole world, but its intended audience at that time were those Arabs who used to circumambulate the House naked. It was said: this was the custom of the Quraysh. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: this was the custom of a tribe from Yemen. It was also said: the Arabs used to circumambulate naked, except the Hums, who are the Quraysh and those who allied with them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the correct view, because when the Quraysh, after the Year of the Elephant, instituted practices by which they magnified their sanctity, this was among them. So an Arab would either have one of the Hums lend him a garment, and he would circumambulate in it, or he would circumambulate in his own garments and then discard them. (p-545) The matter continued until it became for the Arabs an act of devotion. The Arabs would say: "We circumambulate naked, just as we came out from our mothers' bellies, and we do not circumambulate in garments in which we have soiled ourselves with sins." Whoever circumambulated in his own garments, their practice, as we have mentioned, was to throw those garments away and not benefit from them. Those garments were called "al-Laqa" (the discarded). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Enough grief for me is my returning to it, as if it were a discarded thing (laqa) among the circumambulators, a sacred thing (harim)."

A woman would circumambulate naked, to the point that one of them would say:

"Today some of it appears, or all of it, but what appears of it, I do not make lawful."

Allah, Exalted and Majestic, forbade all of that, and in the year nine it was proclaimed in Mecca: "No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no naked person shall circumambulate the House."

And "al-fitnah" (temptation) in this verse means enticement and overpowering of the self. The apparent sense of His saying, ﴿"Let not... tempt you"﴾, is a prohibition directed at Satan, but the meaning is a prohibition of them from themselves, from listening to him and obeying his command, just as they said, "I shall not see you here," where the apparent wording is a prohibition of the speaker himself, but its meaning is a prohibition of the other from remaining where he would be seen. He attributed the removal in this verse to Iblis, and that is a figurative usage, because he was striving toward it and causing it. It is said "ab" (father), and for the mother "abah"; and on this basis it is said "abawan" (two parents). And "yanzi'u" (stripping) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "akhraja" (removed).

The disagreement about the clothing has already been mentioned: from the one who said "the fingernails," and the one who said "the light," and the one who said "the garments of Paradise." Mujahid said: it is a metaphor, and what was meant is the garment of piety that was sent down.

(p-546) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is weak.

And His saying, ﴿"Indeed, he sees you"﴾, to the end of the verse, is an addition to the warning, and an informing that Allah, Exalted and Majestic, has empowered Satan over the children of Adam to this extent, and in accordance with that, caution must be exercised through obedience to Allah, Exalted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Satan exists; the Shariah has established him, and he is a body. "And his tribe" means: his kind, his category, and his offspring. "Haythu" is built on the dhamm (damma); some of the Arabs build it on the fath (fatha), because it indicates a specific place. Al-Zajjaj said: what follows it is its complement, and it is not in an annexed relation to it. Abu 'Ali said: this is not correct; "haythu" is not a relative word, since there is no returning pronoun as in relative constructions, and it is annexed to what follows it.

Then Allah, Exalted and Majestic, informed that He made the devils allies, that is: companions and those who infiltrate the disbelievers who have no faith. Al-Zahrawi mentioned that "ja'ala" here means "described."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a Mu'tazili tendency.

And His saying, ﴿"And when they commit"﴾, and what follows it, is included in the description of "those who do not believe," so that the rebuke falls upon a description of a people made an example of those being rebuked, since their act resembled the act of those made an example of. It is also valid that this verse be detached from the one before it, as a fresh report about the disbelieving Arabs.

As for "al-fahisha" (immorality) in this verse, although the wording is general, it refers to the uncovering of the private parts during circumambulation. It is narrated from al-Zuhri that he said: these verses were revealed about this, and Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said the same. It was the saying of some disbelievers: Allah commanded these practices that we have, and legislated them. So Allah, Exalted, answered them with His saying, ﴿"Say: Indeed, Allah does not command immorality."﴾ Then He rebuked them for their lying, and made them stand before their saying of what they have no knowledge of, and no understanding of, but rather it is a claim and a fabrication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 29–30:

(p-547)His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice. And set your faces upright at every place of prayer, and call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him. As He originated you, you will return.﴾ ﴿A group He has guided, and a group upon whom misguidance has been justly decreed. Indeed, they have taken the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think that they are guided.﴾

His saying, ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice,﴾ includes the meaning "Be just" (aqsitu). For this reason, His saying "and set your faces upright" is joined to it, by taking it according to the meaning. Al-qist means justice and truth. The interpreters (al-mu'awwilun) differed concerning His saying, ﴿and set your faces upright at every place of prayer.﴾ It was said: He intended "toward the Ka'bah." This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. The purpose according to this is the legislation of the qibla and the command to adhere to it. It was also said: He intended the command to bring the intention to Allah, Exalted is He, in every prayer, and to direct the aim toward Him, Exalted is He, as you say: "I have turned my face to Allah, Exalted is He." This was said by al-Rabi'.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The "face" is not to be taken as the bodily organ; rather it is the aim and the intention.

It was also said: the intended meaning of this expression is the permission to pray in every place on the earth, that is: "Wherever you are, it is a mosque for you, and at the time of prayer it is obligatory upon you to set your faces toward Allah, Exalted and Majestic, in it." Some people said its cause was that a people used to pray only in their own mosques, in their own qibla; so when the prayer time came in other mosques, they did not pray in them. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said: the intended meaning of His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He, ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ is the announcement of resurrection. That is: "As He brought you into existence and originated you, so He will restore you after death." According to this interpretation, the pause is on "you will return," and "a group" is in the accusative governed by "He guided." The second is in the accusative governed by a verb whose implied form is: "and He punished a group" or "He misguided a group upon whom misguidance has been decreed..."

(p-548)Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said, and Abu al-'Aliyah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Mujahid also, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah; and its meaning is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): the intended meaning of His saying, ﴿As He originated you, you will return,﴾ is the announcement that the people of wretchedness and disbelief in this world, upon whom it was written, are the people of wretchedness in the Hereafter; and the people of happiness and faith in this world, for whom it was written, are their people in the Hereafter. Nothing changes of the matters that He has decreed, arranged, and executed. According to this interpretation, the pause at His saying "you will return" is not good; and "a group" according to this interpretation is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the second is conjoined to the first. Al-Tabari said: This verse is evidence of the error of the view of one who claims that Allah, Exalted is He, does not punish anyone for a sin he committed or an error he believed in, unless he commits it knowingly, having knowledge of the place of correctness.

Al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl, Sahl ibn Shu'ayb, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read: "anna-humu ittakhadhu" with a fathah on the alif.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 31–32:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿O Children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prostration, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like the excessive.﴾ ﴿Say: "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" Say: "They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely for them on the Day of Resurrection." Thus do We detail the verses for a people who know.﴾

This is a general address to the whole of mankind; and these matters were commanded because of the disobedience, regarding them, of the Arab polytheists present at that time.

As for "al-zinah" (adornment) here: it means the concealing garments. This is said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. Tawus said: "The loincloth is part of the adornment."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It includes what is of perfume for Friday; the siwak (tooth-stick); changing of garments; and everything whose good repute has been found in the Shari'ah, provided its user does not intend by it self-admiration.

As for ﴿at every place of prostration﴾: at every place of prostration. It is thus an indication to the prayers and to covering the private parts therein. This is the most important matter. Along with the prayer, all places of goodness enter in; and along with covering the private parts, what we have mentioned of perfume for Friday and other things enter in. Makki mentioned a hadith that the meaning of ﴿take your adornment﴾ is: pray in your sandals; but I do not think it is sound.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and eat and drink﴾: it is a prohibition of what they had committed themselves to, of forbidding meat and fat during the days of the season. This is said by al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Along with that there also enter the bahirah, the sa'ibah, and the like; and Qatadah explicitly stated this, and said: the bahirah and what resembles it are the intended meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the good things of provision﴾.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿but do not be excessive﴾: its meaning is "do not be negligent." The people of interpretation said: it means "do not be excessive by forbidding for yourselves what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has not forbidden." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: there is no excess in what is lawful; excess is only in committing sins.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He means: "in what is lawful, moderation." The wording requires the prohibition of excess absolutely. So whoever engages in an act of prohibition and thereby interprets his involvement in it, becomes one of the excessive, and the prohibition is directed at him. And whoever engages in a permissible act: if he proceeds in it with moderation and the middle course of matters, it is good; but if he goes to excess until harm enters, he likewise becomes one of the excessive, and the prohibition is directed at him. Like this: "that a person is negligent in buying garments and the like, and exhausts most of his wealth in that, or gives away all his wealth and then struggles with his dependants in poverty after that"; (p-550) and the like. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not love any of this; and the Shari'ah has forbidden it. Therefore the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, restricted the testator to a third, and said: "And a third is much." Some scholars said: If people reduced it to a quarter, that would be in line with the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: "And a third is much." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, also said regarding this verse: Allah, Exalted is He, permitted eating and drinking as long as it was not excess or arrogance.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, to ask them about the one who forbade what Allah, Exalted is He, had made lawful; by way of rebuke and affirmation. This question does not require an answer; what is intended by it is to make them stand upon the evil of the act. Some people mentioned that the question and the answer came in this verse from one direction, and imagined that His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "They are for those who believed"﴾ is the answer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a corrupt view; that is not an answer to the question, and this type of question does not require an answer. "The adornment of Allah" is everything that desire calls for, and the seeking of exaltation on earth, such as wealth and children; and it is the adornment over which the Shari'ah gave preference.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the good things of provision﴾: the majority said: it means the permitted things; and al-Shafi'i and others said: it means the pleasurable things.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: However, that - necessarily - is conditioned to be from the lawful; and what led al-Shafi'i to this was his prohibition of the loathsome things, such as the gecko and others; for he says: they are among the impure things, forbidden.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely for them on the Day of Resurrection."﴾

Nafi' alone read "khalisatun" with a nominative ending; and the rest read "khalisatan" with an accusative ending; and the verse is interpreted in two senses.

The first: that it informs that these good things which exist in this world are, on the Day of Resurrection, purely for the believers in this world; and their purity is that they will not be punished for them, nor tormented. So His saying, ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is connected to "believed"; and to this points the interpretation of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, for he said: "Say: they are for those who believed in the life of this world (p-551): they benefit from them in this world, and their sin does not follow them." As for ﴿"khalisatan"﴾ with a nominative ending: it is the predicate of "they"; and "for those who" is an explanation of the purity; and it is valid that "khalisatun" be a second predicate; and "on the Day of Resurrection" means by it the time of reckoning. Qatadah and al-Kisa'i read: "Say: they are for whoever believed in the life of this world."

The second sense: that it informs that these good things which exist are, in the life of this world, for those who believed, even though they are also for others along with them; and they are, on the Day of Resurrection, purely for them; that is, no one shares with them in their use in the Hereafter. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ibn Juraij and Ibn Zayd. So His saying, ﴿in the life of this world﴾ - on this interpretation - is connected to the omitted element presumed in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿for those who believed﴾; as if He said: "They are purely - or established - in the life of this world for those who believed." And "khalisatun" with a nominative ending is a predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject; its estimate: "and they are purely on the Day of Resurrection." And "on the Day of Resurrection" is intended to mean the continuance of existence in Paradise. As for whoever read "khalisatan" with an accusative ending: it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for those who believed﴾; and the estimate: "they are established - or settled - for those who believed, in a state of purity for them." The governing element in it is the sense of the verb contained in the preposition "li-" in His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿for those who﴾ [al-An'am: 32]. Abu 'Ali said in "al-Hujjah": It is valid that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿in the life of this world﴾ be connected to His saying "harrama" (forbade); and it is not valid that it be connected to "zinata" (adornment), because it is a verbal noun that has already been qualified; and it is valid that it be connected to His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He, ﴿akhraja li-'ibadihi﴾ (He brought forth for His servants); and that is permissible even though the relative clause is separated from its relative by His saying, ﴿Say: "They are for those who believed"﴾; because that is a speech that strengthens the narrative and is not wholly foreign to it; as occurs in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation covers them﴾ [Yunus: 27]; for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and humiliation covers them﴾ [Yunus: 27] is coordinated with "earned," and is within the relative clause. Connecting it to "akhraja" is the view of al-Akhfash. It is valid that it be connected to His saying: ﴿"and the good things"﴾; it is valid that it be connected to His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He, ﴿of provision﴾; and it is valid that it be connected to His saying: ﴿"believed".﴾

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This last is the most correct of the views according to this first interpretation, in the arrangement we have set out here; but according to the other interpretation (p-552) these connections which Abu 'Ali mentioned weaken the meaning of the verse; and it appears only that it be connected to the omitted element presumed in His saying: ﴿for those who believed﴾.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, "thus"; the construction of the speech is: that is, "just as We have detailed these previously mentioned matters, so likewise; and in that form, We detail the verses" - that is, "We make clear the signs, the indications, and the guidances" - "for a people who have knowledge by which they benefit." And "nufassil" (We detail) means: We divide and make clear; because the clarification of matters that are ambiguous is precisely in dividing them into distinct parts.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-A'raf, verses 33–36**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, whether apparent or hidden, sin, unjustified aggression, associating partners with Allah for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know.﴾ ﴿For every community there is a term. When their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ ﴿Children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves, relating My signs to you, then whoever fears Allah and makes amends, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿But those who deny Our signs and are arrogant towards them, they are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein.﴾

When the denial of what the disbelievers had forbidden by their own opinions was mentioned, He followed it with the mention of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden, and its determination.

"Al-fawahish" (indecencies) are what is grotesque and abhorrent. Its root lies in ugliness of appearance, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*A neck like the neck of a gazelle, not ugly when it is adorned,*
*nor bare of ornament.*

His saying, ﴿For every community there is a term﴾, and the rest of the verse, carries threat and warning. The meaning is: "For every community (that is, group and party, a word used for many people) there is a determined term for the coming of punishment when they disbelieve and oppose the command of their Lord. So you too, O community, are like that." This was said by al-Tabari and others.

al-Hasan recited: "When their *ajal* (terms) come" in the plural, and this is also the reading of Ibn Sirin. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said: This is the more apparent, because every person has a term. As for the singular, it is because it is a genus-noun, and its being attached to a plural makes the singular acceptable. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

*...................... in your throats is a bone, and we have been choked.*

His saying, ﴿an hour﴾: a word used to specify a small portion of time, and what is meant is all its parts. That is, they cannot delay by an hour, nor by less than that, nor by more. This is like His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisa': 40]. These are expressions in which a part stands in place of the whole.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It seems that there is an apparent contradiction between this verse and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He defers you to a specified term﴾ [Nuh: 4], since that one indicates a promise of postponement if they believe, and a warning of hastening if they disbelieve.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The truth is the position of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah): that each person has one term, from which he neither delays nor advances. Among the people of Noah, there were those whom Allah knew would disbelieve, and so they were hastened (to punishment), and that was their binding term. And among them were those who would believe, and so they were postponed until their binding term. The distinction between the two groups was hidden from Noah, so he called all of them to the path of salvation, while knowing that each group is hastened or delayed according to its term. It is as if he were saying: "If you believe, we will know that you are among those for whom Allah has decreed belief and a deferred term; and if you disbelieve, we will know that you are among those decreed a hastened term and disbelief."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On this same principle is the call of Muhammad (peace be upon him) to the path of Paradise, while he knew that among them there are those who will disbelieve and enter the Fire. Likewise is the case of a captive, who is told: "Either you believe and are released, or you will be killed."

What is derived from it for those present with Muhammad (peace be upon him) is that this is the ruling of Allah Exalted in the world since He created it. This is in consideration of the time of the revelation of the verse.

al-Tabari traced to Abu Sayyar al-Sulami who said: Allah, Exalted is He, placed Adam (peace be upon him) and his progeny in His palm, and said: ﴿Children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves﴾, to the end of the verse. He said: Then He looked at the messengers and said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously; indeed I am Knower of what you do﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51], ﴿And indeed this, your community, is one community, and I am your Lord, so fear Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 52]. Then He dispersed them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no doubt that this address was in eternity (*al-azal*). It was also said: what is meant by "the messengers" is Muhammad (peace be upon him).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In view of there being no prophet after him. So it is as if those addressed were the intended meaning of "Children of Adam," and no others, since others were not reached by the address. This was reported by al-Naqqash. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then whoever fears Allah and makes amends﴾: "man" may be a conditional, and its answer is ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾. This sentence is in the answer to the first condition, which is ﴿if messengers come to you﴾. And "man" in ﴿whoever fears Allah﴾ may be a relative pronoun. It is as though He intended by the speech a division of people: the first category is ﴿whoever fears Allah﴾, and the second category is ﴿but those who deny Our signs﴾. This division in its entirety is the answer to the condition in His saying ﴿if they come to you﴾. So it is as if He said: "If messengers come to you, then those who are God-fearing, there is no fear for them, and those who deny are the companions of the Fire." That is, this is the fruit and benefit of the message.

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ [al-A'raf: 37]: that is, there is no benefit for the fabricator, nor any worldly aim. So the verse is a clearing of the Prophet (ﷺ) from fabrication, and a rebuke of the fabricators among the disbelievers. Ibn Muhaysin recited: "*fala khawfu*" without tanwin (nunation). It was also said: the intended meaning is "*fala al-khawf*" (there is no fear), then the alif and lam were dropped while the fa' was kept as it is, to indicate the omitted element. The negation of fear and grief encompasses all kinds of distress and aversion of the soul. Fear is likely to be for future matters, and grief for past ones.

﴿But those who deny Our signs and are arrogant towards them﴾: [these two states encompass] everyone who turns away from the message of the Messenger (ﷺ): either he denies according to his belief, or he is arrogant and therefore denies, even if he is not firmly set in belief on denial.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is akin to disbelief out of obstinacy.

When their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ ﴿Children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among yourselves, relating My signs to you, then whoever fears Allah and makes amends, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿But those who deny Our signs and are arrogant towards them, they are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein.﴾

When the denial of what the disbelievers had forbidden by their own opinions was mentioned, He followed it with the mention of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden, and its determination.

"Al-fawahish" (indecencies) are what is grotesque and abhorrent. Its root lies in ugliness of appearance, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*A neck like the neck of a gazelle, not ugly when it is adorned,*
*nor bare of ornament.*

Then it came to be used for what is evil in conduct, for expressions of impropriety and obscenity. From it is the hadith, in the description of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He was not *fahish*" (not coarse in speech). From it also is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Salama ibn Salama ibn Waqsh: "You have been *afhasht* (harsh) towards the man," in the narration of the expeditions. From it also is the saying of the poet al-Hazin, concerning Kuthayyir 'Azza:

*Short of shirt, indecent in his house* ...............

It is likewise used for what is repugnant and abhorrent to souls. Beauty and ugliness in matters are received only from the Law (shari'ah), and so is the indecent. Therefore His saying here, *al-fawahish* (the indecencies), is only a reference to what the Law has explicitly prohibited in other places. Thus everything the Law has forbidden is indecent, even if reason does not deny it, such as wearing silk and gold for men, and the like.

His saying, ﴿whether apparent or hidden﴾, encompasses the whole category, since it is a division from which nothing escapes, and it is a general term covering all indecencies. Mujahid, however, went to restrict it, saying: "What is apparent" is the naked circumambulation (of the Ka'bah), and "the hidden" is fornication. Others have said other things, which are given as examples. The word *ma* (what) is a *badal* (substitution, apposition) of *al-fawahish*, a substitution of part from whole (*badal ba'd min kull*). The two parts together form a substitution of a thing by a thing that is itself.

Also, "*al-ithm*" (sin): its wording is general for all actions and statements for which the perpetrator incurs sin. This is the view of the majority. Some people said that it is wine (*khamr*), and they argued for this with the saying of the poet:

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is rejected, because this surah is Meccan, and the Law did not address the prohibition of wine except in Medina, after Uhud, since a group of the Companions took it on the day of Uhud and died as martyrs while it was in their stomachs. Moreover, the line of verse is said to be fabricated, and if it is authentic, then it contains an omitted *mudaf* (an elided construct). And it seems that the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, according to this view, is that the prohibition of wine comes from His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both is great sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. And in this verse it has already been prohibited. Thus it follows from this that wine is sin, and sin is forbidden, so wine is forbidden.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: But this does not hold, because His saying ﴿in both is sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219] may mean that wine incurs sins from the corruption of the mind, slander, killing a soul and other such wrongs. So it is as if He said: "In wine are these sins," meaning they are caused by it, accompanying it. And these things are forbidden without doubt. On this reading, wine is excluded from prohibition, and the analogy which the proponent of what we mentioned relied upon does not follow. This is reinforced by the fact that we find the Companions drinking wine after the revelation of His saying ﴿In both is sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219]. In some hadiths: "Some people left it because of the sin in it, and some drank it for its benefits." Wine was prohibited only by the apparent meanings of the Qur'an, the texts of the hadiths, and the *ijma'* (scholarly consensus).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 37:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Those will receive their share of the Book until, when Our messengers come to them to take their souls, they say: "Where is that which you used to invoke besides Allah?" They will say: "They have strayed from us," and they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾

(p-558) This is a verse of warning and interrogation, in the form of affirmation; meaning: there is no one more wrong than him. "Iftara" means: he invented (ikhtalaqa). And this, although it is connected to what precedes it, meaning: "How do they make the messengers fabricators? There is no one more wrong than one who fabricates, and the messengers have no portion except that the one who is guided is shown mercy and the one who disbelieves is punished," it also points, in meaning, to every fabricator, to those whose mention came earlier, those who said: ﴿Allah commanded us to do it﴾ [al-A'raf: 28].

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿or denies His signs﴾, is an indication of all the disbelievers. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿their share of the Book﴾: al-Hasan, al-Suddi and Abu Salih said: its meaning is: what is decreed in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). So "the Book" is an expression for the Preserved Tablet, and it is established in the Sharia that their share in it is punishment and wrath. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿of the Book﴾, means: of the wretchedness and happiness that was written for him.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is supported by the well-known hadith which contains that the angel comes when the embryo is formed in the womb, and writes his provision, his term, and whether he is wretched or happy. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, also said, as did Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Dahhak: "the Book" is intended to mean that which the angels write of the deeds of creation, good and evil, so these people receive their share of that, which is disbelief and sins. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Mujahid and al-Dahhak: "of the Book" is intended to mean: "of the Qur'an," and their share in it is that their faces will be blackened on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and Ibn Zayd said: what is meant by the share is what has preceded for them in the Mother of the Book of provision, life span, good and evil, in this world. Al-Tabari preferred this view and argued for it with His saying, Exalted is He, after that: ﴿until, when Our messengers come to them﴾, meaning: "at the end of that," so the meaning of the verse according to this interpretation is: "those enjoy and dispose of [their share] of the world, to the extent of what was written for them, until, when Our messengers come to them for their death..." This is the interpretation of a group regarding the coming of the messengers for taking souls, and upon this is based al-Tabari's preference mentioned earlier.

A group said: "Our messengers" means by them: the angels of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and "they take them in full" means: "they count them in full, driving them to Hell."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is consistent with the earlier interpretations of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿their share of the Book﴾, because the share, according to those interpretations, reaches them only in the Hereafter, and the coming of the messengers of death has already been decreed. His saying, Exalted is He, quoting the messengers: ﴿Where is that which you used to invoke﴾, is an interrogation of affirmation, rebuke, and making them stand before disgrace; and it is an indication of the idols, the images, and everything worshipped besides Allah, Exalted is He. "Tad'un" means: "you worship and hope in." Their saying: "They have strayed" means: they perished, were lost, and went missing. Then He began the report about the polytheists with His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿and they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers﴾. This verse and what resembles it apparently contradict His saying, Exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23]. The reconciling of the two is either that it is among different groups, or at different times, they say in one state, and in another state.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 38–39:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿He will say: "Enter into the Fire among the nations of jinn and men who passed away before you. Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them: 'Our Lord, these led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire.' He will say: 'For each there is double, but you do not know.'"﴾ ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them: "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾

This is a report of what Allah, Exalted is He, will say to them on the Day of Resurrection, through the mediation of the angels of punishment. He expressed "will say" with "said" (qāla) to affirm the certainty of its occurrence and the truthfulness of the account, and this is common.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"among nations"﴾ is connected to ﴿"enter"﴾. It is also possible that it is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: "existing" or "established" among nations, so that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "enter." It has been said that "fī" (in) here means "maʿa" (with). It has also been said that it retains its original meaning, and this is the most correct view. His saying ﴿"who have passed away"﴾ is a qualifier of "nations." His saying ﴿"in the Fire"﴾ may be connected to "enter," and it may be connected to "nations," meaning: among established or settled nations. It may also be connected to the verb within "passed away." The meaning of ﴿"have passed away"﴾ on this connection is: "have gone before and time has passed over them, and they have become known through the long ages." It may also be used even if little time has elapsed, since its original usage concerns people who have died, meaning: "they have gone to the emptiness of the earth." On the first two connections for His saying ﴿"in the Fire"﴾, "passed away" is a report about the state of the worldly life, meaning: "Enter the Fire, among the earlier nations before you in the world, the disbelieving ones." He mentioned the jinn first because they are deeper in disbelief, and Iblis is the origin of misguidance and seduction. This verse is explicit that the disbelieving jinn are in the Fire. What reason requires is that their believers are in the Garden, because they are rational, responsible, sent to, and they believed and affirmed. Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, has a chapter heading: "Chapter on mentioning the jinn and their reward and punishment." ʿAbd al-Jalil mentioned that believing jinn will become dust, like animals, and he cited a hadith in this regard that is unknown (majhūl); I do not think it is sound. And Allah knows best.

The brotherhood in this verse is the brotherhood of religious community and law. Al-Suddi said: "Its last ones curse its first ones." ﴿"Ideraku"﴾ means: they caught up with one another. Its form is "tafā‘alū," its origin is "tadārakū," which was assimilated, so the hamzat al-wasl was brought in. Abu ʿAmr read "idda-rakū" with a hamzat al-wasl cut off. Abu al-Fath said: this is problematic, and it is not permissible to cut it off spontaneously; that occurs only anomalously in poetic necessity. Mujahid read with a cut hamzah and a sukun on the dal, "idrakū," with a fatha on the ra and the alif after the dal omitted, meaning: some of them caught up with others. Ḥumayd read "udrikū," with a damma on the hamzah and a kasra on the ra, meaning: "they were made to enter into its reaching." Makki said, regarding Mujahid's reading, that it is "iddarakū," with a shaddah on the fatḥah dal and a fatḥah on the ra, and said its origin is "idtarakū," and its form is "iftaʿalū." Ibn Masʿud and al-Aʿmash read "tadārakū," and it is narrated from Abu ʿAmr. The majority read "ḥattā idha ad-dārakū." It was also read with the alif of "idhā" omitted, because of the meeting of two sukūns.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"The last of them said of the first of them"﴾: its meaning is: "The last nation, which found established misguidances and false practices in use from the first that instituted them, and fabricated against Allah, Exalted is He, and took the path of misguidance from the beginning, said: Our Lord, these took the paths of misguidance and caused our misguidance. So give them a multiplied punishment, meaning a second one, additional to our punishment, since they are disbelievers and causes of our disbelief." One says "ḍāʿaftu kadhā" when one makes it like the first. The lam in His saying ﴿"of them"﴾ appears to be a lam of cause, since the saying is in fact addressed to the Lord, Exalted is He. His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

It is also possible that it is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: "existing" or "established" among nations, so that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "enter." It has been said that "fī" (in) here means "maʿa" (with). It has also been said that it retains its original meaning, and this is the most correct view. His saying ﴿"who have passed away"﴾ is a qualifier of "nations." His saying ﴿"in the Fire"﴾ may be connected to "enter," and it may be connected to "nations," meaning: among established or settled nations. It may also be connected to the verb within "passed away." The meaning of ﴿"have passed away"﴾ on this connection is: "have gone before and time has passed over them, and they have become known through the long ages." It may also be used even if little time has elapsed, since its original usage concerns people who have died, meaning: "they have gone to the emptiness of the earth." What reason requires is that their believers are in the Garden, because they are rational, responsible, sent to, and they believed and affirmed. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 40–42:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them — the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. Thus do We recompense the criminals.﴾ ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hellfire, and above them coverings. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿But those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾

This verse is general in regard to all disbelievers, past and present. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read: ﴿لا تُفَتَّحُ﴾ (lā tufattaḥu), with a damma on the first tā' and a shadda on the second; Abu 'Amr read: "tuftaḥu", with a damma on the tā', a sukun on the fā', and the second tā' lightened; Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "yuftaḥu", with a yā' at the beginning and the tā' lightened; Abu Haywa and Abu Ibrahim read: "yufattaḥu", with a yā', a fatha on the fā', and a shadda on the tā'. The meaning of the verse is: "No deed, no spirit, and no supplication will ascend for them." It is thus general in negating what is granted to the believers in God, Exalted is He. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others.

al-Tabari mentioned reports concerning the manner of seizing the spirit of the believer and of the disbeliever; I have abridged them, since they are not necessarily implied by the verse, and because of the weakness of their chains.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, negated for them entry into Paradise, and He made it conditional upon an impossible matter that will never occur: that the camel should enter the hole of the needle where the thread enters. The camel is as it is known, and the eye of the needle is as it is known.

The majority of Muslims read: "al-jamal" (الجَمَلُ), the singular of camels. al-Hasan said: it is the camel that stands at the watering-trough (al-mirbad). Once, when they pressed him, he said: it is al-ashtar, and in Persian that is "al-jamal." Another time he said: it is the young of the she-camel, and this was also said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an expression that indicates the embarrassment of the questioner, since the listeners were in doubt about the word because of the differing readings. al-Tabari reported from Mujahid, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he used to read: "hatta yalija al-jamalu al-asfar" (until the yellow camel passes). Abu al-Sammal read: "al-jaml" (الجَمْلُ), with a sukun on the mim. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Malik ibn al-Shikhkhir, and Abu Raja' read: "al-jummal" (الجُمَّلُ), with a damma on the jim and a shadda on the mim, and it is the rope of the ship. Salim al-Afta', Ibn Khayr, and also Ibn 'Amir read: "al-jumal" (الجُمَلُ), with the mim lightened, derived from "al-jummal," and they said: it is the ropes of ships. al-Kisa'i related that the one who transmitted the shadda on the mim from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was a non-Arab, so he doubled the mim because of his non-Arabic speech.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, because of the large number of Ibn 'Abbas's companions who transmitted the aforementioned reading. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as reported from him, read: "al-juml" (الجُمْلُ), with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the mim. Ibn 'Abbas also read: "al-jumul" (الجُمُلُ), with a damma on the jim and the mim.

And "al-samm" (اَلسَّمُّ) is the hole of the needle and other things. It is said "samm," "summ," with fatha, kasra, and damma on the sin. The majority read with a fatha on the sin; Ibn Sirin read with a damma; Abu Haywa read with both damma and kasra, and both forms were reported from him. "al-Khiyat" and "al-mikhyat" mean the needle. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fi samm al-mikhyat" (فِي سَمِّ المِخْيَطِ), with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the kha', and a fatha on the ya'. Talha read: "fi samm al-makhyat" (فِي سَمِّ المَخْيَطِ), with a fatha on the mim; and Ubayy was likewise in this form. Thus are the disbelievers and the people of crimes recompensed by Allah, Blessed and Exalted, with this certain decree and other things.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hellfire﴾: the meaning is that Hell is a bedding for them, a dwelling and a resting place which they prepare for themselves. And "ghawashin" (غَواشٍ) is the plural of "ghashiya," which is what covers a person, that is, envelops and conceals him from above. al-Dahhak said: "al-mihad" is the bedding, and "al-ghawashi" are the coverlets. According to Sibawayh, the tanwin entered "ghawashin" because it lacks the pattern of "mafa'il"; when the preventing structure was removed by deleting the yā' outright, not for the sake of meeting two unvocalized letters, but just as it was deleted in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿wal-layli idha yasr﴾ [al-Fajr: 4] and ﴿dhalika ma kunna nabghi﴾ [al-Kahf: 64], and in the verse of the poet: "...thumma la yafri" — the prohibition was removed. This is like their saying "dhuldhul" with tanwin, while they mean "al-dhaladhil," when the structure was removed. al-Zajjaj said: According to Sibawayh, the tanwin in "ghawashin" is a substitute for the deleted yā'. Abu 'Ali rejected that this is Sibawayh's position. It is permissible to pause with a yā' or without a yā', and the preferred choice is without a yā'.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿But those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ — the verse: this is a verse of promise, informing that all the believers are the companions of Paradise, and for them is eternity therein. Then, in the midst of the speech, after the attribute that He stipulated for the believers, He inserted a parenthetical statement that lightens the condition and gives hope in the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, and informs that His religion is ease.

This verse is explicit that the Shari'a does not establish, among its obligations, anything beyond what cannot be borne. The discussion of the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, and of its occurrence, has already preceded this and needs no repetition.

And "al-wus'" (اَلْوُسْعُ) means capacity: it is the measure that the extent of human ability can contain.
