The majority of Muslims read: "al-jamal" (الجَمَلُ), the singular of camels. al-Hasan said: it is the camel that stands at the watering-trough (al-mirbad). Once, when they pressed him, he said: it is al-ashtar, and in Persian that is "al-jamal." Another time he said: it is the young of the she-camel, and this was also said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an expression that indicates the embarrassment of the questioner, since the listeners were in doubt about the word because of the differing readings. al-Tabari reported from Mujahid, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he used to read: "hatta yalija al-jamalu al-asfar" (until the yellow camel passes). Abu al-Sammal read: "al-jaml" (الجَمْلُ), with a sukun on the mim. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, al-Sha'bi, Malik ibn al-Shikhkhir, and Abu Raja' read: "al-jummal" (الجُمَّلُ), with a damma on the jim and a shadda on the mim, and it is the rope of the ship. Salim al-Afta', Ibn Khayr, and also Ibn 'Amir read: "al-jumal" (الجُمَلُ), with the mim lightened, derived from "al-jummal," and they said: it is the ropes of ships. al-Kisa'i related that the one who transmitted the shadda on the mim from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was a non-Arab, so he doubled the mim because of his non-Arabic speech.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is weak, because of the large number of Ibn 'Abbas's companions who transmitted the aforementioned reading. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as reported from him, read: "al-juml" (الجُمْلُ), with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the mim. Ibn 'Abbas also read: "al-jumul" (الجُمُلُ), with a damma on the jim and the mim.

And "al-samm" (اَلسَّمُّ) is the hole of the needle and other things. It is said "samm," "summ," with fatha, kasra, and damma on the sin. The majority read with a fatha on the sin; Ibn Sirin read with a damma; Abu Haywa read with both damma and kasra, and both forms were reported from him. "al-Khiyat" and "al-mikhyat" mean the needle. Ibn Mas'ud read: "fi samm al-mikhyat" (فِي سَمِّ المِخْيَطِ), with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the kha', and a fatha on the ya'. Talha read: "fi samm al-makhyat" (فِي سَمِّ المَخْيَطِ), with a fatha on the mim; and Ubayy was likewise in this form. Thus are the disbelievers and the people of crimes recompensed by Allah, Blessed and Exalted, with this certain decree and other things.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hellfire﴾: the meaning is that Hell is a bedding for them, a dwelling and a resting place which they prepare for themselves. And "ghawashin" (غَواشٍ) is the plural of "ghashiya," which is what covers a person, that is, envelops and conceals him from above. al-Dahhak said: "al-mihad" is the bedding, and "al-ghawashi" are the coverlets. According to Sibawayh, the tanwin entered "ghawashin" because it lacks the pattern of "mafa'il"; when the preventing structure was removed by deleting the yā' outright, not for the sake of meeting two unvocalized letters, but just as it was deleted in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿wal-layli idha yasr﴾ [al-Fajr: 4] and ﴿dhalika ma kunna nabghi﴾ [al-Kahf: 64], and in the verse of the poet: "...thumma la yafri" — the prohibition was removed. This is like their saying "dhuldhul" with tanwin, while they mean "al-dhaladhil," when the structure was removed. al-Zajjaj said: According to Sibawayh, the tanwin in "ghawashin" is a substitute for the deleted yā'. Abu 'Ali rejected that this is Sibawayh's position. It is permissible to pause with a yā' or without a yā', and the preferred choice is without a yā'.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿But those who believed and did righteous deeds﴾ — the verse: this is a verse of promise, informing that all the believers are the companions of Paradise, and for them is eternity therein. Then, in the midst of the speech, after the attribute that He stipulated for the believers, He inserted a parenthetical statement that lightens the condition and gives hope in the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, and informs that His religion is ease.

This verse is explicit that the Shari'a does not establish, among its obligations, anything beyond what cannot be borne. The discussion of the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, and of its occurrence, has already preceded this and needs no repetition.

And "al-wus'" (اَلْوُسْعُ) means capacity: it is the measure that the extent of human ability can contain.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 43:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this. And we would not have been [able] to be guided had Allah not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth." And they will be called, "This is Paradise; you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do."﴾

This is information from Allah, Exalted and Majestic, that He purifies the hearts of the inhabitants of Paradise from resentment (ghill) and hatred (hiqd), because the one who holds resentment is tormented by it, and there is no torment in Paradise. It has been related in a hadith: "Resentment at the gate of Paradise is like the kneeling camels; Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has removed it from the hearts of the believers."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning of this hadith, if it is taken literally, is that Allah, Exalted and Majestic, creates a substance and places it where it is seen, like the kneeling camels, because resentment is an accident (ʿaraḍ) that does not subsist by itself. If it is said that this is a metaphor, expressing its removal from their souls, then these words are used in the manner of illustration, as you would say: "So-and-so, when he enters upon the amir, leaves his arrogance laid down at the door." This has a basis, but the first (interpretation) is more correct and agrees with the Law in many matters, such as his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Death will be brought on the Day of Resurrection as if it were a ram, and it will be slaughtered," and other such things.

Al-Hasan reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "By Allah, it was revealed concerning us, the people of Badr: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, [as] brothers upon couches facing one another﴾ [al-Hijr: 47]." It is also related from him that he said: "By Allah, it was revealed concerning us: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾." Qatada mentioned that ʿAli said: (p-566) "I hope that I, and ʿUthman, and Talha, and al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them, are among those of whom Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the correct meaning, for the verse is general concerning the people of Paradise. Al-ghill is resentment (al-hiqd) and a hidden enmity in the soul; its plural is ghilal. From it comes al-ghulul, which is taking in secret; from it comes al-inghilal in a thing (entanglement); and from it comes al-mughill bi-l-amana (one who betrays a trust). From it is the saying of ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbda:

"A slender one like the staff of al-Nahdi, around which is wrapped a dark cord of the stone of Qurran, bound with a..."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿rivers will flow beneath them﴾, is clear, because what lies flat upon the earth is beneath what stands upright and rises toward the sky. "Hadana" means "arshadana" (guided us). The indication by "hadha" (this) may be understood as referring to faith and the righteous deeds that lead to entry into Paradise; and it may be understood as referring to Paradise itself, meaning: He guided us to its paths. For each of the two interpretations there are examples in the Qur'an.

Ibn ʿAmir alone recited: "wa-ma kunna li-nahtadiya" without the waw in His saying, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿"wa-ma kunna"﴾; and so it is in the codices of the people of Syria. Abu ʿAli said: The reason for omitting the waw is that the speech is connected and linked to what precedes it.

When they saw the confirmation of what the prophets had brought from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and witnessed the fulfillment of the promises, they said: ﴿The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth﴾. They judged that this was a truth decided by One who perceives directly, whereas in the world they used to judge that it was a truth decided by One who is known through inference. And ﴿"wa-nudu"﴾, i.e., "it was said to them with a cry." This calling was from Allah, Exalted and Majestic. "An" may be understood as explanatory of the meaning of the calling, in the sense of "i.e."; and it may be understood as the lightened form of the heavy (an), with a hidden pronoun in it, its estimate being: "that it is this Paradise." A similar usage is the saying of al-Aʿsha:

"Among youths like swords of India, who know that every one who goes barefoot and sandaled is perishing."

Its estimate: "that he is perishing." From it is also the saying of another:

"I flatter him, and I know that both of us are eager for what harms his companion."

And ﴿tilkumu al-jannatu﴾ is a subject (mubtada') with a qualifier (sifa); and "uriththumuha" is the predicate (khabar). And "tilkum" is a demonstrative containing a sense of absence; either because they had been promised it in the world, so the indication refers to that, i.e., "that, this Paradise," with "this" omitted; or before entering, or after entering while they are gathered in one place of it, each being absent from his own dwelling.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿for what you used to do﴾, is not in the sense that this is obligatory upon Allah, Exalted; rather it is by the indication of His mercy, Exalted, and His covering. Deeds are a sign from Allah, Exalted, and a path to strengthening hope. Entry into Paradise is only by the sheer mercy of Allah, Exalted; and the distribution of stations within it is according to the measure of deeds. And "uriththum" indicates the divisions.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir recited: ﴿"uriththumuha"﴾, and likewise in al-Zukhruf. Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisa'i and Hamza recited: "uriththummuha," with the assimilation of the tha' into the ta', and likewise in al-Zukhruf.

(p-568)

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" They will say, "Yes." Then a caller will proclaim between them: "The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers, who bar (people) from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, and who disbelieve in the Hereafter."﴾

This is a report from God, may He be exalted and glorified, about what will happen from them. He expressed future meanings in the past tense (ṣīgha māḍiya). This is acceptable where the occurrence is certain. This calling from the people of the Garden to the people of the Fire is a rebuke, a reproach and an increase in their distress. It takes place when they look down upon them, and God creates the ability to perceive with their hearing and their sight.

The majority of readers recited *naʿam* ("yes") with a fatḥa on the ʿayn. Al-Kisā'ī recited *naʿim* with a kasra on the ʿayn. It is also reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him, and from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Ibn Wathhāb and al-Aʿmash recited it so. Al-Akhfash said: "They are two dialects." Sībawayh did not report the kasra. He said: *naʿam* is an affirmation of a promise and a confirmation, meaning: once this, and once that. In the book of Abū Ḥātim, from al-Kisā'ī, from a shaykh of the descendants of al-Zubayr, who said: "I did not hear the elders of Quraysh say anything but *naʿim*, with a kasra on the ʿayn, and then I lost it after him." Also in it, from Qatādah, from a man of Khath'am, who said: "I said to the Prophet (ﷺ), 'Do you claim that you are a prophet?' He said, '*Naʿim*.'" with a kasra on the ʿayn. Also in it, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, who said: "ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, asked about something, and they said, '*Naʿam*.' ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'The *naʿam* are camels and sheep; say *naʿim*'," with a kasra on the ʿayn. Abū Ḥātim said: "This dialect is not known today in the two Ḥarams."

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿Then a caller proclaimed between them﴾, and the rest of the verse: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Ṭabarī and others said that *adhdhana muʾadhdhinun* here means *aʿlama muʿlimun* ("a proclaimer proclaimed"). Sībawayh said: "*Adhdhantu*" is informing by means of a sound.

Ibn Kathīr, in the narration of Qunbul, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim recited ﴿*anna laʿnata Allāh*﴾ with the light form of *anna* (*an*) from the heavy, and *laʿnatu* in the nominative. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and Ibn Kathīr in the narration of al-Bizzī and Shibl recited *anna laʿnata* with the heavy *anna* and *laʿnata* in the accusative. All of them recited the one in *al-Nūr* (p-569) *anna laʿnata Allāh* and *anna ghaḍaba Allāh* with a doubled nūn, except Nāfiʿ, who recited both as *an laʿnatu* and *an ghaḍabu*, with the light form. Ibn ʿIṣma (or "Ismah") reported from al-Aʿmash: "*muʾadhdhinun baynahum inna*", with a kasra on the alif, on the assumption of an implied *qāla* ("said").

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Since the *adhān* is speech, and the wrongdoers in this verse are the disbelievers.

Then He began describing them by their deeds in this world, so that it would be a sign that the people of this description are the ones meant on the Day of Resurrection by His words: ﴿The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾. The word ﴿*yaṣuddūna*﴾ means "they turn away." *Al-sabīl* means the road and the path; it may be masculine or feminine, and the feminine is more common. The word ﴿*wa yabghūnahā*﴾ means "they seek it" or "they seek for it." If you take it as "they seek it," then ﴿*ʿiwajan*﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It may also refer to the pronoun returning to *al-sabīl*, meaning "crooked," or to the plural pronoun in ﴿*yabghūnahā*﴾, meaning "crooking it." If "*yabghūnahā*" is taken as "they seek for it," this is the apparent interpretation of al-Ṭabarī, may God have mercy on him; then *ʿiwajan* is the object of *yabghūna*. *Al-ʿiwaj*, with a kasra on the ʿayn, is used for affairs and meanings; *al-ʿawaj*, with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, is used for physical bodies and upright things.

﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-A'raf (7), verses 46–48:**

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights (al-A'raf) are men who recognize each by his mark. They call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," (but) they have not entered it, while they aspire (to enter).﴾ ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And the companions of the heights call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying, "Your gathering has not availed you, nor did your arrogance."﴾

The pronoun in His statement, ﴿"and between them"﴾, refers to Paradise and the Fire. It may also refer to both groups, since His statement, may He be blessed and exalted, ﴿"And the companions of Paradise call out to the companions of the Fire"﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], includes them both.

"Al-hijab" (the barrier) is the wall that He mentioned in His statement: ﴿"So a wall will be set up between them with a gate."﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: "al-A'raf is a barrier between Paradise and the Fire." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: "It is a hill between Paradise and the Fire." al-Zahrawi mentioned a hadith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it, and on the Day of Resurrection it will stand between Paradise and the Fire, and there will be held back upon it peoples (p-570) who recognize each by his mark; they are, if Allah wills, of the people of Paradise." He also mentioned another hadith from Safwan ibn Sulaym that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is upon one of the pillars of Paradise."

"Al-A'raf" is the plural of "'urf," which is an elevated place of the earth. From it is the statement of the poet:

"Every thick-fleshed one whose flesh is firm,
like a mountain rising above the a'raf."

And from it is the statement of al-Shammakh:

"And they remained among high a'raf, as if they were
spears planted, their direction set by the wind."

And from it is "'urf" of the horse (its mane) and "'urf" of the rooster (its comb), because of their height. al-Suddi said: "al-A'raf was named 'a'raf' because its companions recognize people."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a non-Arabic (or foreign) explanation. What is meant by the a'raf of that barrier is its heights.

His statement, ﴿"men" (rijal)﴾: Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd said: They are the angels. The word "rijal" is used metaphorically for them, since they were in the forms of men. He said: They are males, not females.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Allah has also named "rijal" among the jinn.

(p-571) The majority said: They are men from among the human beings. Then they differed. Mujahid said: They are righteous people, jurists and scholars. al-Zahrawi related that they are the "witnesses" of the Resurrection who testify before the people concerning their deeds, and they exist in every community. al-Zajjaj also said this. Some people said: They are prophets. al-Mahdawi said: They are the martyrs. Shurahbil ibn Sa'd said: They are those who were martyred in the way of Allah, who went out disobeying their parents. al-Tabari mentioned a hadith on this from the Prophet (ﷺ), and that their disobedience to their parents was balanced by their martyrdom. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: They are people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In the Musnad of Khaythama ibn Sulayman, at the end of the fifteenth part, there is a hadith from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The scales will be set up on the Day of Resurrection, and the good deeds and bad deeds will be weighed. Whoever's good deeds outweigh his bad deeds by the weight of a sow's hair (su'ubah) enters Paradise, and whoever's bad deeds outweigh his good deeds by the weight of a sow's hair enters the Fire." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what of one whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal?" He said: "Those are the companions of al-A'raf; they have not entered it, while they aspire." Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman said: They are a people whose young children delayed them until they were the last of the people.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that upon the a'raf of that wall, or upon elevated places away from both groups, wherever Allah wills, there are men of the people of Paradise whose entry is delayed, and they experience what has been described of contemplation (i'tibar) concerning both groups.

﴿They recognize each by his mark﴾: that is, by his sign. It is the whiteness of the faces and their beauty for the people of Paradise, and their blackness and ugliness for the people of the Fire, and so on, in the place of these and the place of those. "Al-simaa" (the mark): (p-572) the sign. It is from "wasama," and there is a metathesis (qalb) in it. It is said "sima," with short vowel, and "sima'," with long vowel, and "simiya'," with a kasra on the mim and an added ya'. Its measure (wazn) is "'ifla," despite it being from "wasama." It was also said that it is from "sawama," meaning "to know," and its measure in this case is "fi'la."

Their calling out to the companions of Paradise may be understood as that the companions of Paradise have not yet entered it. Then His statement, ﴿"they have not entered it while they aspire"﴾, may also be understood as referring to the people of Paradise, which is the interpretation of Abu Mijlaz, since he made the companions of al-A'raf angels. It may also be understood as referring to the people of al-A'raf. It may be that their calling out to the people of Paradise with peace is while those people have already entered it; then His statement, ﴿"they have not entered it while they aspire"﴾, can only refer to the people of al-A'raf alone. This is the interpretation of al-Suddi, Qatadah, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan, and he said: By Allah, Allah did not place that aspiration in their hearts except for a good that He intended for them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the most apparent and most fitting, and no one's view is to be considered in the presence of the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ).

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights (al-A'raf) are men who recognize each by his mark. They call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," (but) they have not entered it, while they aspire (to enter).﴾ ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And the companions of the heights call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying, "Your gathering has not availed you, nor did your arrogance."﴾

The pronoun in His statement, ﴿"and between them"﴾, refers to Paradise and the Fire. It may also refer to both groups, since His statement, may He be blessed and exalted, ﴿"And the companions of Paradise call out to the companions of the Fire"﴾ [al-A'raf: 44], includes them both.

"Al-hijab" (the barrier) is the wall that He mentioned in His statement: ﴿"So a wall will be set up between them with a gate."﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: "al-A'raf is a barrier between Paradise and the Fire." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also said: "It is a hill between Paradise and the Fire." al-Zahrawi mentioned a hadith that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it, and on the Day of Resurrection it will stand between Paradise and the Fire, and there will be held back upon it peoples (p-570) who recognize each by his mark; they are, if Allah wills, of the people of Paradise." He also mentioned another hadith from Safwan ibn Sulaym that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Uhud is upon one of the pillars of Paradise."

"Al-A'raf" is the plural of "'urf," which is an elevated place of the earth. From it is the statement of the poet:

"Every thick-fleshed one whose flesh is firm,
like a mountain rising above the a'raf."

And from it is the statement of al-Shammakh:

"And they remained among high a'raf, as if they were
spears planted, their direction set by the wind."

And from it is "'urf" of the horse (its mane) and "'urf" of the rooster (its comb), because of their height. al-Suddi said: "al-A'raf was named 'a'raf' because its companions recognize people."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a non-Arabic (or foreign) explanation. What is meant by the a'raf of that barrier is its heights.

His statement, ﴿"men" (rijal)﴾: Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd said: They are the angels. The word "rijal" is used metaphorically for them, since they were in the forms of men. He said: They are males, not females.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Allah has also named "rijal" among the jinn.

(p-571) The majority said: They are men from among the human beings. Then they differed. Mujahid said: They are righteous people, jurists and scholars. al-Zahrawi related that they are the "witnesses" of the Resurrection who testify before the people concerning their deeds, and they exist in every community. al-Zajjaj also said this. Some people said: They are prophets. al-Mahdawi said: They are the martyrs. Shurahbil ibn Sa'd said: They are those who were martyred in the way of Allah, who went out disobeying their parents. al-Tabari mentioned a hadith on this from the Prophet (ﷺ), and that their disobedience to their parents was balanced by their martyrdom. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: They are people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In the Musnad of Khaythama ibn Sulayman, at the end of the fifteenth part, there is a hadith from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The scales will be set up on the Day of Resurrection, and the good deeds and bad deeds will be weighed. ﴿They recognize each by his mark﴾: that is, by his sign. It is the whiteness of the faces and their beauty for the people of Paradise, and their blackness and ugliness for the people of the Fire, and so on, in the place of these and the place of those. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 49–52:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them any mercy? Enter the Garden; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve.﴾ ﴿The companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour down upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided for you." They will say: "Allah has forbidden both of them to the disbelievers,"﴾ ﴿those who took their religion as amusement and play, and whom the worldly life deceived. So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿And indeed We brought them a Book which We have detailed with knowledge, a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe.﴾

Abu Mijlaz said: The people of the Heights (ahl al-a'raf) are the angels, and they are the ones who say, "Are these...?", pointing to the people of the Garden.

The Qadi, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The saying of those who say that the people of the Heights are prophets and martyrs is similar to this.

Others said: The people of the Heights are mortal believers who have committed sins. His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿"Are these...?"﴾ is from the speech of an angel by the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, pointing to the people of the Heights and addressing the people of the Fire. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Al-Naqqash said: When [the angel] rebuked them with His saying, ﴿Your gathering did not avail you﴾ [al-A'raf: 48], the people of the Fire swore that the people of the Heights would enter the Fire with them; so the angels called out to them: "Are these...?" Then they called out to the companions of the Heights: ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ Some of the interpreters said: The pointing with "these" refers to the people of the Garden, the addressees are the people of the Heights, and those who are addressed are the people of the Fire. The meaning is: "Are these the weak ones in the world, about whom you swore that Allah, Exalted, does not regard them? It was said to them: Enter the Garden"; and what al-Naqqash said has already been mentioned, that the oath was in the Hereafter, made against the people of the Heights.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read: "Adkhilu al-jannah" (with an alif and a kasra on the kha'), meaning "Enter yourselves into the Garden," or it may be addressed to the angels, after which the address returns to the humans in "upon you." 'Ikrimah, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, read: "Dakhalu al-jannah" as a report in the past tense. Talhah ibn Musarrif, Ibn Wathhab, and al-Nakha'i read: "Udkhilu al-jannah" as a passive report.

The Qadi, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The arrangement of each of these readings according to the views on who is addressed by His saying "Are these...?" and who is addressed is possible with the easiest understanding; so I have abbreviated it concisely. Likewise is the shift in the verse from addressing one group to addressing another.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve﴾: its meaning is: "You will not fear what is coming, nor will you grieve over what has passed." al-Tabari mentioned, through the chain of Hudhayfah, that the people of the Heights desire intercession, so they come to Adam, who refers them to Noah; then the prophets push them one to another until they come to Muhammad (ﷺ) so that he may intercede for them; he intercedes, and they enter the Garden, where they are cast into the river of life and become white, and are named "the poor of the Garden." Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah, said: "I wish I were among the people of the Heights."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿The companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden﴾, etc.: the word "call" (nida') implies that the people of the Fire had knowledge that the people of the Garden could hear their call. It is permissible that this happens while they see them through a perception which Allah, Exalted, grants them despite the distance from the low to the high; and it is permissible that this happens while the wall and the barrier mentioned earlier stand between them. It is related that this call takes place when the people of the Garden look down upon them. The "an" in His saying ﴿"an afidu"﴾ is explanatory, in the sense of "that is."

"Fada al-ma'" means the water flowed and poured out; and "afadahu" means someone else caused it to pour. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿or of what Allah has provided for you﴾ refers to food, as said by al-Suddi; so the people of the Garden say to them: "Indeed Allah, Exalted, has forbidden the food and drink of the Garden to the disbelievers."

The Qadi, Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: More shameful for the disbelievers in this statement is that some of them see others, for that is more humiliating and more painful to the soul. The people of the Garden's answer with this ruling is by the command of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. al-Zahrawi mentioned that it was related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The best charity is water," meaning when there is need for it, since it is the most pleasant drink and the most refreshing to the soul. al-Sha'bi asked for a drink from Mus'ab, who said to him: "Which of the drinks do you love?" He replied: "The easiest of them to find and the dearest of them when lacking." Mus'ab said to him: "Boy, bring the water."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾, etc.: the religion is ascribed to them from the standpoint of their acceptance of being bound by it, since it is the religion of Allah, Exalted, in that He commanded it, and the religion of all people in that they were commanded with it. ﴿And the worldly life deceived them﴾: it is possible that this is part of the speech of the people of the Garden, and the speech of Allah, Exalted, begins from His saying "So today..."; it is also possible that the whole statement is from the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning of His saying ﴿took their religion as amusement﴾ is: by turning away and mocking those who call them to Islam. ﴿And the worldly life deceived them﴾: that is, it deceived them with its adornment and their belief that it is the ultimate goal; it is also possible that the word derives from "al-gharr," which is filling the mouth, meaning it satiated them and made them arrogant.

As for His saying, ﴿So today We will forget them﴾: it is an report from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, about what will be done to them. Forgetting in this verse means abandonment, i.e., We will leave them in torment, just as they abandoned looking toward the meeting of this day. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and a group of the exegetes. Qatadah said: They were forgotten from good, and were not forgotten from evil. If forgetting is understood as heedlessness on the part of the disbelievers, then in regard to the remembrance of Allah it is the naming of the punishment by the name of the sin. His saying, ﴿"and they used to"﴾, is coordinated with "ma" in His saying ﴿"as they forgot"﴾; it is also possible that the second "ma" is taken as superfluous, and His saying "kanu" is coordinated with His saying "nasu."

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And indeed We brought them a Book﴾, etc.: He mentioned the excuses made to them immediately after mentioning what is done to them. The lam in His saying, Glorified is He, "la-qad" is the lam of oath, and the pronoun in "ji'nahum" refers to those previously mentioned. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 53–54:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but its final outcome? On the day its final outcome comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth. Do we have any intercessors who might intercede for us, or might we be sent back so that we could act differently from how we used to act?" They have lost their own souls, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which pursues it swiftly, and (He created) the sun, the moon and the stars, subjected by His command. Surely, creation and command belong to Him. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

"Yanzurūn" means "yantaẓirūn" (they await). "Al-ta'wīl" (ultimate outcome, final consequence) here means "al-ma'āl" (the eventual result) and "al-'āqibah" (the end). This is the view of Qatādah, Mujāhid and others. Ibn 'Abbās said: "its ta'wīl" means its eventual outcome on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Suddī said: this refers to the worldly life, such as the Battle of Badr and others, and also to the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: "Are these disbelievers waiting for anything but the eventual outcome of this religion, of what they were called to, and of what they were turned away from, while they believe its outcome will be good for them?" Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then informs that its outcome, when it comes, will be accompanied by their regret. They will say, lamenting what they missed of faith: "The messengers indeed spoke the truth and brought the truth." On this view, al-ta'wīl is derived from the root "āla, ya'ūlu" (to return to, to become). Al-Khaṭṭābī said: "awwaltu al-shay'" means "I returned the thing to its beginning," so the word is derived from "al-awwal" (the first). This is related by al-Naqqāsh.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It has also been said that "awwaltu" means: I sought the first of the aspects and meanings.

As for "nasūhu" (they had forgotten it) in the verse, it is fitting that forgetting here means abandoning (al-tark).

They acknowledge the truth and ask about ways of escape at a time when there is no opportunity for them to be given back their right standing (lā musta'tab lahum). A group read "aw nuraddu" with the verb in the nominative (rafʿ), taking it as "aw hal nuraddu?" (or shall we be returned?), and with "fa-na'mala" in the subjunctive (naṣb) as an answer to this last interrogation. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "aw nuraddu fa-na'malu" with nominative (rafʿ) in both verbs, as a coordination (ʿaṭf) of "na'malu". Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū Ḥaywa read "aw nuradda fa-na'malu," with "nuradda" in the subjunctive. In this reading, the subjunctive of "nuradda" is either by coordination with "fa-yashfaʿū" (so they might intercede), or according to what al-Farrā' related, that "aw" can mean "ḥattā" (until), as in the line of Imru' al-Qays:

"… … … or that we die and are thereby excused."

It has come in the tafsir and in the ḥadīths that Allah, Exalted is He, began creation on Sunday, the creatures were completed on Friday, and then on Saturday nothing was created. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 55–56:

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Indeed, He does not like transgressors.﴾ ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right. And call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾

This is a command to supplicate (du'a'), and an act of worship (ta'abbud) in itself. Then, along with the command to supplicate, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, joined qualities that are fitting alongside it.

(p. 581) His saying, the Exalted, ﴿"tadarru'an"﴾ means: with humility (khushu') and submissiveness (istikana). "Al-tadarru'" is a word that implies being audible, because humbling oneself (tadarru') only takes place through gestures of the limbs and postures of the body that accompany the request. As for "wa-khufyatan," it means: within the self specifically. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has praised this in His saying, ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best remembrance is the hidden one." The Sharia establishes that secrecy in acts of righteousness that are not publicly displayed is greater in reward than open performance. Some scholars interpreted both tadarru' and khufya as meaning secrecy altogether, so that tadarru' is an act of the heart. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan mentioned this meaning and said: "We have met people for whom there was no deed on earth that they could make secret and it would never become public. The Muslims would strive in supplication, yet no sound of them could be heard; there was only a whisper between them and their Lord. That is because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.﴾" He also mentioned a righteous servant whose action He approved, saying: ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿Call upon your Lord﴾ means: worship your Lord; ﴿humbly and in secret﴾ means: with submissiveness and the belief of that in the hearts."

All seven readers recited "wa-khufyatan" with a ḍamma on the kha' (khufyatan). ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), recited it here and in "al-An'am" as "wa-khifyatan" with a kasra on the kha'. Both are dialectal forms (lughatan). It has been said that "khifyatan" with a kasra on the kha' means "fear" (al-khawf) and "awe" (al-rahba), and this appears from the words of Abu 'Ali. A group recited "wa-khifatan" from "al-khawf" (fear), meaning: "Call upon Him with submissiveness and fear." Ibn Sida mentioned it in al-Muhkam without attributing it to anyone. Abu Hatim said: "al-A'mash recited it, according to what they claim."

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, He does not like transgressors﴾ means: in supplication, although the wording is general; to this the indication points. Transgression (i'tida') in supplication takes several forms. Among them is excessive loudness and shouting, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a people who had raised their voices with takbir: "O people, be gentle with yourselves; for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent." Among them is that a person supplicates for a status equal to that of a prophet, or supplicates for something impossible, and other such overreach. Among them is that he supplicates seeking disobedience, and other things. In these examples there is sufficiency.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "Indeed Allah does not like transgressors." The "mu'tadi" is one who exceeds the limit and commits what is prohibited, and this may vary in degree according to what the transgression concerns. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There will be people who overstep in supplication. It is sufficient for a person to say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings closer to it of speech and action, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings closer to it of speech and action."

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ and the rest of the verse: these are general words that encompass every act of corruption, whether small or great, after setting right, whether small or great. The intent of the prohibition is generality, and singling out one matter over another in this is arbitrary, except that it may be said by way of example. Al-Dahhak said: "It means: do not block up flowing water, and do not cut down fruit-bearing trees out of harm." It has also been reported: "Cutting the dinar and the dirham is among corruption on earth." And it has been said: "The commerce of rulers is among corruption on earth." Some people said: "The meaning is: do not commit shirk on the earth after Allah has set it right through the sending of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and the establishment of the laws, and the clarity of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)." The one who said this statement intended the greatest corruption after the greatest reform, so He singled it out for mention.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope﴾ is a command that a person be in a state of watchfulness, grief, and yearning toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that hope and fear are like the two wings of a bird, carrying it along the path of uprightness; if either of them is alone, the person perishes. Many scholars have said: fear should predominate over hope throughout life; when death comes, hope should predominate. Many (p. 583) scholars have held that fear should be far more dominant in a person. All of this is precaution. From this is al-Hasan al-Basri's wish to be the man who is the last to enter Paradise, and Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, wished to be among the People of the Heights (ashab al-A'raf), because his view was that they are sinners.

Then His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ gives reassurance. It is a verse of promise, in which there is a restriction by His saying ﴿to the doers of good﴾. People differed about the reason for omitting the feminine marker (ta') from "qarib" (near), when describing mercy (rahma), into several opinions. Among them: that it is in the sense of a relative adjective (nisba), meaning "possessing nearness." Among them: that since its feminine form is not a true feminine, it follows the pattern of "kaff khadib" (a dyed hand) and "lihya dahin" (an oiled beard). Among them: that it has the meaning of a masculine noun, so the attribute was mentioned in that form. Those who held this view differed about the masculine noun of which it is the substitute: one group said "forgiveness and pardon," another group said "rain," and it has been said other things. Al-Farra' said: "The word 'qurb' (nearness), when used in the sense of kinship and blood relationship, is always accompanied by the ta' with a feminine noun; there is no alternative. When it is used in the sense of nearness of distance, [it may be masculine or feminine]."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Or 'time' (al-zaman), for it may come with a feminine noun with a ta', and it may come without a ta'; and this is of that type. And from this is the saying of the poet:

؎ 'Ashiyyata la 'Afra'a minka qariba ∗∗∗ fa-tadnu wa-la 'Afra'a minka ba'idu

[In an evening when 'Afra' is not near to you, so that she draws close, nor is 'Afra' far from you.]

In this line he combined both forms."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "This is al-Farra's view in his book, and it has passed in some books of exegetes in a restricted form. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view. Abu 'Ubayda said: 'Qarib' in the verse is not an attribute of mercy; rather, it is an adverb of place (zarf) for it, and a location; therefore it comes in this form for the feminine, the dual, and the plural. Likewise 'ba'id' (far). When they make it an attribute in the sense of 'muqarraba' (brought near), they say 'qariba,' 'qaribatan,' and 'qaribat.'" Al-Tabari mentioned that His saying, the Exalted, "qarib," is intended to refer to the closeness of souls to bodies; that is, at that moment mercy reaches them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 55–56:

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Indeed, He does not like transgressors.﴾ ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right. And call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾

This is a command to supplicate (du'a'), and an act of worship (ta'abbud) in itself. Then, along with the command to supplicate, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, joined qualities that are fitting alongside it.

(p. 581) His saying, the Exalted, ﴿"tadarru'an"﴾ means: with humility (khushu') and submissiveness (istikana). "Al-tadarru'" is a word that implies being audible, because humbling oneself (tadarru') only takes place through gestures of the limbs and postures of the body that accompany the request. As for "wa-khufyatan," it means: within the self specifically. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has praised this in His saying, ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best remembrance is the hidden one." The Sharia establishes that secrecy in acts of righteousness that are not publicly displayed is greater in reward than open performance. Some scholars interpreted both tadarru' and khufya as meaning secrecy altogether, so that tadarru' is an act of the heart. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan mentioned this meaning and said: "We have met people for whom there was no deed on earth that they could make secret and it would never become public. The Muslims would strive in supplication, yet no sound of them could be heard; there was only a whisper between them and their Lord. That is because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.﴾" He also mentioned a righteous servant whose action He approved, saying: ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. Al-Zajjaj said: "﴿Call upon your Lord﴾ means: worship your Lord; ﴿humbly and in secret﴾ means: with submissiveness and the belief of that in the hearts."

All seven readers recited "wa-khufyatan" with a ḍamma on the kha' (khufyatan). ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), recited it here and in "al-An'am" as "wa-khifyatan" with a kasra on the kha'. Both are dialectal forms (lughatan). It has been said that "khifyatan" with a kasra on the kha' means "fear" (al-khawf) and "awe" (al-rahba), and this appears from the words of Abu 'Ali. A group recited "wa-khifatan" from "al-khawf" (fear), meaning: "Call upon Him with submissiveness and fear." Ibn Sida mentioned it in al-Muhkam without attributing it to anyone. Abu Hatim said: "al-A'mash recited it, according to what they claim."

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, He does not like transgressors﴾ means: in supplication, although the wording is general; to this the indication points. Transgression (i'tida') in supplication takes several forms. Among them is excessive loudness and shouting, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to a people who had raised their voices with takbir: "O people, be gentle with yourselves; for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent." Among them is that a person supplicates for a status equal to that of a prophet, or supplicates for something impossible, and other such overreach. Among them is that he supplicates seeking disobedience, and other things. In these examples there is sufficiency.

Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "Indeed Allah does not like transgressors." The "mu'tadi" is one who exceeds the limit and commits what is prohibited, and this may vary in degree according to what the transgression concerns. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "There will be people who overstep in supplication. It is sufficient for a person to say: O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings closer to it of speech and action, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings closer to it of speech and action."

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ and the rest of the verse: these are general words that encompass every act of corruption, whether small or great, after setting right, whether small or great. The intent of the prohibition is generality, and singling out one matter over another in this is arbitrary, except that it may be said by way of example. Al-Dahhak said: "It means: do not block up flowing water, and do not cut down fruit-bearing trees out of harm." It has also been reported: "Cutting the dinar and the dirham is among corruption on earth." And it has been said: "The commerce of rulers is among corruption on earth." Some people said: "The meaning is: do not commit shirk on the earth after Allah has set it right through the sending of the Messengers, peace be upon them, and the establishment of the laws, and the clarity of the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ)." The one who said this statement intended the greatest corruption after the greatest reform, so He singled it out for mention.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And call upon Him in fear and hope﴾ is a command that a person be in a state of watchfulness, grief, and yearning toward Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that hope and fear are like the two wings of a bird, carrying it along the path of uprightness; if either of them is alone, the person perishes. Many scholars have said: fear should predominate over hope throughout life; when death comes, hope should predominate. Many (p. 583) scholars have held that fear should be far more dominant in a person. All of this is precaution. From this is al-Hasan al-Basri's wish to be the man who is the last to enter Paradise, and Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, wished to be among the People of the Heights (ashab al-A'raf), because his view was that they are sinners.

Then His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾ gives reassurance. It is a verse of promise, in which there is a restriction by His saying ﴿to the doers of good﴾. People differed about the reason for omitting the feminine marker (ta') from "qarib" (near), when describing mercy (rahma), into several opinions. Among them: that it is in the sense of a relative adjective (nisba), meaning "possessing nearness." Among them: that since its feminine form is not a true feminine, it follows the pattern of "kaff khadib" (a dyed hand) and "lihya dahin" (an oiled beard). Among them: that it has the meaning of a masculine noun, so the attribute was mentioned in that form. Those who held this view differed about the masculine noun of which it is the substitute: one group said "forgiveness and pardon," another group said "rain," and it has been said other things. Al-Farra' said: "The word 'qurb' (nearness), when used in the sense of kinship and blood relationship, is always accompanied by the ta' with a feminine noun; there is no alternative. When it is used in the sense of nearness of distance, [it may be masculine or feminine]."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "Or 'time' (al-zaman), for it may come with a feminine noun with a ta', and it may come without a ta'; and this is of that type. And from this is the saying of the poet:

؎ 'Ashiyyata la 'Afra'a minka qariba ∗∗∗ fa-tadnu wa-la 'Afra'a minka ba'idu

[In an evening when 'Afra' is not near to you, so that she draws close, nor is 'Afra' far from you.]

In this line he combined both forms."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "This is al-Farra's view in his book, and it has passed in some books of exegetes in a restricted form. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view. Abu 'Ubayda said: 'Qarib' in the verse is not an attribute of mercy; rather, it is an adverb of place (zarf) for it, and a location; therefore it comes in this form for the feminine, the dual, and the plural. Likewise 'ba'id' (far). When they make it an attribute in the sense of 'muqarraba' (brought near), they say 'qariba,' 'qaribatan,' and 'qaribat.'" **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 57–58**

His statement, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿It is He who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water therewith and bring forth with it fruits of every kind. Thus do We bring forth the dead, that you may remember. And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord; and that which is corrupt does not yield except scantily. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾

This is a verse of contemplation and inference. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural, and "nushuran" with a damma on the nun and the shin. Abu Hatim said: this is the reading of al-Hasan, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and Abu Raja'. The readings of al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Abu Yahya, and Abu Nawfal, al-A'rabiyyayn, differ from them. Ibn Kathir read "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular, with "nushuran" also with a damma. Ibn 'Amir read "al-riyah" in the plural, with "nushran" having a damma on the nun and a sukun on the shin. Abu Hatim said: this was also transmitted from al-Hasan, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu Raja', Qatada, and Abu 'Amr. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-rih" in the singular, with "nashran" having a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the shin. Abu Hatim said: this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Ibn Thabit, Ibrahim, Talha, al-A'mash, and Masruq ibn al-Ajda'. Ibn Jinni read the reading of Masruq: "nasaran," with a fatha on the nun and the shin. 'Asim read "al-riyah" in the plural of collectivity, with "bushran" having a damma on the ba' and a sukun on the shin. It was also transmitted from him as "bushuran," with a damma on the ba' and the shin. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sulami, and Ibn Abi 'Abla read it so. Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' and Abu Qutayb read "bushra," on the pattern of "fu'la," with a damma on the ba'. It was transmitted from Abu Yahya and Abu Nawfal. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "bashran," with a fatha on the ba' and a sukun on the shin. Al-Zahrawi said: this was also transmitted from 'Asim.

Whoever reads "al-riyah" in this verse in the plural is more fortunate, because wherever "al-riyah" occurs in the Qur'an it is linked with mercy, as in His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾ [al-Rum: 46]; and His saying: ﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾ [al-Hijr: 22]; and His saying: ﴿Allah is He who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. The mention of "al-rih" in the singular is mostly accompanied by a context of punishment, as in His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 41]; and His saying: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious, violent wind﴾ [al-Haqqah: 6]; and His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Rather, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24], ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 25]. Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', and 'Asim followed this approach. In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when the wind blew: 'O Allah, make them winds (riyah) and do not make them a wind (rih).'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The meaning in all of this is clear. The wind that brings rain and sustenance is dispersed and gentle; it comes from here and from there, and scatters. Hence it is appropriate, since its parts are separated and its directions vary a little, to call it "riyah" (winds) in the plural and to describe it with abundance. As for "the wind of cold and punishment," it is violent, storming, a single mass, extremely bitter, destructive by its force, and at times carrying scorching cold. Hence it is appropriate, since it is strongly continuous, to call it "rih" (wind) in the singular. Likewise, the wind is mentioned in the singular in His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿and they sailed with them on a favourable wind﴾ [Yunus: 22], because ships travel with a continuous wind, as if it were one thing; so it is mentioned in the singular for that reason and described as "favourable," to remove the ambiguity between it and the disliked wind. Likewise the wind of Sulayman, peace be upon him: it used to run by his command, or blow strongly over his fields, and it was continuous. Furthermore, whoever reads "al-rih" in the singular in this verse intends by it the generic noun. Also, restricting it with "bushran" (as heralds of good news) removes the ambiguity.

The verb "arsala" (to send) in regard to the wind means to let it flow, release it, and cause it to pour forth. From this is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was more generous with good than the wind that is sent forth." The plural of "rih" is "arwah" for the few, and "riyah" for the many, because the middle letter of "rih" is a waw, which changed into a ya' in the singular due to the kasra before it; the same applies in the plural of abundance. In the plural of paucity it remained sound, because there is nothing in it that requires a change.

As for "nushuran" with a damma on the nun and the shin: it may be the plural of "nashir" (spreading), according to the nisba (relative form), meaning "possessing spreading," from "al-tayy" (folding); or "nushur" from "al-hayat" (life). It may also be that "nushuran" is the plural of "nashur," with a fatha on the nun and a damma on the shin, like "rasul" and "rusul," "sabur" and "subur," "shakur" and "shukur." It may also be that "nushuran" is like the passive participle in meaning, "mansur" (spread out), like "rakub" in the sense of "markub" (ridden). It may also be from the patterns of the active participle, since they spread the clouds. The example of the first (the form "nashir" and "nushur") is "shahid" and "shuhud," "nazil" and "nuzul," as the poet said:

"... or you will alight, for we are a group of guests (nuzul)."

And "qatil" and "qutul," and from it the saying of al-A'sha:

"Indeed we, O our people, are the like of your slain (qutul)."

As for the one who reads "nushran" with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the shin, he has lightened the shin of "nushuran." As for the one who reads "nashran" with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the shin, it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "al-riyah." It may be meant in the sense of "al-nashr," which is the opposite of folding; every remaining of the wind without blowing is folding. It may also be from "al-nashr" meaning revival, as al-A'sha said:

"How strange (is the case) of the dead one who is revived!"

As for the one who reads "nashran" with a fatha on the nun and the shin, which is an anomalous reading, it is a noun, and it is according to the nisba: Abu al-Fath said: meaning "possessing nashar," and "al-nashar" is when sheep spread out at night and graze; thus the cloud is likened, in its spreading and generality, to that.

As for "bushuran" with a damma on the ba' and the shin, it is the plural of "bashir" (bearer of good news), like "nadhir" and "nudhur." "Bushran" with a sukun on the shin is a lightened form of it. "Bashran" with a fatha on the ba' and a sukun on the shin is a verbal noun. "Bushra" is also a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The mercy in this verse is the rain. "Bayna yadayh" means "before" His mercy, in front of it; here it is a metaphor, while its literal sense is what lies before a person of physical things.

"Aqallat" means: it lifted from the earth and carried it; from it comes "al-qillah" (a small quantity), as if the one who lifts sees what he lifts as little when he is able to lift it. "Thiqalan" means: laden with water. The Arabs describe clouds with heaviness and sluggishness, and from this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Nor is there a cloud more beautiful than it, / heavy, its dark parts unveiled."

The wind drives the clouds from behind them, so this is actual driving. The pronoun in "suqnahu" refers to the clouds. The verb is attributed to a pronoun for the name of Allah, Exalted, insofar as it is a blessing. Describing the land as dead is a metaphor because of its dryness, its barrenness, and the withering of its vegetation. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and al-A'mash read "li-baladin mayyitin" with a sukun on the ya'; the rest read it with a shadda. The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"fa-anzalna bihi"﴾ may refer to the clouds, that is, "from it"; it may refer to the land; and it may refer to the water, which is the most evident of these.

Al-Suddi said, in explaining this verse: Allah, Exalted is He, sends the winds, and they bring the clouds from between the two horizons, the edge of the sky and the earth, where they meet; then they bring it out from there, then they spread it, and spread it out in the sky. Then He opens the gates of the sky, and the water flows over the clouds, and then the clouds rain after that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This detailed account has not been established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead﴾ may have two meanings. One is that it means: just as this great power in sending down water and bringing forth fruits by it from barren land is the power to revive the dead from their graves; and this is an example of it. The other is that it means: thus is it done to the dead, by the descent of rain upon them, until they live by it; so the statement is then a report, not a parable. This interpretation rests only on the hadith mentioned by al-Tabari from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "When people die at the first blast, rain will fall upon them from water beneath the Throne, called 'the water of life,' for forty years; and they will grow as plants grow. When their bodies are complete, the spirit will be blown into them. Then a sleep will be cast upon them, and they will sleep; and when the second blast is sounded, they will rise, finding the taste of sleep, and they will say: 'Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?' Then the caller will call out to them: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]."

His saying: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth﴾ is a verse that completes the first meaning in the verse before it, informing about the custom of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, regarding the growth of lands. Whoever wishes to make it an example of the heart of the believer and the heart of the disbeliever, all of that is coherent; but the wording of the verse does not require that the example was intended for that. The use of this as an illustration is related by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi. Al-Nahhas said: it is an example for the intelligent person and for the dull one. "Al-tayyib" is the land of good soil, the noble ground. It was singled out with "bi-idhni rabbihi" (by the permission of its Lord) as praise and honour. This is like when you say to someone you are overlooking: "You are as Allah wills," which is an expression that gives emphasis in praise or in blame. From this is His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], according to some interpretations. "Al-khabith" is salt-marsh and similar poor land. Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Hayawa, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "yukhriju nabatahu" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', and a fatha on the ta'. "Al-nakid" is what is difficult and scant. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Do not fulfil the promise if you promise, and if you give, you give something paltry and grudging."

"Nakida al-rajul" means: when he asked insistently and was embarrassed; from it is the saying of the poet:

"Give what you have given with goodwill; there is no good in the miserly or the one who is grudging."

Most people, and all of the Seven, read "nakidan" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the kaf. Talha ibn Musarrif read "nakdan" with a lightened kaf and a fatha on the nun. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "nakadan" with a fatha on the nun and the kaf. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the reading of the people of Madinah.

﴿Thus do We vary the signs﴾: that is, thus do We make the matters clear. "Yashkurun" means: they believe in the blessings of Allah, Exalted is He, and they praise Him.

"... or you will alight, for we are a group of guests (nuzul)."

And "qatil" and "qutul," and from it the saying of al-A'sha:

"Indeed we, O our people, are the like of your slain (qutul)."

As for the one who reads "nushran" with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the shin, he has lightened the shin of "nushuran." As for the one who reads "nashran" with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the shin, it is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "al-riyah." It may be meant in the sense of "al-nashr," which is the opposite of folding; every remaining of the wind without blowing is folding. It may also be from "al-nashr" meaning revival, as al-A'sha said:

"How strange (is the case) of the dead one who is revived!"

As for the one who reads "nashran" with a fatha on the nun and the shin, which is an anomalous reading, it is a noun, and it is according to the nisba: Abu al-Fath said: meaning "possessing nashar," and "al-nashar" is when sheep spread out at night and graze; thus the cloud is likened, in its spreading and generality, to that.

As for "bushuran" with a damma on the ba' and the shin, it is the plural of "bashir" (bearer of good news), like "nadhir" and "nudhur." "Bushran" with a sukun on the shin is a lightened form of it. "Bashran" with a fatha on the ba' and a sukun on the shin is a verbal noun. "Bushra" is also a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative. The mercy in this verse is the rain. "Bayna yadayh" means "before" His mercy, in front of it; here it is a metaphor, while its literal sense is what lies before a person of physical things.

"Aqallat" means: it lifted from the earth and carried it; from it comes "al-qillah" (a small quantity), as if the one who lifts sees what he lifts as little when he is able to lift it. "Thiqalan" means: laden with water. The Arabs describe clouds with heaviness and sluggishness, and from this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Nor is there a cloud more beautiful than it, / heavy, its dark parts unveiled."

The wind drives the clouds from behind them, so this is actual driving. The pronoun in "suqnahu" refers to the clouds. The verb is attributed to a pronoun for the name of Allah, Exalted, insofar as it is a blessing. Describing the land as dead is a metaphor because of its dryness, its barrenness, and the withering of its vegetation. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and al-A'mash read "li-baladin mayyitin" with a sukun on the ya'; the rest read it with a shadda. The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"fa-anzalna bihi"﴾ may refer to the clouds, that is, "from it"; it may refer to the land; and it may refer to the water, which is the most evident of these.

Al-Suddi said, in explaining this verse: Allah, Exalted is He, sends the winds, and they bring the clouds from between the two horizons, the edge of the sky and the earth, where they meet; then they bring it out from there, then they spread it, and spread it out in the sky. Then He opens the gates of the sky, and the water flows over the clouds, and then the clouds rain after that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This detailed account has not been established from the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead﴾ may have two meanings. One is that it means: just as this great power in sending down water and bringing forth fruits by it from barren land is the power to revive the dead from their graves; and this is an example of it. The other is that it means: thus is it done to the dead, by the descent of rain upon them, until they live by it; so the statement is then a report, not a parable. This interpretation rests only on the hadith mentioned by al-Tabari from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "When people die at the first blast, rain will fall upon them from water beneath the Throne, called 'the water of life,' for forty years; and they will grow as plants grow. When their bodies are complete, the spirit will be blown into them. Then a sleep will be cast upon them, and they will sleep; and when the second blast is sounded, they will rise, finding the taste of sleep, and they will say: 'Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?' Then the caller will call out to them: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]."

His saying: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth﴾ is a verse that completes the first meaning in the verse before it, informing about the custom of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, regarding the growth of lands. Whoever wishes to make it an example of the heart of the believer and the heart of the disbeliever, all of that is coherent; but the wording of the verse does not require that the example was intended for that. The use of this as an illustration is related by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Suddi. Al-Nahhas said: it is an example for the intelligent person and for the dull one. "Al-tayyib" is the land of good soil, the noble ground. It was singled out with "bi-idhni rabbihi" (by the permission of its Lord) as praise and honour. This is like when you say to someone you are overlooking: "You are as Allah wills," which is an expression that gives emphasis in praise or in blame. From this is His saying, Blessed and Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, for him is what has passed, and his affair is up to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 275], according to some interpretations. "Al-khabith" is salt-marsh and similar poor land. Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Hayawa, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "yukhriju nabatahu" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', and a fatha on the ta'. "Al-nakid" is what is difficult and scant. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Do not fulfil the promise if you promise, and if you give, you give something paltry and grudging."

"Nakida al-rajul" means: when he asked insistently and was embarrassed; from it is the saying of the poet:

"Give what you have given with goodwill; there is no good in the miserly or the one who is grudging."

Most people, and all of the Seven, read "nakidan" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the kaf. Talha ibn Musarrif read "nakdan" with a lightened kaf and a fatha on the nun. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "nakadan" with a fatha on the nun and the kaf. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the reading of the people of Madinah.

﴿Thus do We vary the signs﴾: that is, thus do We make the matters clear. "Yashkurun" means: they believe in the blessings of Allah, Exalted is He, and they praise Him.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 59–62:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of his people said: "Indeed, we see you in clear error."﴾ ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and advise you, and I know from Allah what you do not know."﴾

The *lam* (لام) is the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*). Al-Tabari said: Allah swore an oath that He sent Noah (peace be upon him). A group of the exegetes (*mufassirun*, those who practise *tafsir*, exegesis of the Qur'an) said: he was named "Noah" (*Nuh*) because he used to wail (*yanuhu*) over himself.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is weak.

Sibawayh said: "Nuh," "Lut," and "Hud" are non-Arabic names, but they are definite proper names, and therefore they are declined (*sharifat*, i.e. take nunation).

This is a warning from Noah (peace be upon him) to his people. He called them to the worship of Allah alone and to the rejection of their idols, which were named: "Wadd," "Suwa'," "Yaghuth," "Ya'uq," and others that are not well known.

Al-Kisa'i alone read *ghayrihi* (غَيْرِهِ) with a *kasra* on the *ra'* (i.e. *ghayrihi*), as an adjective (*na't*) modifying *ilah* (إلَهٍ). This is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Abu Ja'far. The rest read *ghayruhu* (غَيْرُهُ) with a *damma* on the *ra'* (*raf'*). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *hal min khaliqin ghayri Allah* (هَلْ مِن خالِقٍ غَيْرِ اللهِ) with a *kasra* (*khafd*), and the rest read *ghayru Allah* (غَيْرُ اللهِ) with a *damma* (*raf'*). The *raf'* in the reading of the majority here is in apposition (*badal*) to the phrase *min ilah* (مِن إلَهٍ), because the place (*mawdi'*, grammatical position) of *min ilah* is in the nominative. This is the reading preferred by al-Farisi. It is also permissible for it to be an adjective agreeing with the position (*ala al-mawdi'*), since the sense is: "You have no god other than Him" (*ma lakum ilahun ghayruhu*). Or *ghayr* may be understood as *illa* (إلّا, "except"), and so it takes the case of what follows *illa*. Isa ibn Umar read *ghayrahu* (غَيْرَهُ) with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, as an exception (*istithna'*). Abu Hatim said: That is weak, because of the preceding negation.

His saying, the Exalted, *'adhab* (عَذابَ, "punishment"): it may be intended to mean the punishment of this world, and it may be intended to mean the punishment of the Hereafter.

*Al-mala'* (اَلْمَلَأُ) means the noble assembly (*al-jama'ah al-sharifah*). Al-Tabari said: there are no women among them. Al-Naqqash related from Tha'lab regarding *al-mala'*, *al-rahtu*, *al-nafar*, and *al-qawm* (all meaning a group of men). It was said: they are so named because they fill (*yamla'una*) the soul and the eye (with awe). It may also be that they are so named because when they agree (*tama'alu*) on a matter it is completed.

Salama ibn Salama ibn Waqsh al-Ansari said, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was returning from the Battle of Badr: "We only killed bald old women." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Those are the *mala'* of Quraysh; if you had witnessed their deeds, you would have considered your own deed small."

*Al-mala'* is a predominant descriptive term (*sifah ghalibah*). Its plural is *amla'* (أمْلاءٌ). It is not of the pattern of *rahṭ*, even though both are collective nouns, because *rahṭ* has no singular from its own form, whereas *mala'* has from its own form the word *mali'* (مالِئٌ). Ahmad ibn Yahya said: *al-mali'* is the distinguished man who fills the eye with his presence. It comes like *'azib* and *khadim* and *ra'ih*, for the names of their plurals are *'azab*, *khadam*, and *rawah*. And if the word is from *tama'ala al-qawm 'ala kadha* (they agreed upon such-and-such), then it departs from the pattern of *rahṭ*. From this is the saying of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "I did not kill Uthman, nor did I conspire (*mala'tu*) in his blood."

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: *al-Mala'u* is written with a *waw* (*al-Malau*, مَلَؤُ), and so it is in the codices (*masahif*) of Syria.

Their saying, ﴿*"lanaraka"*﴾ (لَنَراكَ, "we see you"): it may be taken as sight of the eye, and it may be taken as sight of the heart (i.e. knowing), and the latter is more apparent. *Fi dalal* (في ضَلالٍ, "in error") means: in ruin (*itlaf*) and ignorance of what you are pursuing.

His saying to them in reply to this: ﴿"There is no error in me"﴾ is an exaggeration in good manners, a turning away from their harshness, a gentle address, and breadth of chest, as the character of prophethood requires. His saying: ﴿"but I am a messenger"﴾ is an invitation to whoever wishes to consider, investigate, and reflect upon the miracle.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: We must affirm that Noah (peace be upon him), and every prophet sent to creation, had a miracle that breaks the normal course of things. Some of them we know by their miracle, and some we do not know.

The seven readers, apart from Abu 'Amr, read ﴿*"uballighukum"*﴾ (أُبَلِّغُكُمْ) with a *shadda* on the *lam* and a *fatha* on the *ba'*. Abu 'Amr read it with a *sukun* on the *ba'* and without the *shadda* on the *lam*.

His saying: ﴿"and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾. Although it is a general expression covering everything He knows, what is intended here is the matters that are frightening for them (the things they would fear), especially since they had never heard of a nation being punished. Thus the expression contains a warning (*wa'id*).
