The *lam* (لام) is the *lam* of oath (*lam al-qasam*). Al-Tabari said: Allah swore an oath that He sent Noah (peace be upon him). A group of the exegetes (*mufassirun*, those who practise *tafsir*, exegesis of the Qur'an) said: he was named "Noah" (*Nuh*) because he used to wail (*yanuhu*) over himself.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is weak.

Sibawayh said: "Nuh," "Lut," and "Hud" are non-Arabic names, but they are definite proper names, and therefore they are declined (*sharifat*, i.e. take nunation).

This is a warning from Noah (peace be upon him) to his people. He called them to the worship of Allah alone and to the rejection of their idols, which were named: "Wadd," "Suwa'," "Yaghuth," "Ya'uq," and others that are not well known.

Al-Kisa'i alone read *ghayrihi* (غَيْرِهِ) with a *kasra* on the *ra'* (i.e. *ghayrihi*), as an adjective (*na't*) modifying *ilah* (إلَهٍ). This is the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Abu Ja'far. The rest read *ghayruhu* (غَيْرُهُ) with a *damma* on the *ra'* (*raf'*). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *hal min khaliqin ghayri Allah* (هَلْ مِن خالِقٍ غَيْرِ اللهِ) with a *kasra* (*khafd*), and the rest read *ghayru Allah* (غَيْرُ اللهِ) with a *damma* (*raf'*). The *raf'* in the reading of the majority here is in apposition (*badal*) to the phrase *min ilah* (مِن إلَهٍ), because the place (*mawdi'*, grammatical position) of *min ilah* is in the nominative. This is the reading preferred by al-Farisi. It is also permissible for it to be an adjective agreeing with the position (*ala al-mawdi'*), since the sense is: "You have no god other than Him" (*ma lakum ilahun ghayruhu*). Or *ghayr* may be understood as *illa* (إلّا, "except"), and so it takes the case of what follows *illa*. Isa ibn Umar read *ghayrahu* (غَيْرَهُ) with a *fatha* on the *ra'*, as an exception (*istithna'*). Abu Hatim said: That is weak, because of the preceding negation.

His saying, the Exalted, *'adhab* (عَذابَ, "punishment"): it may be intended to mean the punishment of this world, and it may be intended to mean the punishment of the Hereafter.

*Al-mala'* (اَلْمَلَأُ) means the noble assembly (*al-jama'ah al-sharifah*). Al-Tabari said: there are no women among them. Al-Naqqash related from Tha'lab regarding *al-mala'*, *al-rahtu*, *al-nafar*, and *al-qawm* (all meaning a group of men). It was said: they are so named because they fill (*yamla'una*) the soul and the eye (with awe). It may also be that they are so named because when they agree (*tama'alu*) on a matter it is completed.

Salama ibn Salama ibn Waqsh al-Ansari said, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was returning from the Battle of Badr: "We only killed bald old women." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Those are the *mala'* of Quraysh; if you had witnessed their deeds, you would have considered your own deed small."

*Al-mala'* is a predominant descriptive term (*sifah ghalibah*). Its plural is *amla'* (أمْلاءٌ). It is not of the pattern of *rahṭ*, even though both are collective nouns, because *rahṭ* has no singular from its own form, whereas *mala'* has from its own form the word *mali'* (مالِئٌ). Ahmad ibn Yahya said: *al-mali'* is the distinguished man who fills the eye with his presence. It comes like *'azib* and *khadim* and *ra'ih*, for the names of their plurals are *'azab*, *khadam*, and *rawah*. And if the word is from *tama'ala al-qawm 'ala kadha* (they agreed upon such-and-such), then it departs from the pattern of *rahṭ*. From this is the saying of Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "I did not kill Uthman, nor did I conspire (*mala'tu*) in his blood."

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: *al-Mala'u* is written with a *waw* (*al-Malau*, مَلَؤُ), and so it is in the codices (*masahif*) of Syria.

Their saying, ﴿*"lanaraka"*﴾ (لَنَراكَ, "we see you"): it may be taken as sight of the eye, and it may be taken as sight of the heart (i.e. knowing), and the latter is more apparent. *Fi dalal* (في ضَلالٍ, "in error") means: in ruin (*itlaf*) and ignorance of what you are pursuing.

His saying to them in reply to this: ﴿"There is no error in me"﴾ is an exaggeration in good manners, a turning away from their harshness, a gentle address, and breadth of chest, as the character of prophethood requires. His saying: ﴿"but I am a messenger"﴾ is an invitation to whoever wishes to consider, investigate, and reflect upon the miracle.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: We must affirm that Noah (peace be upon him), and every prophet sent to creation, had a miracle that breaks the normal course of things. Some of them we know by their miracle, and some we do not know.

The seven readers, apart from Abu 'Amr, read ﴿*"uballighukum"*﴾ (أُبَلِّغُكُمْ) with a *shadda* on the *lam* and a *fatha* on the *ba'*. Abu 'Amr read it with a *sukun* on the *ba'* and without the *shadda* on the *lam*.

His saying: ﴿"and I know from Allah what you do not know"﴾. Although it is a general expression covering everything He knows, what is intended here is the matters that are frightening for them (the things they would fear), especially since they had never heard of a nation being punished. Thus the expression contains a warning (*wa'id*).

(p-592) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you and that you may fear God, and perhaps you will be shown mercy?﴾ ﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.﴾

This is the interrogative alif entering upon the conjunctive waw. The interrogation here carries the sense of affirmation (taqrir) and reproach (tawbikh). Their wonder that occurred was, as is apparent from their story, only by way of considering it remote and impossible. The word "ʿalā" in His saying "ʿalā rajulin" ("through a man"): it has been said that it means "maʿa" ("with"); and it has been said that it is an elision of a modifier, its estimated sense being "ʿalā lisāni rajulin minkum" ("upon the tongue of a man from among you").

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: It is possible that the verb "jāʾakum" (has come to you) in this place is connected with "ʿalā," since everything that comes from God, blessed and exalted is He, takes the ruling of descent (nuzul). Thus "jāʾakum" means "nazala" (has descended), and so it was fitting to say with it "ʿalā rajulin." The lam in "li-yundhirakum" is the lam of purpose (kay). His saying "wa-laʿallakum" ("and perhaps you"), is an expression of hope (tarajjī), in accordance with the condition and belief of Noah (peace be upon him), because this report was indeed from Noah (peace be upon him) himself.

As for His saying, ﴿But they denied him﴾, etc.: God, exalted is He, informed about them that, after his gentle dealings with them, they denied him; so God saved him and the believers with him in the ship, which is the fulk. "Al-fulk" is used for both the singular and the plural, and it is not of the pattern of "junub" and similar words; rather "fulk" is singular, and it was broken into the plural "fulk," so the damma of the fa' in the singular is not the same as in the plural. "Fuʿl" is a broken (plural) pattern, like "asad" and "usd." What confirms this is their saying in the dual: "fulkān."

In the exegesis it is said that those who were with Noah (peace be upon him) in the ship were forty men, and it has been said: eighty, and it has been said: ten. They were his sons: Yafith, Sam, and Ham. In many books of hadith, in al-Tirmidhi and others (p-593): "Indeed, all of creation now is from the offspring of Noah (peace be upon him)." Al-Zuhri said in the Kitab of al-Naqqash: and in the Qur'an: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [al-Isra: 3].

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: It is possible that the rest of the ten or the forty, according to the difference of opinion, were grandchildren (hafadah) of Noah (peace be upon him) and from his offspring, so that the verse and the hadith are reconciled. It is also possible that those in the ship, other than his sons, did not have descendants (lam yansil), and this has been narrated; otherwise there would be a contradiction between the hadith and the verse.

His saying, ﴿they denied Our signs﴾, implies that Noah (peace be upon him) had signs and miracles.

His saying "ʿamīn" (blind): its form is "faʿīn," and it is the plural of "ʿamin," whose form is "faʿ." It means blindness of insight. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both) that Noah (peace be upon him) was sent at the age of forty. Ibn al-Kalbi said: after Adam (peace be upon him) by eight hundred years. He brought the prohibition of daughters, sisters, mothers, maternal aunts, and paternal aunts. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Noah was sent when he was four hundred years old; it has been said: he was sent at three hundred; it has been said: at fifty. It is narrated that he lived after the flood sixty years. It is narrated that the flood occurred in the year one thousand six hundred of his life (peace be upon him). It is mentioned in the hadith of intercession and elsewhere that Noah (peace be upon him) was the first prophet sent to the people. It is also mentioned that Idris (peace be upon him) was before Noah (peace be upon him), and one of his forefathers. This can be reconciled by saying that the mission of Noah was well known for reforming people and bringing them, through the punishment and destruction, to faith. Thus the meaning is that he was the first prophet sent with this characteristic.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 65–68:**

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿And to ʿĀd, their brother Hūd. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be mindful?"﴾ ﴿The eminent ones among his people who disbelieved said: "Indeed, we see you in folly, and indeed, we think you are among the liars."﴾ ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no folly in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere, trustworthy adviser to you."﴾

"ʿĀd" is the name of the tribe. "Akhāhum" is in the accusative, governed by "arsalnā" (We sent), and it is conjoined (maʿṭūf, grammatically linked) to "Nūḥan" (Nūḥ) in the preceding verse. This is also a warning from Hūd, peace be upon him, to his people. The disagreement over the recitation (qirāʾa, a variant reading) of "ghayruh" has been mentioned earlier. His saying, "Will you not then be mindful?" is an appeal (istiʿṭāf, a tender calling) to piety and faith.

His saying, "The eminent ones said" [al-Aʿrāf: 60], and so on: the discussion of this kind of statement has already been given just above. "Al-safāha" (folly) is a verbal noun, used to express a state that is flimsy, delicate, and without firmness or quality. "Al-safah" in cloth means the lightness of its weave. From this is the saying of the poet:

*They walked as spear-shafts sway when their tips are made light*
*by the passing of the gentle spring breezes.*

Their saying "we think you" (*lanaẓunnuka*) is a supposition in its proper sense, because they had nothing but conjectures and guesswork. The disagreement over the recitation of "ublighukum" has been mentioned. As for his saying, exalted is He, "trustworthy" (*amīn*): it may mean that he is trustworthy regarding the revelation and the remembrance sent down from Allah, exalted and majestic is He. It may also mean that he is trustworthy over them, over what is hidden from them, and in desiring good for them. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is sincere in heart toward so-and-so, trustworthy in what is unseen." It may also mean "amīn" derived from "al-amn" (safety), i.e., my side is safe from lying and deceit.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah 7, verses 69–70:**

(Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:)

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah, and increased you greatly in stature. So remember the favours of Allah, that you may prosper.﴾ ﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾

The discussion of a phrase like "Do you wonder" (*awa 'ajibtum*) has already been given. *Al-dhikr* (the reminder) is a general term for admonitions, commands and prohibitions. His words, "Remember" (*wadhkurū*), up to the end of the verse, are an enumeration of the blessings bestowed upon them. *Khulafā'* (successors) is the plural of *khalīf*, like *zarīf* and *ẓurafā'*, and of *khalīfah*, whose plural is *khalā'if*. The Arabs say both *khalīfah* and *khalīf*. Abu 'Ali recited:

"If a departing one departs, his successor will be found,
but the successor of Abu Wahb is not to be found."

Al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq said: the meaning is, "He made you the inhabitants of the earth after the people of Noah, peace be upon him."

His words, "and increased you in *al-khalq* (stature) *basṭah*" (greatly), mean in creation. *Al-basṭah* is completeness in height and breadth. It was said: "He increased you over the people of your age." Al-Tabari said: the meaning is, "He increased you over the people of Noah," and Qatadah said the same.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The wording requires that the increase be over all the world, and this is what is reported about them. It is narrated that the height of a man among them was one hundred cubits, and the height of the shortest of them was sixty, and similar to this.

*Al-ā'lā'* (favours) is the plural of *ilan*, on the pattern of *mi'an*. Al-Zajjaj recited:

"White, he does not fear poverty, nor does he
sever kinship or betray *ila* (covenant)."

It was also said: the singular of *al-ā'lā'* is *alī*, on the pattern of *qafī*; and it was said: its singular is *ala*, on the pattern of *hasā*. It means blessing and favour. "That you may prosper" (*tufliḥūn*) means: that you may attain your aim and hopes.

Al-Tabari said: These 'Ād, according to what Ibn Ishaq related, were descendants of 'Ād ibn Iram ibn 'Awṣ ibn Sam ibn Noah. Their dwellings were al-Shiḥr in the land of Yemen, and what lies beyond Hadramawt up to 'Oman. Al-Suddi said: they were in al-Aḥqāf, which is sand dunes. Their lands had been the most fertile of lands, but Allah the Exalted turned them into wasteland. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: The grave of Hud, peace be upon him, is there, in a reddish sand hill mixed with clay, having acacia and lote trees. They had spread throughout the whole earth and ruled much by their strength and their numbers, and they oppressed people. They were thirteen tribes, and they were worshippers of idols, among which were one called Sida', another Sumud, and another al-Haba'. So Allah the Exalted sent to them Hud, peace be upon him, from among their best and most noble in lineage, and he called them to the Oneness of Allah the Exalted, and to abandoning injustice. Ibn Ishaq said: He did not command them, as is reported, in anything other than this. They denied him and rebelled, and this continued among them until Allah the Exalted willed to execute His command. He withheld rain from them for three years, and they suffered because of it. In that era, when people were troubled by a matter, they would resort to the Sacred Mosque in Mecca and call upon Allah the Exalted there, out of reverence for it, believers and disbelievers alike. The people of Mecca at that time were the 'Amaliq, and their chief was a man called Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr. 'Ad agreed to send a delegation from among them to Mecca to ask Allah the Exalted for rain on their behalf. They sent Qayl ibn 'Ir, Laqim ibn Hazzal, 'Uqayl ibn Ud ibn 'Ad al-Akbar, Martad ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr, who was a believer concealing his faith, and Jalhamah ibn al-Khaybari, together with seventy men from their people. When they arrived in Mecca, they stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, who was on the outskirts of Mecca, outside the Haram, and he hosted them. They remained with him for a month, drinking wine, while the two singing girls, al-Jaradatan, who belonged to Mu'awiyah, entertained them. When Mu'awiyah saw how long they stayed, though 'Ad had sent them to seek relief, he pitied 'Ad. He was the nephew of theirs, since Kalhadah, daughter of Jalhamah al-Khaybari, was his mother's kin. He said: "My maternal relatives are perishing," and it grieved him to order his guests to leave. So he complained of this to the two singing girls, and they said to him: "Compose a poem for us to sing, perhaps we may awaken them." So he said:

"Oh Qayl, woe to you, rise and hasten,
perhaps Allah will give us rain as a cloud,

that He may water the land of 'Ad, for 'Ad
have become ones who cannot speak clearly

from the severe thirst, so we do not hope
through it for the old man nor the boy,

and their women were once in goodness,
but now their women have become barren,

and the wild beasts come to them openly
and do not fear the arrows of an 'Adi,

and you are here, in what you desire,
your day and your night in continual pleasure,

so may your delegation be disgraced, from a delegation of a people
who will not even be greeted with peace."

The two singing girls sang it. When the people heard it, some of them said: "O people, your people only sent you because of what has befallen them. Enter this Sacred Precinct and supplicate, perhaps Allah the Exalted will relieve them." So they went out for that purpose. Martad ibn Sa'd said to them: "By Allah, you will not be watered because of your supplication, but if you obey your prophet and believe in him, you will be watered." He openly declared his faith that day, but the delegation opposed him and said to Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr and his father Bakr: "Hold Martad back from us, and let him not enter the Sacred Precinct with us, for he has followed Hud." They proceeded to Mecca, and Qayl ibn 'Ir asked for rain, saying: "O our God, if Hud is righteous, then give us water, for we are perishing." Allah the Exalted then produced three clouds: white, red and black. Then a caller called to him from the cloud: "O Qayl, choose for yourself and for your people from among these clouds." Qayl said: "I have chosen the black, for it contains the most water." Then it was called to him: "You have chosen a ruinous dust, which leaves none of 'Ad alive, neither parent nor child, except that it makes them lifeless." Allah the Exalted drove the black cloud that Qayl had chosen toward 'Ad, until it emerged upon them from a valley of theirs called "al-Mughith" (the Helper). When they saw it, they said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain," until it became clear that it was a wind, in which a woman of 'Ad called Mahdad was. She cried out and fell unconscious. When she recovered, she was asked: "What did you see?" She said: "I saw a wind like shooting sparks of fire, with men before it leading it." So Allah the Exalted subjected it against them for eight days and seven nights, *husūm* (continuous). *Al-ḥusūm* means continuous. It left none of 'Ad alive except that he perished. Hud and those with him withdrew into an enclosure, and the wind did not reach them except in a way that was pleasant.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a narrative that occurs at length in the tafsir of al-Tabari, and there is disagreement in it, so I have selected its essential points according to the requirements of brevity. In their report, the wind would strike them with stones and lift the litter, with a woman on it, until it threw her into the sea. In their report, their strongest man would block the path of the wind with his own body until it overpowered him and threw him into the sea, then another would take his place, until they all perished. Zayd ibn Aslam said: It reached me that a hyena reared its young in the eye-socket of a man among them. In their report, when 'Ad perished, Allah the Exalted sent a bird, or it was said lions, which carried their corpses until it cast them into the sea. This is His saying, "So they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings" (Al-Ahqaf 46:25). In some of what is reported about them, the wind was never sent except by measure, except on that day, when it overflowed upon its keepers and overpowered them. This is His saying, may He be blessed and exalted: "So they were destroyed by a violent, furious wind" (Al-Haqqah 69:6). It is also reported that Hud, when 'Ad perished, went with those who believed with him to Mecca, and they remained there until they died. Allah the Exalted knows best which of these was the case.

His saying, "They said: Have you come to us..." (to the end of the verse). The apparent meaning of their words, "alone," is that they denied that they should abandon their idols and single out Allah the Exalted for worship, while acknowledging the Creator, the Originator. It is possible that they were deniers of Allah the Exalted, and their words "that we worship Allah alone" would be according to your words, O Hud. The first interpretation is more apparent regarding them and regarding all idol-worshippers. None of the disbelievers denies the lordship of Allah the Exalted except one whose stupidity is extreme, like Arbad ibn Rabi'ah, or one who claims it for himself, like Pharaoh and Nimrod. Their words, "Then bring us," express determination in denial, contempt for the matter of prophethood, and urgency for punishment. Their words "what you threaten us with" are emphatic, since this promise was explicitly about evil. Had the mention of the promise been unqualified, it would not have come except regarding good.

So remember the favours of Allah, that you may prosper.﴾ ﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we would worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾

The discussion of a phrase like "Do you wonder" (*awa 'ajibtum*) has already been given. *Al-dhikr* (the reminder) is a general term for admonitions, commands and prohibitions. His words, "Remember" (*wadhkurū*), up to the end of the verse, are an enumeration of the blessings bestowed upon them. *Khulafā'* (successors) is the plural of *khalīf*, like *zarīf* and *ẓurafā'*, and of *khalīfah*, whose plural is *khalā'if*. The Arabs say both *khalīfah* and *khalīf*. Abu 'Ali recited:

"If a departing one departs, his successor will be found,
but the successor of Abu Wahb is not to be found."

Al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq said: the meaning is, "He made you the inhabitants of the earth after the people of Noah, peace be upon him."

His words, "and increased you in *al-khalq* (stature) *basṭah*" (greatly), mean in creation. *Al-basṭah* is completeness in height and breadth. It was said: "He increased you over the people of your age." Al-Tabari said: the meaning is, "He increased you over the people of Noah," and Qatadah said the same.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The wording requires that the increase be over all the world, and this is what is reported about them. It is narrated that the height of a man among them was one hundred cubits, and the height of the shortest of them was sixty, and similar to this.

*Al-ā'lā'* (favours) is the plural of *ilan*, on the pattern of *mi'an*. Al-Zajjaj recited:

"White, he does not fear poverty, nor does he
sever kinship or betray *ila* (covenant)."

It was also said: the singular of *al-ā'lā'* is *alī*, on the pattern of *qafī*; and it was said: its singular is *ala*, on the pattern of *hasā*. It means blessing and favour. "That you may prosper" (*tufliḥūn*) means: that you may attain your aim and hopes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 71–73:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "There has already fallen upon you from your Lord abomination and wrath. Do you dispute with me about names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority? Then wait; I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and those with him by mercy from Us, and We cut off the last of those who denied Our signs and were not believers.﴾ ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you a clear sign from your Lord: this is Allah's she-camel as a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you."﴾

He informed them that the decree had been executed, and that the *rijz* (punishment) had descended upon them. *Rijz* means wrath and punishment. It is said that *rijs* and *rijz* have the same meaning; this was stated by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. A poet said:

"When a year of drought spread over Najd,
its *rijs* and its punishment fell upon them."

The word *rijs* is also used to mean stench and filth, and dung is called *rijs* or *rikz*. This sense of *rijs* is the one borrowed for forbidden things, meaning that they should be avoided just as filth is avoided. Similar in meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the report about Jahjah al-Ghifari and Sinan ibn Wabra al-Ansari, when they called out with the calls of the Jahiliyya: "Leave it, for it is foul-smelling."

His saying, ﴿Do you dispute with me about names which you and your fathers have named?﴾ means that they were disputing with him over whether these idols should be called gods. The dispute was over the naming, not over the named things. However, the Qur'an has the verse: ﴿You worship besides Him only names which you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. Here the reference is only to the idols themselves, since the name is meant to refer to the named thing itself.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever holds that the dispute in this verse was over the essences of the idols and their worship interprets it in this way. The word *ism* (name) appears in Arabic speech with the meaning of "naming," and this is the category in which the grammarians treat it. It may also refer to the named thing itself, and the surrounding context shows this. Among such examples is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], although this too is open to interpretation. Also from this is the verse of Labid:

"Until the year is complete, then the *ism* of peace upon you both..."

This line is subject to several interpretations. The issue has already been discussed at the beginning of the book. *Sultan* means proof. His saying, ﴿Then wait; I am with you among those who wait﴾, is a warning and a threat.

The pronoun in His saying, ﴿So We saved him﴾ [al-A'raf: 83], refers to Hud, peace be upon him. That is, Allah brought him out safe and saved, together with those believers who followed him, by the mercy and grace of Allah, Exalted. Hud, peace be upon him, and those who believed with him went out until they reached Makkah, and they stayed there until they died.

﴿And We cut off the last of﴾ is a metaphor (*isti'ara*) used for a people who are uprooted by destruction. *Dabir* means the one who comes after a people and follows behind them. When the cutting off and uprooting reach this point, no one remains. His saying, ﴿who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], indicates a miracle, even if it is not specified.

His saying, Exalted, ﴿And to Thamud﴾ and what follows: this is Thamud, son of Ghabir, son of Iram, son of Sam, son of Nuh, brother of Judays ibn Ghabir. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *wa-ila Thamudin* with a kasra on the dal and tanwin throughout the Qur'an, treating it as the name of a tribe with diptote, and not diptote when it is the name of a tribe. This was stated by al-Zajjaj. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Thamud disbelieved their Lord﴾ [Hud: 68]. The meaning is: "We sent to Thamud their brother Salih," so it is coordinated with Nuh. The brotherhood here is brotherhood of kinship. Al-Zajjaj said that it may be the brotherhood of humanity, and he was called their brother when he was sent to them. They were an Arab people, and Hud and Salih, peace be upon them, were Arabs. Likewise Isma'il and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, were Arabs. So said al-Naqqash, though there is consideration regarding Isma'il, peace be upon him. Salih, peace be upon him, is Salih ibn Ubayd ibn Arim ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, as Makki mentioned. Wahb said: Allah sent him when he was near puberty. When his people perished, he set off with those who were with him to Makkah, and they stayed there until they died. Their graves are between Dar al-Nadwa and al-Hijr.

His saying, *bayyina* (clear), is an adjective. The noun it describes has been omitted and the adjective put in its place. Sibawayh said: this is ugly for an indefinite noun, to omit it and set its adjective in its place. But when the adjective is very common and well known, and it is the thing intended in reports and about peoples, the ugliness disappears, as when you say, "A slave of the sons of so-and-so came to me," meaning "A man, a slave, came to me," because "slave" is an adjective. Likewise His saying here, *bayyina*, means: a sign, or a proof, or a clear admonition. Some people said that Salih, peace be upon him, brought the she-camel of his own accord. A group, which is the majority, said rather that she was requested.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is more fitting with what has come in the reports about their affair. It is narrated that some of them said: "O Salih, if you are truthful, call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from this hill (in another narration: from this rock, a rock at al-Hijr called al-Kathiba) a pregnant she-camel." He said: So he called upon Allah, Exalted, and that hill was seized with labor pains, shook, and split open, bringing forth a great she-camel. It is narrated that she was pregnant and gave birth to her well-known young one. It is also narrated that her young one came out with her from the rock. It is narrated that one of the male camels of Thamud struck her, and she gave birth to her well-known young one. It is said that *Naqat Allah* (Allah's she-camel) is said to honor her and single her out, and it is an attribution of a creature to its Creator. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said that she was a she-camel like the rest of the she-camels, and Allah, Exalted, made for her a share of water one day, and for them a share of water one day. The sign was in her drinking and her milking.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: "She was a she-camel who came out from among their camels, and she did not give milk." But what the people hold is stronger and more sound than this. The commentators said: She was a great wonder; she would come to the water between two mountains, and they would crowd her because of her size. She shared the water with Thamud, day by day. She would come on her day and take the full water of the well of Hamshari, and they would milk her as much milk as they wished. Then she would remain a day, and come again after that every other day. This continued as long as Allah willed, until Thamud killed her. They said: "What do we do with the milk? Water is more beloved to us than it." The cause of the weariness, as is reported, was that she used to spend summer in the bottom of the valley, the Valley of al-Hijr, and winter on its upper part. Their livestock would flee from her, so she summered on the back of the valley for the heat and wintered in its bottom for the cold. Because of this, they were corrupted, so they agreed together to kill the she-camel. Salih, peace be upon him, once said to them: "This month a boy will be born whose hands will bring about your destruction." Ten men had sons born, and nine of them slaughtered their sons, but the tenth remained, and he was Salif, the father of Qidar. Qidar grew up red and blue-eyed. Whenever the nine saw him they said: "If our sons had lived, they would have been like this." This made them resentful, so they killed their sons because of the words of Salih. Then they agreed to kill him, peace be upon him. They went out and hid in a cave to ambush him, peace be upon him, and they swore an oath: ﴿We will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will surely say to his heir: We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾ [al-Naml: 49]. The cave collapsed upon them, and they died. They are the nine men whom Allah, Exalted, mentioned in His Book.

Qidar ibn Salif and Mis'da ibn Mihraj resolved, and they added seven men to themselves, and they determined to hamstring the she-camel. It is narrated that the reason for this was that two women of Thamud, enemies of Salih, peace be upon him, offered themselves and their wealth to Qidar and Mis'da on condition that they hamstring the she-camel. They were women of beauty. It was also said that Qidar drank wine with a people, and they sought water to mix with the wine but did not find it, because the she-camel was drinking it. So they then resolved to hamstring her. They went out and sat on her path, and Qidar hid for her behind a rock. When she came near him, he struck her with a spear, then she fell, and he slaughtered her. Then they pursued the young one, and it fled from them until it climbed a hill, and it cried out three times and called for help. They caught up with it and hamstrung it. In some reports, they found the young one on a high ground, and when they wanted it, it rose with it until it reached the sky, and they could not reach it. The young one cried out, seeking help from Allah, blessed and exalted. So Allah revealed to Salih, peace be upon him, that he should say to them: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days." Al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: Allah, Exalted, made the young one speak, and it called out: "Where is my mother?" Salih, peace be upon him, said to them: "Indeed, the punishment will fall upon you on the fourth day after the hamstringing of the she-camel." It is narrated that she was hamstrung on Wednesday. Salih, peace be upon him, said to them: "Your faces will turn red tomorrow, will turn yellow on the second day, and will turn black on the third day, and the punishment will descend on the fourth day, Sunday." When the sign he had told them about appeared, they were certain, and they prepared themselves, smeared their bodies with *manna*, dug graves, and perfumed themselves with camphor. Then the Shout seized them, and Salih, peace be upon him, and those with him went out until they settled at Ramla in Palestine.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I have condensed this narrative from a lot which al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, related, out of a desire for brevity.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: I came to the land of Thamud and measured the chest of the she-camel, and I found it to be sixty cubits.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The land of Thamud lies between Syria and Madinah. It is the place through which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed with the Muslims during the expedition to Tabuk, and he said: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them." Then he covered his head with his turban and hastened his pace (ﷺ).

It is narrated that the distance whose people the Shout destroyed is eighteen miles. It consists of the land of al-Hijr, its pastures al-Janab, and Hasmi as far as Wadi al-Qura and what surrounds it. It was said of Qidar that he was born out of wedlock, from a man called Zabyan, but he was born on the bed of Salif, so he was attributed to him. Qatada and others mentioned this. al-Tabari mentioned that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by a grave and said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "No." He said: "This is the grave of Abu Righal, who is the father of Thaqif. He was from Thamud. The calamity befell his people while he was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and he was safe. When he went out of the Sacred Precinct, what had befallen them befell him, so he was buried here, and a golden branch was placed with him." Do you dispute with me about names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority? Then wait; I am with you among those who wait."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and those with him by mercy from Us, and We cut off the last of those who denied Our signs and were not believers.﴾ ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you a clear sign from your Lord: this is Allah's she-camel as a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you."﴾

He informed them that the decree had been executed, and that the *rijz* (punishment) had descended upon them. *Rijz* means wrath and punishment. It is said that *rijs* and *rijz* have the same meaning; this was stated by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. A poet said:

"When a year of drought spread over Najd,
its *rijs* and its punishment fell upon them."

The word *rijs* is also used to mean stench and filth, and dung is called *rijs* or *rikz*. This sense of *rijs* is the one borrowed for forbidden things, meaning that they should be avoided just as filth is avoided. Similar in meaning is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the report about Jahjah al-Ghifari and Sinan ibn Wabra al-Ansari, when they called out with the calls of the Jahiliyya: "Leave it, for it is foul-smelling."

The dispute was over the naming, not over the named things. However, the Qur'an has the verse: ﴿You worship besides Him only names which you have named﴾ [Yusuf: 40]. Here the reference is only to the idols themselves, since the name is meant to refer to the named thing itself.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever holds that the dispute in this verse was over the essences of the idols and their worship interprets it in this way. The word *ism* (name) appears in Arabic speech with the meaning of "naming," and this is the category in which the grammarians treat it. It may also refer to the named thing itself, and the surrounding context shows this. Among such examples is the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], although this too is open to interpretation. Also from this is the verse of Labid:

"Until the year is complete, then the *ism* of peace upon you both..."

This line is subject to several interpretations. The issue has already been discussed at the beginning of the book. *Sultan* means proof. His saying, ﴿Then wait; I am with you among those who wait﴾, is a warning and a threat.

The pronoun in His saying, ﴿So We saved him﴾ [al-A'raf: 83], refers to Hud, peace be upon him. That is, Allah brought him out safe and saved, together with those believers who followed him, by the mercy and grace of Allah, Exalted. Hud, peace be upon him, and those who believed with him went out until they reached Makkah, and they stayed there until they died.

﴿And We cut off the last of﴾ is a metaphor (*isti'ara*) used for a people who are uprooted by destruction. *Dabir* means the one who comes after a people and follows behind them. When the cutting off and uprooting reach this point, no one remains. His saying, ﴿who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 64], indicates a miracle, even if it is not specified.

His saying, Exalted, ﴿And to Thamud﴾ and what follows: this is Thamud, son of Ghabir, son of Iram, son of Sam, son of Nuh, brother of Judays ibn Ghabir. They were an Arab people, and Hud and Salih, peace be upon them, were Arabs. Likewise Isma'il and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, were Arabs. So said al-Naqqash, though there is consideration regarding Isma'il, peace be upon him. Salih, peace be upon him, is Salih ibn Ubayd ibn Arim ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, as Makki mentioned. Wahb said: Allah sent him when he was near puberty. When his people perished, he set off with those who were with him to Makkah, and they stayed there until they died. Their graves are between Dar al-Nadwa and al-Hijr.

His saying, *bayyina* (clear), is an adjective. The noun it describes has been omitted and the adjective put in its place. Sibawayh said: this is ugly for an indefinite noun, to omit it and set its adjective in its place. But when the adjective is very common and well known, and it is the thing intended in reports and about peoples, the ugliness disappears, as when you say, "A slave of the sons of so-and-so came to me," meaning "A man, a slave, came to me," because "slave" is an adjective. Likewise His saying here, *bayyina*, means: a sign, or a proof, or a clear admonition. Some people said that Salih, peace be upon him, brought the she-camel of his own accord. A group, which is the majority, said rather that she was requested.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is more fitting with what has come in the reports about their affair. It is narrated that some of them said: "O Salih, if you are truthful, call upon your Lord to bring forth for us from this hill (in another narration: from this rock, a rock at al-Hijr called al-Kathiba) a pregnant she-camel." He said: So he called upon Allah, Exalted, and that hill was seized with labor pains, shook, and split open, bringing forth a great she-camel. It is narrated that she was pregnant and gave birth to her well-known young one. It is also narrated that her young one came out with her from the rock. It is narrated that one of the male camels of Thamud struck her, and she gave birth to her well-known young one. It is said that *Naqat Allah* (Allah's she-camel) is said to honor her and single her out, and it is an attribution of a creature to its Creator. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said that she was a she-camel like the rest of the she-camels, and Allah, Exalted, made for her a share of water one day, and for them a share of water one day. The sign was in her drinking and her milking.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: "She was a she-camel who came out from among their camels, and she did not give milk." But what the people hold is stronger and more sound than this. The commentators said: She was a great wonder; she would come to the water between two mountains, and they would crowd her because of her size. She shared the water with Thamud, day by day. She would come on her day and take the full water of the well of Hamshari, and they would milk her as much milk as they wished. Then she would remain a day, and come again after that every other day. This continued as long as Allah willed, until Thamud killed her. They said: "What do we do with the milk? Water is more beloved to us than it." The cause of the weariness, as is reported, was that she used to spend summer in the bottom of the valley, the Valley of al-Hijr, and winter on its upper part. Their livestock would flee from her, so she summered on the back of the valley for the heat and wintered in its bottom for the cold. Because of this, they were corrupted, so they agreed together to kill the she-camel. Salih, peace be upon him, once said to them: "This month a boy will be born whose hands will bring about your destruction." Ten men had sons born, and nine of them slaughtered their sons, but the tenth remained, and he was Salif, the father of Qidar. Qidar grew up red and blue-eyed. Whenever the nine saw him they said: "If our sons had lived, they would have been like this." This made them resentful, so they killed their sons because of the words of Salih. Then they agreed to kill him, peace be upon him. They went out and hid in a cave to ambush him, peace be upon him, and they swore an oath: ﴿We will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will surely say to his heir: We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾ [al-Naml: 49]. The cave collapsed upon them, and they died. They are the nine men whom Allah, Exalted, mentioned in His Book.

Qidar ibn Salif and Mis'da ibn Mihraj resolved, and they added seven men to themselves, and they determined to hamstring the she-camel. It is narrated that the reason for this was that two women of Thamud, enemies of Salih, peace be upon him, offered themselves and their wealth to Qidar and Mis'da on condition that they hamstring the she-camel. They were women of beauty. It was also said that Qidar drank wine with a people, and they sought water to mix with the wine but did not find it, because the she-camel was drinking it. So they then resolved to hamstring her. They went out and sat on her path, and Qidar hid for her behind a rock. When she came near him, he struck her with a spear, then she fell, and he slaughtered her. Then they pursued the young one, and it fled from them until it climbed a hill, and it cried out three times and called for help. They caught up with it and hamstrung it. In some reports, they found the young one on a high ground, and when they wanted it, it rose with it until it reached the sky, and they could not reach it. The young one cried out, seeking help from Allah, blessed and exalted. So Allah revealed to Salih, peace be upon him, that he should say to them: "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days." Al-Naqqash transmitted from al-Hasan that he said: Allah, Exalted, made the young one speak, and it called out: "Where is my mother?" Salih, peace be upon him, said to them: "Indeed, the punishment will fall upon you on the fourth day after the hamstringing of the she-camel." It is narrated that she was hamstrung on Wednesday. Salih, peace be upon him, said to them: "Your faces will turn red tomorrow, will turn yellow on the second day, and will turn black on the third day, and the punishment will descend on the fourth day, Sunday." When the sign he had told them about appeared, they were certain, and they prepared themselves, smeared their bodies with *manna*, dug graves, and perfumed themselves with camphor. Then the Shout seized them, and Salih, peace be upon him, and those with him went out until they settled at Ramla in Palestine.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I have condensed this narrative from a lot which al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, related, out of a desire for brevity.

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: I came to the land of Thamud and measured the chest of the she-camel, and I found it to be sixty cubits.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The land of Thamud lies between Syria and Madinah. It is the place through which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed with the Muslims during the expedition to Tabuk, and he said: "Do not enter the dwellings of those who wronged themselves unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them." Then he covered his head with his turban and hastened his pace (ﷺ).

It is narrated that the distance whose people the Shout destroyed is eighteen miles. It consists of the land of al-Hijr, its pastures al-Janab, and Hasmi as far as Wadi al-Qura and what surrounds it. It was said of Qidar that he was born out of wedlock, from a man called Zabyan, but he was born on the bed of Salif, so he was attributed to him. Qatada and others mentioned this. al-Tabari mentioned that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by a grave and said: "Do you know what this is?" They said: "No." He said: "This is the grave of Abu Righal, who is the father of Thaqif. He was from Thamud. The calamity befell his people while he was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and he was safe. When he went out of the Sacred Precinct, what had befallen them befell him, so he was buried here, and a golden branch was placed with him." He said: So the people rushed with their swords, and they dug until they brought out the branch.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This report supports what is in the biographies, that Abu Righal was the guide of the Elephant and its leader to Makkah. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 74–76:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of ʿĀd and settled you in the land, taking for yourselves palaces in its plains and carving out the mountains as houses. So remember the bounties of Allah, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief.﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed: "Do you know that Ṣāliḥ is one sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in that with which he has been sent."﴾ ﴿Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that which you have believed."﴾

"Wa-bawwaʾakum" (and He settled you): its meaning is "makkanakum" (He established you). It is used with regard to a place and its locations. You say, "tabawwaʾa fulānun manzilan ḥasanan" (so-and-so occupied a good dwelling). From this is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He settles the believers in positions for battle﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 121]. And al-Aʿshā said:

"Fa-mā bawwaʾa al-Raḥmānu baytaka manzilan / bi-sharqiyyi Ajyādi al-Ṣafā wal-Muḥarrami"
(The Most Merciful did not settle your House in a dwelling / on the eastern side of Ajyād, al-Ṣafā and al-Muḥarram.)

"Al-quṣūr" (palaces): the plural of "qaṣr," which are the houses that are "quṣirat" (confined) to specific plots of land, unlike the houses of tent-poles; and they are "quṣirat" from people entirely.

"Al-naḥt" (carving): cutting and shaving something hard, such as stone, wood, and the like.

al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan read "wa-tanḥatūna" with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ; the majority of people read it with a kasrah and with a tāʾ from above. Ibn Muṣarrif read it with a yāʾ from below and a kasrah on the ḥāʾ; Abū Mālik read it with a yāʾ from below and a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ. They used to carve the mountains because of the length of their lifespans.

"Taʿthaw" (commit corruption): its meaning is "tufsidū" (you cause corruption). It is said: "ʿathā, yaʿthī," and "ʿathā, yaʿthū," and "ʿathiya, yaʿthā," like "nasiya, yansā." The wording of the verse follows the latter. al-Aʿmash read "tiʿthaw" with a kasrah on the tāʾ. "Mufsidīna" (causing mischief) is a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

The discussion of "al-malaʾ" (the eminent ones) has already been mentioned. Ibn ʿĀmir alone read in this place "wa-qāla al-malaʾu," with the conjunctive wāw, which is elided according to all.

"Alladhīna istakbarū" (those who were arrogant) are the notables and great ones who were disbelievers. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-A'raf, verses 77–79:**

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel, and rebelled against the command of their Lord, and said, "O Salih, bring us what you have threatened us with, if you are one of the messengers." Then the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes in the morning.﴾ ﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I have certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord, and advised you, but you do not love those who give advice."﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿"fa-'aqarū"﴾ (so they hamstrung): by including them all in the pronoun, it implies that the hamstringing of the she-camel was done by a unanimous agreement and collective consensus among them. Accordingly, it is related that Qidar did not hamstring her until he had consulted the men, the women and the children. When they all agreed, he took it upon himself and hamstrung her. (p. 605)

As for "wa-'ataw" (and they rebelled): its meaning is that they were arrogant and obstinate, did not submit to the command and the Law, insisted on denying him, and hastened the vengeance by their saying, ﴿"bring us what you threaten us with"﴾. The word "promise" is apt in this context, since it was restricted to being a punishment.

Abu Hatim said: 'Isa and 'Asim read "ītinā" with a hamza and a prolonged ḍamma. Abu 'Amr and al-A'mash read it with the hamza lightened, so that it sounds like a yā' in pronunciation.

As for "al-rajfa" (the earthquake): it is what the cry or the overwhelming calamity produces, by which a person trembles. It means to be shaken, to move, to be agitated, and to quiver. From this comes the saying of Khadija, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned with her, his heart trembling (yarjufu fuʾaduhu)." From this also is the verse of al-Akhtal:

"Though you see me, my white hair has bent me with age, / I tremble like a vulture, while a man is stretched out (on the ground)."

From it also comes "irjāf al-nufūs" (the agitation of souls) for disturbing news, meaning its stirring up. It is related that the cry of Thamud contained the sounds of everything with a terrifying voice, and it was excessive. It split their hearts, so they fell upon their chests. And "al-jāthim" (the prostrate): one who lies flat on the ground upon his chest, with his legs drawn in, as a hare and birds crouch, for their crouching is upon their faces. From it is the saying of Jarir:

"I knew the place of the pitching, and I knew from it / the riding beasts of the cooking-pot like the crouching embers."

Some of the exegetes said: its meaning is "burnt coals, charred like the crouching ashes."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Wherever "al-ramād al-jāthim" (crouching ashes) is found in poetry, it is only used metaphorically for the appearance of ashes before they die down and scatter. The proponent of this view held that the cry was accompanied by burning thunderbolts.

Allah, may He be exalted, informed of Salih's action in turning away from them at the time they hamstrung the she-camel and said, ﴿"bring us what you threaten us with"﴾. This was before the punishment descended. Accordingly, it is related that he, upon him be peace, went out from among them before the punishment descended, and this is what his address to them requires. As for the wording of the verse, it may be that he addressed them while they were dead, out of grief for them and mention of their condition, or for some other reason, just as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed the people of the well of Badr. al-Tabari said: It was said that no nation perishes while its prophet is with it. It is related that he, upon him be peace, set out with those who were with him until he came to Makkah, and he stayed there until he died. The word "turning away" implies despair of their good and certainty of their destruction.

His saying, ﴿"but you do not love those who give advice"﴾, is an expression of their preferring desires over sound judgement, since the speech of the adviser is hard and opposes the desire of the one being advised. For this reason the Arabs say: "The command of your tear-jerkers, not the command of your laughers."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 80–84:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And [We sent] Lot, when he said to his people: "Do you commit an abomination such as no one in the worlds has committed before you?"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, you approach men lustfully instead of women. Rather, you are a people who transgress."﴾ ﴿But the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel them from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was among those who remained behind.﴾ ﴿And We rained upon them a rain [of stones], so observe how was the end of the criminals.﴾

(p-607) "Lot" (peace be upon him): Allah the Exalted sent him to a nation called "Sodom" (Sadum). It is narrated that he was the nephew of Abraham (peace be upon him). His being in the accusative case is either governed by "arsalna" (We sent), mentioned earlier concerning the prophets, or by a verb understood, its implied meaning being: "And mention Lot." His question to them is in the form of rebuke, reproach and censure.

"Al-fahisha" (the abomination) here means having intercourse with men in their anuses. It is narrated that this sin had not been committed by any nation before them.

The shaykh Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Although the wording of the verse implies this, the verse could also mean: "No one preceded you in persisting in it and openly displaying it." It is narrated that they would approach one another; and it is narrated that they used to approach only strangers, as said by al-Hasan al-Basri. 'Amr ibn Dinar said: "No male mounted a male before the people of Lot (peace be upon him)." Al-Naqqash related that Iblis was the origin of their practice, since he invited them to himself. Some scholars said: the perpetrator of sodomy is like the fornicator. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) and others said: he is to be stoned, whether he is married or not. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) burned a man called "al-Fajah" when he committed the deed of the people of Lot (peace be upon him).

Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read "innakum" as a statement, as if it explains the abomination. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him) and Hamza read "a-innakum" with another interrogative; this is because the first is a question about an general matter, and the second about a specified one. Yet Hamza and 'Asim read with two hamzas, while Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir pronounced only one.

"Shahwatan" (lustfully) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), from your saying: "shahiitu al-shay'a, shahaatan" (I desired the thing). The meaning: you leave aside the intended purpose of intercourse, which is seeking the offspring that Allah the Exalted has decreed, and you single out mere desire alone.

His saying: ﴿"Rather, you"﴾ is a turning away from speaking about them, or a confirmation of them in the sin and a leaving of that, moving to the judgment upon them that they are a people who have exceeded the limit and committed what is forbidden. "Al-israf" (transgression) is excessive corruption.

The majority read "jawaba" (answer) in the accusative; al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "jawabu" in the nominative. The response of his people was not by argument from them, nor by rational defence; rather it was by disbelief, harshness and pure abandonment, in their saying: ﴿"Expel them"﴾, and their justification for expulsion by the purity of those who expel. The pronoun refers to Lot (peace be upon him) and his family; although no mention of them had preceded, the meaning requires them. It is narrated that he had with him none but his two daughters, and on this basis the pronoun covers him and his two daughters. "Yatatahharun" means: they keep themselves distant from our condition and our custom. Mujahid said: its meaning is that they keep themselves pure from the anuses of men and women. Qatada said: they found fault with them without fault, and blamed them without cause. The difference regarding "his family" is as previously mentioned.

Allah the Exalted made an exception of Lot's wife (peace be upon him) from those saved, and informed that she perished. "Al-ghabir" means: the remaining. This is the well-known meaning in the language, and from it comes "ghubar al-hayd" (the residue of menstruation), as Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

Free from every residue of menstruation, and from the corruption of a nursing mother and a debilitating disease.

And "ghubar al-laban fi al-dar'" is its remnant: some exegetes said: she was among those who remained behind in the punishment and retribution, meaning: "with those who remain, among those who were not saved." Abu 'Ubayda Mu'ammar said: Allah mentioned her as one who had grown old and remained from his era into the era of others, so she was a remainder until she perished along with her people.

Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems that His saying, "except his wife," suffices by itself to show that she was not saved; then He began describing her afterwards with a description that is related neither to salvation nor to destruction. The first is more apparent. "Al-ghabir" may come in the sense of "the past," and so the lexicographers related "ghabara" in the sense of "remained" and in the sense of "passed away." As for the verse of al-A'sha:

He bit with what the sponsors left him of his mother, in the bygone time.

The apparent meaning is that he meant the past, referring to the time of the satire; it is possible that he meant "in the remaining time," referring to the present, which is a remainder after leaving; and it is possible that "fi al-zaman" is linked to "bit," so that "al-ghabir" means "the remaining" absolutely. The first is more apparent.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿"And We rained upon them"﴾ and the rest of the verse is an explicit statement of rain; and the verses in other surahs are consistent that it was of stones. It is narrated that Allah the Exalted sent Jibril (peace be upon him), who uprooted them with his wing; they were six cities, and it was said five, and it was said four. He lifted them until the people of the heavens heard the braying of donkeys and the crowing of roosters; then he overturned them, made their upper part lower, and sent them down to the earth. The stones followed them besides this, and destroyed whoever among them was on a journey or outside the raised areas. The wife of Lot (peace be upon him), when she heard the commotion, said: "Oh my people!" and turned around; then a rock struck her and killed her.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. So give full measure and weight, and do not deprive the people of their due, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation. That is better for you, if you are believers."﴾ ﴿"And do not sit on every path, threatening and turning away from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He multiplied you. And observe how was the end of the corrupters."﴾

It is said regarding "Madyan" that it is the name of a town and region; it is said that it is the name of a tribe; and it is said that they are descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil ('alayhi al-salam). It is narrated that Lut ('alayhi al-salam) was the maternal grandfather of Shu'ayb; and Makki said: he was the husband of the daughter of Lut. Whoever regards "Madyan" as the name of a man does not declension it, because it is a non-Arabic proper noun; and whoever regards it as the name of a tribe or a land, it is more fitting that it not take declension.

His saying, "akhahum" (their brother), is in the accusative governed by the verb of His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿We sent﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] at the beginning of the narratives. This supports that "Lut" was governed by it, and that the wording is continuous. This brotherhood is one of kinship. The discussion of "ghayruhu" and "ghayrahu" has already been mentioned. "Al-bayyinah" (the clear evidence) refers to his miracle, although we have not been given an explicit text about it.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited: "qad ja'atkum ayatun min Rabbikum" (a sign has come to you from your Lord) in place of "bayyinah".

His saying, ﴿fa-awfu al-kayla﴾ (so give full measure), is a command to them to be upright in giving; and it is, in meaning, [applicable] to both taking and giving. This sin had spread among them in that era, and it was grave alongside their disbelief, on account of which the earthquake (al-rajfah) seized them. "Tabkhasu" (deprive) means: wrong; and from it is their saying: "You consider her foolish, while she is a deceiving wrongdoer" (bakhisun), i.e., unjust and deceptive. "Ashya'ahum" (their due) means their wealth and their goods, of what is measured by volume or weighed.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and do not cause corruption﴾, is a general term for both minor and major corruption; and likewise reform is general. The commentators have stated that the reference to corruption is to disbelief, and to reform is to prophethoods and laws. His saying, ﴿That is better for you﴾, means: beneficial in the sight of Allah Exalted, bringing about His success and His good pleasure, on condition of faith and monotheism; otherwise no deed benefits without faith.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And do not sit on every path﴾, etc. Al-Suddi said: this is a prohibition against tax collectors, toll agents, and the like, from taking people's wealth unjustly. "Al-sirat" means the road. (Their practice was to do much of this, because it is of the same kind as their deprivation and their shortchanging in measure and weight.) Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: it is a prohibition against robbery and highway banditry, and that was their practice; and he narrated in this regard a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 85–86:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. It is said regarding "Madyan" that it is the name of a town and region; it is said that it is the name of a tribe; and it is said that they are descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil ('alayhi al-salam). It is narrated that Lut ('alayhi al-salam) was the maternal grandfather of Shu'ayb; and Makki said: he was the husband of the daughter of Lut. Whoever regards "Madyan" as the name of a man does not declension it, because it is a non-Arabic proper noun; and whoever regards it as the name of a tribe or a land, it is more fitting that it not take declension.

His saying, "akhahum" (their brother), is in the accusative governed by the verb of His saying (Exalted is He) ﴿We sent﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] at the beginning of the narratives. This supports that "Lut" was governed by it, and that the wording is continuous. This brotherhood is one of kinship. The discussion of "ghayruhu" and "ghayrahu" has already been mentioned. "Al-bayyinah" (the clear evidence) refers to his miracle, although we have not been given an explicit text about it.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited: "qad ja'atkum ayatun min Rabbikum" (a sign has come to you from your Lord) in place of "bayyinah".

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 87:

(p-612) His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent and a group who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾

The meaning: "And if you, O my people, have disagreed concerning me, and have split your affair by your disbelief, so that one group has believed and another group has disbelieved, then be patient, O disbelievers, until the judgment of Allah the Exalted comes between me and you."

In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿"Then be patient"﴾, there is the force of threat and warning; this is the apparent sense of the speech, and that the address in the whole verse is to the disbelievers.

Mundhir ibn Sa'id reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the address with His saying "Then be patient" is to the believers, in the sense of a promise to them. Muqatil ibn Hayyan also said this. Al-Naqqash said: Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: the meaning is, "Then be patient, O company of disbelievers."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the view of the majority (al-jama'a).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 88–89:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said: "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion." He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ ﴿We would have fabricated a lie against God if we returned to your religion after God had rescued us from it. It is not for us to return to it, unless God, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In God we put our trust. Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of deciders.﴾

The meaning of "al-mala'" (the eminent ones, the notables) has already been discussed, as has the meaning of arrogance (istikbar). Their saying, ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb﴾ [p. 613], is a threat of exile. "Al-qarya" (the town) is the city that gathers people together, because it "taqarra," that is, it is gathered. Their saying, ﴿or you will return to our religion﴾, means: "or you will become" (in our religion). The verb "'ada" (to return) is used in the speech of the Arabs in two ways:

The first: a thing returns to a state it was in before. In this sense it is intransitive; if it is made transitive, it takes a preposition. From this is the saying of the poet:

"If the scorpion returns, we return to it, and the sandal is ready for it."

From it is the saying of another:

"Would that the days of youth were renewed, and the bygone age would return, O Buthayna."

From it is the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿Even if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. From it is the saying of the poet:

"If the days were kinder to me once, then the sins of those days have returned in turn."

The second way: it means "to become" (sara), and it governs its predicate as "sara" does, and does not imply that the state existed earlier. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Those are noble deeds? Not two bowls of milk mixed with water, which then became urine."

And from it is the saying of another:

"My head became like the thaghama (white plant)."

And from it is the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿until it became like the old curved date-stalk﴾ [Ya-Sin: 39]. However, this is open to interpretation. His saying in the verse, ﴿or you will return﴾, while Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, had never been a disbeliever, requires that the verb here means "become." As for the believers after their disbelief, the other meaning applies to them, and Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, is excluded from it, unless they meant his returning to the state of his silence before he was sent (as a prophet).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Even if we were unwilling?﴾ is a challenge from him to them concerning the heinousness of their disobedience, and a request that they confess with their tongues that they expel the believers in God, the Exalted, by compulsion, unjustly and oppressively.

In His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We would have fabricated a lie against God if we returned to your religion﴾, the apparent meaning is that it is a report from them: that is, "We would indeed be committing a great offence and fabricating against God, the Exalted, a lie, by returning to disbelief." It may also be understood as an oath in the form of a supplication, like the saying of the poet:

"I have remained with my wealth..."

And as you say: "I have fabricated against God, the Exalted, if I speak to so-and-so." The meaning of "iftaraynā" (we fabricated) is: we split (our speech) by the word and disagreed. From this is the saying of 'Aisha, may God be pleased with her: "Whoever claims that Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord has greatly fabricated against God."

Shu'ayb's deliverance from their religion was from the very beginning of his mission, while the deliverance of those who believed with him came after they had fallen into disbelief.

His saying, ﴿unless God wills﴾, may be understood to mean: "unless a bad predestination from God, the Exalted, precedes us in this matter, and a decree that cannot be reversed is carried out by Him, the Exalted."

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: The believers are the ones who might be permitted to do this, but Shu'ayb has been protected by prophethood, and this is the most evident meaning the statement can bear. It may also be understood to mean an exception concerning what God, the Exalted, may be worshipped by the believers through, among the acts of worship performed by the disbelievers. When he said to them, "We will not return to your religion," then feared that God might be worshipped through some of the acts of the disbelievers, so that some heretic would oppose him with this and say, "This is a return to our religion," he made an exception for the will of God, Blessed and Exalted, concerning whatever God may be worshipped through. It may also be understood to mean the sense of remote improbability, as you say: "I will not do such-and-such until the raven turns white, and until the camel passes through the eye of the needle." It is known that this is impossible, so it is a reference to something impossible.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This interpretation belongs only to the Mu'tazila (the rationalist theological school), whose doctrine is that disbelief and faith are not by the will of God, the Exalted. Therefore this interpretation follows only from their view. This is an interpretation transmitted by the exegetes, though they were not aware of its implications. It has also been said that this exception is merely a concealment and a matter of courtesy.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This interpretation is weakened by the position of the exception. Had the statement been "in shā' Allāh" (if God wills) at the beginning, this interpretation would have been stronger.

His saying, ﴿Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, means: "The knowledge of our Lord, the Exalted, encompasses all things," as you say: "Zayd perspired sweat," that is, "the sweat of Zayd perspired." And "wasi'a" (encompassed) is in the sense of "ahāṭa" (surrounded).

His saying, "iftaḥ" (decide), means: "judge." And "al-fātiḥ" and "al-fattāḥ" mean: the judge, in the dialect of Himyar. It has also been said: in the dialect of Murad. Some of them said:

"Ah, convey a message to the Banu Usm, for I am independent of your judgment."

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: Every prophet who wished God, the Exalted, to destroy his people, was commanded to supplicate against them; then God, the Exalted, answered him and destroyed them. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, said: I did not know the meaning of this word until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say to her husband, "Come, let me decide between us (uftiḥuka)," that is, "let me judge between you and me."

His saying, ﴿In God we put our trust﴾, is a submission to God, the Exalted, and a holding fast to His grace. This supports the first interpretation of His saying, ﴿unless God wills﴾.
