Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 90–93:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And the chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "If you follow Shu'ayb, then indeed you will be losers."﴾ ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became in their home prostrate corpses.﴾ ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—it was as if they had never dwelt therein. Those who denied Shu'ayb—they were the losers.﴾ ﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you, so how should I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾

This statement was made by the chiefs (al-mala') to their followers and to the rest of the people who imitated them.

And "al-Rajfah" (the earthquake): a severe quake by which a person is affected with shaking, trembling and agitation.

(p-617) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is possible that one group of the people of Shu'ayb were destroyed by the rajfah and another group by the zullah (the cloud-canopy). It is also possible that the zullah and the rajfah occurred at one and the same time. It has been narrated that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, sent Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to the people of Madyan and to the companions of al-Aykah (the thicket). It was said: they were two groups; and it was said: they were one group. With their disbelief, they used to diminish the measure and the weight. He called them, and they denied him, so this dispute that preceded took place between them. When they transgressed, and the period lengthened for them, Allah the Exalted opened for them a gate from the gates of Hell, and the heat from it destroyed them, so neither shade nor water benefited them. Then He sent a cloud in which was a pleasant wind; they found the coolness and pleasantness of the wind, so they called out to one another: "Take shelter under the zullah!" When they gathered beneath the zullah—and it was that cloud—it closed over them and destroyed them.

al-Tabari said: It reached me that a man from the people of Madyan, called 'Amr ibn Jalha', said when he saw it:

Poetry:
O my people, indeed Shu'ayb is a messenger, so leave aside
from you Samir and 'Imran ibn Shaddad.

I see a cloud, O my people, that has risen,
calling with a voice over the stony valley.

And if you see in it a morning of tomorrow,
there will be nothing but al-Raqim walking between its hills.

Samir and 'Imran: their soothsayers (kahinuhum); and al-Raqim: their dog. It has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when he mentioned Shu'ayb: "That is the orator of the prophets" (dhalika khatib al-anbiya'); in reference to his saying to his people: ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in that which I forbid you from. I intend only reform as much as I am able. And my success is not except through Allah. Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back.﴾ [Hud: 88].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He means: because of the goodness of his re-admonition and the beauty of his gentleness.

al-Tabari related from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Bajali that he said: Abu Jad, Hawwaz, Huttī, (p-618) Kalamun, Sa'fas and Qarshat are the names of the kings of Madyan; and the king on the day of the zullah was "Kalamun." So his sister lamented him, saying:

Poetry:
Kalamun—my pillar has been demolished by his destruction in the midst of the settlement.
The lord of the people, death came upon him, a fire, in the midst of a canopy.
They were made a fire upon them; their dwelling became like something dissolved.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a report that is only supposed (mazhunun bi-ha), and Allah the Exalted knows best. The meaning of "jathimin" has already been mentioned.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein﴾: an expression which contains information about the completeness of their destruction, the descent of retribution upon them, and an alert to the lesson in them. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

Poetry:
As if there had not been between al-Hajun and al-Safa ...................

And "yaghnaw" means: they remained and dwelt.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Ghaniytu fi al-makan" is said only of a stay that is accompanied by luxury and a pleasant, comfortable life; this is what I have inferred from the verses in which the Arabs used this word. Among them is the saying of the poet:

Poetry:
And indeed we dwelt therein, and we saw ages
in which they led us, the tender maidens, gracefully...

(p-619) And from it is the saying of another:

Poetry:
And indeed your neighbours dwelt therein, those
who hold fast to you a covenant and union...

al-Tabari recited it. And from it is the saying of another:

Poetry:
Ala, call out for the sake of the beloved, the abodes (al-maghani)...................

And from it is the saying of Muhalhil:

Poetry:
Our abode in Tihama dwelt in the age, and in it the sons of Ma'add settled...

It is likely that the word is from "al-istighna'" (self-sufficiency). As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as if it had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus: 24]; it contains this meaning, because what is meant is: "as if it had not been luxuriant, fresh and self-sufficient"; and it is not found, to my knowledge, except accompanied by this meaning. As for the saying of the poet:

Poetry:
We were self-sufficient for a time with poverty and wealth, and each of them was given to drink by time in its cup...

(p-620) its meaning is: we were content with that and accepted it, although this word is not connected with a place.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾, up to the end of the verse, is a statement which implies that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, felt within himself, when he saw the destruction of his people, grief and compassion, since his hope for them had been otherwise. (p-5) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Never did We send a prophet to a town without afflicting its people with adversity and hardship, that perhaps they might humble themselves.﴾ ﴿Then We substituted good for evil, until they multiplied and said, "Hardship and ease touched our forefathers too." So We seized them suddenly, while they were unaware.﴾ ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from heaven and earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they had earned.﴾

This verse is a report from God, Mighty and Majestic, that He never sent a prophet to a city (and the city is the qarya) without seizing its people who denied him with hardship (al-ba'sa') — which means calamities in wealth, worries, and the accidents of time — and adversity (al-darra') — which means calamities in the body, such as sicknesses and the like. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and of many of the people of lexicography. He related from al-Suddi something implying that the two terms overlap, so that each is said of both meanings. "Perhaps" (la'alla) expresses expectation according to human belief and assumption. "Yadarra'un" means they submit themselves to faith. Similarly, the saying: "Fever humbled me before You" (al-humma adra'atni laka).

Then He said, Exalted is He, that after carrying out the judgment upon the former peoples, He substituted for the creatures, in place of the evil (which is the hardship and adversity), the good (which is ease and blessing). This is according to what people perceive; otherwise, things may come about as the poet said:

؎ Allah may bestow blessing through trial, however great it is, and He may try some people with blessings.

(p-6) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This holds true only when looking to the Hereafter and its recompense. Absolute blessing is that in which there is no punishment, and absolute trial is that in which there is no reward.

"Hatta 'afaw" means: until they multiplied. It is said: "'afa al-nabat wa al-rish," meaning it grows when its plants multiply. From this meaning is the poet's saying:

؎ But they cut the sword with ... sturdy, fleshy, thick-fleshed (riding camels)...

And on this is his saying, may peace and blessings be upon him: "Trim the mustaches and let the beards grow (a'fu al-lihā)." 'Afa in the language also means to efface and to decay. Some people said it is among the words used for opposites. As for Zuhayr's saying:

؎ ................................ upon the traces of those who passed away, the effacement (al-'afa')

It admits three meanings: a supplication for effacement, a report of it, and a supplication for growth and vegetation, as one says: "The rains poured upon him and the abundant showers watered him." When God changed their condition to good out of kindness toward them, and they multiplied, the creatures, because of the disbelief they were in, saw after that that the befalling of adversity and ease was merely by chance and not by intention, as the Prophet informs; and they believed that what had befallen them of that was like the chance that had befallen their forefathers, so they made it an example, meaning: this has befallen our forefathers, so we should not deny it. God, Exalted, informed that He seized these groups whose belief this is.

(p-7) His saying: "Batghatan" means suddenly and unexpectedly, and a seizing of anger and force, for the wretchedness that preceded them in His eternal knowledge. "Al-sarra'" means joy and delight. "Wa hum la yash'urun" means: while they are deniers who do not perceive anything of it nor sense it through reasoning or otherwise.

His Exalted saying: "Wa law anna ahla al-qura amanu wa-ttaqaw" (Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God): the meaning of this verse is that had they been among those whom God's knowledge had preordained to acquire faith and acts of obedience and to be characterized by piety, then there would have followed from God's bounty, mercy and favor what was mentioned of the blessings of rain and plants; but since they were among those whose disbelief and denial had preceded, there followed God's seizing them for the evil they had committed. Everything is decreed, and reward and punishment are tied to human acquisition (kasb), and by reason of it actions are attributed to them in His saying: "(believed and were mindful)" and in "(denied)."

Six of the seven readers recited "la-fatahna" with a light ta', which is the common reading. Ibn 'Amir alone, along with 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, recited "la-fattahna" with a shadda on the ta'. "Fath al-barakat" means sending them down upon people, and from it is His saying, Exalted: "What God opens to people of mercy" [Fatir: 2]. From it the Sufis said: "al-futuh and al-barakat are growth and increases." "From heaven" refers to the direction of rain, wind and sun; "and the earth" refers to the direction of growing and preserving what grows. This is what human perception grasps, but God has servants other than that whose number is uncounted, and what is in God's knowledge is greater.

So We seized them suddenly, while they were unaware.﴾ ﴿Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from heaven and earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they had earned.﴾

This verse is a report from God, Mighty and Majestic, that He never sent a prophet to a city (and the city is the qarya) without seizing its people who denied him with hardship (al-ba'sa') — which means calamities in wealth, worries, and the accidents of time — and adversity (al-darra') — which means calamities in the body, such as sicknesses and the like. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and of many of the people of lexicography. He related from al-Suddi something implying that the two terms overlap, so that each is said of both meanings. "Perhaps" (la'alla) expresses expectation according to human belief and assumption. "Yadarra'un" means they submit themselves to faith. Similarly, the saying: "Fever humbled me before You" (al-humma adra'atni laka).

Then He said, Exalted is He, that after carrying out the judgment upon the former peoples, He substituted for the creatures, in place of the evil (which is the hardship and adversity), the good (which is ease and blessing). This is according to what people perceive; otherwise, things may come about as the poet said:

؎ Allah may bestow blessing through trial, however great it is, and He may try some people with blessings.

(p-6) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This holds true only when looking to the Hereafter and its recompense. Absolute blessing is that in which there is no punishment, and absolute trial is that in which there is no reward.

"Hatta 'afaw" means: until they multiplied. It is said: "'afa al-nabat wa al-rish," meaning it grows when its plants multiply. From this meaning is the poet's saying:

؎ But they cut the sword with ... sturdy, fleshy, thick-fleshed (riding camels)...

And on this is his saying, may peace and blessings be upon him: "Trim the mustaches and let the beards grow (a'fu al-lihā)." 'Afa in the language also means to efface and to decay. Some people said it is among the words used for opposites. As for Zuhayr's saying:

؎ ................................ upon the traces of those who passed away, the effacement (al-'afa')

It admits three meanings: a supplication for effacement, a report of it, and a supplication for growth and vegetation, as one says: "The rains poured upon him and the abundant showers watered him." When God changed their condition to good out of kindness toward them, and they multiplied, the creatures, because of the disbelief they were in, saw after that that the befalling of adversity and ease was merely by chance and not by intention, as the Prophet informs; and they believed that what had befallen them of that was like the chance that had befallen their forefathers, so they made it an example, meaning: this has befallen our forefathers, so we should not deny it. God, Exalted, informed that He seized these groups whose belief this is.

(p-7) His saying: "Batghatan" means suddenly and unexpectedly, and a seizing of anger and force, for the wretchedness that preceded them in His eternal knowledge. "Al-sarra'" means joy and delight. "Wa hum la yash'urun" means: while they are deniers who do not perceive anything of it nor sense it through reasoning or otherwise.

His Exalted saying: "Wa law anna ahla al-qura amanu wa-ttaqaw" (Had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of God): the meaning of this verse is that had they been among those whom God's knowledge had preordained to acquire faith and acts of obedience and to be characterized by piety, then there would have followed from God's bounty, mercy and favor what was mentioned of the blessings of rain and plants; but since they were among those whose disbelief and denial had preceded, there followed God's seizing them for the evil they had committed. Everything is decreed, and reward and punishment are tied to human acquisition (kasb), and by reason of it actions are attributed to them in His saying: "(believed and were mindful)" and in "(denied)."

Six of the seven readers recited "la-fatahna" with a light ta', which is the common reading. Ibn 'Amir alone, along with 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, recited "la-fattahna" with a shadda on the ta'. "Fath al-barakat" means sending them down upon people, and from it is His saying, Exalted: "What God opens to people of mercy" [Fatir: 2]. From it the Sufis said: "al-futuh and al-barakat are growth and increases." "From heaven" refers to the direction of rain, wind and sun; "and the earth" refers to the direction of growing and preserving what grows. This is what human perception grasps, but God has servants other than that whose number is uncounted, and what is in God's knowledge is greater.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 97–100:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾ ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the morning while they are at play?﴾ ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are lost.﴾ ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its former people that, if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins, and seal over their hearts so that they do not hear?﴾

This verse contains a warning to the disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad (ﷺ), because when he informed them about what He had done to the earlier nations, He said: "Who guarantees these people that there will not descend upon them the like of what descended upon those?" This is a question in the manner of rebuke.

Al-ba's (البَأْس) means punishment. "Bayatan" (بَياتًا) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning the time of their sleeping at night, and it is possible that this is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited "a-amina" (أوأمِنَ) with a sukun on the waw and the two hamzas pronounced clearly. Warsh, on the authority of Nafi', recited "awamina" (أوامِنَ) with a fatha on the waw and the vowel of the second hamza transferred onto it; this reading has the same meaning as the first but is eased. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "a-wa amina" (أوَ أمِنَ) with a fatha on the waw and the two hamzas pronounced clearly. The meaning of this reading is that the interrogative alif entered upon the conjunctive particle (ḥarf al-'aṭf). The meaning of the first reading is that he conjoined with "aw" (أو), which is for one of two things, and the meaning is: "Do they feel secure from this or from that?" as you say: "Did Zayd come or 'Amr?" This "aw" is not the one that is for retraction from the first statement, as you say: "I stand, or I sit," while you intend to retract standing and affirm and establish sitting. Our saying "which is for one of two things" encompasses permission and choice, as in your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or with Ibn Sirin," or your saying: "Sit with al-Hasan or sit with Ibn Sirin."

His saying ﴿yal'abun﴾ (they are at play) means: in the utmost heedlessness and aversion.

﴿Makr Allah﴾ (the plan of Allah) is an idafa of the created to the Creator, as you say: "the she-camel of Allah" and "the House of Allah." What is meant is an action by which the stubborn disbelievers are punished, and it is attributed to Allah because it is the punishment for the sin. The Arabs call a punishment, in whatever form it takes, by the name of the sin upon which the punishment falls. This is explicit in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54]. And in this place too, it is as if their disbelief after the message and the manifestation of Allah's call is a plan, deceit and mockery. It has been said that in such cases and others the wording is treated rather than the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] and "Indeed Allah does not tire until you tire," and other such examples.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land﴾ — the verse. This is an alif of affirmation (taqrir) that entered upon the conjunctive waw. "Yahdi" means: it makes clear and manifest, and al-huda (الهُدى) means the morning. They cited as evidence for this:

"Until I made clear the morning (al-huda), while the wild beasts were rushing, swimming in the mirage, their ears lowered or praying..."

It is possible that the one who makes clear is Allah, exalted is He, and it is possible that the one who makes clear is His saying: ﴿that if We willed﴾, meaning their knowledge of that. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: "yahdi" means: becomes evident. This too is a verse of warning, meaning: has it not become evident to the heirs of the land, after those whose mention has preceded and what befell them, that We are able, if We willed, to strike them with destruction because of their disobediences, as was done to those who came before? "And We seal" means: We set a seal upon their hearts with wretchedness. In this expression there is mention of the people whom it intends, a reminder of the blessing upon them in what they inherited, and an admonition by the state of those who passed away among the destroyed. "And We seal" is conjoined to ("asabnahum") since what is meant by it is the future. It is possible that "wa-natba'" is a separate (munqati') statement, informing of the occurrence of the sealing and not that it is a threat, and the threat of destruction remains, which is by a punishment such as the blast or the drowning or the like. Abu 'Amr recited "wa-natba' 'ala" with the 'ayn assimilated into the 'ayn and with ishmam of the damma, as recorded by Abu Hatim.

This too is a verse of warning, meaning: has it not become evident to the heirs of the land, after those whose mention has preceded and what befell them, that We are able, if We willed, to strike them with destruction because of their disobediences, as was done to those who came before? "And We seal" means: We set a seal upon their hearts with wretchedness. In this expression there is mention of the people whom it intends, a reminder of the blessing upon them in what they inherited, and an admonition by the state of those who passed away among the destroyed. "And We seal" is conjoined to ("asabnahum") since what is meant by it is the future. It is possible that "wa-natba'" is a separate (munqati') statement, informing of the occurrence of the sealing and not that it is a threat, and the threat of destruction remains, which is by a punishment such as the blast or the drowning or the like. Abu 'Amr recited "wa-natba' 'ala" with the 'ayn assimilated into the 'ayn and with ishmam of the damma, as recorded by Abu Hatim.

(p-10) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is like what was said about ﴿Dhālika al-Kitābu﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]: that it is a subject and a predicate, and like the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ulā'ika al-mala'" ("Those are the chiefs"), and like the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"Tilka al-makārim..." [...]

And this is common. It seems that the wording carries a sense of regret over the cities mentioned. The meaning is: We relate to you from the reports of those who passed, so that you may discern the lessons and know the punishments which Allah inflicted upon those who passed.

Then he began the report about all of them with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And certainly their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before.﴾

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement admits four aspects of interpretation. The first: that it means the Messenger came to each group among them, and they denied him at the beginning of his mission. Then his proof became clear, and the signs indicating his truthfulness appeared, along with the continuation of his call, but they persisted in their disbelief and did not believe in what had made their denial evident before. It seems that He described them, according to this interpretation, with obstinacy in disbelief and firmness upon it. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers.﴾ It is possible, in this aspect, that the meaning of ﴿fa-mā kānū li-yu'minū﴾ is: they would not have been granted by Allah the guidance to faith, because they had denied before, so their denial became a cause for being prevented from faith afterward.

The second aspect: that it means: their last generation in time and era would not have been guided and believed in what their first generation in time and era had denied; rather all of them disbelieved, and some of them followed the ways of others in disbelief.

(p-11) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

al-Naqqash pointed to this view. It seems that the pronoun in His saying "kānū" refers to the later ones, and the pronoun in His saying "kadhdhabū" refers to the earlier ones among them.

Mujahid said this and linked it to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they were returned, they would certainly return to what they were forbidden.﴾ [al-An'am: 28]. This is also an eloquent description of obstinacy and persistence in disbelief; indeed it is the ultimate extent of that.

The fourth aspect: it is possible that it means describing them as not being going to believe in what Allah, blessed and exalted is He, had already known in His knowledge that they would deny. So He made the preceding decree upon them equivalent to their denying by themselves, especially since their denial had come into existence at the time the messengers came. This is the saying of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him.

(p-12) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wronged themselves through them. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And Moses said: "O Pharaoh, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. It is fitting for me that I should not say about Allah except the truth. I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel."﴾ ﴿He said: "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the beholders.﴾

The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, "after them" (min ba'dihim), refers to the prophets previously mentioned and to their nations. The "signs" (āyāt) in this verse are general, including the nine and others. As for His saying, ﴿so they wronged themselves through them﴾, the meaning is: they wronged themselves regarding them and because of them, and they also wronged their manifestation and those who followed their manifestation. It has been said: when "zalamū" (wronged) was made equivalent to "kafarū" (disbelieved) and "jaḥadū" (denied), it was made to take the preposition bi (with), as the poet said:

"Indeed Allah has killed Ziyad for me"

So "qatala" (killed) was made equivalent to "ṣaraf" (turned away). Then Allah warned against the end of the corrupters, the wrongdoers, and made them an example with which He threatens the disbelievers of the era of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is the title of every king of Egypt in that time. So Moses, peace be upon him, addressed him with the most magnificent of his names and the most beloved of them to him, since he was among the Pharaohs, like the Namarudhah among the Greeks, Caesar among the Romans, Khosrow among the Persians, and the Negus among the Abyssinians. It is narrated that he was Moses son of 'Imran son of Qahath son of Levi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, the friend of the Most Merciful. It is also narrated that the name of the Pharaoh of Moses, peace be upon him, was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, and it has been said: he was the Pharaoh of Yusuf, and that he lived more than four hundred years.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for one who says that Yusuf who was sent, to whom Moses alluded in His saying, ﴿And Yusuf had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾ [Ghafir: 34], is other than Yusuf the Truthful, there is no need to consider it. But one who says that he is Yusuf the Truthful, what appears from the story of Yusuf opposes him, since he ruled Egypt after its 'Aziz. How, then, could its 'Aziz live until the time of Moses? It is resolved by saying that the 'Aziz was not the king Pharaoh; rather he was his chamberlain.

Nafi' alone read "'alayya" with the preposition 'ala attached to the first person pronoun, while the rest read "'ala" with the yā' silent. Al-Farisi said: the meaning of this reading is that 'ala was placed in the position of bi, as if He had said: "worthy to not say about Allah except the truth," just as bi was placed in the position of 'ala in His saying, ﴿and do not sit at every path﴾ [al-A'raf: 86]; so the meaning is reached through both. And just as 'ala also comes in the sense of 'an (about), from which is the poet's saying describing his bow:

"I shoot from it, and it is a single, unified branch, three cubits and a span long."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Ḥaqīq" according to this means: fitting and deserving. al-Tabari said: some people said: "ḥaqīq" means "eager," so it was connected with 'ala; but in this view there is remoteness. Some people said: "ḥaqīq" is an attribute of "rasūl," and the sentence is complete at that point; "'alayya" is a fronted predicate, and "an lā aqūla" is an inchoative whose predicate has preceded it. The i'rab (grammatical case) of "an," according to the reading of the one who silenced the yā', is in the genitive; according to the reading of the one who vocalized it with a shadda, it is in the nominative. Al-Kisa'i said: in the reading of 'Abdullah: "ḥaqīq bi-allā aqūla." Abu 'Amr said: in the reading of 'Abdullah: "ḥaqīq an aqūla," and al-A'mash read with it. This address, when you reflect, is extremely gentle in the soft speech which he, peace be upon him, was commanded to use.

His saying: ﴿I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord﴾, the verse. Here "al-bayyina" refers to all of his signs, and it is more indicative of the miracle here. This is from Moses a presentation of his prophethood, and from Pharaoh a demand for a breach of the habitual order that indicates truthfulness.

(p-14) The apparent meaning of the verse and others is that the law of Moses, peace be upon him, was not built except upon the Children of Israel alone, and he did not call Pharaoh and his people except to the sending of the Children of Israel. And his mention of it, perhaps, [is so that] he may be mindful or purify himself and believe in the Oneness of God, just as one reminds every disbeliever, since every prophet calls to tawhid, even if he does not practice it or fight for it himself. As for his calling him to believe and to adhere to the entire Shari'a, this is not stated explicitly, and the matter is open to possibility. In sum, the difference between the Children of Israel and Pharaoh and the Copts becomes apparent. Do you not see that the remainder of the Copts, who were the majority, were never returned to by Moses, peace be upon him, nor did he oppose them, and that the Copts were, for example, worshippers of cows and others? He needed only to dialogue with Pharaoh because of his dominion over the Children of Israel.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾, the verse. It is narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, was disturbed by it and by his exchange [with Pharaoh], so Pharaoh said to his helpers: "Seize him." Then Moses threw down the staff, and it became a serpent and moved toward Pharaoh, and he fled from it. al-Suddi said: it renewed and said: "O Moses, restrain it from me," and he restrained it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said something similar.

"Idhā" (when/behold) is a adverb of place in this position according to al-Mubarrad, since it is a predicate about an entity; but the correct view upon which people agree is that it is an adverb of time in every position. It is said that the serpent placed the lower part of its jaw on the ground and its upper part on the battlements of the palace. "Thu'bān" is the male serpent, and it is more terrifying and bolder; this was said by al-Dahhak. Qatada said: it became a male, long-haired serpent. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it planted its tail in the ground and raised its chest toward Pharaoh. His saying: ﴿manifest﴾ means: there is no imagination in it; rather it is clear that it is real, and it is from abāna meaning bāna (to be clear), or from bāna meaning salaba ('an ajzā'ihi) (to be stripped of its parts).

His saying: ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ means: from his pocket or his sleeve, according to the difference of opinion regarding that. His saying: ﴿behold, it was white﴾ — Mujahid said: like milk or whiter. It is narrated that it would appear luminous, translucent, like the sun shining brightly, and Moses, peace be upon him, had a reddish-dark complexion; then he would return his hand, and it would return to the color of his body.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two verses Moses, peace be upon him, presented for confrontation (mu'āraḍa), called to Allah with them, (p-15) broke the habitual order with them, and challenged people to the religion with them. If we make the challenge (taḥaddī) the calling to religion in general, then with them he challenged; and if we make the challenge the calling after the inability to oppose the miracle and the manifestation of that, then the staff alone is singled out at that time, because the opposition and the inability in it had occurred.

It is said: the taḥaddī is the calling to bring forth the like of the miracle. It is narrated from Farqad al-Sabakhi that the mouth of the serpent would open forty cubits wide.

Al-Kisa'i said: in the reading of 'Abdullah: "ḥaqīq bi-allā aqūla." Abu 'Amr said: in the reading of 'Abdullah: "ḥaqīq an aqūla," and al-A'mash read with it. This address, when you reflect, is extremely gentle in the soft speech which he, peace be upon him, was commanded to use.

His saying: ﴿I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord﴾, the verse. Here "al-bayyina" refers to all of his signs, and it is more indicative of the miracle here. This is from Moses a presentation of his prophethood, and from Pharaoh a demand for a breach of the habitual order that indicates truthfulness.

(p-14) The apparent meaning of the verse and others is that the law of Moses, peace be upon him, was not built except upon the Children of Israel alone, and he did not call Pharaoh and his people except to the sending of the Children of Israel. And his mention of it, perhaps, [is so that] he may be mindful or purify himself and believe in the Oneness of God, just as one reminds every disbeliever, since every prophet calls to tawhid, even if he does not practice it or fight for it himself. As for his calling him to believe and to adhere to the entire Shari'a, this is not stated explicitly, and the matter is open to possibility. In sum, the difference between the Children of Israel and Pharaoh and the Copts becomes apparent. Do you not see that the remainder of the Copts, who were the majority, were never returned to by Moses, peace be upon him, nor did he oppose them, and that the Copts were, for example, worshippers of cows and others? He needed only to dialogue with Pharaoh because of his dominion over the Children of Israel.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾, the verse. It is narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, was disturbed by it and by his exchange [with Pharaoh], so Pharaoh said to his helpers: "Seize him." Then Moses threw down the staff, and it became a serpent and moved toward Pharaoh, and he fled from it. al-Suddi said: it renewed and said: "O Moses, restrain it from me," and he restrained it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said something similar.

"Idhā" (when/behold) is a adverb of place in this position according to al-Mubarrad, since it is a predicate about an entity; but the correct view upon which people agree is that it is an adverb of time in every position. It is said that the serpent placed the lower part of its jaw on the ground and its upper part on the battlements of the palace. "Thu'bān" is the male serpent, and it is more terrifying and bolder; this was said by al-Dahhak. Qatada said: it became a male, long-haired serpent. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it planted its tail in the ground and raised its chest toward Pharaoh. His saying: ﴿manifest﴾ means: there is no imagination in it; rather it is clear that it is real, and it is from abāna meaning bāna (to be clear), or from bāna meaning salaba ('an ajzā'ihi) (to be stripped of its parts).

His saying: ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ means: from his pocket or his sleeve, according to the difference of opinion regarding that. His saying: ﴿behold, it was white﴾ — Mujahid said: like milk or whiter. It is narrated that it would appear luminous, translucent, like the sun shining brightly, and Moses, peace be upon him, had a reddish-dark complexion; then he would return his hand, and it would return to the color of his body.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two verses Moses, peace be upon him, presented for confrontation (mu'āraḍa), called to Allah with them, (p-15) broke the habitual order with them, and challenged people to the religion with them. If we make the challenge (taḥaddī) the calling to religion in general, then with them he challenged; and if we make the challenge the calling after the inability to oppose the miracle and the manifestation of that, then the staff alone is singled out at that time, because the opposition and the inability in it had occurred.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is said: the taḥaddī is the calling to bring forth the like of the miracle. This is a third type, and according to it Moses's challenge with both verses together would be (valid), since the apparent sense of his affair is that he presented them together for consideration, even if he did not explicitly call for the bringing of their like. It is narrated from Farqad al-Sabakhi that the mouth of the serpent would open forty cubits wide.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 109–116:

The words of the Most High:

﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer. He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?"﴾ ﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers"﴾ ﴿"who will bring you every knowing sorcerer."﴾ ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh, saying: "Indeed, there will surely be a reward for us if we are the victors."﴾ ﴿He said: "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾ ﴿They said: "O Moses, either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw."﴾ ﴿He said: "Throw." So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people, frightened them, and brought a great magic.﴾

The sorcerer (sāḥir) held the highest rank and the greatest standing among men at that time. But their describing Moses with this, while they were opposing him concerning prophethood, is a great disparagement and debasement. They intended this if they could not do more. Their saying ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ means that he will rule over you by moving your subjects among the Children of Israel, which would lead to the ruin of your dwellings once the servants and the revenue are gone. Also, there is no doubt that they feared he would fight them, and their suspicions roamed in every direction. Al-Naqqāsh said: They used to take from the Children of Israel a tribute like the jizya, and they saw that their rule would go away with the removal of that.

As for their saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, the apparent meaning is that it is from the speech of the chiefs to one another. It was said that it is from Pharaoh's speech to them. Kardam narrated from Nafi‘ the reading "tamurūnī" with a kasra on the nūn, and likewise in al-Shu‘arā’. "Mā" is an interrogative, and "dhā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), so they form a subject and predicate. In "tamurūn" there is a pronoun referring back to "alladhī," its estimated form being "you command with it." It is also permissible to make "mādhā" like a single noun in a position of accusative governed by "tamurūn," and no pronoun is then implied in it. Al-Ṭabarī said: Sihr (magic) is derived from: "saḥara al-maṭar al-arḍ" (the rain struck the land) when it pours heavily upon it until it turns over its plants and uproots them from their roots; so it "saḥara" them with a saḥar, and the land is "maskhūra" (struck).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Rain only "saḥara" the mud when it spoils it so that no work can be done in it. Sihr is the seizing that takes hold of the eye so that one sees the matter as other than what it is, and it may also seize the mind. From this is the saying of Dhū al-Rummah:

"And a sorceress of the mirages across the deserts, (through whose high ground the wild cattle dance)"

He meant: it makes itself appear as water to the eyes.

Then the chiefs advised Pharaoh to put off Moses and Aaron, to leave off considering their affair, and to gather sorcerers from every place, so that Moses' victory would come by a clear, known and manifest proof.

Ibn Kathīr read "arji'hu" with a waw after the dammed hā' and a hamza before the hā'; Abū ʿAmr read "arji'hu" with a hamza and without a waw after it; Nāfi‘, alone in the narration of Qālūn, read "arjihi" with a kasra on the hā'. It may be that the meaning is "delay him," and he eased the hamza. It may also be from "al-raja'" in the sense of "feed him and make him hopeful" (rajjihu), as said by al-Mubarrad. Warsh, from Nāfi‘, read "arjihī" with a yā' after the kasra of the hā'. Ibn ʿĀmir read "arji'hi" with a kasra on the hā' and a hamza before it. Al-Fārisī said: This is an error. ʿĀṣim and al-Kisā’ī read "arjihu" with a damma on the hā' without a hamza; and Abān narrated from ʿĀṣim "arjih" with sukūn on the hā', and this is a dialect that stops on the hā' of the pronoun when the letter before it is vocalized. From it is the saying of the poet:

"Time has humbled me, a man and a hand… he swears: I will not set right except that I corrupt."

So he sets right today and corrupts tomorrow.

Another said:

"When he saw that there was neither contentment nor satisfaction, he inclined to a sandhill's shrub and lay down."

Al-Naqqāsh related that no one who was a bastard (walad ghiyyah) would sit with Pharaoh; rather, they were nobles. For this reason they pointed to delaying (ijrā’) and did not point to killing, and they said: If you kill him, doubt will enter among the people, but overcome him with proof. "Al-madā’in" is the plural of "madīnah," whose form is fa‘īlah from "madana," or mufi‘ah from "dāna yadīnu," and on this basis "madā’in" is hamzated or not hamzated. "Ḥāshirīn" means gathering; the commentators said: they are the police (shuraṭ). Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi‘, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir read "bi-kulli sāḥirin"; Ḥamzah and al-Kisā’ī read "bi-kulli saḥḥārin" in the intensive form, and likewise in Sūrat Yūnus; and they agreed on "saḥḥārin" in Sūrat al-Shu‘arā’. Qatādah said: the meaning of the "delaying" they pointed to is imprisonment and confinement.

As for the words of the Most High ﴿And the sorcerers came﴾ and the verse that follows, there are omitted matters here required by the apparent sense of the speech, namely that he sent to the sorcerers and commanded them to come. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: he sent youths, and they taught them at al-Farama.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfi‘, and ʿĀṣim in the narration of Ḥafṣ read "inna lanā la-ajran" as a statement. In al-Shu‘arā’ they read "ā’inna lanā" with an extended, fathed alif, except ʿĀṣim, who does not extend it. Abū ʿAlī said: it is permissible that it be in the form of a question with its alif dropped, and this has been said regarding His words "an ʿabbadta banī isrā’īl"; and from it is the saying of the poet: "I rejoice that I am bereaved of the noble…"

ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisā’ī read here and in al-Shu‘arā’ "ā’inna" with the interrogative alif before "inna"; a group read "a’inna" without extension; and Abū ʿAmr read here and in al-Shu‘arā’ "ayinna."

"Al-ajr" here means the wage (ujrah); they asked for it if they prevailed, so Pharaoh granted them it, and added to them rank and status. Its meaning: "those brought near to me." It is narrated that the sorcerers who came to Pharaoh were fifteen thousand, said by Ibn Isḥāq; Ibn Jurayj said they were nine hundred; al-Naqqāsh mentioned that they were seventy-two men; ʿIkrimah said they were seventy thousand; Muḥammad ibn al-Mundhir said they were eighty thousand; and al-Suddī said two hundred thousand and more.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These sayings have no chain of transmission to rely upon. Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said they were twelve thousand; al-Suddī said they were some thirty-odd thousand men, each with a rope and a staff; Abū Thumāmah said they were seventeen thousand.

As for the words of the Most High ﴿They said: "O Moses, either you throw"﴾ and the verse that follows: "in" in "immā an" is in a position of accusative, meaning: either you do the throwing; it may also be in a position of nominative, meaning: either it is the throwing. The sorcerers gave Moses the choice of advancing in throwing or delaying.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the act of one who is confident and trusts in himself. The apparent meaning is that advancing in imaginings, tricks and proofs is what matters, since their effect passes into the soul. So that Allah might manifest the matter of Moses' prophethood, He strengthened his soul and certainty, and he trusted in the truth, so He gave them the first throw; they became energetic and delighted, until Allah manifested the truth and nullified their effort.

As for the words of the Most High ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, it is a text that they had an additional action beyond what they produced of deception and effects in the staff and other bodies upon which they exercised their craft. "Istarhabūhum" means: they frightened them, i.e., caused them alarm; so their action required and invited awe from the people. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, described their magic as great, meaning: because of its abundance. It is narrated that they brought three hundred and sixty camels laden with ropes and staves, and when they threw them, they moved and filled the valley, one riding upon another, so the people were terrified and awed by it. Al-Zajjāj said: it was said that they placed mercury in them, so they would not settle.

Also, there is no doubt that they feared he would fight them, and their suspicions roamed in every direction. Al-Naqqāsh said: They used to take from the Children of Israel a tribute like the jizya, and they saw that their rule would go away with the removal of that.

"Mā" is an interrogative, and "dhā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), so they form a subject and predicate. In "tamurūn" there is a pronoun referring back to "alladhī," its estimated form being "you command with it." He meant: it makes itself appear as water to the eyes.

(p-20) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsely fabricated.﴾ ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and turned back humbled.﴾ ﴿And the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission? Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city, to expel its people from it. But you will soon know!﴾ ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides, then I will crucify you all."﴾

"An" (أنْ) is in a position of accusative governed by "awhayna" (We revealed), meaning "bi-an alqi" (that throw). It may also be explanatory, in the sense of "ay" (that is), in which case it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis of the sentence).

It is narrated that when the day of the gathering came, Moses, peace be upon him, went out leaning on his staff with his hand in his brother's hand, and the magicians had lined up before him in a great number, as has been mentioned. When they threw down their ropes and staffs and struck fear into people, God Most High revealed to him, so he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent. It grew until it was like a mountain. It was said that it lengthened until it crossed the Nile. It was said that the gathering was at Alexandria and it lengthened until it passed the city of al-Buhayra. It was said that the gathering was in Egypt and that it lengthened until it crossed the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea) with its tail.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a saying far from the truth, excessively exaggerated, and it should not be given any attention. It is narrated that when the magicians threw down their ropes and Moses threw down his staff, they began to make incantations, and their ropes and staffs grew larger, while Moses' staff grew until it filled the horizon and swallowed them all. Then it returned to being a staff, and at that the magicians believed. It is narrated that Moses' staff was the staff of Adam, peace be upon them both, and that it was from Paradise. It was said that it was from the 'ayn (a spring) that is in the middle of the leaf of basil (rayhan). It was said that it was a branch of khubbayz (mallow). It was said that it had two prongs. It was said that the staffs of the prophets were kept in safekeeping with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. When Moses tended the flock for him, Shu'ayb said to him: "Go and take a staff." He went to the house and the staff flew into his hand. Shu'ayb ordered him to return it and take another, so he did, and that one flew into his hand too. He informed Shu'ayb of this, so Shu'ayb left it to him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: an angel gave the staff to Moses on the road to Madyan.

"Talqaf" (تَلْقَفُ) means: it swallows and gulps down. "Ma ya'ifikun" (ما يَأْفِكُونَ) means: what they had shaped of their falsehood and lying. The majority of readers recited "talaqqafu" (تَلَقَّفُ) with a doubled qaf. Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, recited "talqafu" (تَلْقَفُ) with a sukun on the lam and a fatha on the qaf. In some transmissions from Ibn Kathir, he recited "ttalaqqafu" (تَّلَقَّفُ) with a doubled ta, by assimilation (idgham) of the ta of "tatalaqqafu"; this reading applies only in connected speech and is not possible at the beginning of the verb. Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "talqamu" (تَلْقَمُ) with a mim, meaning it swallows like a morsel (luqma).

It is narrated that the serpent consumed those ropes and staffs entirely, and God, Mighty and Majestic, caused them to vanish. Moses stretched out his hand to its mouth and it returned to being a staff as it had been. At that, the magicians knew that this was not from human beings, so they fell down prostrate, believing in God and His Messenger.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿So the truth took place﴾, "waqa'a" (وَقَعَ) means: it descended and came into being. "Al-haqq" (the truth) refers to the shining forth of the proof, the manifestation of the miracle, and the continuance of the challenge to the whole world until the Day of Judgment. The phrase ﴿what they had been doing﴾ is a general expression that encompasses the magic of the magicians and the efforts of Pharaoh and his faction. The pronoun in His saying "fa-ghulibu" (So they were overcome) refers to all of them, the magicians and the efforts of Pharaoh and his faction. As for His saying ﴿and turned back humbled﴾: if we assume that the whole group turned back before the magicians believed, then the pronoun includes them; if we assume it was after they believed, then they are not included in the pronoun, and the humiliation that God, Blessed and Most High, describes them with does not befall them, because they believed and were martyred, may God be pleased with them.

As for His saying Most High: ﴿And the magicians were cast down prostrate﴾, and the verses that follow: when the magicians saw the great power that made them certain of Moses' prophethood, peace be upon him, they believed in their hearts. Added to that were dread, awe, and fear of the power of God, Blessed and Most High. So they fell down prostrate to God Most High, pressing their faces to the ground, and they believed openly with their tongues. Ibn 'Abbas and others said of them: they became magicians in the morning and martyrs by evening. As for the threat, it was directed at all of them.

(p-20) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsely fabricated.﴾ ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and turned back humbled.﴾ ﴿And the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission? "An" (أنْ) is in a position of accusative governed by "awhayna" (We revealed), meaning "bi-an alqi" (that throw). It may also be explanatory, in the sense of "ay" (that is), in which case it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis of the sentence).

It is narrated that when the day of the gathering came, Moses, peace be upon him, went out leaning on his staff with his hand in his brother's hand, and the magicians had lined up before him in a great number, as has been mentioned. When they threw down their ropes and staffs and struck fear into people, God Most High revealed to him, so he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent. It grew until it was like a mountain. It was said that it lengthened until it crossed the Nile. It was said that the gathering was at Alexandria and it lengthened until it passed the city of al-Buhayra. It was said that the gathering was in Egypt and that it lengthened until it crossed the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea) with its tail.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a saying far from the truth, excessively exaggerated, and it should not be given any attention. It is narrated that when the magicians threw down their ropes and Moses threw down his staff, they began to make incantations, and their ropes and staffs grew larger, while Moses' staff grew until it filled the horizon and swallowed them all. Then it returned to being a staff, and at that the magicians believed. It is narrated that Moses' staff was the staff of Adam, peace be upon them both, and that it was from Paradise. It was said that it was from the 'ayn (a spring) that is in the middle of the leaf of basil (rayhan). It was said that it was a branch of khubbayz (mallow). It was said that it had two prongs. It was said that the staffs of the prophets were kept in safekeeping with Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. When Moses tended the flock for him, Shu'ayb said to him: "Go and take a staff." He went to the house and the staff flew into his hand. Shu'ayb ordered him to return it and take another, so he did, and that one flew into his hand too. He informed Shu'ayb of this, so Shu'ayb left it to him. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: an angel gave the staff to Moses on the road to Madyan.

"Talqaf" (تَلْقَفُ) means: it swallows and gulps down. "Ma ya'ifikun" (ما يَأْفِكُونَ) means: what they had shaped of their falsehood and lying. The majority of readers recited "talaqqafu" (تَلَقَّفُ) with a doubled qaf. Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, recited "talqafu" (تَلْقَفُ) with a sukun on the lam and a fatha on the qaf. In some transmissions from Ibn Kathir, he recited "ttalaqqafu" (تَّلَقَّفُ) with a doubled ta, by assimilation (idgham) of the ta of "tatalaqqafu"; this reading applies only in connected speech and is not possible at the beginning of the verb. Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "talqamu" (تَلْقَمُ) with a mim, meaning it swallows like a morsel (luqma).

It is narrated that the serpent consumed those ropes and staffs entirely, and God, Mighty and Majestic, caused them to vanish. Moses stretched out his hand to its mouth and it returned to being a staff as it had been. At that, the magicians knew that this was not from human beings, so they fell down prostrate, believing in God and His Messenger.

As for His saying, Most High: ﴿So the truth took place﴾, "waqa'a" (وَقَعَ) means: it descended and came into being. "Al-haqq" (the truth) refers to the shining forth of the proof, the manifestation of the miracle, and the continuance of the challenge to the whole world until the Day of Judgment. The phrase ﴿what they had been doing﴾ is a general expression that encompasses the magic of the magicians and the efforts of Pharaoh and his faction. The pronoun in His saying "fa-ghulibu" (So they were overcome) refers to all of them, the magicians and the efforts of Pharaoh and his faction. As for His saying ﴿and turned back humbled﴾: if we assume that the whole group turned back before the magicians believed, then the pronoun includes them; if we assume it was after they believed, then they are not included in the pronoun, and the humiliation that God, Blessed and Most High, describes them with does not befall them, because they believed and were martyred, may God be pleased with them.

As for His saying Most High: ﴿And the magicians were cast down prostrate﴾, and the verses that follow: when the magicians saw the great power that made them certain of Moses' prophethood, peace be upon him, they believed in their hearts. Added to that were dread, awe, and fear of the power of God, Blessed and Most High. So they fell down prostrate to God Most High, pressing their faces to the ground, and they believed openly with their tongues. Their identifying the Lord by mentioning Moses and Aaron removed the lordship of Pharaoh and the false notion, which ignorant people entertained, that he was the lord of people. Aaron, the brother of Moses, was three years older than him.

Pharaoh's saying ﴿before I gave you permission﴾ is evidence of the weakness of his position, because he made their offense only the failure to seek his permission, and he did not make belief itself the offense, except under a condition. Asim, in the transmission of Hafs from him, recited "amantum" (أمَنتُمْ) in every place in the Qur'an as a statement. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir recited "amantum" (آمَنتُمْ) with a hamza and a long vowel, as a question, and likewise in Ta-Ha and al-Shu'ara'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "a'amantum" (أآمَنتُمْ) with two hamzas, the second being long, and al-A'mash related it from Abu Bakr from Asim. Ibn Kathir, in the transmission of Abu al-Ikhrit from him, recited "wa-amantum" (وَآمَنتُمْ), which is with the interrogative alif, except that he made it a waw, treating the separated as if it were joined, as in the expression "tuwada" for "tu'ada". Qunbul, from al-Qawwas, recited "wa-amantum" (وَآمَنتُمْ), which in the reading with two hamzas is "a'amantum", except that he made the interrogative alif a waw and left the alif of "af'altum" as it is.

The pronoun in "bihi" (بِهِ) may refer to the name of God, Blessed and Most High, or to the name of Moses, peace be upon him. Pharaoh rebuked them for believing before his permission, and then he charged them that this had been done by agreement among them. It is narrated on this matter from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with them both, that Moses, peace be upon him, met the chief of the magicians, whose name was Shum'un, and Moses said to him: "Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me?" He said: "Yes." Pharaoh learned of this, and that is why he said: ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city﴾. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 125–127:

(p-23) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿They said, "Indeed, we are to our Lord returning."﴾ ﴿And you do not avenge [i.e., find fault] with us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims.﴾ ﴿And the chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said, "Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land and to abandon you and your gods?" He said, "We will kill their sons and keep their women alive, and indeed we are dominant over them."﴾

This is a submission from the believing magicians, a reliance upon God and a trust in what is with Him.

The majority of readers recited "تَنْقِمُ" (tanqimu) with a kasra on the qaf. Abu Haywa, Abu al-Barhasam, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "تَنْقَمُ" (tanqamu) with a fatha on it. Both are dialects (lughatan). Abu Hatim said: "The preferred reading is with a kasra on the qaf." All the scholars cited the verse of Ibn al-Ruqayyat:

؎ ما نَقَمُوا مِن بَنِي أُمَيَّةَ.... ∗∗∗..............................

with a fatha on the qaf. Its meaning is: "And you do not count against us a sin and hold us accountable for it."

Their saying: ﴿Pour upon us patience﴾ means: "Overwhelm us [with it] as water overwhelms the one upon whom it is poured." Here it is a metaphor (istiʿāra). Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "When the magicians believed, six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel followed Moses." Al-Naqqash transmitted from Muqatil that he said: "Moses remained in Egypt after the belief of the magicians for a year or thereabouts, showing them the signs."

The saying of the chiefs of Pharaoh's people, ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people?﴾, is a statement that includes inciting Pharaoh against Moses and his people, and urging him to kill them or to change their condition, so that they will not leave the religion of Pharaoh. The meaning of ﴿أتَذَرُ مُوسى﴾ is: "Will you leave?" The majority of readers recited "وَيَذَرَكَ" (wa-yadharaka), and its accusative case has two interpretations. One is that it is taken as "وَأنْ يَذَرَكَ" (wa-an yadharaka), so the wāw is the wāw al-ṣarf (the wāw of "with" that governs the subjunctive, i.e., the wāw that introduces a verb in the subjunctive), and they said: "Will you leave him and his leaving you?" That is: "Will you leave him and your abandoning [him]?" The other meaning is that it is conjoined to their saying "لِيُفْسِدُوا" (li-yufsidu).

Nu'aym ibn Maysara and al-Hasan, in one of the transmissions from him, recited "وَيَذَرُكَ" (wa-yadharuka) in the nominative, conjoined to their saying "أتَذَرُ" (ataðaru). Anas ibn Malik recited "وَنَذَرُكَ" (wa-nadharuka) with the nūn and a nominative verb, in the sense of a threat from them, or in the sense of informing that the matter will end up in this.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abd Allah [ibn Mas'ud] recited: "فِي الأرْضِ وقَدْ تَرَكُوكَ أنْ يَعْبُدُوكَ وآلِهَتَكَ" (fi al-ardi wa-qad tarakūka an yaʿbudūka wa-ālihatak). Abu Hatim said: al-A'mash recited: "وَقَدْ تَرَكَكَ وآلِهَتَكَ" (wa-qad taraka-ka wa-ālihatak). The Seven [readers] and most scholars recited: "وَآلِهَتَكَ" (wa-ālihatak) in the plural.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is in accordance with what is reported: that Pharaoh, in his time, had for the people gods of cows, idols and other things, and Pharaoh had instituted this and made himself the Highest God. So his saying, on this basis, ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24] is only in relation to what was between him and the others among the worshipped things. It was also said: Pharaoh used to worship a stone which he hung on his chest like a ruby or the like. Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh had a ḥannāna (an amulet) hung on his breast which he worshipped and prostrated to. Sulayman al-Taymi said: It reached me that he used to worship cows. This was mentioned by Abu Hatim.

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Mas'ud, and Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with them all, and a group and others, recited: "وَإلاهَتَكَ" (wa-ilāhatak), meaning: "and your worship and your humbling yourself to you." This group claimed that Pharaoh did not permit the worship of anything other than himself, and that in his saying "the Most High" he only meant "the Greatest and the Most Great," without any [specific] relation. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship.

Ibn Kathir recited: "سَنَقْتُلُ" (sa-naqtulu) with lightening (تَخْفِيف, takhfif), and "يُقَتِّلُونَ" (yuqattilūna) with intensification (tashdid). Nafi' lightened both of them. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited "يُقَتِّلُونَ" and "سَنُقَتِّلُ" with intensification, for emphasis. The meaning is: "We will continue upon what we were upon of torturing them and cutting them off."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And indeed we are dominant over them﴾ means: in status and in power over the world. "Dominant" (qāhirūn) requires belittling their affair, i.e., they are too insignificant to be given attention.

Ibn Kathir recited: "سَنَقْتُلُ" (sa-naqtulu) with lightening (تَخْفِيف, takhfif), and "يُقَتِّلُونَ" (yuqattilūna) with intensification (tashdid). Nafi' lightened both of them. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i recited "يُقَتِّلُونَ" and "سَنُقَتِّلُ" with intensification, for emphasis. The meaning is: "We will continue upon what we were upon of torturing them and cutting them off."

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And indeed we are dominant over them﴾ means: in status and in power over the world. "Dominant" (qāhirūn) requires belittling their affair, i.e., they are too insignificant to be given attention.

(p-٢٥) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Moses said to his people, "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to Allah; He bequeaths it to whomever He wills of His servants, and the good outcome is for the God-fearing."﴾ ﴿They said, "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us." He said, "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then He will see how you act."﴾ ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, so that they might take heed.﴾

When Pharaoh said, "We will kill their sons," and threatened them, Moses, peace be upon him, said to the Children of Israel, strengthening them and promising them what is with Allah: ﴿Seek help in Allah and be patient.﴾ The apparent meaning of this whole statement is a promise of the unseen, so its force implies that it comes from Allah, though the wording contains nothing of that. The "land" (al-ard) is the land of this world, which is the most apparent meaning. It has been said that what is meant here is the land of Paradise, but in the second instance it is the land of this world only.

A group read "yūrathuhā" with a fatha on the rāʾ. The Seven (al-Sabʿah, the seven canonical Readers) read "yūrithuhā" with a sukūn on the wāw, a light rāʾ, and a kasra. Ḥafṣ, narrating from ʿĀṣim, and the recitation of al-Ḥasan read "yuwarrithuhā" with a shadda on the rāʾ, for emphasis. Patience in this verse encompasses both waiting, which is an act of worship, and patience in direct confrontation.

Their saying, ﴿before you came to us﴾, refers to the slaughter that took place during the period when Pharaoh feared that a child would be born who would ruin his kingdom. Their saying, ﴿after you came to us﴾, refers to Pharaoh's threats and all the intimidation they suffered during that period. Al-Suddī and Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the Children of Israel only said this statement when Pharaoh pursued them and forced them toward the sea, their hearts constricted, and they saw the sea before them and a dense enemy behind them, so they said this statement.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In sum, this is a statement consistent with what is known of the Children of Israel: their restlessness toward their prophets, the weakness of their certainty, and their lack of patience in religion. Moses' appeal to them with the words ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾, and his promise to them of succession in the land, indicate that it calls for souls that are reluctant, and the Children of Israel's taking this path without any narrative context strengthens this assumption. Al-Naqqāsh reported that they said this in Egypt when Pharaoh imposed on them labour they could not bear. It is related that he would assign them the making of bricks while withholding straw from them, so that the work would be hard for them.

His saying, ﴿then He will see how you act﴾, is a warning and an exhortation to uprightness. If this promise is taken to come from Allah, then the words of al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan are construed accordingly: "ʿasā" (it may be) from Allah is binding. They were indeed made successors in Egypt in the time of Dāwūd and Sulaymān, and they conquered Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) with Yūshaʿ.

His saying, ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years﴾, to the end of the verse. He informed that He seized the people of Pharaoh during the period in which Moses was calling them, with "al-sinīn" (years), which means droughts and famines. This is Allah's way with nations, and He did likewise with Quraysh. In the speech of the Arabs, "al-sanah" means dearth, and from it comes Layla's saying: "and the people are in dearth (musntūn)." Words like sanah, ʿiḍah, and others of similar form that are defective (manqūṣah) are pluralised with the wāw and nūn; this is not the sound masculine plural, but a substitute for what was lost. Likewise "arḍ" (land): they assumed that the feminine tāʾ had been dropped in it, since its proper form should have been "arḍah." As for "ḥurrah" and "iḥarrūn," because doubled roots are always subject to alteration, they assumed it to be like the defective type. The kasra on the sīn in "sunūn" and "sinīn," and the addition of the alif in "iḥarrīn," are evidence that it is not a sound plural.

His saying, ﴿and a shortage of fruits﴾: it is reported that a date palm would bear only one fruit. Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywah said something similar. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, intended that they should turn back in repentance and desist from the disbelief in which they were, since circumstances of hardship soften hearts and incline them toward what is with Allah.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 131–133:**

Allah the Almighty and Majestic says:

﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours." And if an evil afflicted them, they ascribed it to the ill omen of Moses and those with him. Surely their omen is with Allah, but most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will not believe you."﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood as distinct signs, but they were arrogant and were a criminal people.﴾

The purpose of their being afflicted with famine and the loss of fruits was that they would turn back in repentance and return (to Allah). Instead, they went astray and made it into an omen of ill fortune from Moses. So, whenever a good outcome came to them in crops and the like, they said, "This is ours, due to us, and truly belongs to us." And whenever harm reached them, they said, "This is because of Moses and his ill omen." This was said by Mujahid and others.

The reading of the majority of people is "yaṭṭayyarū" (يَطَّيَّرُوا), with the ṭāʾ and the final yāʾ doubled. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Talha ibn Musarrif read "tatayyarū" (تَطَيَّرُوا) with the letter tāʾ and a lightened ṭāʾ. Mujahid read "tashā'amū bi-Mūsā" (تَشاءَمُوا بِمُوسى), with tāʾ at the beginning and using the word for ill omen (shu'm).

As for His words, ﴿Surely their omen (ṭāʾir) is with Allah﴾, its meaning is their fortune and their portion. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. It is derived from the driving away of birds (zajr al-ṭayr, the practice of divination by birds). What is with Allah of divine decree for a person is called a "bird" (ṭāʾir), because a person believes that everything that befalls him is according to what he sees in the bird. So the word is used metaphorically. The majority of readers read "ṭāʾiruhum" (طائِرُهُمْ), and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "ṭayruhum" (طَيْرُهُمْ).

As for His words, ﴿but most of them﴾ — all of them do not know. This is either because a few of them did know, like the believing man and Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, or it means the whole, and the expression is figurative for the sake of possibility. It is also possible that the pronoun in "ṭāʾiruhum" refers to all the world, and the specification of "most" then stands on its apparent meaning. It may also be intended that: "but most of them are not close to knowing, due to their being immersed in ignorance." On this interpretation, among them there is a small number who are prepared to know, if Allah grants them success.

The word "mahmā" (مَهْما), according to al-Khalil, originally is "mā mā" (ما ما), and the first alif was changed into a hāʾ. Sibawayh said it is "mah mā" (مَهْ ما), the two being merged, and it is one particle. Others said its meaning is "mah wa-mā," a conditional particle. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. This verse contains their transgression, their obstinacy, and their certainty in disbelief, which is unmixed.

As for His words, ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾, to the end of the verse: al-Akhfash said, "al-ṭūfān" (الطُوفانُ) is the plural of "ṭūfāna" (طُوفانَة). These were punishments and kinds of torment which Allah sent upon them so that they would be deterred and turn back. "Al-ṭūfān" is a verbal noun from your saying, "ṭāfa yaṭūfu" (طافَ يَطُوفُ). It is general for everything that circulates, except that the Arabs' usage of it became frequent for water and heavy rain. From this is the saying of the poet:

*"The fresh traces of its signs were altered by the rough winds and the flood of rain."*

From this also is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*"A flood extended and spread its flow, a month of heavy showers and a month of hail."*

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said that the flood in this verse was heavy rain which struck them and continued upon them until it demolished their houses and constrained them. It was also said that the overflow of the Nile covered them. Many stories have been related about its manner. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said, "From the Prophet (ﷺ): 'The flood intended in this verse is death.'" Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said in some of what is narrated from him: it is an ambiguous verbal noun, meaning something which Allah, blessed and exalted, sent upon them.

The locusts are well known. Al-Akhfash said that it is the plural of "jarāda" (جَرادَة), applicable to both masculine and feminine. If you wish to specify, you say: "I saw a male locust (jarāda dhikran)." It is related that when Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, caused rain to fall upon them, their land was flooded and their cultivation was prevented. They said, "O Moses, pray to remove this from us, and we will believe." He prayed, and Allah removed it from them, and the land produced good growth. Then they transgressed and said, "We do not wish that we had not been rained upon; this is only a favour from Allah to us." Then Allah sent the locusts, which devoured everything the land had produced. Ibn Wahb related from Malik that it is narrated that they ate their doors, and ate iron and nails, and constricted them to the utmost constriction. Allah left them from their vegetation only what would sustain life. They said to Moses, "Pray to remove the locusts from us, and we will believe." He prayed, and it was removed. They returned to their disbelief, and they saw that what sustained their life had sufficed them. So Allah sent upon them the lice (al-qummal, القُمَّلَ), which are the young locusts that jump and do not fly. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada. It was also said that it is the "ḥamnān" (الحَمْنانُ), which is the young of ticks. It was also said that it is fleas. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: al-qummal is the weevil which comes out of wheat. It was also said: al-qummal is a very small black animal, and it is still in the land of Egypt until now. Ḥabib ibn Abi Thabit said: al-qummal is the dung beetles. Al-Hasan read "al-qaml" (القَمْلَ), with a fatḥa on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. On this reading, it is clear, since it is the well-known louse. It is related that Moses walked with his staff to a heap of sand, struck it, and all of it spread out as lice throughout Egypt. Then they said, "Pray to remove this," and he prayed, and they returned to their transgression and disbelief.

Allah, blessed and exalted, sent upon them the frogs, which entered their beds and between their garments. Whenever a man wished to speak, a frog would leap into his mouth. Ibn Jubayr said: a man would sit with the frogs up to his chin. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the frogs were land creatures, but when they were sent upon the family of Pharaoh, they heard and obeyed, so they began to hurl themselves into the cooking pots while they were boiling. Allah rewarded them for their good obedience by returning the water (to its coolness). They said, "Pray to remove this," and he prayed, and it was removed. They returned to their disbelief and obstinacy. Then Allah sent upon them the blood: the water they were drinking, which they were obtaining, turned into blood. It is related that a man among them would draw water from the well, and when the bucket was raised to him, it became blood. It is also related that a Copt and an Israelite would draw water with one vessel, and when the water came out, what was on the side of the Copt was blood, and what was on the side of the Israelite was water. And other such things of punishment by blood that had turned from water. This is the view of the group of interpreters (al-mutaʾawwilūn). Zayd ibn Aslam said: Allah only imposed upon them nosebleeds, and this is the meaning of His words, ﴿and the blood﴾.

As for His words, ﴿distinct signs (āyāt mufaṣṣalāt)﴾: "tafṣīl" (التَفْصِيلُ), in its original sense concerning physical bodies, is the removal of connection, so it is the separation of two things. When it is used for meanings, it is intended that they were separated from one another and their combination and ambiguity were removed, so that clarification results from it. A group of the commentators said: "mufaṣṣalāt" is intended to mean separated in time. The meaning is that the punishment would lift, and then they would remain for a period said to be a month, and it was said eight days, and then the next would come. Thus the intended meaning is that these kinds of punishment did not come all at once, nor in succession, (p-30) Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, described them with arrogance towards the signs and towards faith, and with their having committed a transgression against Allah, blessed and exalted, and against His servants.

*"A flood extended and spread its flow, a month of heavy showers and a month of hail."*

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said that the flood in this verse was heavy rain which struck them and continued upon them until it demolished their houses and constrained them. It was also said that the overflow of the Nile covered them. Many stories have been related about its manner. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said in some of what is narrated from him: it is an ambiguous verbal noun, meaning something which Allah, blessed and exalted, sent upon them.
