They said, "O Moses, pray to remove this from us, and we will believe." He prayed, and Allah removed it from them, and the land produced good growth. Then they transgressed and said, "We do not wish that we had not been rained upon; this is only a favour from Allah to us." Then Allah sent the locusts, which devoured everything the land had produced. Ibn Wahb related from Malik that it is narrated that they ate their doors, and ate iron and nails, and constricted them to the utmost constriction. Allah left them from their vegetation only what would sustain life. They said to Moses, "Pray to remove the locusts from us, and we will believe." He prayed, and it was removed. They returned to their disbelief, and they saw that what sustained their life had sufficed them. The purpose of their being afflicted with famine and the loss of fruits was that they would turn back in repentance and return (to Allah). Instead, they went astray and made it into an omen of ill fortune from Moses. So, whenever a good outcome came to them in crops and the like, they said, "This is ours, due to us, and truly belongs to us." It is derived from the driving away of birds (zajr al-ṭayr, the practice of divination by birds). What is with Allah of divine decree for a person is called a "bird" (ṭāʾir), because a person believes that everything that befalls him is according to what he sees in the bird. So the word is used metaphorically. The majority of readers read "ṭāʾiruhum" (طائِرُهُمْ), and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "ṭayruhum" (طَيْرُهُمْ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 134–136:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) fell upon them, they said: "O Musa, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you and surely send the Children of Israel with you."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them at a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾ ﴿So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾

"Al-rijz": the punishment. The apparent meaning of the verse is that al-rijz refers to the punishment mentioned earlier, such as the flood, the locusts, and others. However, some of the exegetes said: the reference here by al-rijz is only to a plague (ta'un) which He sent upon them, so that seventy thousand Copts died in a single night. It is related concerning this that Musa, peace be upon him, commanded the Children of Israel to slaughter a ram and smear their doors with its blood, so that this would be a distinction between them and the Copts in the descent of the punishment.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. These reports and what resembles them are taken only from the books of the Children of Israel, and therefore they are weak. Their saying "by what He has covenanted" (bi-ma 'ahida) means: by your protection (dhimam) and your pledge to Him. It encompasses all the means between Allah, blessed and exalted, and Musa, from Musa's obedience and a blessing from Allah, blessed and exalted. It is possible that this was from them by way of an oath upon Musa. It is possible that the meaning is: "Call upon your Lord for us, being one who turns to Him by what He has entrusted to you," and it is possible — if he perceived that there was some covenant between Allah, the Exalted, and Musa concerning their affair — that the reference is to it. The first is more general and more binding, and the last requires a narration.

Their saying "if You remove" (la'in kashafta), i.e., by your supplication, "we will surely believe" (lanu'minanna) and "we will surely send" (walanursilanna) is an oath and its answer. This is a covenant from Pharaoh and his chieftains, those who hold the binding and loosing authority, and the plural pronoun in His saying "lanu'minanna" refers to them.

The wording of this verse indicates the difference between the Copts and the Children of Israel in the mission of Musa, because if their faith in him had been on the level of the faith of the Children of Israel, they would not have sent the Children of Israel away nor separated from their religion; rather they would have shared it with the Children of Israel. It is related that when the punishment was lifted, Pharaoh said to Musa: "Go with the Children of Israel wherever you wish." But some of his community opposed him, so he returned and broke his word. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informed that when He removed the punishment from them, they broke the covenant they had given to Musa.

Here "idha" is for surprise (lil-mufaja'a), "ila" is connected to "kashafna," and "ajal" is meant as the end-point of each one of them by the destruction and death specific to him. This is the necessary implication of the wording, as you say: "I took such-and-such until a time," and you do not mean a particular time. Yahya ibn Salam said: "al-ajal" here means drowning.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement is only because he saw that the majority of this group had happened to perish by drowning, so he believed that the reference here by "al-ajal" is to drowning. This is not necessary, because a world of them must have died before the drowning, and they were among those who were delayed and had the punishment removed from them until a term which they reached, and they are included in this verse. So where is the drowning in regard to these? And where is it in regard to those who remained in Egypt and did not drown?

Some people mentioned that the meaning of the statement is: "So when We removed from them the punishment that was deferred until a term which they would reach, behold, they broke their word." The essence of this interpretation is that the punishment was deferred. However, the first meaning is more eloquent, because it contains a certain threat.

Abu al-Barhasam and Abu Haywa read "yankithun" with a kasra on the kaf. Al-naknth is the undoing of what has been fastened, and it is used for physical objects and for abstract meanings. Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr read "al-rujz" with a damma on the ra' throughout the Qur'an. Abu Hatim said: except that Ibn Muhaysin used a kasra in two places: "rijz al-shaytan" and "war-rijza fahjur."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He saw these two with another meaning, as in the sense of filth and impurity from which one must purify oneself.

"Al-yamm": the sea. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

A desert, and darkness of night, as if they were
A sea whose shores the Romans speak among.

The "bi" in His saying "bi-annahum" is the "bi" of causation. The description of the disbelievers as heedless, though they had denied and rejected at the beginning of the verses, is from the standpoint that they were heedless of what the verses contain of guidance and salvation; for this they were heedless.

Abu Hatim said: except that Ibn Muhaysin used a kasra in two places: "rijz al-shaytan" and "war-rijza fahjur."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He saw these two with another meaning, as in the sense of filth and impurity from which one must purify oneself.

"Al-yamm": the sea. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

A desert, and darkness of night, as if they were
A sea whose shores the Romans speak among.

The "bi" in His saying "bi-annahum" is the "bi" of causation. The description of the disbelievers as heedless, though they had denied and rejected at the beginning of the verses, is from the standpoint that they were heedless of what the verses contain of guidance and salvation; for this they were heedless.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 137–138:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We made the people who had been oppressed inheritors of the eastern and western parts of the land, which We had blessed. And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel, because of their patience. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and what they had been building.﴾ ﴿And We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoting themselves to their idols. They said, "O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods." He said, "Indeed you are a people who are ignorant."﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿those who had been oppressed﴾ is a metonymy for the Children of Israel, because of Pharaoh's enslaving them and his domination over them. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ — al-Hasan, Qatada and others said: it means the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria). Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "It is also said that it means the land of Egypt, and this is the saying of al-Hasan in the book of al-Naqqash." And a group said: it means the entire earth.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is plausible either metaphorically, since He gave them control over many lands, or literally, in that He gave control to their descendants, namely Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both. But what fits the meaning of the verse, and what has been narrated concerning it, is that He gave the sons of the oppressed, in their own persons, the eastern and western parts of the land, especially with His description of the land as "the one We had blessed." No land is characterized by this quality and singled out by it more than others except the land of al-Sham, because of its water, trees, blessings and benefits.

al-Tabari related from a speaker he did not name — and al-Zahrawi mentioned that it was al-Farra' — that ﴿the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of place, meaning: they were oppressed in the eastern and western parts of the land; and that His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿which We had blessed﴾ is an object of "We made inheritors." Al-Tabari considered this weak, and it is likewise a view that is not plausible. ﴿Which﴾ (al-LatI) is in the genitive position as a qualifier of "the land," and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative position as a qualifier of "eastern" and "western."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾ means what had preceded in His knowledge and His word in eternity of deliverance from their enemy and their prevailing over him. This was said by Mujahid. al-Mahdawi said: it is His saying: ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5]. It is also said: it is His saying: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾ [al-A'raf: 129], and so on. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr: "kalimat" (plural).

"Ya'rishun" — Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: its meaning is "they build." 'Arasha al-bayt means he roofed it, and al-'arsh means building and arranging. al-Hasan said: it refers to vineyards and what resembles them. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim read it with a kasra on the ra'; the rest — Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim as narrated from him, al-Hasan, Abu Raja' and Mujahid — read it with a damma. Likewise in Surat al-Nahl. Both are dialectal forms. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yu'arrishun" and "ya'kkifun" with a damma on the yaa' in both, a fatha on the 'ayn, and shadda on the ra' and kaf, both kasra.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have seen that al-Hasan al-Basri argued from His saying, "And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled," to the end of the verse, that one should not rebel against wicked kings, but rather should be patient with them, for Allah will destroy them. I have seen another say: when people confront trial with its like, Allah leaves them to it; and when they confront it with patience and awaiting relief, Allah brings relief. This saying is also narrated from al-Hasan.

Most people read "wa-jawaznā" (And We took across), while al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "wa-jawwaznā." Abu Hatim and al-Mahdawi mentioned it. The meaning is: We cut it through with them and made them cross it. This verse begins a report about them. al-Naqqash said: they crossed the sea on the day of 'Ashura', and Moses was given the Torah on the coming Day of Sacrifice, so between the two events there were eleven months. It is narrated that their crossing was from one bank of the sea to the opposite bank, and it is narrated that it was a crossing from the bank to another place on it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Either this was by revelation from Allah and by command, so that His command would be carried out against Pharaoh and his people — and this is the apparent meaning — or it was according to Moses' own judgment in seeking escape, by being between two cliffs or passes and obstacles. It occurs in the book of al-Naqqash that it was the Nile of Egypt.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an error, unsupported by any narration, and the wording does not allow it except by strained interpretation. Rather, it is the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea). The people referred to in the verse are the 'Arab; it is also said they were the Canaanites. Qatada and Abu 'Amr al-Jawni said: they were a people from Lakhm and Judham. "Qawm" in speech specifically means men, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*And I do not know — and I will surely think I know — whether the clan of Hisn are men or women.*

And from it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿let not a people ridicule a people﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], and ﴿nor women [ridicule] women﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "ya'kufun" with a damma on the kaf; Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu 'Amr in the narration of 'Abd al-Warith from him read "ya'kifun" with a kasra. Both are dialectal forms. "al-'Ukuf" means a person's persistent attachment to something and devotion to it; from it comes i'tikaf (retreat) in the mosques, and from it is the saying of the rajiz:

*...the devotion of the Nabat, playing the fanzaja.*

As for the idols in this verse, it is said they were literally cows; Ibn Jurayj said they were images of cows made of stone, wood and the like, and that was the first instance of the fitnah of the calf.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent sense of the words of the Children of Israel to Moses, "make for us a god just as they have gods," is that they admired what they saw of the gods of those people, and wished that this be part of Moses' law and among the things by which one draws near to Allah. Otherwise, it is far-fetched that they would say to Moses, "Make for us an idol which we will single out for worship and disbelieve in your Lord." So Moses, peace be upon him, informed them that this was ignorance on their part, since they asked for a forbidden matter in which there is association in worship, and from it leads to singling out idols for worship and disbelief in Allah, mighty and majestic. In accordance with what I have said, the resemblance arises that the Prophet ﷺ related in the saying of Abu Waqid al-Laythi to him during the Battle of Hunayn, when they passed by a great green lote tree: "O Messenger of Allah, make for us a Dhat Anwat, just as they have a Dhat Anwat." Dhat Anwat was a lote tree belonging to some polytheists, on which they hung their weapons, and on which they had a day when they gathered. Abu Waqid and others wished that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would legislate this in Islam. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw that it was a means to worshipping that tree, so he denounced it and said: "Allahu Akbar! By Allah, you have said just as the Children of Israel said: ﴿make for us a god just as they have gods﴾. Indeed you will follow the ways of those before you."

Abu Waqid did not intend corruption by his words. Some people said that this was disbelief on the part of the Children of Israel, and the word "ilah" (god) implies that, and this is possible; but what I mentioned first is more correct in my view. And Allah, exalted, knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 139–141:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, these people—what they are in is doomed, and what they have been doing is in vain.﴾ ﴿He said, "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has preferred you over the worlds?"﴾ ﴿And [recall] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾

Musa informed them, from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about the corrupt condition of those people, so that what they had admired of their own state would vanish. So he said: ﴿Indeed, these people﴾ refers to those people; ﴿doomed﴾ means destroyed, ruined, of bad outcome. This was said by as-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. And at-tabar (tabar) is destruction and loss of the outcome; and a vessel that is mutabbar means broken, and its fragments are tibr (gold), and from this comes tibr al-dhahab (gold ingot/bullion), because it is broken pieces. His words ﴿what they are in﴾ is a expression that encompasses their entire condition. ﴿And in vain﴾ means: corrupt, gone, dissolved.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿He said, "Shall I seek…"﴾ (the verse), Allah the Exalted commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to confront them and make them acknowledge this statement. It is possible that the statement was from himself, peace be upon him. (p-37) And ﴿abghikum﴾ means: I seek for you, from baghaytu al-shay' (I sought the thing) when you seek it. And "ghayr" is in the accusative governed by an implied verb; this is the apparent reading. It is also possible that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl), as if the sense of the speech were: "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah?" So it occupies the position of an adjective, and when it was fronted, it was put in the accusative as a circumstantial. And ﴿al-ʿālamīn﴾ (the worlds) is a general term intended to restrict it to the world of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is superior to them by consensus, and because of the Exalted's words: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 110]. Except that "favour" may be meant as the abundance of prophets among them, for they were preferred in this respect over the worlds absolutely.

Then, in this verse, He enumerated for them the blessings for which they are obliged not to disbelieve in Him nor to desire the worship of other than Him. One group read "najjaynākum," while the majority of people read "anjaynākum," which has been mentioned. It is also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, "wa-idh anjākum," meaning: Allah saved you; and so it is in the codices of the people of Syria. ﴿Yasūmūnakum﴾ means: they impose upon you and burden you. Then the "evil torment" was explained by his words: (they slaughter and keep alive). And "balāʾ" in this place means testing and trial. The first interpretation is more apparent.

A group said: these verses were addressed by Musa to those of the Children of Israel who were present. Al-Tabari said: rather, this verse was addressed to those who were in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), as a rebuke to them for what was done to their forebears and for what they were recompensed with.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is more apparent and clearer.

You say: sāmahu khuṭṭata khasf (he imposed on him a humiliating condition) and the like. The "musāwamah" of sale looks to this, that each of the two bargainers imposes his desire upon his companion. Then the "evil torment" was explained by his words: (they slaughter and keep alive). And "balāʾ" in this place means testing and trial. His words ﴿dhālikum﴾ refer to the evil torment, though it is possible that he refers by it to the deliverance, so it is as if he said: in your deliverance there is a trial and test for you, whether you will fulfil the gratitude due for the blessing.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first interpretation is more apparent.

A group said: these verses were addressed by Musa to those of the Children of Israel who were present. Al-Tabari said: rather, this verse was addressed to those who were in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), as a rebuke to them for what was done to their forebears and for what they were recompensed with.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first is more apparent and clearer.

(p-38) The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron, "Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾ ﴿When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You." He said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me." When his Lord revealed Himself to the mountain, He reduced it to dust, and Moses fell down in a swoon. When he recovered, he said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers."﴾

Abu 'Amr, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Raja', Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "wa-wa'adna" (with a doubled *waw*), which has already been discussed in al-Baqara. Allah informed Moses, peace be upon him, that he should prepare himself for his intimate conversation (munajah) with Him for thirty nights. Then He added ten more nights to the term. It is reported that Moses, peace be upon him, had told the Children of Israel of his absence as thirty nights. When the ten nights were added during his absence, without the Children of Israel knowing this, their souls became restless because it exceeded what he had told them. Then al-Samiri said to them, "Moses has died and will not return," and he led them astray with the calf, so they followed him. This entire account is transmitted by Ibn Jurayj.

It is also said that Moses had informed them of his absence as forty nights, and that this is how Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, had informed him. This is what is meant by this verse. This is related from al-Hasan, and it is similar to the words of the Exalted: ﴿Fasting three days during the pilgrimage and seven when you return; that makes ten complete﴾ [al-Baqara: 196]. They counted the days and nights, and when forty periods of time had passed, they said, "Moses has broken his promise," and so they went astray.

Mujahid said: The thirty is the month of Dhu al-Qa'da, and the ten is the ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. This is also said by Ibn 'Abbas and Masruq. It is reported that the thirty was promised so that he might fast during them, prepare himself and make ready for the intimate conversation, and that the duration of the intimate conversation is the ten. It is also said that the duration of the intimate conversation is the forty. The fact that Moses willingly accepted the command and committed to it beautifies the term "promise" (mu'ada). Where it is stated that the promise was forty nights, this is a report of the whole matter, while in this verse it is a report of its detail, of how it happened. The word "forty" in this verse and what follows is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal). It is also permissible for "forty" to be an adverbial accusative (zarf), insofar as it is a number of time periods.

In the codex (mushaf) of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, the reading is "wa-tammamnaha" without the alif and with a doubled *mim*. al-Zajjaj reported from some of them that when he fasted thirty days, he noticed the odor of his mouth changing, so he cleaned his teeth with a stick of carob wood. The angels then said, "We used to smell the fragrance of musk from your mouth, and you spoiled it with the siwak (tooth-stick)," so ten nights were added to it.

The word "thirty" (thalathin) is in the accusative on the assumption of the meaning: "We set his term at thirty." It is not in the accusative as an adverbial of time, because the promise did not take place within the thirty. Then He repeated the matter with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾. It is said that this was to clarify that the ten were not hours, and in general it is emphasis and explanation.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Moses said to his brother﴾, the verse means: Moses said when he wished to set out for the intimate conversation and to be absent for it. "Ukhlufni" (take my place) means: be my successor (khalifa). This is a delegation during his lifetime, like an agency (wikala) that ends by the dismissal of the one who appointed the agent or by his death. It does not imply that the appointment continues after his death. Thus on this basis the claim of the Imamiyya is answered. They say that the Prophet ﷺ appointed 'Ali as successor by his saying: "You are to me as Aaron was to Moses," and Moses said: "Take my place," so it follows that 'Ali is the successor of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. What we have mentioned resolves this analogy.

In this verse He commanded him to do right (islah). Then, among the other ways of not following the way of a corrupter, Ibn Jurayj said: Among doing right was that he should rebuke al-Samiri and attack him.

Then Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, informed about Moses, peace be upon him, that when he came to the place that had been set for him and at the time that had been appointed for him, and his Lord spoke to him, he said, out of longing: ﴿My Lord, show me that I may look upon You﴾. The majority read "arini" with a kasra on the *ra*. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "arni" with the *ra* sukun.

The meaning of His words ﴿spoke to him﴾ [Yusuf: 54] is: He created for him a perception by which he heard the speech subsisting in the Essence, the eternal, which is an attribute of the Essence. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, brought Moses close until he heard the scratching of the pens on the Tablet. The speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not resemble any of the speech of created beings, nor is it in any direction. Just as He exists without being like existing things, and is known without being like known things, so His speech does not resemble speech that bears the signs of having come into being. The *waw* is conjunctive, joining "spoke to him" to "came." It is possible that it is the *waw* of circumstance (hal), but the first is clearer.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Allah spoke to Moses in a thousand stations, and after each station he saw light on his face for three days. Moses did not approach women from the time Allah, the Exalted, spoke to him.

The response (jawab) of "lamma" (when) in the words of the Exalted is "qala" (he said). The meaning is that when He spoke to him and singled him out with this rank, his aspiration soared toward the rank of seeing, and he longed for that. So he asked his Lord to show Himself to him. This is said by al-Suddi and Abu Bakr al-Hudhali. al-Rabi' said: We brought him near as one in private conference until he heard the scratching of the pens.

According to the Ash'ariyya and Ahl al-Sunna, seeing Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is rationally permissible, because insofar as He exists, He can be seen. They said: the seeing of a thing does not depend on any of its attributes beyond existence. However, the Sharia has established by explicit text the seeing of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, in the Hereafter, and has prevented it in this world by indications from the revelation. So Moses, peace be upon him, did not ask his Lord for something impossible, but for something permissible.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿You will not see Me, but look at the mountain﴾, this is not an answer to one who asks for something impossible. The Exalted said to Noah: ﴿So do not ask Me for what you have no knowledge of. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant﴾ [Hud: 46]. If Moses had asked for something impossible, the words would have contained a kind of rebuke and clarification. The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿You will not see Me﴾ are a text from Allah, the Exalted, prohibiting seeing in this world. "Lan" (will not) negates the future verb. If we remained with this negation alone, we would conclude that Moses would never see Him, neither now nor in the Hereafter. But it has come through another channel, by the *mutawatir* hadith (a report transmitted by so many chains that its authenticity is certain), that the people of faith will see Allah, the Exalted, on the Day of Resurrection. Thus Moses, peace be upon him, is more deserving of seeing Him. Mujahid and others said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to Moses: ﴿You will not see Me﴾, but I will reveal Myself to the mountain, which is stronger and more solid than you. If it remains firm and can bear the patience required by My awe, then you will be able to see Me.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this view, Allah only made the mountain an example. Another group said: The meaning is: I will manifest Myself to you upon the mountain, and if it remains firm before My greatness, then you will see Me. A long narrative is related concerning how Moses stood and waited for the vision. I have abridged it because of its remoteness and the many points of objection in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 144–145:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. And when he recovered, he said: "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 143] ﴿He said: "O Moses, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the thankful."﴾ ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything. So take them with strength and command your people to take the best of them. I shall show you the abode of the defiant.﴾

The theologians (al-mutakallimun), such as al-Qadi al-Baqillani and others, who interpret, said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created life, sensation and perception in the mountain by which it could see. Then He manifested Himself to it, that is, His dominion appeared and became evident, so the mountain was crushed because of the intensity of the manifestation. When Moses saw what happened to the mountain, he fell unconscious." This meaning is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Tabari transmitted with a chain from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Thabit, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited: "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust," and he placed his thumb near his little finger and said: "The mountain then sank." Humayd said to Thabit: "Do you say this?" Thabit raised his hand and struck his chest and said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says it, Anas says it, and shall I conceal it?"

Another group said: the meaning is: when Allah manifested Himself to the mountain by His power and dominion, the mountain crumbled.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is clung to very firmly by the Mu'tazila in their claim that seeing Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not permissible. Whoever among the People of the Sunna says it does so while believing that seeing is permissible, but he says that it is more fitting to the wording of the verse than to take the verse to mean that the mountain was given perception and life. al-Zajjaj said: whoever says that the implied sense is "when the command of his Lord manifested itself" has erred, and the people of the language do not recognize that. Abu 'Ali replied to him in "al-Aghfal."

Al-dakk means being crushed and pulverized. The Prophet (ﷺ), Ibn Mas'ud, Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "dakkan." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and others read: "dakkha'" on the pattern of "hamra'," and al-dakka' is the she-camel that has no hump. So the meaning is: He made it a level land, like the humpless she-camel. It is related that the mountain went away entirely; it was also said that its top went away and most of it remained. It is also related that the mountain crumbled and was pulverized until it became dust scattered by the winds. Sufyan said: it is related that it sank into the earth and reached the sea beneath the earths. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it keeps sinking in it until the Day of Resurrection. It is related that it broke into six pieces, of which three fell in Makkah: Thabir, the Cave of Thawr, and Hira', and three in Madinah: Uhud, Warqan, and Radwa; this was reported by al-Naqqash. Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said: it sank into the earth and does not appear until the Day of Resurrection.

"Sa'iqan" means: fallen unconscious, like one who is struck by a thunderclap, which is an excessively loud cry. al-Khalil said: it is a violent impact of the sound of thunder. This was said by Ibn Zayd and a group of exegetes. Qatada said: it was death. al-Zajjaj said: this is weak, and the word "recovered" requires otherwise.

His saying, ﴿Glory be to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], means: exalted are You above all imperfection; this is how the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it. His saying, ﴿I repent to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], means: from asking You to see You in this world while You do not permit it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it is possible that this was a statement he uttered, peace be upon him, because of the intensity of the terror of what he witnessed, and he did not mean by it repentance from a specific thing, but it is a word suitable for that situation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What the People of the Sunna guard against is that it be a repentance from asking for the impossible, as the Mu'tazila claimed.

Nafi' read: "wa-ana" with the alif retained in continuous recitation. al-Zahrawi said: the better course is to omit it in continuous recitation, and retaining it is an anomalous dialect, contrary to analogy. As for his saying, "awwal" (first), it may mean: first of his people, the Children of Israel, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid; or first of the believers of his time, if disbelief had spread through the horizons; or it may mean the first of the believers in that you will not be seen in this world. This was said by Abu al-'Aliya.

Then Allah, Exalted, affirmed to Moses his blessings with Him by way of information, contented him with them, and commanded him to be thankful for them, as if He said: and do not go beyond them to other things.

"Istafa" originally was "istafa" (ishtafa), a form of ifta'ala from safa yasfu; the ta' became a ta' because of the preceding sad. Its meaning: I chose you and singled you out. It is used only for good things and favors; one does not say "istafahu" for evil. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿above the people﴾, is general, and the intended meaning is particular, concerning those who shared with Moses in being sent, for the prophets who were sent share with him in being messengers. The apparent meaning of the Law is that Moses was singled out with speech, although many things have been related about Allah speaking to others, the greatest of which is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Adam and said: "He is a prophet who was spoken to."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

However, that has been interpreted as meaning that it happened in Paradise; according to this, the singling out of Moses is preserved, and it is possible that His saying ﴿above the people﴾ is an absolute generality covering both ranks together: messengership and speech.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "bi-risalati" in the plural, since what he was sent with is of various kinds. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read: "bi-risalati" in the singular, which is intended as a plural. Here "risala" is used in place of the verbal noun "irsal." The majority of people read: "wa-bi-kalami." Abu Raja' read: "bi-risalati wa-bi-kalimi." al-A'mash read: "bi-risalati wa-bi-kalimi." al-Mahdawi reported from him: "wa-taklimi," on the pattern of "taf'il-i." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So take what I have given you and be among the thankful﴾, is discipline, contentment, and guidance onto the right path, and an example for everyone in his situation, for all blessings come from Him in measure, and all affairs are under the sight and hearing of Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾ and so on: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to Moses, peace be upon him. The alif and lam in "al-alwah" (the tablets) stand in place of a pronoun that is understood to link "the tablets" and "Moses," peace be upon him; the implied phrase is "on his tablets." This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41], meaning: its refuge. It is said the tablets were two; it is said seven. Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the tablets were of emerald. Ibn Jubayr said: of red ruby. Abu al-'Aliya also said: of topaz. al-Hasan said: of wood. His saying, ﴿concerning everything﴾, is a general term, and what is intended is everything that benefits in the sense of the Law and is needed for welfare. His saying, ﴿a detailed explanation of everything﴾, is similar. Ibn Jubayr said: what they were commanded and forbidden. Mujahid said the same. al-Suddi said: the lawful and the unlawful. His saying, ﴿with strength﴾, means: with earnestness, patience in it, and bearing its burden; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Suddi. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "with strength" here means: with obedience. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to take with greater firmness than what he commanded his people. "Khudh" originally was "u'khudh," the hamza which is the first radical of the verb was dropped contrary to analogy, so the first was dispensed with. His saying, ﴿the best of them﴾, may have two meanings. One of them is comparative: as if He said: when two permissible options present themselves in it, they should take the better of the two, such as pardon or retaliation, patience or retribution.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the view that the comparative form "af'al" is used only where both options share the quality compared. As for the other view, "the best" may mean what is commanded in comparison with what is forbidden, because it is better than it, as with the abrogating text in relation to the abrogated one and the like. al-Tabari took this meaning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What supports this interpretation is that obligations enter into it, and they do not enter into the first interpretation. It is also possible to conceive of a shared goodness between what is commanded and what is forbidden, even in terms of pleasures and the appetites of the commanding self. The other meaning that His saying ﴿the best of them﴾ may bear is that by "the best" is meant describing the Law in its entirety, as if He said: We have made for you a law that is the best, as you say "Allah is greatest" without comparison; then He said: so command them to take the best of it, which We have prescribed for them. There are objections to this interpretation.

Most people read: "sa-urikum" (I shall show you). al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read: "urikum." Abu al-Fath said: the apparent reading of this recitation is rejected, and this is Abu Sa'id, whose eloquence is transmitted. He explained it as meaning "urikum" (I shall show you), with the vowel of the hamza prolonged until a waw arose from it; the waw is appropriate in this place, since it is a place of threat and severity, so the sound was stretched in it. Qasama ibn Zuhayr read: "sa-urithukum" (I shall bequeath to you), as reported by Abu Hatim; al-Mahdawi attributed it to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. The waw was retained in the orthography of the Mushaf, so this variation was difficult, although we do not interpret them and they are only transmitted reports. As for those who read "sa-urikum," the meaning for them is: I shall display to you and make you perceive, so that you may take heed of the condition of the abode of the defiant. The seeing here is sight with the eye, but the meaning includes a promise to the believers and a threat to the defiant. What shows that it is sight with the eye is that its verb is transitive, and it has been made transitive by the hamza to two objects; had it been seeing of the heart, it would have been made transitive by the hamza to three objects. If someone says: the third object is implied by the meaning, so it is understood, that is: destroyed, or ruined, or kindled (according to the one who said it is Hell), it is said to him: it is not permissible to omit this object and be content without it, since the two are introduced on the subject and predicate; and even if it were permitted, it would be a grammatical impropriety unbefitting the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Muqatil, and Qatada, in the book of al-Naqqash, said: the abode of the defiant is Egypt, and the intended people are the family of Pharaoh. Qatada also said: the abode of the defiant is Syria, and the intended people are the 'Amaliqa whom Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to fight. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: the abode of the defiant is Hell, and the intended people are the disbelievers of Moses in general. al-Naqqash reported from al-Kalbi: the abode of the defiant is the dwellings of Thamud, 'Ad, and the bygone nations; that is: we will recount them to you, and you will see them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 144–145:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious. And when he recovered, he said: "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 143] ﴿He said: "O Moses, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the thankful."﴾ ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything. So take them with strength and command your people to take the best of them. I shall show you the abode of the defiant.﴾

The theologians (al-mutakallimun), such as al-Qadi al-Baqillani and others, who interpret, said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created life, sensation and perception in the mountain by which it could see. Then He manifested Himself to it, that is, His dominion appeared and became evident, so the mountain was crushed because of the intensity of the manifestation. When Moses saw what happened to the mountain, he fell unconscious." This meaning is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Tabari transmitted with a chain from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Thabit, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited: "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust," and he placed his thumb near his little finger and said: "The mountain then sank." Humayd said to Thabit: "Do you say this?" Thabit raised his hand and struck his chest and said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) says it, Anas says it, and shall I conceal it?"

Another group said: the meaning is: when Allah manifested Himself to the mountain by His power and dominion, the mountain crumbled.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is clung to very firmly by the Mu'tazila in their claim that seeing Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not permissible. Whoever among the People of the Sunna says it does so while believing that seeing is permissible, but he says that it is more fitting to the wording of the verse than to take the verse to mean that the mountain was given perception and life. al-Zajjaj said: whoever says that the implied sense is "when the command of his Lord manifested itself" has erred, and the people of the language do not recognize that. Abu 'Ali replied to him in "al-Aghfal."

Al-dakk means being crushed and pulverized. The Prophet (ﷺ), Ibn Mas'ud, Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "dakkan." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and others read: "dakkha'" on the pattern of "hamra'," and al-dakka' is the she-camel that has no hump. So the meaning is: He made it a level land, like the humpless she-camel. It is related that the mountain went away entirely; it was also said that its top went away and most of it remained. It is also related that the mountain crumbled and was pulverized until it became dust scattered by the winds. Sufyan said: it is related that it sank into the earth and reached the sea beneath the earths. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it keeps sinking in it until the Day of Resurrection. It is related that it broke into six pieces, of which three fell in Makkah: Thabir, the Cave of Thawr, and Hira', and three in Madinah: Uhud, Warqan, and Radwa; this was reported by al-Naqqash. Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said: it sank into the earth and does not appear until the Day of Resurrection.

"Sa'iqan" means: fallen unconscious, like one who is struck by a thunderclap, which is an excessively loud cry. al-Khalil said: it is a violent impact of the sound of thunder. This was said by Ibn Zayd and a group of exegetes. Qatada said: it was death. al-Zajjaj said: this is weak, and the word "recovered" requires otherwise.

His saying, ﴿Glory be to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], means: exalted are You above all imperfection; this is how the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it. His saying, ﴿I repent to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], means: from asking You to see You in this world while You do not permit it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it is possible that this was a statement he uttered, peace be upon him, because of the intensity of the terror of what he witnessed, and he did not mean by it repentance from a specific thing, but it is a word suitable for that situation.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What the People of the Sunna guard against is that it be a repentance from asking for the impossible, as the Mu'tazila claimed.

Nafi' read: "wa-ana" with the alif retained in continuous recitation. al-Zahrawi said: the better course is to omit it in continuous recitation, and retaining it is an anomalous dialect, contrary to analogy. As for his saying, "awwal" (first), it may mean: first of his people, the Children of Israel, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid; or first of the believers of his time, if disbelief had spread through the horizons; or it may mean the first of the believers in that you will not be seen in this world. This was said by Abu al-'Aliya.

Then Allah, Exalted, affirmed to Moses his blessings with Him by way of information, contented him with them, and commanded him to be thankful for them, as if He said: and do not go beyond them to other things.

"Istafa" originally was "istafa" (ishtafa), a form of ifta'ala from safa yasfu; the ta' became a ta' because of the preceding sad. Its meaning: I chose you and singled you out. It is used only for good things and favors; one does not say "istafahu" for evil. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿above the people﴾, is general, and the intended meaning is particular, concerning those who shared with Moses in being sent, for the prophets who were sent share with him in being messengers. The apparent meaning of the Law is that Moses was singled out with speech, although many things have been related about Allah speaking to others, the greatest of which is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about Adam and said: "He is a prophet who was spoken to."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

However, that has been interpreted as meaning that it happened in Paradise; according to this, the singling out of Moses is preserved, and it is possible that His saying ﴿above the people﴾ is an absolute generality covering both ranks together: messengership and speech.

Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "bi-risalati" in the plural, since what he was sent with is of various kinds. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read: "bi-risalati" in the singular, which is intended as a plural. Here "risala" is used in place of the verbal noun "irsal." The majority of people read: "wa-bi-kalami." Abu Raja' read: "bi-risalati wa-bi-kalimi." al-A'mash read: "bi-risalati wa-bi-kalimi." al-Mahdawi reported from him: "wa-taklimi," on the pattern of "taf'il-i." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So take what I have given you and be among the thankful﴾, is discipline, contentment, and guidance onto the right path, and an example for everyone in his situation, for all blessings come from Him in measure, and all affairs are under the sight and hearing of Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾ and so on: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to Moses, peace be upon him. The alif and lam in "al-alwah" (the tablets) stand in place of a pronoun that is understood to link "the tablets" and "Moses," peace be upon him; the implied phrase is "on his tablets." This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41], meaning: its refuge. It is said the tablets were two; it is said seven. Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the tablets were of emerald. Ibn Jubayr said: of red ruby. Abu al-'Aliya also said: of topaz. al-Hasan said: of wood. His saying, ﴿concerning everything﴾, is a general term, and what is intended is everything that benefits in the sense of the Law and is needed for welfare. His saying, ﴿a detailed explanation of everything﴾, is similar. Ibn Jubayr said: what they were commanded and forbidden. Mujahid said the same. al-Suddi said: the lawful and the unlawful. His saying, ﴿with strength﴾, means: with earnestness, patience in it, and bearing its burden; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Suddi. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: "with strength" here means: with obedience. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to take with greater firmness than what he commanded his people. "Khudh" originally was "u'khudh," the hamza which is the first radical of the verb was dropped contrary to analogy, so the first was dispensed with. His saying, ﴿the best of them﴾, may have two meanings. One of them is comparative: as if He said: when two permissible options present themselves in it, they should take the better of the two, such as pardon or retaliation, patience or retribution.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is according to the view that the comparative form "af'al" is used only where both options share the quality compared. As for the other view, "the best" may mean what is commanded in comparison with what is forbidden, because it is better than it, as with the abrogating text in relation to the abrogated one and the like. al-Tabari took this meaning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What supports this interpretation is that obligations enter into it, and they do not enter into the first interpretation. It is also possible to conceive of a shared goodness between what is commanded and what is forbidden, even in terms of pleasures and the appetites of the commanding self. The other meaning that His saying ﴿the best of them﴾ may bear is that by "the best" is meant describing the Law in its entirety, as if He said: We have made for you a law that is the best, as you say "Allah is greatest" without comparison; then He said: so command them to take the best of it, which We have prescribed for them. There are objections to this interpretation.

Most people read: "sa-urikum" (I shall show you). al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read: "urikum." Abu al-Fath said: the apparent reading of this recitation is rejected, and this is Abu Sa'id, whose eloquence is transmitted. He explained it as meaning "urikum" (I shall show you), with the vowel of the hamza prolonged until a waw arose from it; the waw is appropriate in this place, since it is a place of threat and severity, so the sound was stretched in it. The waw was retained in the orthography of the Mushaf, so this variation was difficult, although we do not interpret them and they are only transmitted reports. If someone says: the third object is implied by the meaning, so it is understood, that is: destroyed, or ruined, or kindled (according to the one who said it is Hell), it is said to him: it is not permissible to omit this object and be content without it, since the two are introduced on the subject and predicate; and even if it were permitted, it would be a grammatical impropriety unbefitting the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Muqatil, and Qatada, in the book of al-Naqqash, said: the abode of the defiant is Egypt, and the intended people are the family of Pharaoh. Qatada also said: the abode of the defiant is Syria, and the intended people are the 'Amaliqa whom Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to fight. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: the abode of the defiant is Hell, and the intended people are the disbelievers of Moses in general. al-Naqqash reported from al-Kalbi: the abode of the defiant is the dwellings of Thamud, 'Ad, and the bygone nations; that is: we will recount them to you, and you will see them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 146–147:

The words of the Most High:

﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth without right. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. And if they see the path of right guidance, they will not take it as a path; and if they see the path of error, they will take it as a path. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾ ﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter—their deeds have become worthless. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾

(p-47) The meaning: "I will prevent and avert." Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "The signs here are every revealed Book."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the meaning is: (turning away) from understanding them and affirming them. Ibn Jurayj said: "The signs are the placed markers that indicate the Oneness (of Allah)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the meaning is: (turning away) from reflecting upon them, contemplating them, and inferring from them. The wording encompasses both meanings.

Those who are arrogant on the earth without right are the disbelievers. The meaning of this verse is: I will make the turning away from the signs a punishment for the arrogant for their arrogance. His saying, may He be blessed and exalted, ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ is a decree from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, upon the group whom He has predestined not to believe. The reading of the majority is "yarau" with a fatha on the ya', recited by Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Shibl, Ibn Wththab, Talha ibn Musarrif, and the rest of the Seven; Malik ibn Dinar read it with a damma on the ya'.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read "al-rushd." Ibn 'Amir—in some of what is narrated from him—and Abu al-Barhasam read "al-rushud" with a damma on the ra' and the shin. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "al-rushd" with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin, and "al-rashad" with fatha on both, with one meaning. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "ar-rushd" with damma on the ra' means righteousness in judgment, and "ar-rashad" with fatha on both means religion. As for Ibn 'Amir's reading with damma on both, the damma followed the damma.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "la yattakhidhuha" and "tattakhidhuha," treating "sabil" as feminine. The word "sabil" is both feminine and masculine. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿That﴾ refers to the turning away, i.e., We turned them away, and Our punishment for them is by their disbelief, their denial, and their heedlessness regarding reflection upon the signs and pausing before the proofs. It is possible that "dhalika" is the predicate of an inchoative, its estimate being: "the matter is that," and it is possible that it is in the accusative position by a verb whose estimate is: "We did that."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, the verse, this verse confirms the previous one, and its placement within the category of what is denied. "The meeting of the Hereafter" is an expression that includes a threat; i.e., there their condition will be exposed to them. "Habitat" means: fell and became corrupt. The root of habat, in what came before, is that its goodness is lost, but it may be used of what was first corrupt, since the end of the doers is one.

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Will they be recompensed﴾ is a question with the meaning of affirmation, i.e., they deserve punishment because of the evil of their deeds. It was permissible to use "habitat" here, since their deeds, according to their beliefs, were proceeding on the path of goodness; so the corruption in them is only according to their beliefs. As for what they are in themselves, they are corrupt from the very beginning. From this word is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, among what spring grass produces is that which kills by habat or causes bloating." That is, corruption due to excessive eating after the goodness that existed at first. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read "habatat" with a fatha on the ba'.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 148–149**

(p-48)

God the Exalted said:

﴿And the people of Musa, after him, took from their ornaments a calf, a body that had a lowing sound. Did they not see that it does not speak to them, nor guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And when they were overcome with regret, and saw that they had gone astray, they said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be among the losers."﴾

The original form of "اتَّخَذَ" (ittakhadha) is "اِيتَخَذَ" (ayttakhadha), whose pattern is "افْتَعَلَ" (ifta'ala), from "تَخِذَ" (takhidha). This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. The pronoun in "بَعْدِهِ" (ba'dihi) refers to Musa, meaning after his departure for the private conversation with God (al-munajah). The ornaments are attributed to the Children of Israel, although they were borrowed from the Copts (al-Qibt), since the Children of Israel had taken possession of them, either because they were given them as a spoil (nafl), as has been narrated. Yahya ibn Sallam reported from al-Hasan that he said: "The Children of Israel borrowed the ornaments of the Copts for the day of festivity. When Musa was commanded to set out with them by night, it became impossible for them to return the borrowed items. Also, they feared that their secret would be exposed. Then God gave them these as a spoil." It is also possible that the ornaments are attributed to the Children of Israel because their hands handled them after the conquest of the people of Pharaoh.

It is narrated that al-Samiri, whose name was Musa ibn Zafar and who was ascribed to a village called Samira, said to Harun when Musa went to the private conversation: "O Harun, the Children of Israel have squandered the ornaments that were borrowed from the Copts. They have disposed of them and spent some of them. If you were to gather them, Musa could see his opinion regarding them." He said: "Harun gathered them. When they were gathered, he said to al-Samiri: 'You are the most worthy of people to have them kept with you.'" So al-Samiri took them, and he was a goldsmith, and he fashioned from them the image of a calf, which is the young of a cow.

"جَسَدًا" (jasadan) means a body (juththa) and inanimate matter. It was said: it was a body without a head. This is an argument based on the linguistic meaning of "jasad," which refers to whatever is other than the head. It was also said: God gave it flesh and blood.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This view is weak, because the reports that Musa filed it down with files contradict it. "الخُوارُ" (al-khuwar) is the lowing of cows. It is narrated that this calf lowed only once, either through a manufactured trick by al-Samiri, or through a magic he had devised from grasping a handful of dust from the trace of the Messenger (al-Rasul), or because God made the calf low as a trial for the Children of Israel. One group recited "لَهُ جُوارٌ" (lahu juwar) with a jim, meaning shouting, and Abu Hatim said: "and intense loudness of voice." Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Shayba recited "مِن حُلِيِّهِمْ" (min huliyyihim) with a dammah on the ha' and a kasrah on the lam. It is the plural of "حَلْيٌ" (hally), on the pattern of "ثَدْيٌ" (thady) and "ثُدِيٌّ" (thudiyy). Its original form is "حُلُوِيٌ" (huluwiyy); the waw was changed into a ya' and assimilated, so "حُلُيٌّ" (hulayyun) resulted, and the lam was given a kasrah to harmonize with the ya'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "مِن حِلِيِّهِمْ" (min hiliyyihim) with a kasrah on the ha', according to the explanation we previously mentioned. Abu Hatim said: "However, they gave the ha' a kasrah to follow the kasrah of the lam." Abu 'Ali said: "The change that entered the plural was strengthened by this later change." He said: "What confirms the kasrah of the fa' in this kind of plural is their saying 'qisiyy' (قِسِيٌّ)." Abu Hatim said: "Yahya ibn Wassab, Talha, al-A'mash and the companions of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited it thus." Ya'qub al-Hadrami recited "مِن حَلْيِهِمْ" (min halyihim) with a fatha on the ha' and sukun on the lam. Then it is either a singular used to mean the plural, or it is the plural of "حِلْيَةٌ" (hilyah), as "تَمْرَةٌ" (tamrah) and "تَمْرٌ" (tamr). The meaning of "الحُلِيِّ" (al-hulli) is what is adorned with, of stones, gold and silver.

Then God the Exalted made clear their corrupt natures and established the corruption of their belief by His saying: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾ (p-49) and the rest of the verse. This is because the silent inanimate object does not possess divinity, and what does not guide to good nor removes distress is likewise. The pronoun in "اتَّخَذُوهُ" (ittakhadhuhu) refers to the calf. His saying "وكانُوا" (wa-kanu) is an informing us about all their states, past, present and future. It is possible that the "و" is a waw of circumstance (waw al-hal). The cause of the taking of the calf and the detailed account of that situation has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah, so what is sufficient there need not be repeated here.

One group recited "سَقَطَ" (saqata) with a fatha on the sin and the qaf, related by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "أُسْقِطَ" (usqita) with a hamzah bearing a dammah and a sukun on the sin. Abu 'Ubayda said: "It is said of one who undertook a matter and failed at it: 'سُقِطَ في يَدِهِ' (suqita fi yadihi)."

As for the fact that most people in this state are accompanied by regret, and that is how it accompanied the Children of Israel mentioned in the verse, the connection between these expressions and the meaning we have mentioned is that the striving, or the turning, or the defending, has fallen into the hand of the one referred to, so that it remains in his hand and does not go beyond it, and has no effect outside it. Al-Zajjaj said: "The meaning is that regret fell into their hands." It is also possible that loss and disappointment fell into their hands.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On all of this it follows that "سَقَطَ" (saqata) is transitive, since "سَقَطَ" implies an object, which here is the verbal noun of the causing to fall (al-isqat), as one says "ذُهِبَ بِزَيْدٍ" (dhuhiba bi-Zayd). In this statement there is weakness. In the language of the Arabs, "al-siqat" (السِّقاط) means much error and regret over it. From it is the saying of Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil:

"How can they hope for my failure, after
the head has been covered with white hair and baldness?"

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 148–149**

(p-48)

God the Exalted said:

﴿And the people of Musa, after him, took from their ornaments a calf, a body that had a lowing sound. Did they not see that it does not speak to them, nor guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿And when they were overcome with regret, and saw that they had gone astray, they said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will certainly be among the losers."﴾

The original form of "اتَّخَذَ" (ittakhadha) is "اِيتَخَذَ" (ayttakhadha), whose pattern is "افْتَعَلَ" (ifta'ala), from "تَخِذَ" (takhidha). This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. The pronoun in "بَعْدِهِ" (ba'dihi) refers to Musa, meaning after his departure for the private conversation with God (al-munajah). The ornaments are attributed to the Children of Israel, although they were borrowed from the Copts (al-Qibt), since the Children of Israel had taken possession of them, either because they were given them as a spoil (nafl), as has been narrated. Yahya ibn Sallam reported from al-Hasan that he said: "The Children of Israel borrowed the ornaments of the Copts for the day of festivity. When Musa was commanded to set out with them by night, it became impossible for them to return the borrowed items. Also, they feared that their secret would be exposed. Then God gave them these as a spoil." It is also possible that the ornaments are attributed to the Children of Israel because their hands handled them after the conquest of the people of Pharaoh.

It is narrated that al-Samiri, whose name was Musa ibn Zafar and who was ascribed to a village called Samira, said to Harun when Musa went to the private conversation: "O Harun, the Children of Israel have squandered the ornaments that were borrowed from the Copts. They have disposed of them and spent some of them. If you were to gather them, Musa could see his opinion regarding them." He said: "Harun gathered them. When they were gathered, he said to al-Samiri: 'You are the most worthy of people to have them kept with you.'" So al-Samiri took them, and he was a goldsmith, and he fashioned from them the image of a calf, which is the young of a cow.

"جَسَدًا" (jasadan) means a body (juththa) and inanimate matter. It was said: it was a body without a head. This is an argument based on the linguistic meaning of "jasad," which refers to whatever is other than the head. It was also said: God gave it flesh and blood.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and Shayba recited "مِن حُلِيِّهِمْ" (min huliyyihim) with a dammah on the ha' and a kasrah on the lam. It is the plural of "حَلْيٌ" (hally), on the pattern of "ثَدْيٌ" (thady) and "ثُدِيٌّ" (thudiyy). Its original form is "حُلُوِيٌ" (huluwiyy); the waw was changed into a ya' and assimilated, so "حُلُيٌّ" (hulayyun) resulted, and the lam was given a kasrah to harmonize with the ya'. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "مِن حِلِيِّهِمْ" (min hiliyyihim) with a kasrah on the ha', according to the explanation we previously mentioned. Abu Hatim said: "However, they gave the ha' a kasrah to follow the kasrah of the lam." Abu 'Ali said: "The change that entered the plural was strengthened by this later change." He said: "What confirms the kasrah of the fa' in this kind of plural is their saying 'qisiyy' (قِسِيٌّ)." Abu Hatim said: "Yahya ibn Wassab, Talha, al-A'mash and the companions of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited it thus." Ya'qub al-Hadrami recited "مِن حَلْيِهِمْ" (min halyihim) with a fatha on the ha' and sukun on the lam. Then it is either a singular used to mean the plural, or it is the plural of "حِلْيَةٌ" (hilyah), as "تَمْرَةٌ" (tamrah) and "تَمْرٌ" (tamr). The meaning of "الحُلِيِّ" (al-hulli) is what is adorned with, of stones, gold and silver.

Then God the Exalted made clear their corrupt natures and established the corruption of their belief by His saying: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾ (p-49) and the rest of the verse. This is because the silent inanimate object does not possess divinity, and what does not guide to good nor removes distress is likewise. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 150:

(p-52) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿When Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me. Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by his head, dragging him toward himself. He said: "O son of my mother! The people deemed me weak and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies rejoice over me, and do not place me with the wrongdoing people."﴾

He means: he returned from the private communion (munajah). It is narrated that when he drew near the encampment of the Children of Israel, he heard their voices and said: "These are the voices of people at play." But when he realized that they were devoted to the worship of the calf, anger and grief overcame him and he threw down the Tablets. This is what Ibn Ishaq said. Al-Tabari said: God informed him, before his return, that they had been seduced by the calf, and therefore he returned while angry. Grief (asaf) may mean intense anger, but it most often means sorrow, and both meanings apply here. The "ma" attached to "bi'sa" is verbal-masdariyya (it forms a verbal noun with the following verb); this is the view of al-Kisa'i, and there is a difference of opinion about it that was discussed earlier in Surah al-Baqarah. The meaning is: evil is your succession to me after me. One says "khalafahu bi-khayr aw bi-sharr" when a person does good or evil to those he leaves behind after him. One says "ajila fulan al-amr" when he got ahead in it. So His saying "a-'ajiltum" means: Did you race ahead of your Lord's decree and hasten my coming before the time that was appointed for it?

As for His, the Exalted, saying "and he threw down the Tablets," etc., Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the cause of his throwing down the Tablets was his anger at his people for their worship of the calf and his anger at his brother for neglecting their affair. Qatada said, if it is authentically transmitted from him: Rather, it was because he saw in them the excellence of the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and he desired that this should belong to his own community; when he learned that it belonged to others, he became angry.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a poor opinion, and Moses, peace be upon him, should not be described by it. The first view is the correct one. In general, there was a narrowness of temper in Moses' character, and this is established in more than one place. It is also narrated that the Tablets were two tablets, and the dual was expressed in the plural form since the dual is a kind of plural. It is further narrated that they were a load of seventy camels, from which one part could be read in a year.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak and excessive; it was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Ibn 'Abbas said: When Moses threw them down, they broke, and most of them were lifted up, the part containing the detailed explanation of everything; what remained in his copy was guidance and mercy, and it is that which he took afterward. The discussion of what the Tablets were made of has already been mentioned earlier. His seizing his brother by the head and beard is part of the aforementioned disposition; this is the apparent meaning of the wording. It is also narrated that this was only because of his left hand, and Harun feared that an onlooker might suppose it was from anger, so he forbade him and entreated him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak; the first view is the correct one, because of His saying: ﴿You caused a division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94]. His saying "son of my mother" is an appeal for tenderness by the bond of the mother, since it is the closest of kinships. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim read "ibna umma" with a fatha on the mim. The Kufans said: its origin is "ibna ummaha," which was elided for lightness. Sibawayh said: they are two nouns built on fatha like a single noun, as with fifteen and the like. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr), Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ibna ummi" with a kasra on the mim, so the origin is "ibna ummi" with the ya' elided, either by analogy with their elision in "la ubali" and "la adri" for lightness, or because they treated the first and the last as a single noun and then added to it, as in your saying "ya ahada 'ashara aqbilu," as Sibawayh said. This is more analogical than elision for lightness. Then they added it to the ya' of the speaker, and the ya' was elided from "ummi" according to the dialect of one who says "ya ghulami," eliding it in the vocative. Had one not supposed that the first and last form a single noun, the elision would not be valid, because "umm" is not a vocative.

"Istada'uni" means: they considered me weak. His saying "kadu" means they came close but did not do it.

Most readers recite "fa-la tushmit biya al-a'da'a" with a damma on the ta', a kasra on the mim, and a fatha on "al-a'da'a." Mujahid, as transmitted by Abu Hatim, recited "fa-la tashmat biya" with a fatha on the ta' and the mim and a damma on "al-a'da'u." Abu Hatim transmitted this. Mujahid also recited, as transmitted by Abu al-Fath: "fa-la tashmat biya al-a'da'a" with a fatha on the ta' and the mim and a fatha on "al-a'da'a," on the basis that "shamita" is made transitive. This has also been narrated. Abu al-Fath said: "So do not rejoice over me, you, O Lord," and this is permissible, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] and similar expressions. Then he returned to the intended meaning and supplied a verb which governs "al-a'da'a" in the accusative, as if he said: "Do not let the enemies rejoice over me," as in the reading of the majority.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is contrivance in this statement of Abu al-Fath. Al-Mahdawi related from Ibn Muhaysin: "tashmit" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the mim, and "al-a'da'a" in the accusative. Shamata (gloating) is the enemy's joy at his enemy's calamity. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾ means the worshippers of the calf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 151–153:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. And thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾ ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed—indeed, your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Musa (Moses) sought forgiveness for his own action with his brother, and for his haste in throwing down the Tablets. He sought forgiveness for his brother for his action in being patient with the Children of Israel. It is possible that the seeking of forgiveness was for something other than this, which we do not know, and God knows best.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾, the verse is an address from God Most High to Musa, peace be upon him, given His saying ﴿will be overtaken﴾. That overtaking occurred in the time of Musa, peace be upon him. The wrath and humiliation are the command to them to kill themselves; this is the apparent meaning. Some of the exegetes said: "Humiliation" is the jizya (poll tax). The rationale for this view is that the wrath and humiliation remained among the descendants of those originally addressed, and it is as if the intended meaning is: "will overtake their descendants." Ibn Jurayj said: the reference in His saying "those who" is to those among the worshippers of the calf who died before repentance by the killing of souls, and to those who fled and were not present at the time of the killing.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to this view, the wrath and humiliation are the punishment of the Hereafter. The wrath of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, if taken in the sense of will, is an attribute of essence; and if taken in the sense of punishment and the descent of vengeance, it is an attribute of action. (p-55) As for His saying: ﴿And thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, the primary intended referents are those who fabricated lies against God regarding the worship of the calf, while the general force of the wording encompasses every fabricator until the Day of Resurrection. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, Abu Qilaba and others said: every possessor of innovation (bid'a) or slander is abased, and they took this verse as evidence.

As for His saying Exalted is He: ﴿But those who committed evil deeds﴾, this verse contains the promise that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forgives those who repent, and the reference is to those among the Children of Israel who repented. The verse contains the ordering of faith after repentance. The meaning of this is that by His saying "and believed," He intended that repentance is beneficial for them and saving, so they should hold fast to it; this is a specific faith following faith in the absolute sense. It is also possible that by His saying "and believed" He means "and did the deeds of believers until they died upon that." It is also possible that He intends emphasis, so He mentioned repentance and faith, since they are mutually entailing; except that repentance, on this view, would be from disbelief necessarily, so "repented and believed" would have one meaning. This does not apply to repentance from sins, since faith necessarily precedes that, and faith and repentance from disbelief are mutually entailing. His saying ﴿indeed, your Lord﴾ is an affirmation and a hopeful promise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that His saying "repented and believed" means that the order of the two verbs was not intended, according to the usage of the conjunction "wa" which does not necessarily imply order, and "and believed" would mean: "while they are believers before and after," as if He said: "among their attributes is that they believed."
