The verse contains the ordering of faith after repentance. The meaning of this is that by His saying "and believed," He intended that repentance is beneficial for them and saving, so they should hold fast to it; this is a specific faith following faith in the absolute sense. It is also possible that by His saying "and believed" He means "and did the deeds of believers until they died upon that." It is also possible that He intends emphasis, so He mentioned repentance and faith, since they are mutually entailing; except that repentance, on this view, would be from disbelief necessarily, so "repented and believed" would have one meaning. This does not apply to repentance from sins, since faith necessarily precedes that, and faith and repentance from disbelief are mutually entailing. His saying ﴿indeed, your Lord﴾ is an affirmation and a hopeful promise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that His saying "repented and believed" means that the order of the two verbs was not intended, according to the usage of the conjunction "wa" which does not necessarily imply order, and "and believed" would mean: "while they are believers before and after," as if He said: "among their attributes is that they believed."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 151–153:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. And thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾ ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed—indeed, your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Musa (Moses) sought forgiveness for his own action with his brother, and for his haste in throwing down the Tablets. He sought forgiveness for his brother for his action in being patient with the Children of Israel. It is possible that the seeking of forgiveness was for something other than this, which we do not know, and God knows best.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾, the verse is an address from God Most High to Musa, peace be upon him, given His saying ﴿will be overtaken﴾. That overtaking occurred in the time of Musa, peace be upon him. The wrath and humiliation are the command to them to kill themselves; this is the apparent meaning. Some of the exegetes said: "Humiliation" is the jizya (poll tax). The rationale for this view is that the wrath and humiliation remained among the descendants of those originally addressed, and it is as if the intended meaning is: "will overtake their descendants." Ibn Jurayj said: the reference in His saying "those who" is to those among the worshippers of the calf who died before repentance by the killing of souls, and to those who fled and were not present at the time of the killing.

(p-56) The meaning of this verse is that when Musa's anger had subsided (peace be upon him), he took up the tablets that he had thrown down. It has already been mentioned that it is narrated that most of them were lifted up, or that they were broken into pieces. His saying ﴿sakata﴾ ("subsided") is a metaphorical expression: he likened the dying down of anger to the cessation of a speaker's speech, which is his silence. Yunus ibn Habib said: the Arabs say, "The valley flowed for two days, then it fell silent." Al-Zajjaj and others said: the verbal noun of your saying, "The anger fell silent" (sakata al-ghadab), is sakt, and the verbal noun of your saying, "The man fell silent" (sakata al-rajul), is sukut. This implies that it is a separate verb and not the silence of people. It has also been said that there is an inversion (qalb) in the meaning, and the intended sense is: "When Musa fell silent from anger." This is of the type of: "I put my mouth into the stone" and "I put the cap on my head." In this too there is a metaphor, since anger does not speak so as to be described as falling silent. Mu'awiya ibn Qurra read, "Wa-lamma sakana" ("when it calmed"). In the Mushaf (written codex) of Hafsa, it reads, "Wa-lamma sakata." In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud, it reads, "Wa-lamma sabara 'an Musa al-ghadab" ("when anger was patient toward Musa"). Al-Naqqash said: in the Mushaf of Ubayy, it reads, "Wa-lamma ushtuqqa 'an Musa al-ghadab" ("when anger was split away from Musa").

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿wa-fi nuskhatiha﴾ means: "and in what is copied from them and recited." The lam in His saying, ﴿li-rabbihim﴾, may carry several meanings. The view of al-Mubarrad is that it is connected to a verbal noun, as if he had said: "those whose awe is for their Lord." It may also be that, since the object was placed first, the verb became weakened, so it became strong enough to transitively govern with the lam. It may also mean: "they, for the sake of obeying their Lord and fearing their Lord, dread the punishment and the threat, and the like of this."

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿wa-ikhtara Musa qawmahu﴾ (to the end of the verse). The meaning of this verse is that Musa (peace be upon him) chose from his people this number so that he might take them to a place of worship, supplication and entreaty, so that there would be from him and from them an apology to Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, for the error of the Children of Israel in worshipping the calf, and a request for the complete pardon of those among them who remained. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that their selection was due to the Children of Israel's saying: "Musa killed Harun when he went with him and did not return." So he chose these people so that they might go and Harun would speak to them, (proving) that he had died of his own term. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿li-miqatina﴾ supports the first view and contradicts this view, because it implies that that was at a appointed time set by Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, and a promise of a specific time and place. The construction of the speech is: "And Musa chose from his people," and when the preposition was omitted, the verb became transitive and took the accusative. This is common in the speech of the Arabs.

(p-57) The scholars differed about the cause of the quake (al-rajfa) that struck them. It has been said: it was a punishment for them because of their silence and their turning a blind eye to the worship of the calf. It has been said: it was for their own worship of the calf, and this was hidden from Musa at the time of the selection until Allah informed him; this was said by al-Suddi. It has been said: it was a punishment for them because, when they drew near and knew that Musa was hearing the speech of Allah, they said to him: "Show us your Lord," and then the quake seized them. It has been said: it was a punishment for their excess in supplication, when they said: "O Allah, give us what You have given no one before us and will not give to anyone after us," and then the quake seized them. It has been said: it only seized them when they heard the speech of Harun while he was dead; that is because Musa and Harun went off to worship or something similar, then Harun died, and Musa buried him and returned. The Children of Israel said: "Where is Harun?" He said: "He has died." They said: "No, you have killed him, because you envied us for his good character and his companionship." So he chose the seventy so that they might go with him until they saw the proof of what he had said to them. When they arrived, Musa said to him: "O Harun, were you killed or did you die?" He called out to him from the grave: "I died," and then the quake seized the people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is narrated that they died in this quake, and it is possible that it was like a swoon or the like. The rajfa is trembling and shaking because of a great terror. When Musa saw that, he grieved over them, and he knew that the affair of the Children of Israel would become scattered upon him if he did not bring back the people. So he began to implore his Lord, saying: "My Lord, if You had destroyed them before this state, and me too, it would have been more fitting for me. This is a time of their destruction which causes corruption for me and harm to me."

Then he questioned in the manner of desire, humility and submission. His saying, ﴿Rabbi law shi'ta ahlaktahum min qablu wa-iyya﴾, may mean the time when they turned a blind eye to the worship of the calf, that is, the time of their worship, according to that view. In his own self, it is the time of his killing of the Qibti (the Egyptian man), that is: "You had covered and pardoned at that time, so how is it now, since my returning without them causes corruption for the Children of Israel?" So the aim of the speech, according to this, is purely seeking compassion, and according to the first interpretation, its aim is presenting the argument in the form of a plea for compassion. When we say that the cause of the quake was the worship of the calf, the pronoun in His saying, ﴿a-tuhlikuna﴾, refers to him and to the seventy. The "foolish ones" (al-sufaha') refers to the worshippers from among the Children of Israel. Likewise, when its cause was the saying of the Children of Israel to him: "You killed Harun." When the cause of the quake was their request to see (Allah) and their excess in supplication, or their worshipping the calf themselves, the pronoun in His saying, ﴿a-tuhlikuna﴾, is intended to refer to himself and the Children of Israel, that is: destruction would come to them through division, disbelief and disobedience. The word "foolish ones" would then refer to the seventy. It is narrated that among the seventy there was no one older than forty nor younger than twenty. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were all brought back to life and made prophets.

A group said: when Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, informed Musa (peace be upon him) that the seventy had worshipped the calf, he was astonished and said: ﴿in hiya illa fitnatuka tudillu biha man tasha'﴾ ("It is only Your trial: You send astray by it whom You will"), that is: the matters are in Your hand, and You do what You wish. It has also been said: when Allah, may He be exalted, informed Musa of the worship of the calf by the Children of Israel and of its description, Musa said: "O Lord, and who made it?" He said: "I did." Musa said: "Then You led them astray; it is only Your trial." It is possible that by "it" (hiya) he refers to their saying, "Show us Allah," since it was a trial from Allah that necessitated the quake. In this verse there is a refutation of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). The meaning of ﴿righfir﴾ ("forgive") is: cover (istur).

"واكْتُبْ" means: decree and ordain. "Writing" (al-katb) is used for what is lasting. "Hasanah" is a general term for everything good in this world, such as well-being, wealth, obedience to Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and other things. The "good" of the Hereafter is Paradise: there is no good beyond it and no goal beyond it. "Hudna" with a dammah on the ha' means: we have repented (tubna). Abu Wajza read "Hidna" with a kasrah on the ha', meaning: we moved ourselves and drew ourselves toward Your obedience. It is derived from hada, yahidu, meaning "to move."

[p-59] As for His saying, ﴿My punishment: I afflict with it whom I will﴾, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: the earthquake (al-rajfa) that descended upon the people is My punishment, with which I afflict whom I will. Then He informed of His mercy. It is also possible, and this is the more apparent view, that the speech was intended as a report about His punishment and His mercy from the very beginning, and the matter of the people of the earthquake is included in the generality of His saying: ﴿My punishment: I afflict with it whom I will﴾.

Al-Hasan, Tawus, and 'Amr ibn Fa'id read "man asa'" (whoever does evil) from al-isa'a, meaning whoever does what is not righteous. The Mu'tazila have two connections with this reading: first, the enforcement of the threat (al-wa'id); second, that man creates his own actions, and that "asa'" has no act of Allah in it. These two connections have a possibility that can be resolved from them, as with the rest of the apparent meanings. However, the reciters went to great lengths to guard against this reading. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: this reading is not authentic from al-Hasan, Tawus, and 'Amr ibn Fa'id, who was an evil man (rajul su'). Abu Hatim mentioned that Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna once recited it and approved of it, so 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqbiri stood up to him, shouted at him, and made him hear. Sufyan said: "I did not know, and I did not perceive what the people of innovation (ahl al-bid'a) were saying." This is excessive zeal from those close to Allah, and their caution about religion and their assumption that escaping the Mu'tazila's connection is impossible led them to it.

Then Allah, Blessed and Exalted, described His mercy as encompassing everything. Some scholars said: it is general regarding mercy, and specific in His saying ﴿everything﴾, and what is meant is those whom it has already been known in Allah's knowledge that He will show mercy to, to the exclusion of others. Some said: it is general regarding the mercy of this world, because the disbeliever, the believer, and all animals are continually subject to Allah's worldly mercy. A group said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and My mercy﴾ refers to repentance (tawba), and on this view it is specific in mercy and in things, because what is meant is those from whom repentance may occur. Nawf al-Bakali said: when Iblis heard Allah's saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and My mercy encompasses everything﴾, he hoped for Allah's mercy. But when he heard ﴿So I will decree it for those who fear Me and give zakah﴾, Iblis despaired, and the Jews and Christians remained. When the description was completed, it became clear that what is meant is the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the Jews and Christians despaired of the verse. Qatada said something similar.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So I will decree it﴾, meaning: I will determine it and ordain it. Nawf al-Bakali said: Musa (peace be upon him) said: "My Lord, I have made my delegation (wifada) for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ)." Nawf al-Bakali also said: so praise Allah, who made the delegation of the Children of Israel for you.

As for His saying "yattaqun" (they fear/guard against) in this verse, a group said: it means they guard against shirk (associating partners with Allah), and a group said: they guard against sins (ma'asi).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever says "only shirk and nothing else" has departed into the view of the Murji'a (those who postpone judgment on works). The verse refutes him with the condition of deeds in His saying, Blessed and Exalted, ﴿and they give zakah﴾. Whoever says "sins, without exception" has departed into the view of the Mu'tazila. The correct position is that the term is general, but we should not say "guarding against sins is necessary," rather we should say: "together with the fact that the occurrences of sins are within the will of Allah, Exalted is He." The meaning of "yattaqun" is that they place between themselves and what they guard against a shield (wiqaya) and a barrier (hijab). Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the lofty rank so that the listeners would race toward it.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and they give zakah﴾: the apparent meaning from His saying ﴿and they give﴾ is that it is the zakah specific to wealth. He singled it out here for mention to honor it, and to make it an example for all acts of obedience. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, as is narrated from him: "and they give" refers to the deeds by which they purify their souls.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 157:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the vile things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honour him, support him, and follow the light that has been sent down with him — it is they who are the successful.﴾

These words removed the Jews and the Christians from the shared address that appears in His saying: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Me﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], and this promise was restricted to the community of Muhammad ﷺ. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and others.

"Yattabi'ūn" means: following his law and religion. "Al-Rasūl" (the Messenger) and "al-Nabī" (the Prophet) are two names for two meanings, for the Messenger is more specific than the Prophet; this is so with regard to human beings, because the sense of sovereignty is shared in the word "Messenger." (p-61) "Al-Nabī" is derived from "al-naba'" (news). It was also said: since he is a path to the mercy of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and a means to it, he was likened to the "nabī" (the raised path/road), which is the way. They recited:

"It would have become crumbled pebbles in place of the nabī from the rocky ground."

Its original form has a hamza, but it was lightened; this is what Sibawayh said, and it is like their lightening of khābiyah (a pit), from khabba'a. Its lightened form came into use, so much so that it has been narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not pronounce my name with a hamza." The word "Messenger" was placed first out of concern for the meaning of "risalah" (mission) for those addressed by the Qur'an; otherwise the meaning of prophethood is the one that comes first. Likewise, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ responded to al-Bara' ibn 'Azib when he said: "I believed in Your Book which You sent down, and in Your Messenger whom You sent," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "And in Your Prophet whom You sent," so that the speech would be arranged as the matter is arranged in itself, for he was first made a prophet and then sent as a messenger. Also, in the reversed phrasing there would be a repetition of "mission," which is one meaning.

"Al-Ummī" with a damma on the hamza: it was said to be a relative noun referring to Umm al-Qura, which is Makkah.

(p-62) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this, the word is specific to the Prophet ﷺ and does not imply the meaning of not writing. It was also said that it is a relative noun, on account of not writing and not reckoning, derived from "umm" (mother), meaning he is in the state of one who comes forth from his mother, in not writing. A group said it is a relative noun derived from "ummah" (community), and this too implies not writing, because the community as a whole is non-writing until writing occurs among it like other crafts. Some reciters, as Abu Hatim mentioned, read "al-Ummī" with a fatha on the hamza, and it is a relative noun derived from "umm," which means "intent" (qasd), that is, because this Prophet is the intended goal of people and the place of a "mother" to which they turn in their deeds and their legislation. Ibn Jinni said: this reading may intend "al-Ummī," but it was altered in the manner of relative nouns.

The pronoun in His saying "yajidūnahu" refers to the Children of Israel, and the hā' in it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, and what is meant is his description and attributes. It is narrated that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said to Musa: "Say to the Children of Israel: I will make the earth for you a place of prostration and purification, and I will place the tranquility (sakinah) with you in your houses, and I will make you recite the Torah from the memory of your hearts." Musa informed the Children of Israel, and they said: "We only want to pray in the churches, and for the tranquility to be as it was in the ark, and not to recite the Torah except by looking at it." So it was said to them: "Then We will write it for those who fear Me," meaning the community of Muhammad ﷺ. It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, in al-Bukhari and others, that in the Torah there is a description of Muhammad ﷺ: "O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bearer of good news, a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My messenger; I have named you the one who relies (al-Mutawakkil). He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets, and he does not repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks. I will not take him until through him I have set straight the crooked community, so that they say there is no god but Allah, and by him We open hearts that are veiled, ears that are deaf, and eyes that are blind." In al-Bukhari: "So by him We open blind eyes, deaf ears, and veiled hearts."

The text of Ka'b al-Ahbar is similar in these wordings, except that he said: "veiled hearts and deaf ears (ādhānan summuman)." Al-Tabari said: this is a Himyarite dialect, and it has been narrated as "ghulufiyā wa summūmiyā."

(p-63) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I think this is an error and a non-Arabic usage.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿who enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong﴾ may be taken as beginning a description of the Prophet ﷺ by Allah, Blessed and Exalted; it may also be taken as connected to "yajidūnahu" in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), in a figurative sense, meaning: they find him written in the Torah as one who commands on condition of his existence. The first meaning does not require that they knew from the Torah that he would command, forbid, make lawful, and make unlawful; the second meaning requires that. According to this second meaning, it is a censure of them. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj inclined to this. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said in "al-Aghfal": "Yamurruhum" is, in my view, an explanation of what was written of his mention, just as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] is an explanation of the example, and it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yajidūnahu," because the pronoun refers to the mention and the name, and the mention and the name do not command.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What I have put forward regarding figurative usage and the condition of existence comes close to what Abu 'Ali prohibited; consider this. "Bil-ma'rūf" means what the Law recognised; and every good deed from the standpoint of manliness is recognised by the Law, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "I was sent to perfect noble character." "Al-munkar" is its opposite.

As for "al-tayyibāt," some of the exegetes said regarding it that it refers to the baḥīrah and the like. The position of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, is that they are the lawful things; so he described them as good, since it is a word that carries praise and honour. On this basis he says regarding "al-khabā'ith" that they are the unlawful things. Likewise Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "al-khabā'ith" are the flesh of swine, usury, and other things. On this basis Malik made lawful what is loathsome, such as snakes, beetles, scorpions and the like. The position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, is that "al-tayyibāt" are in terms of taste, except that the word for him is not on its full generality, because its generality in this sense of taste would require the permissibility of wine and swine; rather, he sees it as specific to what the Law has made lawful. He sees "al-khabā'ith" as a general term for what is unlawful by the Law and for what is loathsome, so he prohibits scorpions, beetles, geckos, and what is of this kind. People hold these two positions, though there is disagreement about specifying the "khabā'ith," which is not the place to pursue it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and relieves them of their burden﴾ and the verse continues. "Yaḍa'" by analogy should have been "yaḍi'" with a kasra on the ḍād, but the guttural letter turned it to a fatḥa on the ḍād. Abu Hatim said: Abu 'Amr assimilated "yaḍa' 'anhum" the ayn into the ayn, and Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' gave it the sound of a raised vowel (ishmām al-raf') and prolonged it. Talha recited: "wa yudhhibu 'anhum israhum" (and removes from them their burden). "Al-isr" means the weight, and Qatada, Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid explained it here in this sense. "Al-isr" also means the covenant, and Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and others explained it so. This verse combines both meanings, for a covenant had been taken from the Children of Israel that they would perform heavy deeds, so that covenant and the weight of those deeds were lifted from them by Muhammad ﷺ. Abu Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "al-isr" is the severity of worship. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and the people read "israhum," while Ibn 'Amir alone, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, Ya'la ibn Hakim, Abu Siraj al-Hudhali and Abu Ja'far read "aṣārahum" in the plural, because the deeds were many, so their weights were varied. Whoever uses the singular "isr" is using a singular noun of genus which is meant as a plural. Abu Hatim said: in the book of some scholars: "uṣuraham," singular with an open hamza, from Nafi', 'Isa and al-Zayyat, and that is an error. Makki mentioned it from Abu Bakr from 'Asim and said: it is a dialect.

﴿And the shackles that were upon them﴾ is also a figurative expression for those burdens, like cutting off the skin at the place of urine, and that there is no blood-money and that the killer must be killed, and abandoning work on the Sabbath; for it has been narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, saw a man on the Sabbath carrying reeds and struck off his neck. This is the saying of the majority of exegetes. This is like your saying: "the collar of so-and-so is such-and-such" when one imposes it upon him; and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Take it away, take it away... you were encircled with it, the collar of the dove!"

That is: its shame clung to you. (p-65) From this same meaning is the saying of al-Hudhali:

"It is not like the old covenant of the abode, O Umm Malik, but the chains have encircled the necks."

"The youth has returned like a man of middle age, saying nothing except the truth, and the blamers have rested."

He means the commands of Islam and the obligations of faith, which restrained recklessness, as the Prophet ﷺ said. Ibn Zayd said: what is meant here by the shackles is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, about the Jews: ﴿Their hands are chained﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]; so whoever believes in Muhammad ﷺ, the call and its chaining are removed from him.

Then Allah, Exalted, informed about the state of the believers, saying: ﴿So those who believe in him, honour him, support him﴾. Al-Jahdari, Sulayman al-Taymi, Qatada and 'Isa read "'azzarūhu" with lightening, while the majority of people read it with doubling of the zay; and its meaning in both readings is "they revered him" (waqqarūhu). "Al-ta'zīr" and "al-nasr" are a special witnessing for the Companions, while following the light is shared with them by believers until the Day of Resurrection. "Al-nūr" is a metaphor for the whole of the Law, and His saying "ma'ahu" (with him) contains an elision of a word in construct; the implied meaning is: "with his sending" or "with his prophethood" or something similar. The Law and guidance were likened to light, since hearts are illuminated by it just as sight is illuminated by light. "Al-mufliḥūn" means: those who attain their desire; and this encompasses the meanings of success, for whoever remains (in Paradise) has attained his desire.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 158–159:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all, [the Messenger of] He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet who believes in Allah and His words, and follow him that you may be guided."﴾ ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it establish justice.﴾ ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.﴾ [al-A'raf: 160]

(p-66) This is a command from Allah the Mighty and Majestic to His Prophet to make the call public and to urge people to enter the Law. When He had given hope to the community that follows the unlettered Prophet, for whom He had prescribed His mercy, He followed this with calling people to the following (ittiba') through which those ranks are attained. This verse is specific to Muhammad ﷺ among the messengers, for Muhammad ﷺ was sent to all people and to the jinn; this was said by al-Hasan, and the hadiths require it. Every other prophet was sent only to a particular group, not to all. Then, when he was made public with the message from Allah, blessed and exalted is He, He followed it with an attribute of Allah that requires submission to Him: that He is the owner of the heavens and the earth through creation, origination, giving life and causing death. There is no deity except Him, and there is no one worshipped besides Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ to the end of the verse is the urging to follow Muhammad ﷺ. His saying ﴿who believes﴾ means: who affirms ﴿in Allah and His words﴾. The "words" here are the revealed verses from Him, such as the Torah and the Gospel.

Jumhur al-nas (the majority of readers) read "kalimatihi" in the plural. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "kalimatihi" in the singular, which is meant as a plural. al-A'mash read "alladhi yu'minu billahi wa-ayatihi" instead of "kalimatihi." Mujahid and al-Suddi said that what is meant by "kalimatihi" or "kalimatihi" is 'Isa ibn Maryam.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may be guided﴾ means: in accordance with your hope and according to what you see. His saying "wa-ittaba'uhu" (and follow him) is a general expression that includes all the obligations of the Law. May Allah make us among those who follow him in what is incumbent upon us, by His favour and mercy.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the people of Moses﴾ to the end of the verse. "Yahduna" means: they guide themselves aright. This statement may be understood as describing the righteous believers among the Children of Israel in the time of Moses and what followed of the era, so He informs that among the Children of Israel, despite their rebelliousness and opposition, there were those who were guided, were God-fearing and acted justly. It may also be understood as referring to the group among the Children of Israel who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, as an enticement toward the faith of all of them. It may also refer to what is narrated: that when the Children of Israel were divided, a community of them separated, withdrew, and entered beneath the earth, walking in a tunnel under the earth for a year and a half until they emerged behind China; there, beyond a valley of honey, they uphold the Law and guide by the truth. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj, and part of it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.

(p-67) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a far-fetched narration. Some people read "wa-qatta'nahum" with a doubled ta' (shadda on the ta'). Abu Hayawa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa-qata'nahum" with the ta' unstressed; it is transmitted by Aban from 'Asim. Its meaning is: We separated them, from qat' (cutting). The majority of readers read "'ashrata" with a sukun on the shin, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, and Talha ibn Sulayman, with a variant reading, read "'ashrata" with a fatha on the shin. This group also read, as did Talha ibn Musarrif and Abu Hayawa, "'ashirata" with a kasra on the shin, which is the dialect of Tamim. Abu Hatim said: It is strange that Tamim lighten what is of this pattern, while the people of the Hijaz vocalise it fully, and they contradict one another over this letter. His saying "asbatan" is a substitute (badal) for "ithnata." The specifier (tamyiz) that goes with the number is elided and understood: "ithnata 'ashrata firqatan" (twelve groups) or "qit'atan" (twelve portions), "asbatan." Or it may be removed from the specifier and understood as: "wa-qatta'nahum firaqan ithnata 'ashrata," then "asbatan" is substituted. The first is better and clearer. It is not permissible for "asbatan" to be a specifier, because a specifier must be singular and indefinite, and furthermore "sibt" is masculine while it is counted as feminine. Moreover, this reason alone would prevent it, since "sibt" means "community." al-Tabari said: Some of the Kufans said: since "sibt" carries the meaning of "community," the feminine was given precedence, and this is like the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, these Kilab are ten bellies, and you are innocent of their ten tribes."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This Kufan overlooked the plural of "asbat," and what he held would only be permissible if the sentence were "ithnata 'ashrata sibtan." "Sibt" among the progeny of Isaac is like "qabila" (tribe) among the progeny of Ishmael. al-Zajjaj and others said that "sibt" derives from "sabat," which is a tree.

(p-68) The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Rather, the more evident view is that it is a Hebrew word that was Arabicised.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 160:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We inspired Moses, when his people asked him for water: "Strike the rock with your staff." So there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew their drinking place. And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quail. "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

The matter of the rock and the seeking of water, and where that was, and the matter of the shading and the sending down of the manna and the quail, has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah, and we mentioned that there in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary.

"Fa-nbajasat" means "fa-nfajarat" (gushed forth), except that inbijas (a gentler seeping forth) is lighter than infijar (a forceful bursting forth). Al-A'mash and 'Isa al-Hamdani read "Kulu min tayyibati ma razaqnakum" with the pronoun in the singular (ﻛُﻠِﻲ ﻣِﻦْ ﻃَﻴِّﺒَﺎتِ ﻣَﺎ ﺭَﺯَﻗْﻨَﺎﻛُﻢْ), i.e., with the singular form of the pronoun.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 161–163:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when it was said to them: "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say, 'Remission,' and enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins and We will increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted a saying other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the sky for what they had been doing wrongly.﴾ ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them. Thus We tested them for what they used to defy.﴾

The meaning: "Remember when it was said to them," and what is intended are those who came before among the Children of Israel. That is because when they came out of the wilderness (al-tih), it was said to them: "Dwell in this town." The "qaryah" in the speech of the Arabs is the city, the gathering place of dwellings, and the reference here is to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

This is the saying of al-Tabari. It was also said: it refers to Jericho (Ariha). "Wherever you wish" means: it and its bounties are permitted to you. The Seven Readers, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Mujahid and others read "ḥiṭṭah" with a nominative ending (raf'). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "ḥiṭṭatan" with an accusative ending (naṣb). The nominative is the predicate of an implied subject, its implied sense being: "our request is ḥiṭṭah" (ḥiṭṭah, meaning "remission" or "lowering of burdens"). The accusative is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "lower our sins by a lowering." This is on the basis that they were commanded to utter a word whose meaning is ḥiṭṭah. Some people have said: they were commanded to utter a good saying that implies faith and gratitude to God, so that it would be a remission for their sins; the statement, according to this, is like your saying: "Say something good." The full explanation of this is mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "naghfir" with a nun, "lakum khaṭī'ātikum" with a ta' and a hamza, in the plural. Abu 'Amr read "naghfir" with a nun, "lakum khaṭāyākum" on the pattern of "qaḍāyākum", and this is the reading of al-Hasan and al-A'mash. Nafi' read "tughfar" with a ta' that is damma, "lakum khaṭī'ātukum" with a hamza and a damma on the ta', in the plural; and it was transmitted by Mahbub from Abu 'Amr.

Ibn 'Amir read "tughfar" with a ta' that is damma, "lakum khaṭī'atukum," singular, with a hamza and a nominative ending. Abu Hatim said: al-A'raj and a group read "taghfir" with a ta' and a fatha, in the sense that the ḥiṭṭah forgives, since it is the cause of forgiveness.

"Baddala" means: he changed the wording without removing all of it; "abdala" means: he removed it and brought another word. The reference of "the saying" is to the saying of the Children of Israel: "a grain in a hair or wheat in a barley-corn." The punishment (rijz) sent upon them was plague (ṭā'ūn); it is said that seventy thousand died from it in one day. The exhaustive explanation of this verse has also been mentioned previously.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ — the verse. Some of those who interpreted said: the Jews who opposed Muhammad ﷺ said: the Children of Israel had no disobedience or obstinacy in what they were commanded. So this verse came rebuking them and establishing what the people of this town had done. Their questioning was in the manner of rebuke. The town here is Madyan; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). It was also said: it is Aylah, said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abdullah ibn Kathir, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi and al-Thawri. Qatadah said it is "Muqna" with a qaf and sukun. Ibn Zayd said it is Maqnah, the coast of Madyan; it is also said Maghna, with a ghayn with fatha and a shaddah nun. It was also said: it is Tiberias, said by al-Zuhri.

"Ḥāḍirah" may be understood as the meaning of presence, i.e., the sea is present in it; and it may be understood as the meaning of civilization, in honour of it, i.e., it is the foremost of the cities of the sea. "Idh ya'dūna" means: they transgress the Law, from 'adā ya'dū. Shahr ibn Ḥawshab and Abu Nuhayk read "ya'addūna," and Abu al-Fath said: he meant "ya'tadūna," so he sukkined the ta' to assimilate it into the dal, and transferred its fatha to the 'ayn, so it became "ya'addūna" with a fatha on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the damma-ed dal. The transgression of them on the Sabbath is the very act and occupation, whether hunting or otherwise, except that in this incident it was by hunting. God, the Mighty and Majestic, had tested them concerning the matter of the fish, by its disappearing from them throughout the whole week; then when the Sabbath day came it would come to them in the water openly, i.e., approaching them lined up, as you say: "the spears were levelled" when they are extended in a line. This may occur from the fish by a sending from God, like the sending of clouds, or by revelation and inspiration like the revelation to the bee, or by a sense on that day in the manner God gives animals a sense on Friday of the matter of the Hour, according to what the saying of the Prophet ﷺ implies: "There is no creature except that it is attentive on Friday until the sun rises, out of fear of the Hour." It may also be that this was from the fish, a feeling of safety on that day, in the manner of the feeling of safety of the pigeons of the Sacred Precinct (Ḥaram).

The narrators of this story said: the fish would draw near and multiply until it could be taken by hand. Then, when it was Sunday night, it would disappear entirely; it was also said: its abundance disappeared and there remained only the little that wearies its hunter. ﴿And when it was said to them: "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say, 'Remission,' and enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins and We will increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted a saying other than what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the sky for what they had been doing wrongly.﴾ ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them. The meaning: "Remember when it was said to them," and what is intended are those who came before among the Children of Israel. That is because when they came out of the wilderness (al-tih), it was said to them: "Dwell in this town." The "qaryah" in the speech of the Arabs is the city, the gathering place of dwellings, and the reference here is to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

This is the saying of al-Tabari. It was also said: it refers to Jericho (Ariha). "Wherever you wish" means: it and its bounties are permitted to you. The Seven Readers, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Mujahid and others read "ḥiṭṭah" with a nominative ending (raf'). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "ḥiṭṭatan" with an accusative ending (naṣb). The nominative is the predicate of an implied subject, its implied sense being: "our request is ḥiṭṭah" (ḥiṭṭah, meaning "remission" or "lowering of burdens"). The accusative is as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "lower our sins by a lowering." This is on the basis that they were commanded to utter a word whose meaning is ḥiṭṭah. Some people have said: they were commanded to utter a good saying that implies faith and gratitude to God, so that it would be a remission for their sins; the statement, according to this, is like your saying: "Say something good." The full explanation of this is mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 164–166:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" They said, "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment because they were defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿So when they exceeded in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and expelled."﴾

The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: The Children of Israel divided into three groups. One group disobeyed and hunted (fish on the Sabbath), a second group forbade (the evil) and openly spoke out, and a third group withdrew and neither disobeyed nor forbade. When this third group saw the open rebuke of those who forbade and the rebellion and defiant excess of the disobedient, they said to those who forbade, "Why do you admonish a people" – meaning the disobedient – "whom Allah is going to destroy or punish," on the basis of strong assumption and what was known of Allah's dealings with disobedient nations at that time. Then those who forbade said, "Our admonition is an excuse before Allah." Then they differed after this. One group said: The group that neither disobeyed nor forbade was destroyed along with the disobedient as a punishment for abandoning the forbidding. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who also said: "I do not know what was done to them." Another group said: Rather, they were saved along with those who forbade, because they did not disobey and were not pleased (with the sin). This was said by 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and others. Ibn al-Kalbi said, in what al-Tabari narrated from him (p-72): The Children of Israel divided only into two groups: a group that disobeyed and openly transgressed, and a group that forbade, sought to change (the evil), and withdrew. The latter said to the disobedient, "Indeed Allah will destroy them and punish them." So a community of the disobedient said to those who forbade, mockingly: "Why do you admonish a people whom you know Allah is going to destroy or punish?"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first opinion is more correct, and the pronouns in His saying "to your Lord and perhaps they" support it, for this address requires a speaker, an addressee, and a referred-to party. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "ma'dhiratun" (an excuse) in the nominative, meaning: our admonition is an excuse, i.e., the establishment of an excuse. 'Asim – in some of what is transmitted from him – and 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Talha ibn Musarrif read "ma'dhiratan" in the accusative, meaning: we admonish as an excuse. Abu 'Ali said: Its proof is that Sibawayh said: If a man said to a man, "An excuse before Allah and before you for such-and-such," it would be in the accusative.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The man speaking in this example is making an excuse for himself, and the Children of Israel who forbade were not in that situation, so reflect.

The meaning of "muhlikuhum" is (destroying them) in this world, or "mu'adhdhibuhum" (punishing them) in the Hereafter. His saying, exalted is He, "perhaps they will fear Him," requires pure hope, because it is the speech of human beings.

The pronoun in His saying "nasu" (they forgot) refers to those who were forbidden. It is abandonment, called forgetting, since the strongest degree of abandonment is that the abandoned is forgotten. "Ma" in His saying "ma dhukkiru bihi" carries the sense of "alladhi" (that which). It may mean the reminder itself, or it may mean that in which the reminder was present. "Su'" (evil) is a general word for all sins, but what is specifically intended here, according to the narrative of the verse, is hunting the fish. "Alladhina zalamu" (those who wronged) are the disobedient. His saying, exalted is He, "bi-'adhabin ba'is" means: painful, agonizing, severe.

Nafi' and the people of Medina – Abu Ja'far, Shayba and others – read "biys" with a kasra on the ba', a sukun on the ya', a kasra on the sin, and tanwin, understood as a verb used as a name, like His saying ﷺ: "I forbid you from qil wa-qal" (saying and said). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "bi'sa," as you say: bi'sa al-rajulu (wretched is the man). Abu Hatim considered this weak. Abu 'Amr said: It is reported from al-Hasan "bi'sa" with a hamza between the ba' and the sin. Nafi', as transmitted by Kharija, read "bays" with a fatha on the ba', a sukun on the ya', a kasra on the sin with tanwin. Malik ibn Dinar related from Nasr ibn 'Asim "bays" on the pattern of jamal and jabal. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri read "ba'is" with a fatha on the ba', a kasra hamza, and a tanwinned sin on the pattern of fa'il, and from it is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"Would that I might meet Ruqayya in a secluded place, free from what is wretched."

Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: This is the reading of Nasr ibn 'Asim and Talha ibn Musarrif. It is reported from Nasr "bay'is" with a kasra on the ya' without hamza. Al-Zahrawi said: It is reported from al-A'mash "ba'iss," with the ba' fatha, the hamza kasra and shadda, and the sin kasra with tanwin. A group read "ba'issa" as the one before, except with a fatha on the sin. Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned it from what Ya'qub related. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' (in the transmission of Abu Qurra from him) and 'Asim (in the transmission of Hafs from him) read "ba'isin" with a ya' after the kasra hamza and the tanwinned sin, on the pattern of fa'il. This is a description by way of the verbal noun, like their saying "'adhir al-hayy" and al-nadhir and al-nakir and the like. It is the reading of al-A'raj, Mujahid, the people of the Hijaz, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Nasr ibn 'Asim and al-A'mash, and it is the one Abu Hatim preferred. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Isba' al-'Adwani:

"Angry with me, and I see no evil from either of them to me, wretched."

(p-74) The people of Mecca read "bi'isin" like the first, except with a kasra on the ba', on the pattern of fi'il. Abu Hatim said: They are two dialects. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him, read "bay'isin" with a fatha on the ba', a sukun on the ya', and a fatha on the hamza, on the pattern of fay'al, meaning: severe. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis al-Kindi:

"Both were a chief, severe, striking the helmet on the day of tumult."

It is an adjective like daygham and haydar, and it is the reading of al-A'mash. 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-A'mash (with a variant from him) read "bay'isin" like the one before, except with a kasra on the hamza, on the pattern of fay'il. This is anomalous, because fay'il does not occur in sound (triliteral) roots; it occurs only in defective roots, such as sayyid and mayyit. Al-Zahrawi said: Nasr related from 'Asim "bayyisin" on the pattern of mayyit, and this is taken as from the root ba's (misery), with no basis in hamza. Abu Hatim said: 'Asim claimed that al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "bi'yais," with the ba' kasra, the hamza sakin, and the ya' fatha, on the pattern of khidyam; Abu Hatim considered this weak. Among the seven, Ibn 'Amir read "bi'sin" with a kasra on the ba', a sukun on the hamza, and tanwin on the kasra sin. Some read "ba'sin" with a fatha on the ba' and a sukun on the alif. Abu al-Raja' read "ba'isin" on the pattern of fa'il. Some read "bayasa" with fatha on the ba', ya' and sin, on the pattern of fa'ala. Malik ibn Dinar read "ba'sa" with fatha on the ba' and sin and sukun on the hamza, on the pattern of fa'la, not declined. Some read "ba'sin" declined. Abu Hatim related "bayasin." Abu al-Fath said: This is the reading of Nasr ibn 'Asim. Al-Zahrawi related from Ibn Kathir and the people of Mecca "bi'sa," pronounced with a light hamza.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

He did not clarify whether the hamza is kasra or sakin.

His saying, exalted is He, "bima kanu yafsuqun" means: because of that, and as a punishment for it.

"Utuww" means: defiance and lack of obedience.

His saying, exalted is He, "qulna lahum" may be a saying in words from an angel who made them hear it, which would be more humiliating, degrading and abasing. It may also be an expression for the power that formed them into apes. "Khasi'in" means: banished, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ibn Sayyad: "Begone (ikhsa')!", and as one says to a dog: "Begone (ikhsa')!" So "khasi'in" is a predicate following a predicate; this is the view chosen by Abu al-Fath, who considered the qualifier weak, and so it is, because the intent is not comparison to banished apes.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Khasi'in" may also be a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "kunu," and the qualifier is also valid, though weak. It is reported that the young among them were transformed into apes and the old men were transformed into swine. It is reported that their transformation came two years after the sin of hunting the fish. Ibn al-Kalbi said: Their destruction occurred in the time of Dawud. It is reported that those who forbade divided the city between themselves and the disobedient by a wall. His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" They said, "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment because they were defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿So when they exceeded in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and expelled."﴾

The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: The Children of Israel divided into three groups. One group disobeyed and hunted (fish on the Sabbath), a second group forbade (the evil) and openly spoke out, and a third group withdrew and neither disobeyed nor forbade. Then those who forbade said, "Our admonition is an excuse before Allah." Then they differed after this. One group said: The group that neither disobeyed nor forbade was destroyed along with the disobedient as a punishment for abandoning the forbidding. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who also said: "I do not know what was done to them." Another group said: Rather, they were saved along with those who forbade, because they did not disobey and were not pleased (with the sin). This was said by 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan and others. Ibn al-Kalbi said, in what al-Tabari narrated from him (p-72): The Children of Israel divided only into two groups: a group that disobeyed and openly transgressed, and a group that forbade, sought to change (the evil), and withdrew. The latter said to the disobedient, "Indeed Allah will destroy them and punish them." So a community of the disobedient said to those who forbade, mockingly: "Why do you admonish a people whom you know Allah is going to destroy or punish?"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first opinion is more correct, and the pronouns in His saying "to your Lord and perhaps they" support it, for this address requires a speaker, an addressee, and a referred-to party. Abu 'Ali said: Its proof is that Sibawayh said: If a man said to a man, "An excuse before Allah and before you for such-and-such," it would be in the accusative.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The man speaking in this example is making an excuse for himself, and the Children of Israel who forbade were not in that situation, so reflect.

The meaning of "muhlikuhum" is (destroying them) in this world, or "mu'adhdhibuhum" (punishing them) in the Hereafter. His saying, exalted is He, "perhaps they will fear Him," requires pure hope, because it is the speech of human beings.

"Ma" in His saying "ma dhukkiru bihi" carries the sense of "alladhi" (that which). It may mean the reminder itself, or it may mean that in which the reminder was present. "Su'" (evil) is a general word for all sins, but what is specifically intended here, according to the narrative of the verse, is hunting the fish. "Alladhina zalamu" (those who wronged) are the disobedient. His saying, exalted is He, "bi-'adhabin ba'is" means: painful, agonizing, severe.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "bi'sa," as you say: bi'sa al-rajulu (wretched is the man). Abu Hatim considered this weak. Abu 'Amr said: It is reported from al-Hasan "bi'sa" with a hamza between the ba' and the sin. Nafi', as transmitted by Kharija, read "bays" with a fatha on the ba', a sukun on the ya', a kasra on the sin with tanwin. Malik ibn Dinar related from Nasr ibn 'Asim "bays" on the pattern of jamal and jabal. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri read "ba'is" with a fatha on the ba', a kasra hamza, and a tanwinned sin on the pattern of fa'il, and from it is the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"Would that I might meet Ruqayya in a secluded place, free from what is wretched."

Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: This is the reading of Nasr ibn 'Asim and Talha ibn Musarrif. It is reported from Nasr "bay'is" with a kasra on the ya' without hamza. Al-Zahrawi said: It is reported from al-A'mash "ba'iss," with the ba' fatha, the hamza kasra and shadda, and the sin kasra with tanwin. A group read "ba'issa" as the one before, except with a fatha on the sin. Abu 'Amr al-Dani mentioned it from what Ya'qub related. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 167–168:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And [recall] when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would afflict them with the worst torment. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into nations: among them are the righteous, and among them are those other than that. And We tested them with good times and bad that they might return.﴾

The form "ta'adhdhana" (تَأذَّنَ) is one that implies acquisition (al-takassub), from adhina (أذِنَ), meaning "he knew," and ādhana (آذَنَ), meaning "he informed," like karuma (كَرُمَ), akrama (أكْرَمَ) and takarrama (تَكَرَّمَ). However, when a verb of this kind (and what follows its pattern) is attributed to the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it does not carry the sense of acquisition that applies to created beings. Rather, it is construed with the meaning of knowledge as an attribute, not as acquisition, and it is an eternal attribute inherent in the Essence. The poet alludes to this meaning in his saying:

؎ "Know (ta'allam), may you not be disgraced (abayta al-la'n)"

He did not command him to "learn" in the sense that implies ignorance; rather he meant to make him aware of the strength of his knowledge. From the same usage is the saying of Zuhayr:

؎ "Know (ta'allam) that the worst of people is the living one / ... whose slogan is called out as Yasar"

So the meaning of this verse is: "And when Allah knew that He would surely send against them..." The strength of the speech implies that this knowledge from Him is coupled with execution and enforcement, just as you say of a matter you have resolved upon with utmost determination: "Allah knows I will surely do such-and-such." This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Fārisī. Al-Ṭabarī and others said: "ta'adhdhana" means "a'lama" (he made known). This is problematic from the standpoint of morphology, since the attribution of "ta'adhdhana" to the agent differs from that of "a'lama," and this becomes clear from transitivity and other features. Mujāhid said: "ta'adhdhana" means "qāla" (he said); and it is narrated from him that it means "amara" (he commanded). A group said: its meaning is "ta'allā" (he swore).

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What led them to this view is the entry of the lām (لَ) into the response (jawāb), but the word itself is far from this.

The pronoun in "'alayhim" refers to those of the Children of Israel who remained, not to the pronoun in "lahum." His words, Exalted is He: ﴿who would afflict them﴾ — Sa'īd ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the punishment. Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his community.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that it is general, encompassing everyone with whom the Jews are in this condition. "Yasūmuhum" means: he imposes upon them and burdens them. "Sū' al-'adhāb" (the worst torment) is apparently the jizya (poll tax) and humiliation. Allah has decreed this against them and brought down their dominion, so there is no banner of a Jew upon the earth. Ibn al-Musayyib said: it is recommended that the Jews be made to suffer under the jizya. It is related that a group of the Romans took control of their region, so they sold the neighboring Jews who lived among them and made them their possessions.

Then it is fitting, at the end of this verse—because it contains the infliction of punishment upon them and a warning—to alert to the swiftness of Allah's punishment and to frighten all people with this as a general warning; then He gave hope of this, as an act of kindness from Him, blessed and exalted is He.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them﴾ mean: We scattered them upon the earth. Al-Ṭabarī related from a group of exegetes: there is no patch of earth but that there is a group of Jews in it. The apparent meaning regarding those referred to in this verse is that they are those who came after Solomon at the time his kingdom ended, and it is apparent that this was before the period of 'Īsā, peace be upon him, since there were no righteous ones among them after their disbelief in 'Īsā (ﷺ). In the histories concerning this section there are conflicting reports. The words "al-ṣāliḥūn" (the righteous) and "dūna dhālika" (other than that) are expressions that may be understood as referring to the righteousness of faith: "dūna" in the sense of "ghayr" (other than) is taken to refer to the disbelievers; and if "ṣalāḥ" is taken to mean worship, good and the consequences of faith, then "dūna dhālika" may be understood as referring to believers.

﴿And We tested them﴾ means: We examined them. "Al-ḥasanāt" (good things) are health, ease and the like, which are according to the judgment and perception of the children of Adam; "al-sayyi'āt" (bad things) are their opposites. His words, "la'allahum" (that they might), mean: according to your opinion, if you were to witness that; and the meaning is: that perhaps they would return to obedience and repent of disobedience.

Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into nations: among them are the righteous, and among them are those other than that. And We tested them with good times and bad that they might return.﴾

The form "ta'adhdhana" (تَأذَّنَ) is one that implies acquisition (al-takassub), from adhina (أذِنَ), meaning "he knew," and ādhana (آذَنَ), meaning "he informed," like karuma (كَرُمَ), akrama (أكْرَمَ) and takarrama (تَكَرَّمَ). However, when a verb of this kind (and what follows its pattern) is attributed to the Name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, it does not carry the sense of acquisition that applies to created beings. Rather, it is construed with the meaning of knowledge as an attribute, not as acquisition, and it is an eternal attribute inherent in the Essence. The poet alludes to this meaning in his saying:

؎ "Know (ta'allam), may you not be disgraced (abayta al-la'n)"

He did not command him to "learn" in the sense that implies ignorance; rather he meant to make him aware of the strength of his knowledge. From the same usage is the saying of Zuhayr:

؎ "Know (ta'allam) that the worst of people is the living one / ... whose slogan is called out as Yasar"

So the meaning of this verse is: "And when Allah knew that He would surely send against them..." The strength of the speech implies that this knowledge from Him is coupled with execution and enforcement, just as you say of a matter you have resolved upon with utmost determination: "Allah knows I will surely do such-and-such." This is the view of Abu 'Ali al-Fārisī. Al-Ṭabarī and others said: "ta'adhdhana" means "a'lama" (he made known). This is problematic from the standpoint of morphology, since the attribution of "ta'adhdhana" to the agent differs from that of "a'lama," and this becomes clear from transitivity and other features. Mujāhid said: "ta'adhdhana" means "qāla" (he said); and it is narrated from him that it means "amara" (he commanded). A group said: its meaning is "ta'allā" (he swore).

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What led them to this view is the entry of the lām (لَ) into the response (jawāb), but the word itself is far from this.

The pronoun in "'alayhim" refers to those of the Children of Israel who remained, not to the pronoun in "lahum." His words, Exalted is He: ﴿who would afflict them﴾ — Sa'īd ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the punishment. Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it refers to Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his community.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that it is general, encompassing everyone with whom the Jews are in this condition. "Yasūmuhum" means: he imposes upon them and burdens them. "Sū' al-'adhāb" (the worst torment) is apparently the jizya (poll tax) and humiliation. Allah has decreed this against them and brought down their dominion, so there is no banner of a Jew upon the earth. Ibn al-Musayyib said: it is recommended that the Jews be made to suffer under the jizya. It is related that a group of the Romans took control of their region, so they sold the neighboring Jews who lived among them and made them their possessions.

Then it is fitting, at the end of this verse—because it contains the infliction of punishment upon them and a warning—to alert to the swiftness of Allah's punishment and to frighten all people with this as a general warning; then He gave hope of this, as an act of kindness from Him, blessed and exalted is He.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them﴾ mean: We scattered them upon the earth. Al-Ṭabarī related from a group of exegetes: there is no patch of earth but that there is a group of Jews in it. The apparent meaning regarding those referred to in this verse is that they are those who came after Solomon at the time his kingdom ended, and it is apparent that this was before the period of 'Īsā, peace be upon him, since there were no righteous ones among them after their disbelief in 'Īsā (ﷺ). In the histories concerning this section there are conflicting reports. The words "al-ṣāliḥūn" (the righteous) and "dūna dhālika" (other than that) are expressions that may be understood as referring to the righteousness of faith: "dūna" in the sense of "ghayr" (other than) is taken to refer to the disbelievers; and if "ṣalāḥ" is taken to mean worship, good and the consequences of faith, then "dūna dhālika" may be understood as referring to believers.

﴿And We tested them﴾ means: We examined them. "Al-ḥasanāt" (good things) are health, ease and the like, which are according to the judgment and perception of the children of Adam; "al-sayyi'āt" (bad things) are their opposites. His words, "la'allahum" (that they might), mean: according to your opinion, if you were to witness that; and the meaning is: that perhaps they would return to obedience and repent of disobedience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 169–170:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life and saying, "It will be forgiven us." And if goods like it come to them, they will take them. Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they would not say about Allah except the truth, and they studied what is in it? And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Allah. Will you not then use reason?﴾ ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer—indeed, We do not waste the reward of the reformers.﴾

"Khalafa" means: it occurred behind them and after them. "Khalf" with a sukun on the lam is used most commonly in disparagement, and from it is the saying of Labid:

Those by whose flanks one used to live have gone, and I remain among a later generation like the skin of a mangy camel.

It may also be used in praise, and from it is the saying of Hassan:

For us is the first step towards You, and those after us are followers of our first ones in obedience to Allah.

And "khalaf" with a fatha on the lam is used—most commonly—in praise. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj said: it may also be used in disparagement, and from it is the saying of the poet:

Ah, that is the blind successor.

Mujahid said: the intended meaning of "khalf" here is the Christians, but al-Tabari considered this weak. Al-Hasan al-Basri read "wurrithu al-kitab" with a damma on the waw and a shadda on the ra. His saying ﴿taking the goods of this lower life﴾ is an allusion to bribery and corrupt gains. "Ard" is what is displayed and passes by and does not endure, and "al-adna" is an allusion to the life of this world.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and they say, "It will be forgiven us"﴾ is a rebuke of them for their delusion, and their saying "It will be forgiven" while knowing what is in the Book of Allah of the threat against sins, and their persistence in them, and that whenever they are given the opportunity again they commit them—these are the incapable, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The incapable is one who follows his soul's desires and wishes for things from Allah." They are persistent, and only one who has ceased and repented says "It will be forgiven us."

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Was not the covenant taken from them﴾ to the end of the verse is an emphasis on the obligation to speak the truth about Allah in the Law and in judgments among people, and that bribery should not incline judges toward falsehood. "The Book" here means the Torah, and its covenant: the hardships contained in it in this regard. His saying ﴿that they would not say about Allah except the truth﴾ may mean by it their saying falsehood in a judgment that comes before them, and it may mean their saying "It will be forgiven us," while they knew the truth of Allah's prohibition, blessed and exalted, against that. Jumhur al-Nas read "yaqulu" with a ya' below, and al-Jahdari read "taqulu" with a ta' above.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿and they studied﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿Was not [the covenant] taken﴾ to the end of the verse, in the sense of the past tense, and it is to be understood as: "Was it not the case that the covenant of the Book was taken from them and they studied what is in it?" By these two verbs the proof is established against them in their saying falsehood. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "wadda-rasu ma fihi." Al-Tabari and others said: His saying "and they studied" is conjoined to His saying ﴿who inherited the Book﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this there is consideration, because of the distance of what is conjoined from it, since with the saying "and they studied" the sense of establishing the proof through the construction in His saying "Was not" is lost. Then, blessed and exalted, He admonished and reminded with His saying ﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Allah﴾. Jumhur al-Nas read "Will you not then use reason?" with a ta' above, and Abu 'Amr and the people of Makkah read "ya'qilun" with a ya' below.

His, the Exalted, saying ﴿And those who﴾ is conjoined to His saying "for those who fear Allah." Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs, Abu 'Amr, and the people read "yumassikuna" with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the sin. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, Abu al-'Aliya, and 'Asim alone in the transmission of Abu Bakr read "yumsikuna" with a sukun on the mim and a lightening of the sin. All of them lightened "wa la tumsiku bi-'isam al-kawafir," except Abu 'Amr, who read "wa la tumassiku" with a fatha on the mim and a shadda on the sin. Al-A'mash read "wa-alladhina istamsakû," and in the reading of Ubayy: "wa-alladhina masakû." These are two dialects with one meaning. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

So he did not hold fast to the pledge that she claimed, except as a sieve holds water.

As for the shadda on the sin, it goes with the transitive use with the preposition "bi."
