Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-A'raf, verses 171–172:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And when We lifted the mountain above them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of Allah."﴾ ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." This, lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾

"Nataqna" means: We uprooted and raised. The meaning of *al-natq* is the uprooting of a thing. The Arabs say: "I pulled the butter out of the mouth of the waterskin" (*natqtu al-zubda min fami al-qirba*). From this is the line of the poet:

"And they uprooted our heavy dreams."

And *al-nati* is the womb that expels the child from the man. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Their mothers were not deprived of the goodness of the morning meal, and they were not deprived... (the womb) that bore a male child, which was bound to you."

It is related in a hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Marry virgins, for they are more *antaq* in wombs and sweeter in mouths." The hadith continues. In this story, the Qur'an uses in place of this word the exact word "raised" (*rafa'na*), and "above them" (*fawqahum*) gives the sense of raising, with an added indication: that the angels uprooted the mountain and Allah commanded it.

It is narrated that when Musa (peace be upon him) brought them the Torah and said, on behalf of Allah the Exalted: "This is the Book of Allah. Will you accept it with what is in it? Indeed it contains the explanation of what is permitted to you, what is forbidden to you, what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you." They said: "Recite to us what is in it. If its obligations are light and its limits are easy, we will accept it." He said: "Accept it with what is in it." They said: "No." Musa returned to them, and they refused three times. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed to the mountain, and it uprooted itself and rose above their heads. Musa (ﷺ) said to them: "Do you not see what my Lord says? If you do not accept the Torah with what is in it, I will surely drop this mountain upon you." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "When they looked at the mountain, each one of them fell prostrate on his left cheek (*hajib*), and looked at the mountain with his right eye, fearing that it would fall upon him. Therefore, there is no Jew on earth who prostrates except on his left cheek. They say: 'This is the prostration by which the punishment was lifted from us.'"

*Al-zulla* is that which provides shade. From it is: ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210], and from it is: ﴿the punishment of the Day of the Canopy﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:189]. From it is the statement of Usayd ibn Hudayr to the Prophet ﷺ: "Last night I was reciting, and something covered the house like a canopy (*zulla*), in which were like lamps." The Prophet ﷺ said: "That was the *sakina* (tranquility) that descended for the Qur'an."

If it is asked: "If the mountain was a canopy, what is the meaning of 'as though' (*ka'annahu*)?" The answer is that people are accustomed to these earthly bodies being canopies only when they are on pillars. Since the mountain was not on pillars, it was said: ﴿as though it were a canopy﴾, meaning: as though it were on pillars. "And they thought" (*wa zannu*): the exegetes said its meaning is: they were certain (*ayqanu*).

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The matter is not so in my view. Rather, it is the place of predominant assumption (*ghalabat al-zann*) together with the persistence of hope. How could they be certain of its falling, when Musa (peace be upon him) says that the throwing of it is only on the condition that they do not accept the Torah? Assumption (*zann*) occurs and is used for certainty only when the object of certainty has not come out to the senses (*hawass*), and this has been clarified earlier in this book. Then they were told at the time the mountain was raised: ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾, so they took it and bound themselves to all that it contained of hardship and ease, yet they did not fulfill it. Most people read: "and remember" (*wa-dhkuru*), while al-A'mash read, as Abu al-Fath related from him: "wa-dhdhakkaru" (with the verb in the form that assimilates the letters). His saying "that you may" (*la'allakum*) is according to their hoping (*tarajjihim*), and this is an emphasis on preserving it and being attentive to its command.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord took﴾, the verse. The estimate (*taqdir*) is: "And remember when your Lord took." His saying: ﴿from their loins﴾: the grammarians said it is a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion) for His saying: ﴿from the Children of Adam﴾. The wording of this verse requires that the taking was from the Children of Adam, from their loins, and there is no mention of Adam in the verse according to the wording. The hadiths explaining this verse from the Prophet ﷺ have been transmitted in multiple chains (*mutawatir*), through 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), and others, that when Allah the Mighty and Majestic created Adam (and in some narrations: when He sent Adam down to earth in Dahna' in the land of Sind, as Ibn 'Abbas said; and in some narrations that this was at Nu'man, which is 'Arafat and what is near it, also said by Ibn 'Abbas and others), He wiped over his back (and in some narrations with His right hand, and in some narrations He struck his shoulder). Then He brought out from it (that is, from the wiping or the striking) the *nasamah* (souls) of his offspring. In some narrations they were like ants (*dharr*), and in others like mustard seeds. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: they are the spirits, to which were given likenesses (*mithalat*). 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both) related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "They were taken from his back as a comb takes hair from the head. Allah gave them intellects like the ant of Sulayman (peace be upon him). He took from them the covenant that He is their Lord and that there is no god but Him. They acknowledged this and bound themselves to it. He informed them that He would send messengers to them as reminders and callers, and some of them testified against others."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: He took as witness against them the seven heavens. There is no one born until the Day of Resurrection except that the covenant has been taken from him on that day and in that station. As-Suddi said: the disbelievers gave the covenant that day unwillingly, in the manner of *taqiyya* (dissimulation).

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a summary of the collected lengthy narrations. It seems that the wordings of these hadiths do not harmonize with the wording of the verse. People have greatly exerted themselves in attempting to reconcile them. Some people said: the verse points to this procreation that exists in the world, and "took" (*akhadha*) means "brought into existence" according to the customary usage, and that the "making them testify" (*al-ishhad*) takes place at the time of the maturity of the responsible person (*mukallaf*), who has been given understanding, and this craft that indicates the Maker has been set up for him. Al-Zajjaj inclined to this meaning, and it is a meaning the wording can bear. But there is an objection to it: the interpretation of the verse by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) with the hadith mentioned, and their transmitting that from the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Jurjani extended his discussion on this issue, and the core of his speech is that the wiping and the bringing out of the offspring from the back of Adam is according to the hadith. It was said regarding the verse: "He took from their loins," since the bringing out from the back of Adam, who is the origin, is a bringing out from the loins of his sons, who are the branches, since the branch and the origin are one thing. And this is to a great extent of speech that does not withstand critique.

Others said: All that is in the hadith of wiping with His right hand, striking his shoulder, and the like, is only an expression for the bringing into existence of those souls from him, and the right hand is an expression for power. Or the one who wipes is an angel by the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Thus the hadith includes the beginning of the story and the bringing into existence of the souls from Adam, and this is an addition beyond what is in the verse. Then the verse includes what happened after this, from the taking of the covenant, and the souls are present existing beings. The verse may bear two meanings:

The first: that "took" (*akhadha*) governs "a covenant" (*'ahd*) or "a pledge" (*mithaq*), which you estimate after His saying: "their descendants," and His saying: "from their loins" is to explain the kind of the offspring, since what is meant by all of them is procreation. "The Children of Adam" includes his sons by his loins and his sons by compassion and tenderness. His saying: "their descendants" is a substitute for "the Children of Adam."

The second meaning: that since every soul there has a relation to the one from whose back it comes, the specification of that relation was taken from the back, since it will come out from it. So it is the thing that follows. The meaning is: when they were specified with this relation and recognized by it, that is a kind of taking. And "took," according to this, governs "their descendants," and it does not mean "wiped" or "brought into existence." Rather, their bringing into existence had already occurred, as the mentioned hadith shows. So the hadith adds a meaning beyond the verse, which is the mention of Adam and how the first bringing into existence of souls took place.

Al-Tartushi said: This covenant binds humankind even if they do not remember it in this life, just as divorce binds the one against whom it was witnessed even if he has forgotten it. And he went on to other things that are not exegesis nor from its path.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read: "dhurriyyatihim" (the plural of the plural). Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read: "dhurriyyatahum" (the singular form functioning as a collective). The discussion of the word *dhurriyya* has already been presented in Surah Al 'Imran.

It is related in the stories of this verse that the prophets (peace be upon them) were among those souls, and that Adam (peace be upon him) saw Dawud and was pleased with him. He said: "Who is this?" It was said: "A prophet from your descendants." He said: "How old is he?" It was said: "Sixty years." He said: "Add to his life forty years from mine." So it was added. He said: Adam's life was a thousand years. When he completed nine hundred and sixty, the Angel of Death came to him. Adam said to him: "Forty years remain for me." So the Angel of Death returned to his Lord and informed Him. He said: "Tell him: You gave them to your son Dawud." So Adam (peace be upon him) died after he disputed over the forty years.

Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: Whoever dies young is under the first covenant, and whoever reaches maturity has been taken by the second covenant, meaning the one in this present life of reason. Al-Zajjaj related from some people that they said: this verse is an expression that every soul, when it is born and reaches maturity, its looking at the established proofs is a covenant upon it to believe and to know Allah. This view has already been mentioned. It is a weak opinion, set aside from the transmitted hadiths and discarded.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿We testify﴾ may be from the speech of some souls to others, meaning: we testify against you lest you say on the Day of Resurrection: "We were unaware of knowing Allah and believing in Him." This would then be a statement from these to those. Al-Tabari mentioned this. On this view, it is not good to pause at His saying "Yes" (*bala*). It may also be that His saying, glorified is He: "We testify" is from the speech of the angels, and then it is good to pause at "Yes." Al-Suddi said: the meaning is: Allah and His angels said: "We testify." 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) related it from the Prophet ﷺ.

All seven readers except Abu 'Amr read: ﴿an taqulu﴾ ("that you say") addressing present listeners. Abu 'Amr alone read: ﴿an yaqulu﴾ ("that they say") as a report about absent ones. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Muhaysin. Both readings are explained according to the two meanings mentioned. And *an* is in the position of the accusative, with the estimate: "lest" (*makhafata an*).

﴿And when We lifted the mountain above them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of Allah."﴾ ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" "And they uprooted our heavy dreams."

And *al-nati* is the womb that expels the child from the man. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"Their mothers were not deprived of the goodness of the morning meal, and they were not deprived... (the womb) that bore a male child, which was bound to you."

It is related in a hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Marry virgins, for they are more *antaq* in wombs and sweeter in mouths." The hadith continues. In this story, the Qur'an uses in place of this word the exact word "raised" (*rafa'na*), and "above them" (*fawqahum*) gives the sense of raising, with an added indication: that the angels uprooted the mountain and Allah commanded it.

It is narrated that when Musa (peace be upon him) brought them the Torah and said, on behalf of Allah the Exalted: "This is the Book of Allah. Will you accept it with what is in it? Indeed it contains the explanation of what is permitted to you, what is forbidden to you, what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you." They said: "Recite to us what is in it. If its obligations are light and its limits are easy, we will accept it." He said: "Accept it with what is in it." They said: "No." Musa returned to them, and they refused three times. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic revealed to the mountain, and it uprooted itself and rose above their heads. Musa (ﷺ) said to them: "Do you not see what my Lord says? If you do not accept the Torah with what is in it, I will surely drop this mountain upon you." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "When they looked at the mountain, each one of them fell prostrate on his left cheek (*hajib*), and looked at the mountain with his right eye, fearing that it would fall upon him. Therefore, there is no Jew on earth who prostrates except on his left cheek. They say: 'This is the prostration by which the punishment was lifted from us.'"

*Al-zulla* is that which provides shade. From it is: ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210], and from it is: ﴿the punishment of the Day of the Canopy﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:189]. From it is the statement of Usayd ibn Hudayr to the Prophet ﷺ: "Last night I was reciting, and something covered the house like a canopy (*zulla*), in which were like lamps." The Prophet ﷺ said: "That was the *sakina* (tranquility) that descended for the Qur'an."

If it is asked: "If the mountain was a canopy, what is the meaning of 'as though' (*ka'annahu*)?" The answer is that people are accustomed to these earthly bodies being canopies only when they are on pillars. Since the mountain was not on pillars, it was said: ﴿as though it were a canopy﴾, meaning: as though it were on pillars. "And they thought" (*wa zannu*): the exegetes said its meaning is: they were certain (*ayqanu*).

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The matter is not so in my view. Rather, it is the place of predominant assumption (*ghalabat al-zann*) together with the persistence of hope. How could they be certain of its falling, when Musa (peace be upon him) says that the throwing of it is only on the condition that they do not accept the Torah? Assumption (*zann*) occurs and is used for certainty only when the object of certainty has not come out to the senses (*hawass*), and this has been clarified earlier in this book. Then they were told at the time the mountain was raised: ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾, so they took it and bound themselves to all that it contained of hardship and ease, yet they did not fulfill it. Most people read: "and remember" (*wa-dhkuru*), while al-A'mash read, as Abu al-Fath related from him: "wa-dhdhakkaru" (with the verb in the form that assimilates the letters). His saying "that you may" (*la'allakum*) is according to their hoping (*tarajjihim*), and this is an emphasis on preserving it and being attentive to its command.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord took﴾, the verse. The estimate (*taqdir*) is: "And remember when your Lord took." His saying: ﴿from their loins﴾: the grammarians said it is a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute of inclusion) for His saying: ﴿from the Children of Adam﴾. The wording of this verse requires that the taking was from the Children of Adam, from their loins, and there is no mention of Adam in the verse according to the wording. The hadiths explaining this verse from the Prophet ﷺ have been transmitted in multiple chains (*mutawatir*), through 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), and others, that when Allah the Mighty and Majestic created Adam (and in some narrations: when He sent Adam down to earth in Dahna' in the land of Sind, as Ibn 'Abbas said; and in some narrations that this was at Nu'man, which is 'Arafat and what is near it, also said by Ibn 'Abbas and others), He wiped over his back (and in some narrations with His right hand, and in some narrations He struck his shoulder). Then He brought out from it (that is, from the wiping or the striking) the *nasamah* (souls) of his offspring. In some narrations they were like ants (*dharr*), and in others like mustard seeds. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: they are the spirits, to which were given likenesses (*mithalat*). 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with them both) related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "They were taken from his back as a comb takes hair from the head. Allah gave them intellects like the ant of Sulayman (peace be upon him). He took from them the covenant that He is their Lord and that there is no god but Him. They acknowledged this and bound themselves to it. He informed them that He would send messengers to them as reminders and callers, and some of them testified against others."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: He took as witness against them the seven heavens. There is no one born until the Day of Resurrection except that the covenant has been taken from him on that day and in that station. As-Suddi said: the disbelievers gave the covenant that day unwillingly, in the manner of *taqiyya* (dissimulation).

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a summary of the collected lengthy narrations. It seems that the wordings of these hadiths do not harmonize with the wording of the verse. People have greatly exerted themselves in attempting to reconcile them. Some people said: the verse points to this procreation that exists in the world, and "took" (*akhadha*) means "brought into existence" according to the customary usage, and that the "making them testify" (*al-ishhad*) takes place at the time of the maturity of the responsible person (*mukallaf*), who has been given understanding, and this craft that indicates the Maker has been set up for him. Al-Zajjaj inclined to this meaning, and it is a meaning the wording can bear. But there is an objection to it: the interpretation of the verse by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) with the hadith mentioned, and their transmitting that from the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Jurjani extended his discussion on this issue, and the core of his speech is that the wiping and the bringing out of the offspring from the back of Adam is according to the hadith. It was said regarding the verse: "He took from their loins," since the bringing out from the back of Adam, who is the origin, is a bringing out from the loins of his sons, who are the branches, since the branch and the origin are one thing. And this is to a great extent of speech that does not withstand critique.

Others said: All that is in the hadith of wiping with His right hand, striking his shoulder, and the like, is only an expression for the bringing into existence of those souls from him, and the right hand is an expression for power. Or the one who wipes is an angel by the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Thus the hadith includes the beginning of the story and the bringing into existence of the souls from Adam, and this is an addition beyond what is in the verse. Then the verse includes what happened after this, from the taking of the covenant, and the souls are present existing beings. The verse may bear two meanings:

The first: that "took" (*akhadha*) governs "a covenant" (*'ahd*) or "a pledge" (*mithaq*), which you estimate after His saying: "their descendants," and His saying: "from their loins" is to explain the kind of the offspring, since what is meant by all of them is procreation. "The Children of Adam" includes his sons by his loins and his sons by compassion and tenderness. His saying: "their descendants" is a substitute for "the Children of Adam."

The second meaning: that since every soul there has a relation to the one from whose back it comes, the specification of that relation was taken from the back, since it will come out from it. So it is the thing that follows. The meaning is: when they were specified with this relation and recognized by it, that is a kind of taking. And "took," according to this, governs "their descendants," and it does not mean "wiped" or "brought into existence." Rather, their bringing into existence had already occurred, as the mentioned hadith shows. So the hadith adds a meaning beyond the verse, which is the mention of Adam and how the first bringing into existence of souls took place.

Al-Tartushi said: This covenant binds humankind even if they do not remember it in this life, just as divorce binds the one against whom it was witnessed even if he has forgotten it. And he went on to other things that are not exegesis nor from its path.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read: "dhurriyyatihim" (the plural of the plural). Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read: "dhurriyyatahum" (the singular form functioning as a collective). The discussion of the word *dhurriyya* has already been presented in Surah Al 'Imran.

It is related in the stories of this verse that the prophets (peace be upon them) were among those souls, and that Adam (peace be upon him) saw Dawud and was pleased with him. He said: "Who is this?" It was said: "A prophet from your descendants." He said: "How old is he?" It was said: "Sixty years." He said: "Add to his life forty years from mine." So it was added. He said: Adam's life was a thousand years. When he completed nine hundred and sixty, the Angel of Death came to him. Adam said to him: "Forty years remain for me." So the Angel of Death returned to his Lord and informed Him. He said: "Tell him: You gave them to your son Dawud." So Adam (peace be upon him) died after he disputed over the forty years.

Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: Whoever dies young is under the first covenant, and whoever reaches maturity has been taken by the second covenant, meaning the one in this present life of reason. Al-Zajjaj related from some people that they said: this verse is an expression that every soul, when it is born and reaches maturity, its looking at the established proofs is a covenant upon it to believe and to know Allah. This view has already been mentioned. It is a weak opinion, set aside from the transmitted hadiths and discarded.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿We testify﴾ may be from the speech of some souls to others, meaning: we testify against you lest you say on the Day of Resurrection: "We were unaware of knowing Allah and believing in Him." This would then be a statement from these to those. Al-Tabari mentioned this. On this view, it is not good to pause at His saying "Yes" (*bala*). It may also be that His saying, glorified is He: "We testify" is from the speech of the angels, and then it is good to pause at "Yes." Al-Suddi said: the meaning is: Allah and His angels said: "We testify." 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) related it from the Prophet ﷺ.

All seven readers except Abu 'Amr read: ﴿an taqulu﴾ ("that you say") addressing present listeners. Abu 'Amr alone read: ﴿an yaqulu﴾ ("that they say") as a report about absent ones. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Muhaysin. Both readings are explained according to the two meanings mentioned. And *an* is in the position of the accusative, with the estimate: "lest" (*makhafata an*).

(p-87) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Or [lest] you should say, "It was only that our forefathers associated others with Allah before, and we were [merely] offspring after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ ﴿And thus We detail the verses, and perhaps they will return.﴾ ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our verses, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became of those who are misguided.﴾

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of these verses is that if a covenant had not been taken from the disbelievers, and no messenger had come to them reminding them of what the covenant contained of the Oneness of Allah and worshipping Him, they would have had two arguments: the first, "We were heedless," and the second, "We were followers of our predecessors. So how shall we be destroyed, when the sin belongs only to the one who led us astray and misguided us?" Thus the testimony of some of them against others, or the testimony of the angels against them, came to pass, so that these arguments would be cut off for them. The variant reading in "taqulu" or "yaqulu" depends on the first [interpretation].

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And thus We detail the verses﴾, its implied sense is: just as We did these things and carried out these decrees, so likewise We detail the verses and make them clear to those who lived in your time and to whom you were sent. "And perhaps," in accordance with their hope and your hope and by the reckoning of humans, ﴿they will return﴾ to obedience to Allah, and enter into His Oneness and worship of Him. A group recited it as "yufassilu" with the letter ya'.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And recite to them﴾ the verse. "Recite" (wa-tlu) means: relate and narrate in sequence. The pronoun in "ʿalayhim" refers to the disbelievers present with Muhammad ﷺ and others. The commentators differed about the one who was given the verses. ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud and others said: he was a man from the Children of Israel whom Musa, peace be upon him, sent to the king of Madyan, calling to Allah the Exalted and to the Law, and he taught him from the signs of Allah what he could use to call people with and towards. When he arrived, the king bribed him and gave him gifts on condition that he abandon the religion of Musa and follow the king in his religion, and he did so. The king tempted the people through him and misguided them. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: he was a man of the Canaanite tyrants named Bal'am; it was also said: Bal'am ibn ʿAbir, and it was said: ibn ABir, and it was said other than this, which is too lengthy to mention. He was among the tyrants whom Musa, peace be upon him, fought. When Musa drew near them, they sought refuge with Bal'am, who was righteous and whose supplication was answered. It was said: he had knowledge from the scrolls of Ibrahim and the like. Mujahid said: he had been nominated for prophethood and was given it, but his people bribed him to remain silent, and he did so.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement is rejected and is not authentically attributed to Mujahid, for whoever is given prophethood is necessarily given infallibility; this is established by the Shariah. The meaning of what I have said has been explicitly stated by Abu al-Ma'ali in his book al-Shamil. It was also said: he knew the Greatest Name of Allah, as Ibn ʿAbbas also said. This difference concerns the intended meaning of His saying "Our verses." His people said to him: Invoke Allah, the Exalted, against Musa and his army. He said to them: How can I invoke against a sent prophet? They kept at him until they tempted him. He went out until he reached a mountain from which the army of Musa could be seen. He had told his people: I will not do it until I consult my Lord. He did so, and He remained silent toward him, so he informed them. They said to him: Allah has not left your prohibition except that He wanted this. So he went out, and when he overlooked the army he began to invoke against Musa, but his tongue turned to supplication for Musa and against his own people. They said to him: What are you saying? He said: I cannot control anything but this, and he knew that he had erred. It is narrated that his tongue hung out upon his chest. He said to his people: I have indeed been ruined, but there remains for you only a stratagem. So send the women out to the army of Musa, unveiled and otherwise, and command them that no woman refuse any man, for when they commit fornication they will be destroyed. They did so, the women went out, and the men of the Children of Israel committed fornication with them. Then Fannuhas ibn al-ʿIzar ibn Harun came, and he skewered a woman and a man of the Children of Israel on his spear and raised them on top of the spear. Plague then struck the Children of Israel, and seventy thousand of them died in a single hour. Then al-Mu'tamir reported from his father that Musa, peace be upon him, afterward killed the man who had withdrawn from the signs of Allah. Al-Mahdawi said: it is narrated that he invoked against Musa that he not enter the city of the tyrants, and he was answered; and Musa, peace be upon him, invoked against him that he forget the Greatest Name of Allah, and he was answered. Al-Zajjaj said: it was also said that the reference is to the hypocrites of the People of the Book.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view on this is to say: it refers to the open disbelievers among the People of the Book, for there were no hypocrites among them; rather they were openly opposed. This story has many reports, which I have abridged because their authenticity is unattainable, and I have confined myself to what pertains to the wording of the verse.

A group said: the one referred to in the verse was a man who had been given three answered supplications, but he refrained from using them for the welfare of people. He prayed with one that his wife would return to being the most beautiful of women, and that happened. When she saw herself thus, she hated him and despised him. He then invoked against her a second time, and she was transformed into a female dog. Her sons interceded for her with him, so he prayed for her a third time, and she returned as she had been, and then she went back to her former state, and the supplications were gone.

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the one referred to in the verse is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, who had been given knowledge. It is narrated that he came intending to embrace Islam, and reached Badr a day or so after the battle. He said: Who killed these people? It was said: Muhammad ﷺ. He said: I have no need for the religion of one who killed these people. He apostatized and returned, saying: Now wine is lawful for me, though he had forbidden it to himself. He went on until he joined a group of the kings of Himyar, drinking with them until he died.

"Insalakha" is an expression for disengaging from it, separating and distancing oneself, like stripping off garments or skin. "Atbaʿahu" means: he made him a follower. Al-Tabari said so, either by a misguidance he set down for him, or by himself. The majority recited "fa-atbaʿahu" with an initial alif cut and the taʾ sukun, and this is preferred because it implies that he caught up with him and became with him. Likewise, "fa-atbaʿahu shihabun" [al-Hijr: 18] and "fa-atbaʿahum Firʿawn." Al-Hasan, as transmitted from him by Harun, recited "fa-ittaba'ahu" with a connecting alif and a doubled taʾ, and likewise Talha ibn Musarrif with a variant; and the variant from al-Hasan is in the same sense: he kept to him and followed him with seduction until he seduced him. "Min al-ghawin" means: of the misguided.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: he was a man of the Canaanite tyrants named Bal'am; it was also said: Bal'am ibn ʿAbir, and it was said: ibn ABir, and it was said other than this, which is too lengthy to mention. He was among the tyrants whom Musa, peace be upon him, fought. When Musa drew near them, they sought refuge with Bal'am, who was righteous and whose supplication was answered. It was said: he had knowledge from the scrolls of Ibrahim and the like. Mujahid said: he had been nominated for prophethood and was given it, but his people bribed him to remain silent, and he did so.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This statement is rejected and is not authentically attributed to Mujahid, for whoever is given prophethood is necessarily given infallibility; this is established by the Shariah. The meaning of what I have said has been explicitly stated by Abu al-Ma'ali in his book al-Shamil. It was also said: he knew the Greatest Name of Allah, as Ibn ʿAbbas also said. This difference concerns the intended meaning of His saying "Our verses." His people said to him: Invoke Allah, the Exalted, against Musa and his army. He said to them: How can I invoke against a sent prophet? They kept at him until they tempted him. He went out until he reached a mountain from which the army of Musa could be seen. He had told his people: I will not do it until I consult my Lord. He did so, and He remained silent toward him, so he informed them. They said to him: Allah has not left your prohibition except that He wanted this. So he went out, and when he overlooked the army he began to invoke against Musa, but his tongue turned to supplication for Musa and against his own people. They said to him: What are you saying? He said: I cannot control anything but this, and he knew that he had erred. It is narrated that his tongue hung out upon his chest. He said to his people: I have indeed been ruined, but there remains for you only a stratagem. So send the women out to the army of Musa, unveiled and otherwise, and command them that no woman refuse any man, for when they commit fornication they will be destroyed. They did so, the women went out, and the men of the Children of Israel committed fornication with them. Then Fannuhas ibn al-ʿIzar ibn Harun came, and he skewered a woman and a man of the Children of Israel on his spear and raised them on top of the spear. Plague then struck the Children of Israel, and seventy thousand of them died in a single hour. Then al-Mu'tamir reported from his father that Musa, peace be upon him, afterward killed the man who had withdrawn from the signs of Allah. Al-Mahdawi said: it is narrated that he invoked against Musa that he not enter the city of the tyrants, and he was answered; and Musa, peace be upon him, invoked against him that he forget the Greatest Name of Allah, and he was answered. Al-Zajjaj said: it was also said that the reference is to the hypocrites of the People of the Book.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view on this is to say: it refers to the open disbelievers among the People of the Book, for there were no hypocrites among them; rather they were openly opposed. This story has many reports, which I have abridged because their authenticity is unattainable, and I have confined myself to what pertains to the wording of the verse.

A group said: the one referred to in the verse was a man who had been given three answered supplications, but he refrained from using them for the welfare of people. He prayed with one that his wife would return to being the most beautiful of women, and that happened. When she saw herself thus, she hated him and despised him. He then invoked against her a second time, and she was transformed into a female dog. Her sons interceded for her with him, so he prayed for her a third time, and she returned as she had been, and then she went back to her former state, and the supplications were gone.

ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the one referred to in the verse is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, who had been given knowledge. It is narrated that he came intending to embrace Islam, and reached Badr a day or so after the battle. He said: Who killed these people? It was said: Muhammad ﷺ. He said: I have no need for the religion of one who killed these people. He apostatized and returned, saying: Now wine is lawful for me, though he had forbidden it to himself. He went on until he joined a group of the kings of Himyar, drinking with them until he died.

"Insalakha" is an expression for disengaging from it, separating and distancing oneself, like stripping off garments or skin. "Atbaʿahu" means: he made him a follower. Al-Tabari said so, either by a misguidance he set down for him, or by himself. The majority recited "fa-atbaʿahu" with an initial alif cut and the taʾ sukun, and this is preferred because it implies that he caught up with him and became with him. Likewise, "fa-atbaʿahu shihabun" [al-Hijr: 18] and "fa-atbaʿahum Firʿawn." Al-Hasan, as transmitted from him by Harun, recited "fa-ittaba'ahu" with a connecting alif and a doubled taʾ, and likewise Talha ibn Musarrif with a variant; and the variant from al-Hasan is in the same sense: he kept to him and followed him with seduction until he seduced him. "Min al-ghawin" means: of the misguided.

(p-90)The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but he clung to the earth and followed his own desire. His likeness is that of a dog: if you attack him he pants, and if you leave him he pants. That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories, perhaps they will reflect.﴾ ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided, and whomever He leaves astray, it is they who are the losers.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind.﴾

Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, says: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them.﴾ One group said: its meaning is "We would have seized him," as you say, "the wrongdoer was raised" when he perished. The pronoun in "by them" refers to the sin of "shedding" (al-insilakh, i.e., departing from the signs). He then began describing his condition with the words of the Exalted: ﴿but he clung to the earth﴾. So this is an expression for Allah giving him respite and leaving him to continue. Ibn Abi Najih said: "We would have raised him" means "We would have caused him to die before he fell into sin and We would have raised him away from it." According to this view, the pronoun refers to the signs. Then he began describing his condition. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and a group with him said: "We would have raised him" means "We would have elevated his remembrance and raised his rank with Us through these signs which We gave him." ﴿But he clung to the earth﴾: so the speech is connected, and it mentions the cause for which he was not raised or honoured, as was done for others who were given this.

"Akhlada" (أخلد) means: he remained, became lax, and was steadfast. The "mukhlid" is one whose youth remains firm so that grey hair does not overtake him, and from this comes "al-khuld" (eternity). From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"To whom do these abodes belong? You passed by them at al-Fadfad,
like the writing in the stone-channel of the lasting watercourse."

The phrase ﴿to the earth﴾ may mean: to its desires, its pleasures, and what it contains of delights; this was said by al-Suddi and others. It may also mean an expression for what is lowest and most base, as one says, "So-and-so is in the lowland (al-hadid)." This is supported by the rational meaning, because the earth and what is fixed upon it is this world, and everything upon it is perishing. Whoever clings to it has been deprived of the portion of the enduring Hereafter.

The Exalted's words: ﴿His likeness is that of a dog﴾. Al-Suddi and others said: this man was punished in this world by panting as the dog pants, so he was likened to it in form and appearance. Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: he was likened to it in that he was astray before he was given the signs, and then when he was given them he remained astray, the signs not benefiting him. Thus he is like the dog in that it does not cease panting, whether a burden is placed upon it or it is left without one. The clarification of the meaning: the thing that souls imagine of his condition is what they imagine of the condition of the dog. With this interpretation, it is correct for the "kaf" (ك, "like") to enter upon "mathal" (مَثَل, "likeness"). "Al-lahth" (اللهث) is breathing rapidly with movement of the mouth's organs along with it and extension of the tongue; it most often occurs with heat and fatigue. In the case of a horse it is called "dabh" (ضبح). It is the nature of the dog that it pants in every state. Al-Tabari mentioned that the meaning of ﴿if you attack him, he pants﴾ is "if you chase him away," and he related this from Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That is included within the category of hardship which we mentioned.

The Exalted's words: ﴿That is the likeness of the people﴾, i.e., this likeness, O Muhammad, is the likeness of these people who were astray before you brought them guidance and the message; then you came to them with that, but they remained in their error and did not benefit from it. So their likeness is that of the dog. His words ﴿So relate the stories﴾ mean: recount to them what they know to be among the unseen matters which only the people of the earlier scriptures know, and you are not one of them, ﴿perhaps they will reflect﴾ upon that and believe.

The Exalted's words: ﴿Evil is a likeness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the estimated construction is "evil is a likeness, the likeness of the people," because what follows "bi'sa" (بئس, "evil") and "ni'ma" (نعم, "excellent") is explained by its kind, as you say, "Zayd is an evil man (bi'sa rajulan Zaydun)." When "mathal" is elided, "al-qawm" (the people) is placed in its position, and the nominative in that case is by inception (al-ibtida'), with the predicate being what came before. Al-Jahdari read "sa'a mathalu al-qawmi" (ساء مَثَلُ القَوْمِ), and the nominative of "mathal" in this reading is by "sa'a," but "sa'a" does not operate like "bi'sa" unless what follows it is in the accusative. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: al-Jahdari read "mithlu" (مِثْلُ) with a kasra on the mim and a damma on the lam, and al-A'mash read "mathalu" (مَثَلُ) with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the lam.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This contradicts what Abu Hatim mentioned, for he said: al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read "sa'a mathalu" with the nominative.

These verses, which contain the error of peoples and the discussion of it, are concluded with the statement that all of that is from Allah: the guidance is from Him, by His creation and origination, and likewise the misguidance. Whoever is led astray has been judged to be among the losers, and reward and punishment are linked to the earning of the son of Adam.

"O mother of Farwa, cease blaming and acknowledge,
for every mother gives birth to one who will be removed (al-muntaʼa)."

So relate the stories, perhaps they will reflect.﴾ ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided, and whomever He leaves astray, it is they who are the losers.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind.﴾

Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, says: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them.﴾ One group said: its meaning is "We would have seized him," as you say, "the wrongdoer was raised" when he perished. The pronoun in "by them" refers to the sin of "shedding" (al-insilakh, i.e., departing from the signs). He then began describing his condition with the words of the Exalted: ﴿but he clung to the earth﴾. So this is an expression for Allah giving him respite and leaving him to continue. Ibn Abi Najih said: "We would have raised him" means "We would have caused him to die before he fell into sin and We would have raised him away from it." According to this view, the pronoun refers to the signs. Then he began describing his condition. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and a group with him said: "We would have raised him" means "We would have elevated his remembrance and raised his rank with Us through these signs which We gave him." ﴿But he clung to the earth﴾: so the speech is connected, and it mentions the cause for which he was not raised or honoured, as was done for others who were given this.

"Akhlada" (أخلد) means: he remained, became lax, and was steadfast. The "mukhlid" is one whose youth remains firm so that grey hair does not overtake him, and from this comes "al-khuld" (eternity). From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"To whom do these abodes belong? You passed by them at al-Fadfad,
like the writing in the stone-channel of the lasting watercourse."

The phrase ﴿to the earth﴾ may mean: to its desires, its pleasures, and what it contains of delights; this was said by al-Suddi and others. It may also mean an expression for what is lowest and most base, as one says, "So-and-so is in the lowland (al-hadid)." This is supported by the rational meaning, because the earth and what is fixed upon it is this world, and everything upon it is perishing. Whoever clings to it has been deprived of the portion of the enduring Hereafter.

The Exalted's words: ﴿His likeness is that of a dog﴾. Al-Suddi and others said: this man was punished in this world by panting as the dog pants, so he was likened to it in form and appearance. Al-Jumhur (the majority) said: he was likened to it in that he was astray before he was given the signs, and then when he was given them he remained astray, the signs not benefiting him. Thus he is like the dog in that it does not cease panting, whether a burden is placed upon it or it is left without one. The clarification of the meaning: the thing that souls imagine of his condition is what they imagine of the condition of the dog. With this interpretation, it is correct for the "kaf" (ك, "like") to enter upon "mathal" (مَثَل, "likeness"). "Al-lahth" (اللهث) is breathing rapidly with movement of the mouth's organs along with it and extension of the tongue; it most often occurs with heat and fatigue. In the case of a horse it is called "dabh" (ضبح). It is the nature of the dog that it pants in every state. Al-Tabari mentioned that the meaning of ﴿if you attack him, he pants﴾ is "if you chase him away," and he related this from Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That is included within the category of hardship which we mentioned.

The Exalted's words: ﴿That is the likeness of the people﴾, i.e., this likeness, O Muhammad, is the likeness of these people who were astray before you brought them guidance and the message; then you came to them with that, but they remained in their error and did not benefit from it. So their likeness is that of the dog. His words ﴿So relate the stories﴾ mean: recount to them what they know to be among the unseen matters which only the people of the earlier scriptures know, and you are not one of them, ﴿perhaps they will reflect﴾ upon that and believe.

The Exalted's words: ﴿Evil is a likeness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the estimated construction is "evil is a likeness, the likeness of the people," because what follows "bi'sa" (بئس, "evil") and "ni'ma" (نعم, "excellent") is explained by its kind, as you say, "Zayd is an evil man (bi'sa rajulan Zaydun)." When "mathal" is elided, "al-qawm" (the people) is placed in its position, and the nominative in that case is by inception (al-ibtida'), with the predicate being what came before. Al-Jahdari read "sa'a mathalu al-qawmi" (ساء مَثَلُ القَوْمِ), and the nominative of "mathal" in this reading is by "sa'a," but "sa'a" does not operate like "bi'sa" unless what follows it is in the accusative. Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: al-Jahdari read "mithlu" (مِثْلُ) with a kasra on the mim and a damma on the lam, and al-A'mash read "mathalu" (مَثَلُ) with a fatha on the mim and a damma on the lam.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This contradicts what Abu Hatim mentioned, for he said: al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read "sa'a mathalu" with the nominative.

These verses, which contain the error of peoples and the discussion of it, are concluded with the statement that all of that is from Allah: the guidance is from Him, by His creation and origination, and likewise the misguidance. In the verse there is an expression of wonder at the condition of those mentioned. Whoever is led astray has been judged to be among the losers, and reward and punishment are linked to the earning of the son of Adam.

The Exalted's words: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾ are a report from Allah, the Exalted, that He created many for dwelling in Hell and for burning in it, and within it is a threat to the disbelievers. "Dhara'a" (ذرأ) means: He created and brought into existence with dispersal and spreading out. A group said: the lam in His words "li-Jahannama" (لجهنم) is "lam al-'aqibah" (لام العاقبة, the lam of consequence), meaning: so that their outcome and final destination would be Hell.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not correct. The lam of consequence is only conceivable when the act of the doer was not intended for what the matter ends up being. This lam is like the one in the words of the poet:

"O mother of Farwa, cease blaming and acknowledge,
for every mother gives birth to one who will be removed (al-muntaʼa)."

As for here, the act was intended for what the matter ends up being: their dwelling in Hell. Al-Tabari related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The children of fornication are among those whom Allah created for Hell." Then he traced a hadith from the chain of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr from the Prophet ﷺ. The Exalted's word "kathiran" (كثيرًا, "many") does not explicitly state that the disbelievers are more numerous than the believers, but it refers to that in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah said to Adam: 'Bring forth the group for the Fire.' So he brought forth from every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 180:

The Exalted said:

﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾ [al-A'raf: 179] ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾

This category, the disbelievers who turn away from reflecting on the signs of Allah, is described as having hearts that do not comprehend, (p-94) eyes that do not see, and ears that do not hear. The purpose of this is not to negate these perceptions from their senses entirely. Rather, the purpose is to negate them in some respect, as you say: "So-and-so is deaf to obscenity." From this is the saying of Miskin al-Darimi:

Blind when my neighbour goes out, until the curtain conceals my neighbour.
Deaf to what happens between them, deliberately, though there is nothing wrong with my hearing.

From this is another's saying:

I have turned deaf to an ugly speech, though I could hear it if I wished.
And to a hasty outburst I restrained my soul, though the ribs still held the remnants of anger.

From this is another's saying in advising one who enters the house of a king:

Enter, when you enter, blind, and leave, when you leave, mute.

So it is as if these people, since reflection with the heart, with the eye, and with what they heard of the signs and admonitions did not benefit them, deserved the description that they do not understand, do not see, and do not hear. Mujahid explained this by saying: "They have hearts with which they do not understand anything of the matter of the Hereafter, and eyes with which they do not see guidance, and ears with which they do not hear the truth." "Those" refers to the disbelievers mentioned earlier, (p-95) and they are likened to livestock, in that livestock's hearts do not comprehend things and do not reason through analogies. Likewise, what they see does not settle in them as it should. So too these people: what they see and hear does not produce in them knowledge of it as it truly is when they see and hear it. Then they are judged to be further astray, because the livestock have that nature and creation, neglecting nothing, and have no way to other than that. These people, however, are prepared for understanding, and faculties have been created for them that they can employ, and they have been given paths of reflection. Yet, by their heedlessness and turning away, they join themselves to the livestock, so they are further astray on this account. Then, by His saying: ﴿Those are the heedless﴾ [al-A'raf: 179], He explained the way by which they became more astray than livestock, which is heedlessness and negligence.

As for His saying: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ and the rest of the verse, the cause of this verse, according to what is related, is that Abu Jahl heard some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ reciting, mentioning Allah in their recitation, and at another time reciting and mentioning the Most Merciful (al-Rahman), and similar things. So he said: "Muhammad claims that the God is one, yet he worships many gods." So this verse was revealed.

"Names" (al-asma') here means "designations" (al-tasmiyat), by the consensus (ijma') of the interpreters, and nothing else is possible. "Most beautiful" (al-husna) is a verbal noun described by it. It is also permissible to consider "al-husna" to be the feminine form of "ahsan" (more beautiful), so that the adjective for a plural of non-rational things is singular, as He said: ﴿other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], and as He said: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10]. This is common. The beauty of the names is only attributed to them by the Law's approval of their use and by the textual authority concerning them, and in addition to this, they include noble and beautiful meanings.

People differed concerning a name that indicates unmixed praise, to which no doubt or shared meaning attaches, but which is not found explicitly stated, as to whether it may be used and whether Allah may be named by it. Ibn al-Baqillani explicitly permitted this, while Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari explicitly prohibited it, and the jurists and the majority prohibited it. The correct position is that Allah the Exalted is not named except by a name that the Law has permitted and which it has also established. For the condition attached to permitting its use, namely that it be unmixed praise with no doubt or shared meaning, is something only a small minority of the people of knowledge can judge well. If that were permitted, someone who thinks himself competent, but is not, would storm in and add to the names of Allah what is impermissible by consensus.

It is also disputed concerning the verbs in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] and ﴿the plotting of Allah﴾ [al-A'raf: 99], and similar, whether the active participle may be derived from them. One group said: it may not be used in any way. Another group permitted that it be said with restriction to its cause, so it is said: "Allah is one who mocks the disbelievers," and "a plotter against those who plot against the religion." As for using it without restriction, that is forbidden by consensus. The first position is stronger, and there is no necessity compelling one to the second, because the form of the verb in the Book of Allah suffices. Among the names of Allah are those that came in the Qur'an, and among them are those that came in the hadith and were transmitted with certainty (tawatur). This is what should be relied upon. Al-Tirmidhi has a hadith from Abu Hurayra that specified ninety-nine names, and some of them are anomalous. That hadith is not mutawatir. What is mutawatir from it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever counts them enters Paradise." The meaning of "counts them" (ahsaha) is that he enumerates and memorises them, and this includes belief in them, glorifying them, desiring them, and reflecting upon their meanings. This is the hadith of al-Bukhari. What is derived from it is that these names of Allah, blessed and exalted, are permitted to be used. It is also reported in some of the supplications of the Prophet ﷺ: "O Most Compassionate, O Most Bountiful" (ya hannan ya mannan), but these two names do not occur in al-Tirmidhi's enumeration.

His saying: ﴿so call upon Him by them﴾ is a permission to use them. As for His saying: ﴿and leave those who﴾, Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: leave them, do not argue with them, and do not confront them. Thus the verse, on this view, is abrogated (mansukha, from naskh) by fighting. It was also said: its meaning is a threat, like His saying: ﴿Leave Me with whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], and His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾ [al-Hijr: 3]. It is said: alhada and lahada both mean "deviated, inclined, and swerved." Alhada is the more common, and from it is the saying of the poet:

...........................  the Imam is not a miser, nor one who swerves.

Abu 'Ali said: it is hardly heard from anyone. In the Qur'an: ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj: 25]. From it is the niche (lahd) of the grave, which inclines to one of its two sides.

(p-98) Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read "yulhidun" with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the ha, and likewise in al-Nahl and al-Sajda. Hamza read all three occurrences as "yalhadun" with a fatha on the ya and the ha. Likewise Ibn Wathhab, Talha, 'Isa, and al-A'mash.

The meaning of deviation (ilhad) concerning the names of Allah the Mighty and Majestic is that they give the name of al-Lat as an equivalent to the name of Allah the Exalted, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and al-Uzza as an equivalent to al-'Aziz (the Mighty), as said by Mujahid. They call Allah "Lord" (rabb) and they call their idols "lords" (arbab), and similar things.

His saying: ﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ is a pure threat of the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Kisa'i went to distinguish between alhada and lahada, claiming that alhada means "inclined and swerved," and lahada means "settled and submitted." Al-Tabari said: Al-Kisa'i used to read everything in the Qur'an with a damma on the ya and a kasra on the ha, except the one in al-Nahl, which he read with a fatha on the ya and the ha, claiming that it means "submission (rukun)." Likewise Abu 'Ali mentioned this from him.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 181–185:**

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And among those We created is a nation that guides by the truth and by it acts justly.﴾ ﴿As for those who denied Our signs, We will lead them step by step from where they do not know.﴾ ﴿And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion. He is only a clear warner.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth, and at what Allah has created of things, and that perhaps their term has drawn near? Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾

This verse informs about a people who oppose those previously mentioned, who were people of faith, uprightness and guidance. The apparent wording of this verse implies every believer from the time of Adam, peace be upon him, until the Hour. Al-Nahhas said: "The world is never, at any time, free of a caller who calls to the truth."

(p-99)The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Whether his voice is far-reaching or he is obscure."

It is related from many of the exegetes that it refers to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ. And there is a hadith of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in this regard, who said: "This verse is for you, and a similar one has already come for the people of Musa."

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, the verse is a threat, and the reference is to the disbelievers. The meaning of ﴿We will lead them step by step﴾ (سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهُمْ, from الاستدراج, "gradual leading") is: We will drive them one thing after another and one degree after another, through blessings upon them and granting them respite, until they become deceived and think that no punishment will reach them. His saying ﴿from where they do not know﴾ means: from where they do not know that it is a gradual leading. This is a punishment from Allah for denying the signs. When He had decreed the punishment upon them, He granted them respite so that they would increase in sin. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i recited سَيَسْتَدْرِجُهُمْ with a ya' (the third-person form, "He will lead them").

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿I will give them respite (أُمْلِي)﴾, its meaning is: I will delay them for a period (مُلاءة) of time, that is, a duration. There are three dialectal forms of its vowel: fat-ha, damma and kasra on the mim. Abd al-Hamid, from Ibn Amir, recited أَنَّ كَيْدِي ("that My plan..."), meaning: because My plan is.... The majority of people and the rest of the Seven read إِنَّ كَيْدِي ("indeed My plan..."), as an independent, resumptive statement.

(p-100)And مَتِينٌ (matin) means "strong." The poet said:

"For a kinsman upon us is a duty we will not neglect,
Whose strength is firm, its cord not frayed."

Ibn Ishaq narrated in this verse أَمِينٌ قُواهُ ("trustworthy in his strength"). The word derives from المَتْن, the back, which is carried upon because of its strength. From it is the saying of the poet, Imru' al-Qays:

"She has two backs (matnatan), which are stretched taut
As the leopard lies with its forelegs spread..."

These are the two sides of the spine. From it is also the saying of another:

"They swerved the swerving of despair, and it tested
The strong backs of the swift, with varied gaits..."

From it is also the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And he drives over hard, smooth, firm-jointed (ملاطس) [mounts],
Strong in their tight build, supple, firm-backed (متان)..."

(p-101)From it is also the hadith about the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq: "So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pressed on (فَمَتَنَ) with the people." That is, he traveled with them at a harsh pace so that the talk would be cut off, [the talk] of Ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: ﴿If we return to Madinah...﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8], to the end of the verse.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion﴾, it is an affirmation accompanied by a rebuke of the disbelievers. The pause is on His saying ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾, and then the speech begins with negating what they claimed: ﴿There is no madness in their companion (بِصاحِبِهِمْ)﴾, that is, in Muhammad ﷺ. It is possible that the meaning is: "Have they not reflected that there is no madness in their companion?"

The reason for the revelation of this verse, as related, is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ascended al-Safa at night and began calling the clans of Quraysh: "O Banu so-and-so, O Banu so-and-so," warning them and inviting them to Allah. Some of the disbelievers said when they woke in the morning: "This is a madman who spent the night shouting until morning." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated what they said in that situation and in others, for madness was among what they accused him of, until Allah made His light manifest. Then He informed that he is a nadhir (نذير), that is, one who warns of punishment. The word نِذارة, when it comes unrestricted, refers only to evil, though it may be used for good when qualified. It appears from the arrangement of the verse that it urges them to reflect on the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and that there is no madness in him. Just as He referred them after this verse to looking, and then explained what is to be looked at, so here He referred them to reflection and then explained what is to be reflected upon.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and at what Allah has created of things?﴾, this too is a rebuke of the disbelievers and an affirmation. Looking here is with the heart, as a lesson and reflection. مَلَكُوت is a form denoting greatness and intensity. His saying, glorified be He: ﴿and at what Allah has created of things﴾ is a word encompassing everything that is looked at and used as evidence: from the craftsmanship which points to the Craftsman, from the self of man and his senses, and from the places of his provision. الشيء (thing) applies to all existent things.

His saying ﴿and that perhaps﴾ (وأن عسى) is coordinated with His saying ﴿in the dominion﴾. The second وأنْ is in the position of a nominative after عسى. The meaning is to make them stand before the fact that no looking has occurred on their part into any of this, nor into the fact that their terms have drawn near, so that they die and the time for making up is lost, and the warned-against consequence becomes binding upon them.

(p-102)Then He made them stand before the question: "In what statement or matter will their faith and acceptance occur, if it does not occur through the matter in which their salvation and entry into Paradise lies?" A similar line is the saying of the poet:

"And for whose soul after my soul shall I fight?"

The pronoun in His saying, glorified be He, بَعْدَهُ ("after it"), is taken to refer to the Qur'an. It was said that it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, his story and his entire affair. It was also said that it refers back to the term (الأجل), since there is no action after death.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 186–187:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Whomever God leads astray, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their rebellion, wandering blindly.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal it at its time but He. It is heavy upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except suddenly." They ask you as if you were well-informed about it. Say: "Its knowledge is only with God, but most people do not know."﴾

This is a conditional clause (shart) with its response (jawab), whose implied meaning is despair of them and condemnation of them, because the intended meaning is that this [state] has already befallen them, and that they are an example of it.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Qatada read "wa-nadharuhum" with a nun and a raised ra'. ‘Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, also reads it this way. Hafs, in his transmission from him, reads "wa-yadharuhum" with a ya' and a raised ra'. The people of Makka also read it this way. This reading is either on the assumption of an omitted subject, "wa-nahnu nadharuhum" ("and We leave them"), or on the basis of breaking off the verb and beginning a new statement. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr, according to what Abu Hatim reported, read it with a ya' and jazm (the jussive). Talha ibn Musarrif and al-A'mash also read "wa-yadharhum" with a ya' and jazm, as a conjunction with the position of the fa' and what follows it in His words, "there is none to guide him" (fa-la hadiya lahu), because that position is jussive. A similar usage appears in the verse of Abu Dawud:

Then test me with your trials, perhaps
I may reconcile you and gradually win over Nawiyy

(p-103) From the same usage is the saying of another:

Wherever you go, I am your enemy ... and, despite your diminishing me in life, I shall increase

Abu 'Ali said: A similar case of applying the rule to the position is the words of the Most High: ﴿If only You would delay me to a near term, so that I might give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10], because if you did not attach the fa', you would say "asaddaq" (without the fa' it would be jussive). Kharija reported from Nafi': "wa-nadharhum" with a nun and jazm. Al-tughyan (rebellion) means excess in a thing, and it seems to be used for what is not righteous. Al-'amah means bewilderment.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ and the rest of the verse, Qatada ibn di'ama said: The meaning is that the disbelievers of Quraysh ask you, because Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, we are your kin, so inform us of the time of the Hour." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: The verse refers to the Jews, because Jabal ibn Abi Qushayr and Samawil ibn Zayd said to him: "If you are a prophet, inform us of the time of the Hour, for we know it. If you are truthful, we will believe in you."

Al-sa'a (the Hour) is the Resurrection: the death of everything that was then alive and the raising of all of them. The whole of it is called by the name "the Hour" and the name "the Resurrection." Ayyana means "when," and it is a question about time. Because it includes the notion of time, it is indeclinable (mabni). The majority of people read "ayyana" with a fatha on the hamza. al-Sulami read "iyyana" with a kasra on the hamza. Its original form is probably "ayyu an" (which?), and it is built on fatha. The poet said:

When will my need be fulfilled, when?
Do you not see its time has come?

Abu al-Fath said: The pattern of "ayyana" with a fatha on the hamza is fa'lan, and with a kasra it is fi'lan; the nun in both is an extra letter. Murṣaha is a nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the predicate is ayyana. The view of al-Mubarrad is that murṣaha is raised by an implied verb, and its meaning is "its establisher and its终 end (muntaha)," derived from arsa yursi (to fix firmly). Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded that the matter be referred back to Him and that one submit to His knowledge. Yujalliha means it reveals it. Al-jala' is clear evidence and witnessing, and this is what Zuhayr intends with his words:

..................... an oath, or a flight, or a clear sign

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 186–187:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Whomever God leads astray, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their rebellion, wandering blindly.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal it at its time but He. It is heavy upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except suddenly." They ask you as if you were well-informed about it. Say: "Its knowledge is only with God, but most people do not know."﴾

This is a conditional clause (shart) with its response (jawab), whose implied meaning is despair of them and condemnation of them, because the intended meaning is that this [state] has already befallen them, and that they are an example of it.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman and Qatada read "wa-nadharuhum" with a nun and a raised ra'. ‘Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, also reads it this way. Hafs, in his transmission from him, reads "wa-yadharuhum" with a ya' and a raised ra'. The people of Makka also read it this way. This reading is either on the assumption of an omitted subject, "wa-nahnu nadharuhum" ("and We leave them"), or on the basis of breaking off the verb and beginning a new statement. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr, according to what Abu Hatim reported, read it with a ya' and jazm (the jussive). Talha ibn Musarrif and al-A'mash also read "wa-yadharhum" with a ya' and jazm, as a conjunction with the position of the fa' and what follows it in His words, "there is none to guide him" (fa-la hadiya lahu), because that position is jussive. A similar usage appears in the verse of Abu Dawud:

Then test me with your trials, perhaps
I may reconcile you and gradually win over Nawiyy

(p-103) From the same usage is the saying of another:

Wherever you go, I am your enemy ... and, despite your diminishing me in life, I shall increase

Abu 'Ali said: A similar case of applying the rule to the position is the words of the Most High: ﴿If only You would delay me to a near term, so that I might give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 10], because if you did not attach the fa', you would say "asaddaq" (without the fa' it would be jussive). Kharija reported from Nafi': "wa-nadharhum" with a nun and jazm. Al-tughyan (rebellion) means excess in a thing, and it seems to be used for what is not righteous. Al-'amah means bewilderment.

Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: The verse refers to the Jews, because Jabal ibn Abi Qushayr and Samawil ibn Zayd said to him: "If you are a prophet, inform us of the time of the Hour, for we know it. If you are truthful, we will believe in you."

Al-sa'a (the Hour) is the Resurrection: the death of everything that was then alive and the raising of all of them. The whole of it is called by the name "the Hour" and the name "the Resurrection." Ayyana means "when," and it is a question about time. Because it includes the notion of time, it is indeclinable (mabni). The majority of people read "ayyana" with a fatha on the hamza. al-Sulami read "iyyana" with a kasra on the hamza. Its original form is probably "ayyu an" (which?), and it is built on fatha. The poet said:

When will my need be fulfilled, when?
Do you not see its time has come?

Abu al-Fath said: The pattern of "ayyana" with a fatha on the hamza is fa'lan, and with a kasra it is fi'lan; the nun in both is an extra letter. Murṣaha is a nominative by way of the inceptive (mubtada'), and the predicate is ayyana. The view of al-Mubarrad is that murṣaha is raised by an implied verb, and its meaning is "its establisher and its终 end (muntaha)," derived from arsa yursi (to fix firmly). Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded that the matter be referred back to Him and that one submit to His knowledge. Yujalliha means it reveals it. ..................... an oath, or a flight, or a clear sign
