Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verse 188–189:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: I have no power to benefit or harm myself, except as Allah wills. And had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no evil would have touched me. I am only a warner and a bringer of good tidings for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate, that he might find tranquility in her. And when he covered her, she bore a light burden and carried it about. Then when she became heavy, they both invoked Allah, their Lord: "If You give us a righteous child, we will surely be among the grateful."﴾

This is a command to fully submit, and to disassociate oneself from any share in the power and the unseen of Allah, and for him to describe himself to these questioners by the attribute of one who is incapable of knowing the unseen and must not claim it. So He informed that he does not possess the benefits and harms of his own self except what Allah has granted him, willed, and facilitated. This exception is disconnected (munqati'). He also informed that if he knew the unseen, he would act according to what is to come and would prepare for everything with the preparation of one who knows the measure of what he must prepare for. This is a general expression covering everything. People have specified it: Ibn Jurayj and Mujahid said: "If I knew my term (ajal), I would have acquired much righteous deed." Another group said: "The times of victory, to be ready for them." Makki related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning of ﴿And had I known﴾ is a year of drought, so that I would have stored up from a fertile year for it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The words of the verse encompass this and other than this.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿وَما مَسَّنِيَ﴾ (and no evil would have touched me), it admits of two aspects, and both have been stated. One: that "ما" is conjoined to His saying ﴿لاسْتَكْثَرْتُ﴾ (I would have acquired), meaning: and evil would not have touched me. The second: that the speech is cut off and complete at His saying ﴿I would have acquired much good﴾, and he begins to inform of the negation of evil from himself, which is the madness they attributed to him. Al-Mu'arrij al-Sadusi said: "al-Su' (evil) means madness in the dialect of Hudhayl." Then he informed of the totality of what he is: warning and good tidings. And ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ (for a people who believe) admits of two meanings: One: that he intends he is a warner and bringer of good tidings to a people from whom faith is sought and to whom it is called, and these are all people. The second: that he informs that he is a warner, and the speech is complete, then he begins to inform that he is a bringer of good tidings to those who believe in him, so in this is a promise for those whose faith has been realized.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي خَلَقَكم مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ﴾ (It is He who created you from a single soul), the verse...

Most of the exegetes said: by the single soul is meant Adam, peace be upon him, and by His saying ﴿وَجَعَلَ مِنها زَوْجَها﴾ (and made from it its mate) is Eve. His saying "from it" refers to what was mentioned earlier, that Adam slept and the lowest of his ribs was extracted, and Eve was created from it. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿لِيَسْكُنَ إلَيْها﴾ means: that he might find intimacy and tranquility. All of this was in Paradise.

Then he began with another state, which is in this world after their descent, so he said: ﴿فَلَمّا تَغَشّاها﴾ (when he covered her), that is, he came upon her, and it is a metaphor for intercourse. The light burden (haml khafif) is the seminal fluid that the woman carries in her womb. Most reciters read "ḥamlan" with a fatha on the ḥā'; Hammad ibn Salama, from Ibn Kathir, read "ḥimlan" with a kasra on the ḥā'. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿فَمَرَّتْ بِهِ﴾ means: she continued with it. Ayyub said: "I asked al-Hasan about His saying ﴿فَمَرَّتْ بِهِ﴾ and he said: 'If you were an Arab man, you would know what it is; the meaning is only: she continued with it (fa-istamarrat bihi).'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some have considered it to be inverted (ʿalā al-qalb), as if the intended meaning is: he continued with her, as you say: "I put the cap on my head." Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read—according to what al-Naqqash related—"fa-marat bihi" with a light rā'; its meaning: she doubted about what had befallen her, whether it was a pregnancy or an illness or the like. Ibn 'Abbas read "fa-istamarrat bihi." Ibn Mas'ud read "fa-istamarrat bi-ḥamlihā." 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As read "fa-mārat bihi," and its meaning: she came with it, went, and moved about, as you say: "the wind moved (māratī-l-rīḥu) mawran." "Athqalat" means she entered into heaviness, as you say: "asbaha" and "amsa," meaning: she became one with weight, as you say: "atmara al-rajul" and "albana" when he became one with dates and milk. The pronoun in "da'awā" refers to Adam and Eve.

It is related in the narratives of this verse that when Eve first conceived, she did not know what it was, and this strengthens the reading of whoever read "fa-marat bihi" with a light rā'; she was distressed by that, and Iblis found his way to her. He said to her: "What will you know of what is in your womb? Perhaps it is a pig, or a snake, or a beast of some kind. And what will you know of where it will come out? Will your belly be split open for it so that you die, or from your mouth, or from your nose? But if you obey me and name him 'Abd al-Harith..."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Al-Harith is the name of Iblis." "I will deliver him to you and make him a human like you. And if you do not do so, I will kill him for you." He said: Hawwa informed Adam, and he said to her: "That is our companion who deceived us in Paradise; we will not obey him." When she gave birth, they named him 'Abd Allah, and the boy died. It is narrated that Allah empowered Iblis over killing him; she conceived another, and he did the same to her. She conceived a third, and when she gave birth to him, they obeyed Iblis and named him 'Abd al-Harith, out of eagerness for his life. This is the association (shirk) which they made for Allah, that is, in the naming only.

As for "ṣāliḥan," al-Hasan said: its meaning is: a boy. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both—and this is the most apparent—said: a human being, whole and sound. Its accusative is as the second object. In "al-Mushkil" by Makki, it is stated that it is an adjective of a verbal noun, i.e., a righteous coming (atyan ṣāliḥan). Some people said: the meaning of this verse is to clarify the state of the disbelievers, so He enumerated the blessings that encompass the disbelievers and others of mankind, then He confirmed that with the evil act of the polytheists, so the proof was established against them and punishment became obligatory. That is because He said, addressing all of mankind: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate﴾, meaning Adam and Eve, i.e., and your state continued as one like that. This is a blessing that pertains to each person with a portion of it. Then His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿فَلَمّا تَغَشّاها﴾ to the end of the verse is a description of the state of mankind one by one, i.e., this is how they act. When Allah gives them a righteous, sound child as He wished, they turn him away from the natural disposition (fitra) to association. This is the act of the polytheists, in which the proof is established by its conjunction with the general blessing. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan—as al-Tabari related from him—said: the meaning of the verse ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul﴾ is an indication of the spirit that is breathed into each person.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That is: He created you from a single kind, and made the females from it. Then His, blessed and exalted is He, saying ﴿فَلَمّا تَغَشّاها﴾ to the end of the verse is a description of the state of mankind one by one, in the order mentioned in the preceding statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 190–193:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿So when He gave them a righteous child, they ascribed to Him partners in what He had given them. But exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Do they associate with Him those who create nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ ﴿And they cannot give them help, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is all the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent.﴾

It is said: the preceding verse concerns Adam and Hawwa' (Eve), and the pronoun in His saying "ataahuma" (He gave them) refers back to the two of them. It is also said that the association (shirk) which they ascribed is in obedience, meaning they obeyed Iblis in naming (the child) 'Abd al-Harith, but they were otherwise obedient to Allah. al-Tabari cited a hadith in this regard through the chain of Samura ibn Jundub. It is also possible that the association lies in their making his servitude (ubudiyya) by name to be to other than Him. al-Tabari and al-Suddi said concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾: it is a separate statement, not part of the first; and the account of Adam and Hawwa' ended at His saying ﴿what He had given them﴾, and that this statement is meant for the idolaters of the Arabs.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 7, verses 194–196:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides Allah are servants like you. So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they strike? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ ﴿Say: Call upon your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, my protector is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He takes charge of the righteous.﴾

Most of the reciters read: "Inna alladhina tadʿuna min duni Allahi ʿibadun amthalukum" with the (inna) emphasized and ʿibadun in the nominative. This is an address to the disbelievers, belittling their idols in their own eyes: these idols are created and originated, since they are bodies and physical forms; they are thus "worshipped," that is, "owned" (mutamallaka). Muqatil said: the intended people in this verse are a group of Arabs from Khuza'a who used to worship the angels, so Allah informed them that they are servants like them, not gods.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr read: "In alladhina tadʿuna min duni Allahi ʿibadan amthalakum," with the nun of (inna) lightened, so that it has the meaning of (ma) (not), and with the accusative on His saying "ʿibadan" and "amthalakum." The meaning according to this reading is belittling the status of the idols and negating their likeness to humans; rather, they are lesser and more contemptible, since they are inanimate objects that neither understand nor reason. Sibawayh holds that (in), when it has the meaning of (ma), is weaker in rank than (ma), so the predicate remains nominative and (in) enters upon the subject and predicate without putting the predicate in the accusative. Thus the proper reading in his view of this recitation is: "In alladhina tadʿuna min duni Allahi ʿibadun amthalukum." Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Mubarrad permits that it operates like (ma) in putting the predicate in the accusative. Al-Kisa'i claimed that (in) with the meaning of (ma) only occurs when followed by (illa), as in His Exalted saying: ﴿In al-kafirun illa fi ghurur﴾ [al-Mulk: 20]. Then Exalted God established the proof by His saying: ﴿fadʿuhum﴾, that is: test them; if they do not respond, then they are as we have described.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿Do they have feet﴾ and the verse that follows, the purpose of this verse is: Do they have the senses and attributes of a living being? If they say "No," they have judged that they are inanimate objects. So these details came to explain that general statement on which affirmation was intended. When acknowledgment of the details of the matter occurs, acknowledgment of its generality necessarily follows, and its explanation becomes stronger, leaving no room for doubt. Al-Zahrawi said: the meaning is: You are better than them by these beneficial limbs, so how can you worship them?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The reading of Saʿid ibn Jubayr is strengthened by this interpretation, since it implies that the idols are not servants like humans.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 197–200:

The Exalted said:

﴿Those you invoke besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿If you call them to guidance, they do not hear; and you see them looking at you, yet they do not see.﴾ ﴿Take what is freely given, enjoin what is customary, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ ﴿And if an evil prompting from Satan should stir you, seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is Hearing, Knowing.﴾

The pronoun in His words "besides Him" refers to the name of Allah, the Exalted. This pronoun clarifies what we mentioned about the weakness of the reading of the one who reads "Indeed, the guardian (waliyy) of Allah" as referring to Jibril (ﷺ). This verse also explains the condition of those idols, their corruption, and their inability to help even themselves, let alone others.

As for His words, "And if you call them" (the verse), one group said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community, and the ha' and mim in His words "you call them" refer to the disbelievers. Describing them as not hearing and not seeing is because looking and listening have yielded them no benefit and they have gained nothing of substance from them. This was said by al-Suddi and Mujahid. Al-Tabari said: the intended referent of the mentioned pronoun is the idols, and describing them with looking is a metaphor for facing and confronting, and the imagery of looking that it carries, as you say: "So-and-so's house looks toward so-and-so's house." The meaning of the verse on this view is to make clear the lifelessness of the idols and the insignificance of their status. Some of the Mu'tazilites argued from this verse that the servants will look at their Lord and not see Him, but there is no proof for them in the verse, because looking applied to idols is purely metaphorical.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This matter was repeated and these verses recurred concerning it because the matter of the idols and their veneration was firmly rooted in the souls of the Arabs at that time and dominated their minds, so the discourse on it was made comprehensive out of Allah's kindness toward them.

As for His words, "Take what is freely given" (the verse), it is a charge from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to His Prophet (ﷺ) that encompasses all of his community, and a command to all noble characteristics. The majority said regarding His words, glorified is He: "Take what is freely given" means: accept from people, in their characters, their words, and their dealings, what comes easily without strain. Thus al-'Afw here means the surplus and the ease that comes without hardship. This was said by 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr in the Musannaf of al-Bukhari, and by Mujahid and 'Urwa. From it is the verse of Hatim al-Ta'i:

"Take the easy from me, that you may keep my affection, and do not speak harshly when I am angry."

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi said: this verse concerns wealth. (It was also said: it was before the obligation of zakat, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to take what was easy from people's wealth.) "'Afa" means: it exceeded and increased, from the saying "the plants and the hair 'afa'," meaning they became abundant. Then zakat and its limits were revealed, and it abrogated this verse. Makki reported from Mujahid that "Take what is freely given" means: take the obligatory zakat.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is anomalous (shadhdh).

As for His words, "and enjoin what is customary," its meaning is: everything that souls recognize as good and that the Shari'a does not reject. It was narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Jibril: "What is this 'urf which I have been commanded to enjoin?" He said: "I do not know until I ask the knowledgeable one." So he returned to his Lord, asked Him, then came back and said: "O Muhammad, it is that you give to the one who withholds from you, join ties with the one who cuts you off, and pardon the one who wronged you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the establishing of the ultimate points, and what is intended is that whatever falls short of this is also among the doing of good. 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "bil-'urf" with a damma on the ra' (bi-'urfi, as reported by Abu Hatim), and al-'urf and al-'urf have the same meaning: the known (al-ma'ruf).

As for His words, "and turn away from the ignorant," it is a firm, continuing ruling that applies to people for as long as they endure. This is the view of the majority of scholars. Ibn Zayd, regarding His words "Take what is freely given" up to "the ignorant," said: the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded with this only to conciliate the disbelievers of Quraysh, and then it was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The hadith of al-Hurr ibn Qays, when he brought his uncle 'Uyayna ibn Hisn in to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, is evidence that it is muhkam and continuing, because al-Hurr argued with it against 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he affirmed it and stopped at it.

As for His words, "And if an evil prompting from Satan should stir you," it is a charge from Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to His Prophet (ﷺ) that encompasses his community, man by man. The nazgh is a movement in which there is corruption, and it is rarely used except for the action of Satan, because his movements are swift and corrupting. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you should point at his brother with a weapon, for Satan may stir (yanzagh) in his hands."

The meaning of this verse is: if a passing thought from Satan touches you, then seek refuge in Allah. The prompting of Satan is general, covering anger, making sins appear attractive, acquiring calamities, and other things. In the Musannaf of al-Tirmidhi, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The angel has a lamma (touch of inspiration), and Satan has a lamma."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two lammas are the promptings of good and evil. "Hearing" in this verse fits with seeking refuge, and also fits with the words of the disbelievers, which anger Satan for that reason; and "Knowing" is likewise. Ibn al-Qasim based on this verse his statement that the seeking of refuge at the time of recitation is: "I seek refuge in Allah, the Hearing, the Knowing, from Satan the accursed."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 201–203:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of God, when an evil suggestion from Satan touches them, remember [God], and at once they see clearly.﴾ ﴿Yet their brothers [the devils] keep drawing them into error, and they do not hold back.﴾ ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say: "Why have you not devised it?" Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This [Qur'an] is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe."﴾

"Those who are mindful" (ittaqaw) here is general, covering mindfulness of shirk and mindfulness of sins, as evidenced by the fact that the word is used in praise of them. There is no basis for restricting it to avoiding shirk alone. Also, the mindful person who seeks refuge may still be touched by an evil suggestion from Satan, since infallibility belongs only to the prophets, peace be upon them.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "ṭā'if" (ṭā'ifun). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "ṭayf" (ṭayfun). Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "ṭayyif" (ṭayyifun). The word may derive either from ṭāfa, yaṭūfu, or from ṭāfa, yaṭīfu (with a fatha on the ya'), and the latter is attested from the Arabs. Abu 'Ubayda cited in support of this:

"Whenever the phantom visits you, it wanders, and its wandering for you is remembrance and passion."

So "ṭā'if" is an active participle like qā'il from qāla, yaqūlu, and bā'i' from bāʿa, yabīʿu. "Ṭayyif" is also an active participle, like mayyit from māta, or like bayyi' and layyin from bāʿa, yabīʿu and lāna, yalīnu. "Ṭayf" may be a lightened form of "ṭayyif," like mayt from mayyit. If we take the word from ṭāfa, yaṭīfu, then "ṭayf" is a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi inclined to this view, treating the ṭā'if as like the khātir and the ṭayyib as like the khaṭra. Al-Kisa'i said: "ṭayf" is lamam (a passing touch), and "ṭā'if" is whatever circles around a person.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

How is this so, when al-A'sha said:

"And she rises after the fatigue of travel, as if there had visited her a wandering jinn, mad."

The meaning of the verse: when anger touches them, and Satan adorns with it what is not fitting. His saying "remember" (tadhakkarū) refers to the seeking of refuge commanded earlier, and to what God, Mighty and Majestic, has commanded and forbidden in the event where Satan's incitement occurs. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "min al-shayṭān ta'ammalū fa-idhā hum" (reflect). In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "idhā ṭāfa min al-shayṭān ṭā'ifun ta'ammalū." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Anger is a host from the host of the jinn. Do you not see the redness of the eyes and the swelling of the veins? When that happens, then the earth, the earth!" His saying "mubṣirūn" (seeing clearly) derives from başīra (insight), meaning: then they have clearly recognised the truth and turned towards it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yet their brothers keep drawing them into error⦆ — in these pronouns there are possibilities. Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is connected in meaning to His saying: ﴿nor can they help them, nor can they help themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 192].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this there is room for scrutiny.

The majority said: the verse is in its proper place, but the pronoun in His saying "wa-ikhwānuhum" (and their brothers) refers to the devils, and the pronoun in His saying "yamuddūnahum" (they keep drawing them) refers to the disbelievers, who are meant by "the brothers." The word "Satan" in the verse before this is generic, which is why a plural pronoun returns to them here. The sense on this interpretation is: and there are brothers of the devils, whom the devils keep drawing into error. Qatadah said: both pronouns in the hā' and mīm refer to the disbelievers.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this view the verse is set in opposition to the one before it: the mindful have such-and-such a state, and these disbelievers are drawn on by their brothers among the devils, and then they do not hold back.

His saying "fi al-ghayy" (into error) may be connected to "yamuddūnahum," and on this basis the interpretation mentioned first from the majority follows. It may also be connected to "ikhwān," and then the two pronouns may refer to the disbelievers, as we mentioned from Qatadah, or both may refer to the devils, meaning: the brothers of the devils in error, unlike the brotherhood in God, who drive the devils on by their obedience to them and their acceptance of them. This interpretation does not follow if "fi al-ghayy" is connected to "al-imdad," because humans do not lead devils into error. The purpose of this verse is to describe the state of the disbelievers with the devils, just as the state of the mindful with them was described before.

All seven readers except Nafi' read "yamuddūnahum" from madadtu. Nafi' alone read "yumiddūnahum" with a ḍamma on the ya', from amdadtu. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: madda al-shay' is used when the increase is of its own kind, and amadda it when the increase is of something else.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is not consistently applied. The majority said: they have the same meaning, except that "amadda" is used for what is loved, as in His saying: ﴿Do we bestow on them wealth and children?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55], and His saying: ﴿And We provided them with fruit﴾ [al-Tur: 22], and His saying: ﴿Will you provide me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml: 36]; and "madda" is used for what is disliked, as in His saying: ﴿And He lets them continue in their transgression﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. The drawing of the devils into error for the disbelievers is their adorning of it for them and their continuous misleading. Whoever reads "yamuddūnahum" with a ḍamma on the mim, it is in the usual manner. Whoever reads "yumiddūnahum" it is restricted by His saying "fi al-ghayy," just as one may restrict glad tidings, saying: "I gave him good news of evil." Al-Jahdari read "yumadduhum."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then they do not hold back﴾ refers to all of them, meaning: these do not hold back from obeying the devils and from disbelieving in God, Mighty and Majestic. The majority of people read "yuqṣirūn" from aqṣara, while Ibn Abi 'Ablah and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "yaqṣurūn" from qaṣara.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign﴾. Its occasion, as is related, is that revelation was sometimes delayed for the Prophet ﷺ, so the disbelievers would say: "Why have you not devised it?" The meaning of the word in Arab speech is: you chose it and selected it. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others said: what is meant by this word is: "Why did you not choose it and invent it yourself, from your own side and of your own accord?" The sense is: since all your speech is like that, according to what Quraysh claimed. Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did al-Dahhak: what is meant is: "Why did you not receive it from God and select it upon Him, since you claim to be a prophet and that your station with Him is the station of messengership?" So God, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him to answer by submitting to God, Exalted is He, and that the matter of revelation rests with Him, Who sends it down whenever He wills, with no one to repel His judgment in that. So He said: ﴿Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."﴾ Then by His saying "this" He indicated the Qur'an, and He described it as "insights," meaning signs of guidance and lights that illumine hearts. A group said: the meaning is: "this possesses insights," and the sentence is sound without positing an elided genitive, since what is indicated by "this" is only suras, verses and wisdoms; it may be indicated by "this" because its name is masculine, and it may be described as "insights" insofar as it is suras and verses.

﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾, that is, for these in particular. Al-Tabari said: as for one who does not believe, it is for him a blindness, as a punishment from God, Exalted is He.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 201–203:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of God, when an evil suggestion from Satan touches them, remember [God], and at once they see clearly.﴾ ﴿Yet their brothers [the devils] keep drawing them into error, and they do not hold back.﴾ ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say: "Why have you not devised it?" Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This [Qur'an] is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe."﴾

"Those who are mindful" (ittaqaw) here is general, covering mindfulness of shirk and mindfulness of sins, as evidenced by the fact that the word is used in praise of them. There is no basis for restricting it to avoiding shirk alone. Also, the mindful person who seeks refuge may still be touched by an evil suggestion from Satan, since infallibility belongs only to the prophets, peace be upon them.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "ṭā'if" (ṭā'ifun). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "ṭayf" (ṭayfun). Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "ṭayyif" (ṭayyifun). The word may derive either from ṭāfa, yaṭūfu, or from ṭāfa, yaṭīfu (with a fatha on the ya'), and the latter is attested from the Arabs. Abu 'Ubayda cited in support of this:

"Whenever the phantom visits you, it wanders, and its wandering for you is remembrance and passion."

So "ṭā'if" is an active participle like qā'il from qāla, yaqūlu, and bā'i' from bāʿa, yabīʿu. "Ṭayyif" is also an active participle, like mayyit from māta, or like bayyi' and layyin from bāʿa, yabīʿu and lāna, yalīnu. "Ṭayf" may be a lightened form of "ṭayyif," like mayt from mayyit. If we take the word from ṭāfa, yaṭīfu, then "ṭayf" is a verbal noun. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi inclined to this view, treating the ṭā'if as like the khātir and the ṭayyib as like the khaṭra. Al-Kisa'i said: "ṭayf" is lamam (a passing touch), and "ṭā'if" is whatever circles around a person.

How is this so, when al-A'sha said:

"And she rises after the fatigue of travel, as if there had visited her a wandering jinn, mad."

The meaning of the verse: when anger touches them, and Satan adorns with it what is not fitting. His saying "remember" (tadhakkarū) refers to the seeking of refuge commanded earlier, and to what God, Mighty and Majestic, has commanded and forbidden in the event where Satan's incitement occurs. Ibn al-Zubayr read: "min al-shayṭān ta'ammalū fa-idhā hum" (reflect). In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "idhā ṭāfa min al-shayṭān ṭā'ifun ta'ammalū." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Anger is a host from the host of the jinn. Do you not see the redness of the eyes and the swelling of the veins? When that happens, then the earth, the earth!" His saying "mubṣirūn" (seeing clearly) derives from başīra (insight), meaning: then they have clearly recognised the truth and turned towards it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yet their brothers keep drawing them into error⦆ — in these pronouns there are possibilities. Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is connected in meaning to His saying: ﴿nor can they help them, nor can they help themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 192].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this there is room for scrutiny.

The majority said: the verse is in its proper place, but the pronoun in His saying "wa-ikhwānuhum" (and their brothers) refers to the devils, and the pronoun in His saying "yamuddūnahum" (they keep drawing them) refers to the disbelievers, who are meant by "the brothers." The word "Satan" in the verse before this is generic, which is why a plural pronoun returns to them here. The sense on this interpretation is: and there are brothers of the devils, whom the devils keep drawing into error. Qatadah said: both pronouns in the hā' and mīm refer to the disbelievers.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this view the verse is set in opposition to the one before it: the mindful have such-and-such a state, and these disbelievers are drawn on by their brothers among the devils, and then they do not hold back.

His saying "fi al-ghayy" (into error) may be connected to "yamuddūnahum," and on this basis the interpretation mentioned first from the majority follows. It may also be connected to "ikhwān," and then the two pronouns may refer to the disbelievers, as we mentioned from Qatadah, or both may refer to the devils, meaning: the brothers of the devils in error, unlike the brotherhood in God, who drive the devils on by their obedience to them and their acceptance of them. This interpretation does not follow if "fi al-ghayy" is connected to "al-imdad," because humans do not lead devils into error. The purpose of this verse is to describe the state of the disbelievers with the devils, just as the state of the mindful with them was described before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 7, verses 204–206:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain from His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate.﴾

Al-Tabari and others mention that the occasion of this verse was that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were in Makkah speaking during the obligatory prayer about their needs, shouting at the verses of mercy and punishment, and one of them would say when he came to them: "Did you pray? And how many [rak'ahs] remain?" and they would inform him, and similar things. So the verse was revealed commanding them to listen and be silent during the prayer. As for the saying of one who said: "It is about the khutbah (sermon)," it is weak, because the verse is Makkan, and the khutbah did not exist except after the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration from Makkah. Likewise what al-Zahrawi mentioned from (p-124) that it was revealed because of a young man from the Ansar who was reciting during the prayer while the Prophet (ﷺ) was reciting. As for listening and being silent from speech during the prayer, there is consensus (ijma') on it. As for refraining and remaining silent from recitation, one group said: the follower (ma'mum) refrains from recitation entirely, whether the imam recites aloud or silently. Another group said: the follower recites when the imam recites silently, and refrains when he recites aloud. Another group said: the follower refrains from reciting the chapter during the imam's audible recitation and recites the Opening (al-Fatihah).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Along with this view there are sound hadiths from the Prophet (ﷺ). So this verse makes it obligatory in the prayer to be silent from speech and from anything other than the recitation. It is also obligatory regarding the khutbah by the Sunnah, not by this verse; and it is obligatory from the verse to listen and be silent when the preacher recites the Qur'an during the khutbah. The ruling of this verse outside the prayer is recommended (nadb), I mean the act of silence and listening itself when a person hears the recitation of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. As for what the words contain and what they convey of honouring and glorifying the Qur'an, that is obligatory in every situation. And "al-insat" means silence, and "la'allakum" [that you may] indicates hope on the part of humans.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

We have not exhaustively covered the disagreement of the scholars about recitation behind the imam, since the wording of the verse does not address that; but since it came up in mentioning the occasion, we have mentioned a portion of it.

Al-Tabari reports from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said regarding the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ — he said: silence is on the day of Eid al-Adha, the day of Eid al-Fitr, the day of Friday, and in what the imam recites audibly in the prayer.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view that combines what this verse and other Sunnah require regarding silence. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that ﴿listen to it and be silent﴾ means: act upon what is in it and do not transgress it.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾ — the verse. It is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) that encompasses all his Ummah, and it is a command from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to remember Him by glorifying Him, mentioning Him, sanctifying Him, and praising Him with His attributes of praise. The majority hold that dhikr does not occur only within the self and is not fulfilled except with movement of the tongue, and what indicates this from this verse is His saying: ﴿and without loudness of speech﴾, for this is the rank of secrecy and speaking in a low voice. (p-125) "Tadarru'an" means humbling oneself and submission; "khifatan" originally was "khawfatan" (fear), the waw being changed to ya' because of the preceding kasrah. His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾ means continually, every day, and at the edges of the day. One group said this verse was during the prayer of the Muslims before the obligation of the five daily prayers. Qatadah said: "al-Ghuduww (the mornings) is the Fajr prayer, and al-Asal (the evenings) is the 'Asr prayer." "Al-Asal" is the plural of "asal," and "asal" is the plural of "asil," which is the late afternoon. It was said: "al-Asal" is the plural of "asil" without a medial alif, like "iman" the plural of "yamin"; and "asal" is also the plural of "asa'il," so it is a plural of a plural. Abu Majlaz recited "wal-Isal," a verbal noun like "al-Isbah" and "al-Imsa'," meaning: when you enter the asil (late afternoon). In al-Tabari: Abu Wa'il said to his servant: "Have we entered the late afternoon yet?" ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ is a warning.

When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said ﴿and do not be among the heedless﴾, He then placed after it an example of the diligence of the angels, to stir earnestness in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. His saying "those who" intends the angels, and His saying "with" (ʿinda) means in rank, honour and nearness of status, not in place; so they are "with Him" in that sense. Then He, the Exalted, described their state of humility, their constancy in worship, glorification and prostration. In a hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of a hand's breadth in it except that there is an angel standing, bowing, or prostrating." This is a place of prostration. Al-Nakha'i said in the book of al-Naqqash: "If you wish, bow, and if you wish, prostrate."

The Surah al-A'raf is completed by the success granted by Allah, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

"Al-Asal" is the plural of "asal," and "asal" is the plural of "asil," which is the late afternoon. It was said: "al-Asal" is the plural of "asil" without a medial alif, like "iman" the plural of "yamin"; and "asal" is also the plural of "asa'il," so it is a plural of a plural. Abu Majlaz recited "wal-Isal," a verbal noun like "al-Isbah" and "al-Imsa'," meaning: when you enter the asil (late afternoon). In al-Tabari: Abu Wa'il said to his servant: "Have we entered the late afternoon yet?" ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ is a warning.

When Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said ﴿and do not be among the heedless﴾, He then placed after it an example of the diligence of the angels, to stir earnestness in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. His saying "those who" intends the angels, and His saying "with" (ʿinda) means in rank, honour and nearness of status, not in place; so they are "with Him" in that sense. Then He, the Exalted, described their state of humility, their constancy in worship, glorification and prostration. In a hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space of a hand's breadth in it except that there is an angel standing, bowing, or prostrating." This is a place of prostration. Al-Nakha'i said in the book of al-Naqqash: "If you wish, bow, and if you wish, prostrate."

The Surah al-A'raf is completed by the success granted by Allah, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
